43806.q: What share of Swiss companies are SMEs?
43806.e: Almost all companies in Switzerland are small and medium-sized enterprises. They employ about two thirds of the workforce.
43806.m: Over 99 per cent of Swiss firms are SMEs.

43807.q: From what number of employees is a company no longer counted as an SME in Swiss statistics?
43807.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office's definition, SMEs are companies with fewer than 250 employees. From 250 employees, they are called large companies.

43808.q: Which world economic meeting takes place every January in Davos?
43808.e: At the WEF in Davos, politicians, business leaders and experts from all over the world meet. Smaller Swiss associations hold their conferences in other places in the Grisons, such as Klosters.
43808.m: The WEF takes place every year in Davos.

43809.q: Which recurring concern is particularly prominent for the Trade Association?
43809.e: The SGV criticises that rules and red tape burden small firms more than large ones. It therefore campaigns for less regulation and lower administrative costs.
43809.m: The Trade Association fights unnecessary red tape.

43810.q: In which city is the Swiss Trade Association based?
43810.e: The SGV is based in Bern, near the Federal Palace. This keeps it close to political events.
43810.m: The Trade Association is based in Bern.

43811.q: Which newspaper does the Swiss Trade Association publish?
43811.e: The Schweizerische Gewerbezeitung is the SGV's official paper. “Work”, by contrast, is Unia's newspaper, and “Schweizer Bauer” is a farming paper.
43811.m: The Schweizerische Gewerbezeitung is the mouthpiece of the Trade Association.

43812.q: Which area of education does the Trade Association support particularly strongly, since many SMEs are involved in it?
43812.e: A large share of apprenticeships are offered by SMEs. That is why the SGV strongly supports dual vocational training with a training company and a vocational school.
43812.m: SMEs provide many of the apprenticeships in Switzerland.

43813.q: On which date was the Peace Agreement in the engineering and metal industry signed?
43813.e: The Peace Agreement was concluded on 19 July 1937. It is seen as a milestone for cooperation between employers and trade unions.
43813.m: The Peace Agreement dates from 19 July 1937.

43814.q: Which trade union leader signed the 1937 Peace Agreement on the workers' side?
43814.e: Konrad Ilg was president of the Swiss Metal and Watch Workers' Union (SMUV). He negotiated the agreement with Ernst Dübi from the employers' side.
43814.m: Konrad Ilg was the trade unionist behind the Peace Agreement.

43815.q: Between whom was the 1937 Peace Agreement concluded?
a: Between the Confederation and the cantons
43815.e: The employers' association of the engineering and metal industry and the industry's trade unions concluded the agreement. The state was not a party to it.
43815.m: The Peace Agreement is a contract between the social partners.

43816.q: What did the parties to the Peace Agreement give up in principle?
43816.e: The agreement committed both sides to absolute industrial peace. Conflicts were to be solved through negotiation and, if necessary, arbitration instead of industrial action.
43816.m: In the Peace Agreement, both sides gave up strikes and lockouts.

43817.q: Under the Peace Agreement, which body was to decide disputes if negotiations failed?
43817.e: The agreement set out a step-by-step procedure: first negotiations within the company, then between the associations and finally an arbitration tribunal. The state was not involved.
43817.m: Under the Peace Agreement, an arbitration tribunal decided if negotiations failed.

43818.q: Which event of 1918 is seen as the background to the later wish for industrial peace?
a: The founding of the League of Nations
The general strike in Geneva in 1902
43818.e: In the General Strike of November 1918, the conflict between workers and the middle classes escalated and the army was deployed. This experience shaped the later search for compromise.
43818.m: The 1918 General Strike showed how dangerous harsh class conflict was.

43819.q: Why did the idea of industrial peace become particularly important in the late 1930s?
a: Because of the threat from the neighbouring dictatorships
Because of the introduction of women's suffrage
Because of the building of the Gotthard tunnel
43819.e: Faced with Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy, people wanted to strengthen unity at home. The Peace Agreement fitted in with the Spiritual National Defence.
43819.m: The threat from abroad in the 1930s encouraged unity at home.

43820.q: Which present-day industry association is the successor to the employers' association that signed the Peace Agreement in 1937?
43820.e: The employers' association of the engineering and metal industry (ASM) merged with the VSM in 1999 to form Swissmem. On the union side, the SMUV later became part of Unia.
43820.m: Swissmem continues the tradition of the employers of the Peace Agreement.

43821.q: Since which constitution has the right to strike been expressly laid down in the Swiss Federal Constitution?
43821.e: Article 28 of the 1999 Federal Constitution guarantees freedom of association and allows strikes and lockouts under certain conditions. One of these is that no obligation to keep industrial peace stands in the way.
43821.m: The right to strike has been expressly in the Federal Constitution since 1999.

43822.q: In which law are the provisions on the collective labour agreement (GAV) mainly set out?
43822.e: The GAV is regulated in Articles 356 ff. of the Code of Obligations. The Labour Act, by contrast, mainly regulates health protection and working hours.
43822.m: The collective labour agreement is regulated in the Code of Obligations.

43823.q: Who concludes a collective labour agreement on the employees' side?
a: The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs
43823.e: A GAV is concluded between employers or their associations and employees' associations. So on the employees' side, trade unions or staff associations are always the parties to the agreement.
43823.m: On the employees' side, a GAV is always signed by associations.

43824.q: What form does the law require for concluding a GAV?
43824.e: Under Article 356c of the Code of Obligations, a GAV must be concluded in writing. This makes the agreed rules clear to everyone.
43824.m: A GAV must be concluded in writing.

43825.q: What does it mean when a GAV is declared generally binding (AVE)?
a: It applies to all businesses in the industry
It only applies to trade union members
It can no longer be terminated
43825.e: With an AVE, a GAV is extended to all employers and employees in an industry, including non-members. This prevents undercutting of wages by non-organised firms.
43825.m: A GAV declared generally binding applies to the whole industry.

43826.q: Who declares a GAV covering several cantons generally binding?
43826.e: If the scope extends across several cantons, the Federal Council is responsible. If the GAV affects only one canton, the cantonal government decides.
43826.m: For GAVs covering several cantons, the Federal Council decides on general applicability.

43827.q: Under the law, what obliges the parties to a GAV not to take industrial action on matters regulated in the agreement?
43827.e: Article 357a of the Code of Obligations obliges the parties to keep industrial peace on the matters regulated in the GAV. This relative peace obligation can also be made absolute by contract.
43827.m: While a GAV is in force, the peace obligation applies to the matters it regulates.

43828.q: What is the GAV for the main construction industry in Switzerland called?
43828.e: The National Framework Agreement regulates wages and working conditions in the main construction industry. The L-GAV, by contrast, is the GAV of the hospitality industry.
43828.m: The National Framework Agreement applies in the main construction industry.

43829.q: What applies if an individual employment contract departs from the GAV in the employee's favour?
43829.e: Under the favourability principle in Article 357 of the Code of Obligations, departures are allowed if they benefit the employees. Conditions worse than in the GAV, by contrast, are void.
43829.m: You may only depart from the GAV in the employees' favour.

43830.q: Which measures to protect against wage dumping made it easier from 2004 to declare GAVs generally binding?
a: The accompanying measures to the free movement of persons
43830.e: Accompanying measures were introduced with the free movement of persons with the EU. If wages are repeatedly undercut, they allow GAVs to be declared generally binding more easily.
43830.m: The accompanying measures protect Swiss wages from being undercut.

43831.q: How old is the umbrella organisation Travail.Suisse compared with the Swiss Trade Union Federation (SGB)?
a: Much younger, it was founded in 2002
The same age, both were founded in 1880
Slightly younger, it was founded in 1918
43831.e: Travail.Suisse was founded in Bern in 2002. The Swiss Trade Union Federation, by contrast, has existed since 1880.
43831.m: Travail.Suisse is a young umbrella organisation, founded in 2002.

43832.q: What was the character of many of the trade unions that joined together to form Travail.Suisse in 2002?
43832.e: Travail.Suisse grew out of the Christian National Trade Union Federation and the Federation of Swiss Employees' Associations. The Christian social tradition still shapes the organisation today.
43832.m: Travail.Suisse unites the Christian trade unions and the employees' associations.

43833.q: Which trade union is a large member of Travail.Suisse?
43833.e: Syna is the largest member union of Travail.Suisse. Unia, VPOD and SEV, by contrast, belong to the Swiss Trade Union Federation.

43834.q: What task does an employees' umbrella organisation such as Travail.Suisse carry out?
a: It represents employees' concerns in politics
43834.e: Umbrella organisations bring together the voices of many trade unions. They give their views in consultations, for example, and run referendum campaigns.
43834.m: Employees' umbrella organisations represent employees towards politics and employers.

43835.q: What position does Travail.Suisse hold among the employees' umbrella organisations in Switzerland?
43835.e: The largest employees' umbrella organisation is the SGB. With its member associations, Travail.Suisse is the second largest independent umbrella organisation.
43835.m: After the SGB, Travail.Suisse is the second largest employees' umbrella organisation.

43836.q: Roughly how many members do the associations of Travail.Suisse represent?
43836.e: Together, the member associations of Travail.Suisse represent about 150,000 members. The SGB, with over 300,000 members, is much larger.
43836.m: The associations of Travail.Suisse have about 150,000 members.

43837.q: Whom does the staff association Transfair, a member of Travail.Suisse, represent?
a: Public service employees, for example at Swiss Post and SBB
43837.e: Transfair is the Christian-based staff association of the public service. Among others, it represents employees of Swiss Post, SBB and Swisscom.
43837.m: Within Travail.Suisse, Transfair represents public service staff.

43838.q: Which association from the hospitality industry is a member of Travail.Suisse?
43838.e: The Hotel & Gastro Union represents employees in hotels and catering and belongs to Travail.Suisse. Gastrosuisse and Hotelleriesuisse, by contrast, are employers' associations.
43838.m: The Hotel & Gastro Union is an employees' association within Travail.Suisse.

43839.q: Who elects the members of the federal extra-parliamentary commissions?
43839.e: The members of extra-parliamentary commissions are elected by the Federal Council. The commissions are attached to the Federal Council and the administration, not to Parliament.
43839.m: Extra-parliamentary commissions are elected by the Federal Council.

43840.q: How long is the term of office on an extra-parliamentary commission?
43840.e: The term of office is four years and matches the legislative period. Re-election is possible afterwards.
43840.m: Commission members are elected for four years at a time.

43841.q: Which federal extra-parliamentary commission takes action against cartels and illegal price-fixing?
43841.e: Weko applies the Cartel Act and can fine firms that fix prices. It is an independent decision-making commission.

43842.q: Why does the Confederation set up extra-parliamentary commissions with outside experts?
a: To bring expert knowledge into the administration
To vote out members of the Federal Council
43842.e: The commissions include experts and representatives of associations. They contribute knowledge that the administration lacks.
43842.m: Extra-parliamentary commissions bring in expert knowledge from outside.

43843.q: What are extra-parliamentary commissions that can make decisions themselves, such as the Competition Commission, called?
43843.e: Decision-making commissions have powers to decide; one example is Weko. Administrative commissions, by contrast, only advise and prepare business.
43843.m: Decision-making commissions decide themselves; administrative commissions advise.

43844.q: What is the main task of federal administrative commissions?
a: To advise the Federal Council and the administration
43844.e: Administrative commissions bring external expertise and the views of interest groups into the administration. They advise and prepare business but do not make binding decisions.
43844.m: Administrative commissions bring outside expertise into the federal administration.

43845.q: Which independent federal decision-making commission supervises the Swiss electricity market?
43845.e: The Federal Electricity Commission ElCom supervises electricity prices and security of supply. ComCom is responsible for telecommunications and PostCom for the postal market.
43845.m: ElCom is the supervisory authority for electricity.

43846.q: What must members of extra-parliamentary commissions disclose before they are elected?
43846.e: Like members of parliament, commission members must disclose their interests and affiliations. Anyone who refuses cannot become a member.
43846.m: Members of federal commissions must also declare their interests.

43847.q: Which commission is an example of an advisory extra-parliamentary commission?
a: Finance Committee of the Council of States
43847.e: The Federal Commission against Racism (EKR) is an extra-parliamentary commission of the Federal Council. The other answers are committees of Parliament.
43847.m: The Commission against Racism is an extra-parliamentary commission.

43848.q: What is the procedure in which cantons, parties and associations can comment on a draft law called?
43848.e: In the consultation, preliminary drafts are submitted to interested parties for their views. Resolving differences, the conciliation conference and the final vote, by contrast, are part of the parliamentary procedure.
43848.m: In the consultation, cantons, parties and associations comment on proposals.

43849.q: At what stage of law-making does the consultation take place?
a: Before the Federal Council submits the proposal to Parliament
During the debate in the Council of States
43849.e: The consultation is laid down in Article 147 of the Federal Constitution. It belongs to the pre-parliamentary procedure, before the debate in Parliament.
43849.m: The consultation takes place before Parliament debates a proposal.

43850.q: Under the Consultation Procedure Act, what is the minimum length of a consultation period as a rule?
43850.e: The Consultation Procedure Act provides for a period of at least three months. If holidays or public holidays fall within it, it is extended accordingly.
43850.m: As a rule, a consultation lasts at least three months.

43851.q: Who may submit a response to a federal consultation?
a: In principle any person or organisation
Only parties large enough for a parliamentary group
43851.e: The law names recipients who are expressly invited, such as cantons, parties and umbrella organisations. Beyond that, any person or organisation can give their view.
43851.m: Anyone can take part in a consultation.

43852.q: What is the document called with which the Federal Council submits a draft law to Parliament after the consultation?
43852.e: The dispatch explains the draft law and takes the results of the consultation into account. Motions, interpellations and postulates, by contrast, are parliamentary procedural requests.
43852.m: With the dispatch, the Federal Council passes a proposal to Parliament.

43853.q: Who usually draws up the first draft of a new federal law?
a: The federal administration, for example a federal office
43853.e: Usually a federal office drafts a preliminary version. Then other offices review the text, the consultation follows and finally the Federal Council's dispatch to Parliament.
43853.m: Draft laws are usually drawn up in the federal administration.

43854.q: What happens to the responses from a federal consultation?
a: They are evaluated and published in a report
They are put to the people in a vote
43854.e: The 2005 Consultation Procedure Act requires the results to be summarised and published. The Federal Council takes them into account in its dispatch to Parliament.
43854.m: The results of a consultation are made public.

43855.q: Which political effect is often attributed to the consultation?
a: It makes proposals safer from referendums
It cuts Parliament's work to nothing
It prevents any change in the law
43855.e: If the concerns of key players are taken into account early, the risk of a successful referendum falls. That is why the consultation is seen as a tool for building consensus.
43855.m: The consultation helps produce sound proposals that can survive a referendum.

43856.q: In which law is the obligation for members of parliament to disclose their interests set out?
43856.e: Article 11 of the Parliament Act obliges members to disclose their interests and affiliations. The information is recorded in a public register.
43856.m: The Parliament Act requires the disclosure of interests.

43857.q: Who keeps the public register of the interests of members of the Federal Parliament?
43857.e: The register is kept by the Parliamentary Services and is publicly available on Parliament's website. This means anyone can see the members' affiliations.
43857.m: The Parliamentary Services keep the register of interests.

43858.q: When must members of parliament first disclose their interests?
43858.e: When joining the council, members must report their interests in writing. Changes are then added as they happen and updated every year.
43858.m: Interests are disclosed as soon as someone joins Parliament.

43859.q: Which of these is one of the interests that must be disclosed?
43859.e: Among other things, professional activities, positions on management and supervisory bodies such as boards of directors, and advisory work for interest groups must be disclosed. Wealth and income do not have to be declared.
43859.m: Board seats held by members of parliament are publicly visible.

43860.q: Since a revision, what additional information does the register require for each position?
a: Whether the position is paid or unpaid
The exact annual amount in francs
43860.e: Since a revision, it must be stated whether an activity is unpaid or paid. The amount of payment, however, does not have to be disclosed.
43860.m: The register shows whether a position is paid, but not how much it earns.

43861.q: What must members do when they speak in the council on a matter affecting their personal interests?
43861.e: The Parliament Act requires members to point out a personal interest when they speak. There is no general duty to step aside, as there is for authorities.
43861.m: Members must declare their interests before speaking on a matter that affects them.

43862.q: Which exception applies to the disclosure of interests?
a: Members of the Council of States are completely exempt
43862.e: The Parliament Act reserves professional secrecy as defined in the Criminal Code, for example for lawyers or doctors. Otherwise, the disclosure obligation applies to all members.
43862.m: Only professional secrecy limits the disclosure obligation.

43863.q: Which civil society platform also documents the links between members of parliament and interest groups?
43863.e: Lobbywatch is an independent platform that compiles members' interests and access badges for the Federal Palace. Smartvote, by contrast, is a voting advice tool and Swissvotes a database of votes.
43863.m: Lobbywatch makes lobbying links in the Federal Palace visible.

43864.q: Why do members of the Federal Parliament have particularly many interests and affiliations?
a: Because Parliament is seen as a militia parliament
Because side jobs are required by law
Because associations are allocated seats in the council
Because members of parliament receive no pay
43864.e: In a militia parliament, many members have a job and other posts alongside their mandate. This creates numerous links to companies and associations.
43864.m: Side jobs are widespread in the militia parliament.

43865.q: How many people can a member of the Federal Assembly give a permanent access badge to the Parliament Building?
43865.e: Under the Parliament Act, each member can give two people a permanent access badge. These people and their role are entered in a public register.
43865.m: Each member may give two people a permanent badge for the Federal Palace.

43866.q: What is the system in which members of parliament personally give lobbyists access informally called?
43866.e: Because lobbyists need a member as a “Götti” or “Gotte” (Swiss German for godfather or godmother) to get a badge, people speak of the Götti system. Critics complain that it depends on personal connections.
43866.m: In the Götti system, members of parliament give lobbyists access.

43867.q: In which room of the Federal Palace do lobbyists typically meet members of parliament?
a: In the Council of States chamber
In the domed hall of the National Bank
43867.e: The Wandelhalle lies next to the National Council chamber and serves as a meeting place during sessions. Lobbyists hold talks with members of parliament there.
43867.m: The Wandelhalle is the main meeting place for lobbyists in the Federal Palace.

43868.q: Besides the person's name, what is recorded in the public register of access badges?
43868.e: The register of people with access records the person's name and role. This shows which member gives access to whom.
43868.m: The access register shows which lobbyists hold whose badge.

43869.q: Which professional association of public affairs specialists has issued a code of conduct for lobbyists in Switzerland?
43869.e: SPAG is the professional association of public affairs specialists. Its members commit to a code of conduct with transparency rules.
43869.m: SPAG commits its members to a lobbying code.

43870.q: Which criticism is often made of the access system for lobbyists in the Federal Palace?
a: There is a lack of full transparency about clients
There are too many seats for guests
Lobbyists have to pay to get in
43870.e: Critics complain that lobbyists also get access with day passes or through personal connections without fully disclosing their mandates. Various proposals for more transparency have failed in Parliament.
43870.m: Swiss lobbying is criticised mainly for its lack of transparency.

43871.q: Besides permanent badges, what kind of access can members also give visitors?
43871.e: Members can give guests access for single days. These day visits do not appear in the register of permanent badges.
43871.m: With day passes, visitors enter the Federal Palace without a register entry.

43872.q: Where do the discussions take place in which lobbyists particularly want to influence the details of laws early on?
a: At the Federal Chancellery during vote counting
43872.e: The preparatory committees work through draft laws in detail before they come to the council. Because their meetings are confidential, contact with committee members is especially valuable for lobbyists.
43872.m: Lobbyists often seek contact with members of the preparatory committees.

43873.q: How many forms of government does Aristotle distinguish in his classical theory of forms of government?
43873.e: Aristotle distinguishes three good and three corrupt forms, depending on whether one, a few or many rule. That makes six forms of government.
43873.m: Aristotle's theory of forms of government has three good and three corrupt forms.

43874.q: What does Aristotle call the corrupt form of rule by one person?
43874.e: Monarchy is the good form of rule by one person. If that person rules only for their own benefit, Aristotle speaks of tyranny.
43874.m: A tyrant rules for their own benefit instead of for the good of all.

43875.q: In Aristotle, which form of government is the good rule of a few, directed at the common good?
43875.e: When a few rule for the good of all, Aristotle calls it aristocracy, the rule of the best. The corrupt form is the oligarchy of the rich.
43875.m: For Aristotle, aristocracy is the good rule of the best.

43876.q: What does Aristotle call the good rule of the many, directed at the common good?
43876.e: For Aristotle, polity is rule by the many for the common good. It is seen as a mixture of elements of oligarchy and democracy.
43876.m: Polity is Aristotle's good form of rule by the people.

43877.q: Which form of government does Aristotle count among the corrupt forms of rule by the many?
43877.e: For Aristotle, democracy is rule by the poor in their own interest, and therefore a corruption. Only later writers such as Polybius called this ochlocracy.
43877.m: Aristotle saw democracy as rule by the poor for their own benefit.

43878.q: Which term does Aristotle use to describe humans as social beings?
43878.e: Aristotle describes humans as a “zoon politikon”, a living being made for the community of the polis. Only within it can a person lead a good life.
43878.m: According to Aristotle, humans are political beings by nature.

43879.q: What is the work in which Aristotle systematically examines the forms of government called?
43879.e: In the “Politics”, Aristotle compares constitutions and develops his theory of forms of government. “The Republic” and “The Laws” are by Plato.
43879.m: Aristotle's theory of forms of government is in his work “Politics”.

43880.q: Whom did Aristotle teach at the Macedonian royal court?
43880.e: King Philip II brought Aristotle to the court as teacher of his son Alexander. Aristotle himself had earlier been a pupil of Plato in Athens.
43880.m: Aristotle was the teacher of the young Alexander the Great.

43881.q: By which two criteria does Aristotle classify the forms of government?
a: Number of rulers and the common good
Size of the state and wealth
Religion and origin of the rulers
43881.e: Aristotle asks whether one, a few or many rule, and whether they serve the common good or their own interest. Combining these gives his forms of government.
43881.m: Aristotle always asks who rules and in whose interest.

43882.q: Which innovation under Pericles allowed poorer citizens to serve in the people's courts?
43882.e: Pericles introduced pay for the jurors of the people's courts. This allowed citizens without wealth to make up for lost earnings.
43882.m: Pay for jurors made political participation possible for the poor too.

43883.q: What was the assembly of Athenian citizens called?
43883.e: In the Ekklesia, citizens gathered on the Pnyx and decided on laws, war and peace. The Heliaia, by contrast, was the people's court.
43883.m: The Ekklesia was the people's assembly of Athens.

43884.q: How were most offices filled in Athenian democracy?
43884.e: Drawing lots was seen as especially democratic, because every citizen had the same chance. Only offices that needed expert knowledge, such as that of general (strategos), were elected.
43884.m: In Athens, many offices were decided by lot.

43885.q: What was the Athenian procedure by which a citizen could be banished for ten years called?
43885.e: In ostracism, citizens scratched a name on pieces of pottery. Whoever got the most votes had to leave Athens for ten years.
43885.m: Ostracism protected Athens from individuals becoming too powerful.

43886.q: Which building on the Acropolis was built as part of the building programme under Pericles?
43886.e: From 447 BC, the Parthenon was built under Pericles for the goddess Athena. The Colosseum and the Pantheon are in Rome.
43886.m: The Parthenon is a monument of Athens' golden age under Pericles.

43887.q: With what money did Athens under Pericles fund large parts of its building programme?
a: With contributions from the Delian League
43887.e: The treasury of the Delian League was moved from Delos to Athens in 454 BC. Pericles also used these funds for buildings in Athens, which the allies criticised.
43887.m: Athens also funded its magnificent buildings with its allies' money.

43888.q: What right did every citizen have in the Athenian assembly?
a: The right to speak and make proposals
The right to pass on offices to heirs
The right to make laws alone
43888.e: In Athens, every citizen had the same right to speak in the assembly, known as isegoria. However, women, slaves and foreigners were excluded.
43888.m: In Athens, every citizen could speak in the assembly.

43889.q: What was the Council of 500, which prepared the decisions of the Athenian assembly, called?
43889.e: The members of the Boule were chosen by lot every year, 50 from each of the ten tribes. The Gerousia was Sparta's council of elders.
43889.m: In Athens, the Boule prepared the business of the assembly.

43890.q: In which century did Thomas Hobbes's “Leviathan” appear?
43890.e: Hobbes published “Leviathan” in London in 1651. The work was written under the impact of the English Civil War.
43890.m: “Leviathan” appeared in the 17th century, shortly after the English Civil War.

43891.q: How does Hobbes describe the state of nature of humans without a state?
a: As a war of all against all
43891.e: Without a higher power, people distrust each other and fight to survive. Hobbes calls this the “war of all against all”.
43891.m: For Hobbes, without a state there is a war of all against all.

43892.q: Which Latin phrase does Hobbes use for the relationship between people in the state of nature?
43892.e: In the dedication of “De Cive”, Hobbes takes up the phrase “Man is a wolf to man”. It sums up his pessimistic view of human nature.
43892.m: For Hobbes, man is a wolf to man.

43893.q: Where does the name “Leviathan” originally come from?
43893.e: The Leviathan is a huge sea monster from the Bible, for example in the Book of Job. Hobbes uses it as an image for the all-powerful state.
43893.m: Hobbes named his state after a biblical monster.

43894.q: Which event particularly influenced Hobbes when writing “Leviathan”?
43894.e: Between 1642 and 1649, King and Parliament fought each other in England. This experience of chaos and violence shaped Hobbes's call for a strong state.
43894.m: The turmoil of the Civil War made Hobbes a theorist of security.

43895.q: How does Hobbes characterise life in the state of nature in a famous list?
a: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short
43895.e: Chapter 13 of “Leviathan” says “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”. Without a state there is neither security nor culture nor prosperity.
43895.m: According to Hobbes, without a state life is short and miserable.

43896.q: For Hobbes, what is the most important purpose of the state?
43896.e: People transfer their rights to a sovereign so that he protects their lives. The state is justified by the security it creates.
43896.m: Hobbes justifies the state by the need for protection.

43897.q: Which kind of rule does Hobbes consider the best solution?
43897.e: For Hobbes, the highest power must not be divided, otherwise civil war threatens again. For this he prefers monarchy.

43898.q: What does the famous title page of “Leviathan” show?
a: A ruler whose body is made up of many people
A sea monster swallowing a ship
A wolf in front of a burning city
43898.e: The frontispiece shows a crowned giant with a sword and a bishop's staff, whose body is made up of countless tiny people. This shows that the sovereign unites the citizens.
43898.m: On the title page of “Leviathan”, the citizens together form the body of the state.

43899.q: What is John Locke's main political work called?
43899.e: The “Two Treatises of Government” were published anonymously in 1689. In them Locke argues for a government based on consent that protects the rights of citizens.
43899.m: Locke's theory of the state is in the “Two Treatises of Government”.

43900.q: According to Locke, which natural rights should the state protect?
43900.e: Locke sums up these rights under the term “property”. The state is founded to secure them better than in the state of nature.
43900.m: Locke names life, liberty and property as natural rights.

43901.q: According to Locke, what may citizens do if a government permanently violates their rights?
43901.e: If the government breaks the citizens' trust, power returns to the people. Locke uses this to justify a right of resistance against tyranny.
43901.m: For Locke, the people have a right to resist tyranny.

43902.q: Which event in England did Locke's writings justify after the fact?
43902.e: In 1688 King James II was deposed and William of Orange came to the throne. Locke's treatises provided the justification for this change of power.
43902.m: Locke is seen as an intellectual forerunner of the Glorious Revolution.

43903.q: Which third power does Locke name besides the legislative and the executive?
43903.e: For Locke, the federative power is responsible for war, peace and alliances with other states. Only Montesquieu emphasised the judiciary as a separate power.
43903.m: Locke separated foreign policy off as the federative power.

43904.q: How does Locke justify acquiring property?
43904.e: According to Locke, whoever mixes their labour with something from nature makes it their property. This labour theory of property became very influential.
43904.m: For Locke, property comes from labour.

43905.q: How does Locke's state of nature differ from Hobbes's?
a: It is already governed by the natural law of reason
It is a permanent war of all against all
It already has kings and courts
It consists only of families without rights
43905.e: For Locke, people in the state of nature are free and equal and bound by natural law. But there is no impartial judge, so they found a state.
43905.m: Locke's state of nature is free and equal, but insecure.

43906.q: Which document took over Locke's ideas on natural rights particularly clearly?
43906.e: In 1776 Thomas Jefferson named life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness as unalienable rights. This wording draws on Locke.
43906.m: The US Declaration of Independence bears Locke's mark.

43907.q: What did Locke argue for in his “Letter Concerning Toleration”?
43907.e: Locke demanded that the state should not interfere in faith as long as peace is kept. State and church have different tasks.
43907.m: Locke argued for separating faith and state power.

43908.q: In which city was Jean-Jacques Rousseau born?
43908.e: Rousseau was born in 1712 in what was then the Republic of Geneva. On the title page of the “Contrat social” he calls himself “citoyen de Genève”.
43908.m: Rousseau was a citizen of Geneva.

43909.q: What is the famous first sentence of the first chapter of the “Contrat social”?
a: “L'homme est né libre, et partout il est dans les fers.”
43909.e: Rousseau states that man is born free but is everywhere in chains. He asks how this order can become legitimate.
43909.m: Rousseau begins with the contrast between freedom and chains.

43910.q: In which year did Rousseau's “Du contrat social” appear?
43910.e: “The Social Contract” appeared in 1762, the same year as the novel on education “Émile”. Both books were banned and burned in Geneva.

43911.q: For Rousseau, what distinguishes the general will from the will of all?
a: The general will aims at the common good
The general will is the will of the government
The general will is a simple majority
The general will applies only to nobles
43911.e: The “volonté de tous” is just the sum of private interests. The “volonté générale”, by contrast, is always directed at the common good.
43911.m: The general will is more than the sum of individual interests.

43912.q: Why does Rousseau reject elected representatives as holders of sovereignty?
a: Only the king may represent the people
43912.e: For Rousseau, the sovereignty of the people is inalienable and indivisible. Deputies can only be agents; the people must make the laws themselves.
43912.m: For Rousseau, sovereignty always stays with the people.

43913.q: About which people did Rousseau write that they were free only during parliamentary elections?
43913.e: In the “Contrat social”, Rousseau mocks that the English people are only free when electing members of parliament. After that, they are slaves again.

43914.q: According to Rousseau, what happens to someone who refuses to obey the general will?
a: They will be forced to be free
They are banished from the country
They may found their own community
43914.e: Rousseau writes that such a person will be forced to be free. For him, true freedom means following the law you have given yourself.
43914.m: For Rousseau, freedom means obeying the law you have given yourself.

43915.q: In his discourse on inequality, what does Rousseau see as a main cause of inequality among people?
43915.e: Rousseau describes the first person who fenced off a piece of land and called it “mine” as the founder of civil society. With property came competition and inequality.
43915.m: For Rousseau, inequality began with private property.

43916.q: Which of Rousseau's works is a novel about bringing up a child?
43916.e: In “Émile, or On Education”, Rousseau describes an education in harmony with nature. “Julie” is a love story; “Candide” is by Voltaire.
43916.m: Rousseau's novel on education is called “Émile”.

43917.q: Who was NOT one of the authors of the Federalist Papers?
43917.e: The Federalist Papers were written by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay. Thomas Jefferson was in Paris as an envoy at the time.
43917.m: Hamilton, Madison and Jay wrote the Federalist Papers.

43918.q: How many essays make up the Federalist Papers?
43918.e: Between 1787 and 1788, most of the 85 essays appeared in New York newspapers; the last eight first appeared in a book edition. Collected, they are called “The Federalist”.
43918.m: The Federalist Papers consist of 85 essays.

43919.q: Under which shared pen name were the Federalist Papers published?
43919.e: The authors chose the name Publius after Publius Valerius Publicola, a co-founder of the Roman Republic. Brutus and Cato were pen names of their opponents.
43919.m: The Federalist Papers appeared under the name Publius.

43920.q: What were the Federalist Papers originally written for?
a: To get the US Constitution accepted
43920.e: The essays urged the citizens of the state of New York to ratify the constitution drafted in 1787. Today they are seen as the most important commentary on it.
43920.m: The Federalist Papers campaigned for the new US Constitution.

43921.q: Which three politicians wrote the Federalist Papers together?
43921.e: Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay wrote the essays in 1787 and 1788. Hamilton wrote by far the most.
43921.m: Hamilton, Madison and Jay wrote the Federalist Papers.

43922.q: Which famous sentence comes from Federalist No. 51?
a: “If men were angels, no government would be necessary.”
“Give me liberty, or give me death!”
“Government of the people, by the people, for the people.”
43922.e: With this, Madison explains why controls on power are needed. Ambition should counteract ambition, so that the powers limit each other.
43922.m: Because people are not angels, government needs mutual checks.

43923.q: What were the opponents of the new US Constitution of 1787 called?
43923.e: The Anti-Federalists feared too strong a central government. Their pressure helped lead to the Bill of Rights being added in 1791.
43923.m: The Anti-Federalists distrusted a strong central government.

43924.q: Which principle do the Federalist Papers defend so that no branch of government becomes too powerful?
43924.e: The authors wanted to divide the legislative, executive and judiciary so that they limit each other. In English this is called “checks and balances”.
43924.m: The Federalist Papers defend “checks and balances”.

43925.q: What is Alexis de Tocqueville's best-known work called?
43925.e: “De la démocratie en Amérique” appeared in two volumes in 1835 and 1840. In it Tocqueville analyses American society and politics.
43925.m: Tocqueville described democracy using the example of the USA.

43926.q: What was the official reason for Tocqueville's journey to the USA in 1831?
43926.e: Tocqueville travelled with Gustave de Beaumont on behalf of the French government to study American prisons. On the way he gathered material for his main work.
43926.m: A report on prisons took Tocqueville to America.

43927.q: Which danger of democracy did Tocqueville particularly warn against?
43927.e: A majority can oppress minorities and stifle dissenting opinions. Tocqueville saw this as a new form of unfreedom.
43927.m: Tocqueville warned against the tyranny of the majority.

43928.q: Which basic fact of American society did Tocqueville put at the centre?
a: The Church's influence on the state
43928.e: For Tocqueville, “égalité des conditions” was the defining feature of America. He saw it as a development that would also prevail in Europe.
43928.m: For Tocqueville, equality of conditions shaped democracy.

43929.q: Which institutions did Tocqueville see as an important counterweight to isolation in democracy?
43929.e: Tocqueville observed that Americans found associations for almost every purpose. These train citizens and limit the power of the state.
43929.m: According to Tocqueville, associations strengthen freedom in democracy.

43930.q: Which late work by Tocqueville examines the causes of the French Revolution?
a: The Old Regime and the Revolution
Reflections on the Revolution in France
43930.e: In “L'Ancien Régime et la Révolution” of 1856, Tocqueville shows that centralisation had already begun before 1789. So the Revolution continued much of what came before.
43930.m: Tocqueville saw much continuity between the old regime and the Revolution.

43931.q: How does Tocqueville describe the new form of despotism he feared in democracies?
43931.e: Tocqueville feared a state that, like a guardian, takes care of everything and keeps citizens dependent. This despotism would be mild but paralysing.
43931.m: Tocqueville feared a gentle despotism of patronising care.

43932.q: What was Tocqueville's basic attitude to democracy?
a: He thought it unstoppable but also saw its dangers
He rejected it and wanted the monarchy back
He was not interested in politics
43932.e: Tocqueville saw the spread of equality as an irreversible development. At the same time he warned against the tyranny of the majority and a gentle despotism.
43932.m: Tocqueville saw democracy coming and warned of its weaknesses.

43933.q: Which work did John Stuart Mill publish in 1859?
43933.e: In “On Liberty”, Mill examines how far society may interfere in the life of the individual. The book is a key text of liberalism.
43933.m: Mill's “On Liberty” is a classic of liberalism.

43934.q: What is Mill's principle that coercion is only allowed to prevent harm to others called?
43934.e: Under the harm principle, a person's freedom may only be restricted to protect others. What concerns only themselves, they decide alone.
43934.m: For Mill, freedom ends where others are at risk of harm.

43935.q: Like Jeremy Bentham, which ethical school did Mill follow?
43935.e: Utilitarianism judges actions by how much they contribute to the happiness of as many people as possible. Mill was brought up in this tradition by his father James Mill.
43935.m: Mill held a refined form of utilitarianism.

43936.q: According to Mill, why should even a wrong opinion not be suppressed?
a: Because truth stays alive through debate
Because all opinions are equally true
Because the state cannot check opinions
43936.e: Without challenge, even a true opinion becomes a dead dogma. Also, a wrong opinion often contains part of the truth.
43936.m: For Mill, truth needs open challenge.

43937.q: What did Mill campaign for in 1867 as a member of the British House of Commons?
43937.e: Mill proposed replacing the word “man” with “person” in the electoral reform bill. The proposal failed but was a milestone for the women's movement.
43937.m: Mill was one of the first members of parliament to call for votes for women.

43938.q: Which 1869 work by Mill calls for legal equality for women?
a: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
43938.e: In “The Subjection of Women”, Mill criticises women's legal subordination in marriage and society. He named his wife Harriet Taylor Mill as an important source of ideas.
43938.m: With “The Subjection of Women”, Mill fought for equal rights.

43939.q: Which controversial idea did Mill put forward in his “Considerations on Representative Government”?
43939.e: Mill wanted to give all adults a vote, but give educated citizens extra votes. This plural voting was meant to ensure the quality of decisions.
43939.m: Mill combined universal suffrage with extra weight for education.

43940.q: How does Mill add to utilitarianism in his famous comparison with the pig?
a: There are higher and lower pleasures
All pleasures are worth the same
43940.e: Mill writes that it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied. For him, pleasures of the mind are worth more than purely physical ones.
43940.m: Mill distinguished higher mental pleasures from lower ones.

43941.q: What is Hannah Arendt's main work on National Socialism and Stalinism, published in 1951, called?
a: The Open Society and Its Enemies
43941.e: In it Arendt analyses antisemitism, imperialism and totalitarian rule. For her, terror and ideology are the hallmarks of totalitarianism.
43941.m: Arendt examined the origins of totalitarianism.

43942.q: Which expression did Arendt coin in her report on the trial of Adolf Eichmann?
43942.e: Arendt observed the trial in Jerusalem in 1961. Eichmann did not seem to her a demon, but a thoughtless bureaucrat.
43942.m: Arendt spoke of the banality of evil.

43943.q: Which three basic activities does Arendt distinguish in “The Human Condition” (Vita activa)?
43943.e: Labour secures survival; work creates lasting things. For Arendt, only action among people is political in the true sense.
43943.m: For Arendt, acting together is the political activity.

43944.q: How does Arendt distinguish power from violence?
a: Power is the same as violence
Power always belongs to one individual
43944.e: In “On Violence”, Arendt stresses that power only arises when people join together. Violence can destroy power but cannot create it.
43944.m: For Arendt, power arises from many people acting together.

43945.q: Under which philosopher, who later taught in Basel, did Arendt write her doctoral thesis?
43945.e: Arendt gained her doctorate in Heidelberg in 1928 under Karl Jaspers, on the concept of love in Augustine. Jaspers taught at the University of Basel from 1948.
43945.m: Arendt's doctoral supervisor Karl Jaspers later taught in Basel.

43946.q: Which basic condition of action does Arendt emphasise again and again?
43946.e: For Arendt, politics exists only because different people live in the world together. The variety of perspectives is the precondition for action.
43946.m: Arendt saw plurality as the foundation of politics.

43947.q: Which two revolutions does Arendt compare in her book “On Revolution”?
43947.e: Arendt considers the American Revolution more successful, because it created lasting institutions of freedom. The French Revolution, she argues, failed over the social question.
43947.m: Arendt saw the American Revolution as a successful founding of freedom.

43948.q: Why did Arendt lose her German citizenship in 1937?
a: The Nazis stripped her of it
43948.e: As a Jew, Arendt fled Germany in 1933 and was stripped of her citizenship in 1937. She was stateless until she became a US citizen in 1951.
43948.m: Arendt experienced for herself what it means to be stateless.

43949.q: What is Karl Popper's main political work of 1945 called?
a: The Open Society and Its Enemies
43949.e: In it Popper defends liberal democracy against totalitarian ideas. The work appeared in two volumes in London.

43950.q: Which thinkers does Popper criticise in “The Open Society” as enemies of freedom?
43950.e: Popper accuses them of justifying closed societies or inevitable laws of history. He devotes the first volume to Plato and the second to Hegel and Marx.
43950.m: Popper saw the roots of closed societies in Plato, Hegel and Marx.

43951.q: For Popper, what is the decisive feature of a democracy?
a: The government can be voted out without bloodshed
The people vote directly on everything
43951.e: Popper replaces the question “Who should rule?” with the question of how to get rid of bad rulers. Democracy allows a peaceful change of power.
43951.m: For Popper, democracy means the government can be voted out peacefully.

43952.q: What does Popper call a policy of small, testable reform steps?
43952.e: Instead of rebuilding society according to an overall plan, individual problems should be fixed step by step. That way mistakes can be spotted and corrected.
43952.m: Popper recommended gradual reforms instead of grand utopias.

43953.q: What criterion does Popper set in the philosophy of science for scientific statements?
43953.e: For Popper, a theory is only scientific if it can fail when tested against experience. He developed this in “The Logic of Scientific Discovery”.
43953.m: According to Popper, scientific theories must be refutable.

43954.q: What does Popper's paradox of tolerance state?
43954.e: Anyone who tolerates even the intolerant without limit risks them abolishing tolerance. An open society may therefore protect itself against its enemies.
43954.m: A tolerant society must be able to defend itself against intolerance.

43955.q: What does Popper criticise under the term “historicism”?
a: The belief in predictable laws of history
43955.e: Historicists believe they can predict the course of history. Popper considers this unscientific and dangerous for freedom.
43955.m: Popper denied that history follows fixed laws.

43956.q: Where did the Vienna-born Popper write “The Open Society and Its Enemies”?
43956.e: Popper emigrated to New Zealand in 1937 and taught in Christchurch. There he wrote his main political work during the Second World War.
43956.m: Popper wrote his main political work in exile in New Zealand.

43957.q: What term does Robert Dahl use for democracies that actually exist?
43957.e: Dahl speaks of polyarchy, the rule of the many. He uses it to distinguish real systems from the ideal of perfect democracy.

43958.q: By which two dimensions does Dahl measure polyarchies?
43958.e: A system is more polyarchic the more people may take part and the freer opposition and competition are. Both dimensions must be strongly present.
43958.m: Polyarchy combines broad participation with free competition.

43959.q: Why does Dahl prefer to speak of polyarchy rather than democracy?
a: No state fully reaches the ideal of democracy
The word democracy is too short
For him democracy is a dictatorship
Polyarchy means rule by the king
43959.e: For Dahl, democracy is an ideal that states can only approach. Polyarchy describes the imperfect form actually achieved.
43959.m: For Dahl, democracy remains an ideal.

43960.q: What did Robert Dahl conclude in his study “Who Governs?” about power in a US city?
a: The church held all the power
43960.e: In 1961 Dahl examined who actually influences decisions in New Haven. He found various groups with changing influence instead of a single elite.
43960.m: In New Haven, Dahl found many groups with changing influence.

43961.q: Which institution is NOT one of Dahl's minimum conditions for polyarchy?
43961.e: Dahl lists, among others, elected officials, free elections, freedom of expression, alternative sources of information and freedom of association. Referendums as in Switzerland are not a minimum condition.
43961.m: A polyarchy needs free elections and free opinions.

43962.q: Which theoretical school did Dahl represent with his study of how power is distributed?
43962.e: Dahl concluded that power is spread across many competing groups. In doing so he contradicted the idea of a single power elite.
43962.m: Dahl saw power in democracies as spread across many groups.

43963.q: What does Dahl call a system with low participation and no public contestation?
43963.e: In a closed hegemony both dimensions are weak. Polyarchy is the opposite, with high participation and strong competition.
43963.m: Closed hegemony is the opposite of polyarchy.

43964.q: In which subject was Robert Dahl one of the best-known researchers?
43964.e: Robert Dahl was a professor of political science at Yale University for decades. He coined terms such as polyarchy.
43964.m: Robert Dahl was an important political scientist.

43965.q: Which early work by Habermas examines how the bourgeois public sphere came about?
a: The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere
43965.e: His 1962 habilitation thesis describes how a reasoning public emerged in salons and coffee houses. Later Habermas saw it threatened by the mass media.
43965.m: Habermas described the structural transformation of the public sphere.

43966.q: Which phrase describes, for Habermas, the only thing that should count in an ideal discourse?
a: The unforced force of the better argument
43966.e: In discourse only reasons should convince, not power or pressure. Whoever has the better argument should win without coercion.
43966.m: For Habermas, only the better argument counts in discourse.

43967.q: What is the name of the two-volume main work Habermas published in 1981?
a: The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere
43967.e: In it Habermas distinguishes between action aimed at success and action aimed at mutual understanding. Understanding is the basis of social order.
43967.m: For Habermas, communicative action aims at mutual understanding.

43968.q: What does Habermas call the idealised conversation without coercion and with equal chances for everyone?
43968.e: In the ideal speech situation all participants may speak freely and question any claim. The “veil of ignorance”, by contrast, comes from John Rawls.
43968.m: The ideal speech situation is a yardstick for fair discourse.

43969.q: In which 1992 work does Habermas develop his theory of law and democracy?
a: On the Logic of the Social Sciences
43969.e: Habermas shows there how law gains legitimacy through democratic procedures. The work is regarded as a foundation of deliberative democratic theory.
43969.m: Habermas set out his theory of democracy in “Between Facts and Norms”.

43970.q: Which school of thought is Jürgen Habermas counted as part of?
43970.e: Habermas was Theodor W. Adorno's assistant at the Frankfurt Institute for Social Research. He is regarded as the most important member of the second generation of Critical Theory.
43970.m: Habermas shaped the second generation of the Frankfurt School.

43971.q: Which term coined by Dolf Sternberger did Habermas make especially well known in Germany?
43971.e: Constitutional patriotism means attachment to the values of the constitution rather than to origin or nation. Habermas made the term widely known from the 1980s.
43971.m: Constitutional patriotism binds citizens to shared constitutional values.

43972.q: Where do political decisions get their legitimacy in Habermas' deliberative democracy?
a: From the origin of the rulers
From the will of a single person
43972.e: Deliberation means consultation: decisions are legitimate if they come from an open exchange of reasons. Elections alone are not enough for this.
43972.m: Deliberative democracy lives on the public exchange of reasons.

43973.q: Which large forest in Germany is close to Basel?
43973.e: The Black Forest is a range of low mountains in south-west Germany. Its southern part reaches close to Basel.
43973.m: The Black Forest is just north of Basel in Germany.

43974.q: Which famous collectors of fairy tales come from Germany?
43974.e: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm collected fairy tales such as “Hansel and Gretel” and “Little Red Riding Hood”. They lived in Germany.
43974.m: The Brothers Grimm collected many well-known fairy tales.

43975.q: What is the highest mountain in Germany called?
43975.e: The Zugspitze is about 2,962 metres high. It is in Bavaria on the border with Austria.
43975.m: The Zugspitze is Germany’s highest mountain.

43976.q: Which long loaf of bread is typical of France?
43976.e: The baguette is a long, thin white loaf with a crispy crust. In France people often buy it fresh every day.
43976.m: The baguette is a typically French bread.

43977.q: Which large lake does Switzerland share with France?
43977.e: The northern shore of Lake Geneva belongs to Switzerland, and most of the southern shore belongs to France. In French it is called “Lac Léman”.
43977.m: Lake Geneva lies between Switzerland and France.

43978.q: Which famous food comes from Italy?
43978.e: Pizza comes from Italy, especially from the area around Naples. Today people eat it all over the world.

43979.q: Which city in Italy has canals instead of streets and gondolas as boats?
43979.e: Venice is built on lots of small islands. Instead of cars, boats and gondolas travel along the canals.
43979.m: In Venice you travel by boat instead of by car.

43980.q: In which Italian city does the famous Leaning Tower stand?
43980.e: The Tower of Pisa is a bell tower. Because the ground is soft, it leans.
43980.m: The Leaning Tower stands in Pisa.

43981.q: Which Italian village on Lake Lugano is completely surrounded by Switzerland?
43981.e: Campione d'Italia belongs to Italy but lies in the middle of Ticino. Gandria, Morcote and Brissago are villages in Ticino.
43981.m: Campione d'Italia is an Italian village inside Switzerland.

43982.q: What is the name of the big volcano on the Italian island of Sicily?
43982.e: Etna is the highest active volcano in Europe. It is on Sicily and erupts again and again.
43982.m: Etna is a volcano on Sicily.

43983.q: Which famous chocolate cake comes from Austria?
43983.e: The Sachertorte is a chocolate cake with apricot jam. It was invented by Franz Sacher in 1832.
43983.m: The Sachertorte is a cake from Austria.

43984.q: What is the highest mountain in Austria called?
43984.e: The Grossglockner is about 3798 metres high. It is the highest mountain in Austria.
43984.m: The Grossglockner is Austria's highest mountain.

43985.e: The Grisons borders Austria in the east. The canton of St Gallen also has a border with Austria.
43985.m: The Grisons is a neighbour of Austria.

43986.q: Which animals show off their tricks at the Spanish Riding School in Austria?
43986.e: At the Spanish Riding School, white horses called Lipizzaners perform difficult jumps and steps.
43986.m: At the Spanish Riding School, horses dance.

43987.q: How many federal states does Austria have?
43987.e: Austria is divided into 9 federal states, for example Tyrol, Salzburg and Vorarlberg.

43988.q: Roughly how many people live in Liechtenstein?
43988.e: About 40,000 people live in Liechtenstein (as of 2024). That is fewer than in the city of Lucerne.

43989.q: Which two Swiss cantons does Liechtenstein border?
43989.e: In the west Liechtenstein borders the canton of St Gallen, and in the south the canton of the Grisons.
43989.m: Liechtenstein borders St Gallen and the Grisons.

43990.q: Which of Switzerland's neighbouring countries is the smallest?
43990.e: Liechtenstein covers only about 160 square kilometres. It is one of the smallest countries in the world.

43991.q: What is the name of the Swiss office responsible for customs?
a: Federal Office for Customs and Border Security
43991.e: Since 2022 the Swiss customs authority has been called the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security, or FOCBS (BAZG in German).
43991.m: In Switzerland the FOCBS looks after customs.

43992.q: Which village in the Grisons is duty-free?
43992.e: Samnaun lies outside the Swiss customs area. There you can buy many goods without paying duty.
43992.m: In Samnaun you do not have to pay customs duty.

43993.q: What do you call it when someone secretly takes goods across the border?
43993.e: Anyone who takes goods across the border secretly and without declaring them is smuggling. This is against the law and is punished.

43994.q: Who checks at the border what you bring back from abroad?
43994.e: Customs officers work at the border. They check which goods you bring with you and sometimes ask for money for them.
43994.m: At the border, customs checks the goods.

43995.q: In which city do the Swiss government and parliament work?
43995.e: Bern is called the federal city. The Federal Council and parliament meet in the Federal Palace.
43995.m: Bern is the federal city of Switzerland.

43996.q: How do you say ‘Good day’ in French?
43996.e: “Bonjour” means “good day”. “Buongiorno” is Italian, “Hello” is English and “Hola” is Spanish.

43997.q: How do you say ‘Thank you’ in Italian?
43997.e: “Grazie” means “thank you”. “Prego” means “you're welcome” and “Ciao” means “hello” or “bye”.

44000.q: Which national language of Switzerland is spoken almost only in the canton of the Grisons?
44000.e: Romansh is spoken mainly in the Grisons, for example in the Engadine. It is the smallest of the four national languages.
44000.m: Romansh is spoken mainly in the Grisons.

44001.q: Which flying machine used to be built in Friedrichshafen on Lake Constance?
44001.e: Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin built large airships on Lake Constance. The first Zeppelin rose above the lake in 1900.
44001.m: The Zeppelin comes from Lake Constance.

44002.q: What is the highest mountain in the Alps, on the border between France and Italy, called?
44002.e: Mont Blanc is about 4800 metres high. It lies on the border between France and Italy.
44002.m: Mont Blanc is the highest mountain in the Alps.

44003.q: What is the famous cycle race that goes through France every summer called?
44003.e: The Tour de France has existed since 1903. The riders are on the road for about three weeks.
44003.m: The Tour de France is the most famous cycle race in the world.

44004.q: Which warm sea does France border in the south?
44004.e: In the south France lies on the Mediterranean, for example at Marseille and Nice. In the west it borders the Atlantic.
44004.m: France lies on the Mediterranean in the south.

44005.q: Which purple flowers bloom in huge fields in Provence in summer?
44005.e: Provence is in the south of France. Huge lavender fields grow there and smell very strongly.
44005.m: Lavender blooms in Provence in summer.

44006.q: Which enormous palace did King Louis XIV have built in France?
44006.e: The Palace of Versailles is near Paris. It has a famous Hall of Mirrors and a huge park.
44006.m: Louis XIV had the Palace of Versailles built.

44007.q: Which animal is a well-known symbol of France?
44007.e: The Gallic cockerel is an old symbol of France. You often see it on sports teams.
44007.m: The cockerel is a symbol of France.

44008.q: Which soft cheese comes from France?
44008.e: Camembert comes from Normandy in the north of France. It is soft inside and has a white rind.
44008.m: Camembert is a cheese from France.

44009.q: Which German city has the biggest port in the country?
44009.e: Hamburg lies on the river Elbe, not far from the North Sea. Huge container ships dock there.
44009.m: Hamburg has the biggest port in Germany.

44010.q: In which German city on the Rhine is there a famous cathedral with two tall towers?
44010.e: Cologne Cathedral is over 150 metres high. People worked on building it for over 600 years.
44010.m: Cologne Cathedral stands on the Rhine.

44011.q: In which German city does the Oktoberfest take place every year?
44011.e: The Oktoberfest in Munich is the biggest folk festival in the world. It already starts in September.
44011.m: The Oktoberfest takes place in Munich.

44012.q: Which two seas does Germany border?
a: The North Sea and the Baltic Sea
The Mediterranean and the North Sea
The Baltic Sea and the Mediterranean
The Black Sea and the Baltic Sea
44012.e: In the north Germany lies on the North Sea and the Baltic Sea. There are lots of islands and beaches there.
44012.m: Germany lies on the North Sea and the Baltic Sea.

44013.q: Which fairy-tale castle stands in Bavaria?
44013.e: King Ludwig II had Neuschwanstein Castle built. It looks like a castle from a fairy tale.
44013.m: Neuschwanstein is a fairy-tale castle in Bavaria.

44014.q: How many neighbouring countries does Germany have?
44014.e: Germany borders nine countries, for example Switzerland, France, Poland and Denmark.

44015.q: Which large island in the Mediterranean belongs to Italy?
44015.e: Sardinia lies west of the Italian mainland and belongs to Italy. Corsica belongs to France.

44016.q: Which big Italian city lies not far from Ticino and is known for fashion?
44016.e: Milan is in Lombardy, about an hour's drive from Lugano. The city is famous for fashion and its cathedral.
44016.m: Milan is a big fashion city near Switzerland.

44017.q: What is the longest river in Italy called?
44017.e: The Po flows through northern Italy to the Adriatic Sea. It is the longest river in the country.
44017.m: The Po is the longest river in Italy.

44018.q: Which neighbouring country lies to the south of Switzerland?
44018.e: South of the Alps, Valais, Ticino and the Grisons border Italy.
44018.m: Italy lies to the south of Switzerland.

44019.q: Which breaded meat dish is typical of Austria?
44019.e: Wiener Schnitzel is a thin, breaded veal escalope. It is a national dish of Austria.
44019.m: Wiener Schnitzel is a typical dish from Austria.

44020.e: Austria lies in the middle of Europe and has no coast. Just like Switzerland, it is a landlocked country.

44021.q: Which city in Tyrol has hosted the Winter Olympics twice?
44021.e: Innsbruck hosted the Winter Olympics in 1964 and 1976. The city lies right in the middle of the Alps.
44021.m: Innsbruck has hosted the Winter Olympics twice.

44022.q: Which river flows from the Engadine to Austria?
44022.e: The Inn rises in the Engadine in the Grisons. It flows through Tyrol and later joins the Danube.
44022.m: The Inn flows from the Engadine to Austria.

44024.q: What has Liechtenstein not had since 1868?
44024.e: Liechtenstein abolished its army in 1868. Since then the country has had no soldiers.

44025.q: What is the well-known ski resort in Liechtenstein called?
44025.e: Malbun lies in the mountains of the municipality of Triesenberg. It is the only big ski resort in Liechtenstein.

44026.q: What is Liechtenstein famous for among collectors?
44026.e: For over 100 years Liechtenstein has issued its own beautifully designed stamps. There is even a postal museum in Vaduz.
44026.m: Liechtenstein is known for its stamps.

44027.e: Liechtenstein is too small for its own airport. People who want to fly usually travel to Zurich.
44027.m: Liechtenstein has no airport of its own.

44028.q: Which border town in Ticino lies at the very south of Switzerland?
44028.e: Chiasso lies right on the border with Italy. The southernmost point of Switzerland is near Chiasso.
44028.m: Chiasso lies at the very south of Switzerland.

44029.q: Where does the border run in Lake Geneva?
a: Through the middle of the lake
44029.e: The border between Switzerland and France runs through the water in the middle of Lake Geneva.
44029.m: The border runs through the middle of Lake Geneva.

44030.q: Which pass takes you from Valais straight to Italy?
44030.e: The Great St Bernard links Valais with the Aosta Valley in Italy. The border is at the top of the pass.
44030.m: You can get to Italy over the Great St Bernard.

44031.q: What do you call a piece of a country that is completely surrounded by another country?
44031.e: An exclave belongs to one country but lies completely within the territory of another. One example is Büsingen.
44031.m: An exclave is surrounded by a foreign country.

44032.q: What were the officials called who guarded Switzerland's open border away from the crossings?
44032.e: Border guards also checked the border away from the crossing points. Today they are part of Swiss customs.
44032.m: Border guards watched over the border.

44033.q: Which river forms part of the border with France in the Jura?
44033.e: The Doubs flows through the Jura. Over a long stretch it separates Switzerland from France.
44033.m: The Doubs forms the border with France in the Jura.

44034.q: What is it called when people from Switzerland go shopping more cheaply in a nearby country?
44034.e: Many people cross the border to shop because lots of things are cheaper there. This is called shopping tourism.
44034.m: Shopping abroad is called shopping tourism.

44035.q: Since 2025, up to what value per person per day can you bring purchases into Switzerland without paying VAT?
44035.e: Since 1 January 2025 the duty-free allowance has been 150 francs per person per day. Before that it was 300 francs.
44035.m: The duty-free allowance is 150 francs per person per day.

44036.q: Why are you not allowed to bring ivory souvenirs into Switzerland?
44036.e: Ivory comes from elephants' tusks. To protect these animals, trading in ivory is forbidden.
44036.m: Ivory may not be imported because elephants are protected.

44037.q: What is the money called that you have to pay for some goods at the border?
44037.e: If you buy a lot abroad, you sometimes have to pay customs duty at the border. This money goes to the state.
44037.m: For some goods you pay customs duty at the border.

44038.q: In which city is the Swiss embassy in Germany?
44038.e: Embassies are usually in the capital. That is why the Swiss embassy in Germany is in Berlin, near the Federal Chancellery.
44038.m: The Swiss embassy in Germany is in Berlin.

44039.q: Which country does the ground under a foreign embassy in Bern belong to?
44039.e: The ground of an embassy remains part of the host country. However, the embassy is specially protected.
44039.m: Even under an embassy, the ground is Swiss territory.

44040.q: Which letters are on diplomats' number plates in Switzerland?
44040.e: CD stands for “Corps Diplomatique”. This is how you recognise cars belonging to embassies and diplomats.
44040.m: Diplomats' cars have the letters CD.

44041.q: Which holiday do Swiss embassies abroad celebrate with guests?
44041.e: 1 August is the Swiss National Day. Many Swiss embassies then invite guests to a celebration.

44042.q: Since 1980, which country has Switzerland represented as a protecting power in Iran?
44042.e: Since 1980 the USA and Iran have had no embassies in each other's countries. That is why Switzerland represents the USA in Iran.
44042.m: Switzerland represents the USA in Iran.

44044.q: In which city is the Swiss embassy in Italy?
44044.e: Embassies are usually in a country's capital. That is why the Swiss embassy in Italy is in Rome.
44044.m: The Swiss embassy in Italy is in Rome.

44045.q: How many embassies does a country usually have in another country?
44045.e: A country usually has only one embassy in another country. Sometimes there are also consulates in other cities.
44045.m: A country usually has just one embassy in each country.

44046.q: Which capital of a country neighbouring Switzerland has the most inhabitants?
44046.e: About 3.7 million people live in Berlin (as of 2024). That is more than in any other capital of a neighbouring country.
44046.m: Berlin is the biggest capital among the neighbouring countries.

44047.q: In which capital is the famous Ferris wheel in the Prater?
44047.e: The Ferris wheel in Vienna's Prater was built in 1897. It is one of the city's landmarks.
44047.m: The Ferris wheel in the Prater is in Vienna.

44048.e: The Spree flows right through Berlin, past the Reichstag building.

44049.q: Which capital is also a federal state of Austria in its own right?
44049.e: Vienna is a city and at the same time one of Austria's federal states.
44049.m: Vienna is both a city and a federal state.

44050.q: Which famous church in Paris burned in 2019 and reopened in 2024?
44050.e: In April 2019 the roof of Notre-Dame Cathedral burned. After being rebuilt, it reopened in December 2024.
44050.m: Notre-Dame in Paris was rebuilt after the fire.

44051.q: Which animal is on the coat of arms of Berlin, just like Bern?
44051.e: Berlin's coat of arms has a black bear on it. The city of Bern also has a bear on its coat of arms.
44051.m: Berlin and Bern both have a bear on their coats of arms.

44052.q: What is the Italian word for ice cream?
44052.e: Ice cream is “gelato” in Italian. In Italy there are lots of gelaterias.
44052.m: Ice cream is gelato in Italian.

44054.q: What do you say in French when saying goodbye?
44054.e: “Au revoir” means “goodbye”. “Merci” means “thank you” and “S'il vous plaît” means “please”.
44054.m: To say goodbye in French you say “Au revoir”.

44055.q: Which train do many cross-border commuters from France take to Geneva?
44055.e: The Léman Express has run between Geneva and France since 2019. It links places such as Annemasse with the city of Geneva.
44055.m: The Léman Express links Geneva with France.

44056.q: Why do many people from neighbouring countries work in Switzerland?
44056.e: In Switzerland people usually earn more money than in the neighbouring countries. That is why many cross the border to work.
44056.m: Many cross-border commuters come because of the higher wages.

44057.q: What are cross-border commuters called in French?
44057.e: “Frontière” means “border”. That is why cross-border commuters are called “frontaliers” in French.
44057.m: Cross-border commuters are called frontaliers in French.

44058.q: Which country do most cross-border commuters working in Schaffhausen come from?
44058.e: The canton of Schaffhausen is almost completely surrounded by German territory. That is why its cross-border commuters come mainly from Germany.
44058.m: Many cross-border commuters from Germany work in Schaffhausen.

44059.q: Which two neighbouring countries does the city of Basel border?
44059.e: Basel lies on the Rhine where three countries meet. Many cross-border commuters from France and Germany work in Basel.

44060.q: Why do many cross-border commuters live abroad rather than in Geneva?
44060.e: In Geneva flats are very expensive and hard to find. In nearby France housing is usually cheaper.
44060.m: Many cross-border commuters live abroad because housing is cheaper there.

44061.q: Are cross-border commuters counted as part of Switzerland's population?
44061.e: Cross-border commuters work in Switzerland but live abroad. That is why they are not counted in Switzerland's resident population.
44061.m: Cross-border commuters are not part of Switzerland's resident population.

44062.q: Which language do cross-border commuters from France usually speak at work in Geneva?
44062.e: French is the official language in Geneva. So cross-border commuters from France can speak their own language at work.
44062.m: In Geneva people mostly work in French.

44063.q: What is the smaller, western part of Lake Constance called?
44063.e: Lake Constance is made up of the large Obersee and the smaller Untersee. Steckborn, for example, lies on the Untersee.
44063.m: The smaller part of Lake Constance is called the Untersee.

44064.q: Which German town on Lake Constance has its old town on an island?
44064.e: Lindau's old town lies on an island in Lake Constance. A causeway and a bridge link it to the mainland.
44064.m: Lindau has an old town on an island.

44065.q: Which island in Lake Constance is known for vegetables and old monasteries?
44065.e: Lots of vegetables are grown on the island of Reichenau. Its old churches are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
44065.m: Reichenau is the vegetable island in Lake Constance.

44066.q: Which old houses can you visit at Unteruhldingen on Lake Constance?
44066.e: At Unteruhldingen there are rebuilt houses standing on stilts in the water. This is how people lived by the lake thousands of years ago.
44066.m: You can visit pile dwellings on Lake Constance.

44067.q: Why is the water of Lake Constance important for millions of people?
44067.e: Lots of drinking water is taken from Lake Constance. It flows through long pipes far into southern Germany, for example to Stuttgart.
44067.m: Lake Constance supplies drinking water for millions of people.

44069.q: Which fish is caught especially often in Lake Constance?
44069.e: Whitefish is the most important food fish in Lake Constance. It is often served fried.
44069.m: In Lake Constance people mainly catch whitefish.

44070.q: According to the Federal Constitution, what applies to all authorities?
a: They may only act if the law allows it
They may do what they like
They must have every decision approved by the people
They must always obey the President of the Confederation
44070.e: Article 5 says that the law is the basis and the limit of state action. So authorities always need a rule that allows them to act.
44070.m: The state may only act on the basis of the law.

44072.q: Which legal text is at the very top of the order of law in Switzerland?
a: An ordinance of the Federal Council
44072.e: The Federal Constitution is the highest law of the country. Federal acts and ordinances must be compatible with it.
44072.m: The Federal Constitution is the highest law in Switzerland.

44073.q: Which four national languages does the Federal Constitution name?
44073.e: Article 4 of the Federal Constitution names German, French, Italian and Romansh as national languages.

44074.q: What is the Federal Constitution called in French?
44074.e: The Federal Constitution is published with equal status in the official languages. In French it is called “Constitution fédérale”, in Italian “Costituzione federale”.
44074.m: In French the Federal Constitution is called “Constitution fédérale”.

44075.q: According to Article 5 of the Federal Constitution, what must the federal government and the cantons respect besides national law?
44075.e: Article 5 paragraph 4 says: “The Confederation and the cantons shall respect international law.” This includes international treaties, for example.
44075.m: The federal government and the cantons must respect international law.

44076.q: The state must act “proportionately”. What does that mean?
a: It may not intervene more strictly than necessary
It must always spend the same amount of money
It may only act once a year
44076.e: A measure must be suitable and may not restrict more than necessary. This is stated in Article 5 of the Federal Constitution.
44076.m: Proportionate means no stricter than necessary.

44078.q: What is the majority of the cantons in a vote on the constitution called?
44078.e: In votes on the constitution, what counts besides the people is in how many cantons a majority agrees. This is called the majority of the cantons.
