44771.m: The General Assembly's general debate takes place every September.

44772.q: Which country traditionally gives the first speech by a member state in the general debate?
44772.e: Since the 1950s Brazil has opened the series of country speeches, followed by the host country, the USA. The custom is said to have begun because in the early years hardly any country wanted to speak first, and Brazil volunteered.
44772.m: Brazil traditionally gives the first country speech in the general debate.

44774.q: For how long is the President of the General Assembly elected?
a: For one session lasting a year
44774.e: The presidency changes with every regular session, so every year. It rotates among the five regional groups.
44774.m: The presidency of the General Assembly changes every year.

44775.q: What do countries such as Switzerland present at the annual UN forum on the 2030 Agenda?
a: Their candidates for the Security Council
44775.e: At the High-Level Political Forum, under the Economic and Social Council, countries review the Sustainable Development Goals every July. Many present voluntary national reports there.
44775.m: At the UN forum on the 2030 Agenda, countries report on their progress.

44776.q: Who elects the members of the UN Economic and Social Council?
44776.e: The General Assembly elects the members for three years at a time. The Council started in 1945 with 18 members and was later enlarged to 54.
44776.m: The General Assembly elects the members of the Economic and Social Council.

44777.q: What is the UN Economic and Social Council responsible for?
a: Cooperation on economic, social and environmental issues
44777.e: The Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) coordinates the UN's work on economic and social matters and sustainable development. It is set out in Chapter X of the Charter.
44777.m: The Economic and Social Council coordinates the UN's economic and social work.

44778.q: How many regional economic commissions belong to the Economic and Social Council?
44778.e: There is one commission each for Europe, Africa, Asia and the Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, and Western Asia. They promote economic cooperation in their region of the world.
44778.m: The Economic and Social Council has five regional economic commissions.

44779.q: Which region of the world is the UN economic commission CEPAL (ECLAC) responsible for?
44779.e: CEPAL was founded in 1948 and is based in Santiago de Chile. It is one of the UN's five regional economic commissions.
44779.m: CEPAL is the UN economic commission for Latin America and the Caribbean.

44780.q: Which ECOSOC functional commission, based in Vienna, is the main UN body for drug control?
44780.e: The Commission on Narcotic Drugs decides, for example, which substances are placed under international control. It was founded in 1946 and meets in Vienna.
44780.m: The Commission on Narcotic Drugs in Vienna is the central UN body for drug control.

44781.q: Which advisory body did ECOSOC set up in 2000 for the concerns of indigenous peoples?
44781.e: The Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues advises ECOSOC on the economy, culture, environment, education and human rights of indigenous peoples. It meets every year in New York.
44781.m: The Permanent Forum advises the UN on the concerns of indigenous peoples.

44782.q: Which trust territory was the last to gain independence, in 1994?
44782.e: Palau was part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands and became independent in October 1994. After that the Trusteeship Council had no more territories to administer.
44782.m: Palau was the last trust territory to become independent.

44783.q: How many territories in total were placed under the United Nations trusteeship system?
44783.e: In total eleven territories were placed under trusteeship, mainly in Africa and the Pacific. All later became independent or joined a neighbouring state.
44783.m: The UN trusteeship system covered eleven territories in total.

44784.q: Why does the UN Trusteeship Council still formally exist, even though it no longer administers any territories?
a: It was never removed from the UN Charter
It replaces the Security Council in case of vetoes
44784.e: The Trusteeship Council is one of the main organs of the UN and is set out in the Charter. Removing it would require amending the Charter, so it formally continues to exist.
44784.m: The Trusteeship Council now exists only on paper.

44785.q: Which League of Nations system was the forerunner of the UN trusteeship system?
44785.e: After the First World War the victorious powers administered former German and Ottoman territories as League of Nations mandates. Many of these mandates became UN trust territories in 1946.
44785.m: The League of Nations mandates were the forerunners of the UN trust territories.

44786.q: Which countries make up the Trusteeship Council today?
a: The five permanent members of the Security Council
44786.e: Since the administering powers gave up their territories, only the five permanent members of the Security Council sit on the Trusteeship Council. It now meets only when needed.
44786.m: Today only the five permanent members belong to the Trusteeship Council.

44787.q: What was the aim of the UN trusteeship system for the territories it administered?
a: To lead them to self-government or independence
To keep them as colonies for ever
To divide them among all UN members
To turn them into UN military bases
44787.e: The administering powers had to prepare the territories for self-government or independence. The first territory to leave the system was British Togoland, which became part of Ghana in 1957.
44787.m: The trusteeship system was meant to lead territories to independence.

44788.q: Which country administered the trust territory of Somalia from 1950 to 1960?
44788.e: The former colony of Italian Somaliland was handed to Italy as a trust territory for ten years. In 1960 it united with British Somaliland to form independent Somalia.
44788.m: Italy administered Somalia as a UN trust territory for ten years.

44789.q: Which UN body can decide on binding enforcement measures against a country that threatens peace?
44789.e: Under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Security Council determines whether peace is threatened. Only it can then decide on binding sanctions or military action.
44789.m: Only the Security Council can decide on binding enforcement measures.

44790.q: Which measure can the Security Council decide on under the UN Charter without the use of armed force?
44790.e: The Charter mentions, for example, cutting off economic relations, transport links and diplomatic relations. Most UN sanctions are based on this.
44790.m: The Security Council can impose sanctions without using weapons.

44791.q: What is needed for the Security Council to decide on a military operation?
a: At least nine votes in favour and no veto
A two-thirds majority of the General Assembly
44791.e: The Security Council has 15 members. A decision needs nine yes votes, and none of the five permanent members may vote against it with a veto.
44791.m: A Security Council decision needs nine votes and no veto.

44792.q: Which five countries have a veto in the UN Security Council?
44792.e: The five permanent members are the victorious powers of the Second World War. Each of them can block a decision with a veto.
44792.m: The five permanent members of the Security Council have a veto.

44793.q: With which phrase does the Security Council usually authorise countries to use military force?
44793.e: This phrase first became well known in Resolution 678 of 1990 against Iraq after its occupation of Kuwait. In UN language it means permission for military action.
44793.m: In the Security Council, the words “all necessary means” mean permission to use force.

44794.q: Which chapter of the Charter deals with the peaceful settlement of disputes?
44794.e: Chapter VI names means such as negotiation, mediation, arbitration and judicial settlement. Only when peace is threatened does Chapter VII come in, with enforcement measures.
44794.m: Chapter VI relies on peaceful means to settle disputes.

44795.q: Why does the UN still have no standing army of its own?
a: Countries never firmly pledged troops to it
The Charter forbids any military force
The General Assembly abolished it in 1990
NATO takes over all UN operations
44795.e: The Charter foresaw agreements through which countries would firmly pledge troops to the Security Council. Because of the Cold War these never came about, so countries provide troops for each operation separately.
44795.m: The UN has no army of its own because countries never firmly pledged troops to it.

44796.q: What role does the UN Secretary-General have under the Charter of the United Nations?
a: He commands the armies of the member states
He is the UN's highest judge
He has a veto in the Security Council
44796.e: According to Article 97, the Secretary-General is the chief administrative officer of the organisation. He heads the Secretariat but has no power to give orders to countries.
44796.m: The Secretary-General is the UN's chief administrative officer.

44797.q: Which office of the UN Secretariat coordinates humanitarian aid worldwide in disasters and crises?
44797.e: The Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) is headed by the Emergency Relief Coordinator. Besides New York, it has an important base in Geneva.
44797.m: OCHA makes sure the UN's humanitarian aid is coordinated.

44798.q: According to Article 101 of the Charter, which principle must be considered alongside expertise when hiring UN staff?
a: As wide a geographical spread as possible
The size of a country's army
The size of a country's contributions
A fixed quota per official language
44798.e: Staff should be chosen for efficiency, competence and integrity. At the same time they should come from as many regions of the world as possible.
44798.m: The UN should choose its staff by ability and from as many world regions as possible.

44799.q: Which office in the Secretariat investigates misconduct, fraud and mismanagement within the UN?
44799.e: The Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS) was created in 1994. It carries out audits, evaluations and investigations and works independently of the heads of departments.
44799.m: The Office of Internal Oversight Services checks the UN from the inside.

44800.q: What is the task of the UN Deputy Secretary-General?
a: To support and stand in for the Secretary-General
To elect the judges of the International Court of Justice
44800.e: The post was created in 1998 to ease the Secretary-General's workload; the first holder was the Canadian Louise Fréchette.
44800.m: The Deputy Secretary-General eases the Secretary-General's workload.

44801.q: Besides New York, which cities are the main duty stations of the UN Secretariat?
44801.e: The Secretariat has its headquarters in New York and further duty stations in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi. Its departments are headed by Under-Secretaries-General.
44801.m: The UN has duty stations in New York, Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi.

44802.q: According to UN calculations, roughly how many people live on Earth today?
44802.e: The Population Division of the UN Secretariat regularly publishes the “World Population Prospects”. According to its calculations, the 8 billion mark was reached in November 2022.
44802.m: Just over 8 billion people live on Earth today.

44803.q: Which country was suspended as a member of the Human Rights Council in April 2022?
44803.e: On 7 April 2022 the General Assembly voted with 93 yes votes for the suspension, because of reports of serious crimes in Ukraine. It was only the second suspension, after Libya in 2011.
44803.m: Russia was suspended as a member of the Human Rights Council in 2022.

44804.q: What majority does the General Assembly need to suspend a country's membership of the Human Rights Council?
a: A two-thirds majority of those voting
44804.e: According to its founding resolution, the General Assembly can suspend a member for gross and systematic human rights violations with two thirds of the members present and voting. Abstentions do not count.
44804.m: A suspension from the Human Rights Council needs a two-thirds majority.

44805.q: After how many consecutive terms can a country not be re-elected to the Human Rights Council straight away?
44805.e: A country may sit on the Council for at most two terms in a row. After a break it can stand again.
44805.m: After two terms in a row, a country must take a break from the Human Rights Council.

44806.q: What are the independent experts called who report on particular countries or topics on behalf of the Human Rights Council?
44806.e: Special rapporteurs belong to the so-called special procedures. They work unpaid and independently of governments.
44806.m: Special rapporteurs report independently to the Human Rights Council on countries and topics.

44807.q: Which country announced its withdrawal from the Human Rights Council in June 2018?
44807.e: The US government justified its withdrawal with criticism of members with poor human rights records and of how Israel was treated. The USA had already voted against founding the Council in 2006.
44807.m: The USA left the Human Rights Council in 2018.

44808.q: Who elects the members of the UN Human Rights Council?
44808.e: The General Assembly elects the 47 members by secret ballot for three years. The seats are shared out by world region; Africa and Asia-Pacific have 13 each.
44808.m: The General Assembly elects the Human Rights Council.

44809.q: Which Swiss Federal Councillor called for reform of the UN Commission on Human Rights in 2003, giving the impetus for the Human Rights Council?
44809.e: On behalf of the foreign minister, the Bern international law expert Walter Kälin drafted the concept. Kofi Annan took up the idea in 2005.
44809.m: The idea of the Human Rights Council has roots in Swiss foreign policy.

44810.q: What is the task of the UN's unarmed military observers, who include Swiss officers?
a: They guard UN buildings in New York
They train the armies of member states
44810.e: The oldest peace mission still running, UNTSO, has monitored ceasefires in the Middle East since 1948. Swiss officers have also worked there since 1990.
44810.m: UN military observers monitor ceasefires, with Swiss participation too.

44811.q: Why is it said that classic blue helmet operations are based on “Chapter Six and a Half” of the Charter?
a: They sit between peaceful settlement and enforcement
The Charter has half a chapter on them
They were added as an extra chapter in 1965
They last only six and a half months
44811.e: Peace operations are not explicitly mentioned in the Charter. They go beyond the means of Chapter VI but are not enforcement measures under Chapter VII; the expression is attributed to Dag Hammarskjöld.
44811.m: Legally, peace operations sit between Chapter VI and Chapter VII.

44812.q: What does it mean when a blue helmet mission is given a “robust mandate”?
a: It may use force to protect civilians
It may act without the consent of all UN states
44812.e: A robust mandate is usually based on Chapter VII and allows force beyond pure self-defence, for example to protect the population. Such mandates became more common after the experiences of the 1990s.
44812.m: A robust mandate allows blue helmets to protect civilians, by force if needed.

44813.q: Which event in 1995 showed the failure of UN blue helmets especially clearly?
44813.e: In July 1995 Dutch blue helmets could not prevent Bosnian Serb troops from taking the Srebrenica safe area and murdering around 8,000 Bosniaks.
44813.m: The failure at Srebrenica in 1995 shaped the debate on UN peace operations.

44814.q: In which country was a UN mission unable to prevent a genocide in 1994?
44814.e: The commander of the UN mission in Rwanda warned early of massacres but was not given permission to intervene. The mission was even reduced during the genocide.
44814.m: Rwanda in 1994 showed the limits of UN peacekeeping.

44815.q: How is the mandate of a blue helmet mission usually extended?
a: By a new Security Council resolution
By a decision of the host country alone
By a vote in the Human Rights Council
44815.e: Mandates are time-limited, usually to one year. The Security Council has to renew them with a resolution and can adjust tasks and troop numbers.
44815.m: The Security Council extends blue helmet mandates with a new resolution each time.

44816.q: Where do the soldiers of UN peace missions come from?
a: They are provided by member states
From a standing UN army of its own
44816.e: The UN has no army of its own. For each mission, member states voluntarily provide troops, police and experts.
44816.m: Blue helmets come from the armies of member states.

44817.q: Which task is today one of the core tasks of almost all large blue helmet missions?
44817.e: Since 1999 missions have been explicitly tasked with protecting civilians from threatened violence, first in Sierra Leone. Today this is part of the mandate almost everywhere.
44817.m: Protecting civilians is a core task of today's blue helmet missions.

44818.q: At which summit did UN member states first commit to the Responsibility to Protect (R2P)?
44818.e: In the outcome document of the 2005 World Summit, heads of state and government recognised the Responsibility to Protect in two paragraphs. The concept is a political commitment, not a treaty.
44818.m: Countries recognised the Responsibility to Protect at the 2005 World Summit.

44819.q: Which events of the 1990s was the concept of the Responsibility to Protect a response to?
a: The genocide in Rwanda and the Kosovo war
The fall of the Berlin Wall
44819.e: A commission set up by Canada coined the term “Responsibility to Protect” in 2001. It asked when the international community may intervene if a state does not protect its population.
44819.m: The Responsibility to Protect is a response to Rwanda and Kosovo.

44820.q: Which crime is one of the four crimes to which the Responsibility to Protect applies?
44820.e: The Responsibility to Protect refers to genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity. Other threats are not covered.
44820.m: The Responsibility to Protect applies only to four serious mass atrocity crimes.

44821.q: What does the first pillar of the Responsibility to Protect say?
a: Every state must protect its own population
The UN must intervene militarily at once
Neighbouring states must take in refugees
The Security Council gives up vetoes
44821.e: The first pillar stresses the primary responsibility of the state. The second concerns help from the international community, the third decisive collective action if a state fails.
44821.m: First of all, every state is responsible for protecting its own population.

44822.q: In which country did the Security Council invoke the Responsibility to Protect in 2011 to allow military action?
44822.e: Resolution 1973 allowed a no-fly zone and the protection of civilians. Critics later accused the intervening states of using the mandate for regime change.
44822.m: The 2011 intervention in Libya is the most important and most disputed case of the Responsibility to Protect.

44823.q: Under the Responsibility to Protect, who must authorise military enforcement measures?
44823.e: If a state fails to protect its population, the international community can act. According to the 2005 World Summit, enforcement measures up to military action need a Security Council decision.
44823.m: Military steps under the Responsibility to Protect need the Security Council.

44824.q: Which basic idea underlies the Responsibility to Protect?
44824.e: The diplomat Francis Deng shaped the idea that sovereignty also means duties towards one's own population. If a state fails, the responsibility can pass to the international community.
44824.m: Under the Responsibility to Protect, sovereignty also brings duties.

44825.q: Which role did Switzerland take on for one month each in 2023 and 2024 in the UN Security Council?
44825.e: The presidency rotates every month in the alphabetical order of the members. Switzerland held it in May 2023 and October 2024.
44825.m: Switzerland held the Security Council presidency twice.

44826.q: Which President of the Swiss Confederation chaired an open Security Council debate on protecting civilians in May 2023?
44826.e: Alain Berset was President of the Confederation in 2023 and travelled to New York during the Swiss presidency. He stressed that international humanitarian law applies to all parties to a conflict.
44826.m: President Alain Berset chaired a debate on protecting civilians in 2023.

44827.q: How long was Switzerland a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council?
44827.e: Non-permanent members are elected by the General Assembly for two years. The Federal Council had already announced the candidacy in 2011.
44827.m: Switzerland sat on the Security Council in 2023 and 2024.

44828.q: Which topic was one of Switzerland's four priorities on the Security Council in 2023 to 2024?
44828.e: Switzerland focused on sustainable peace, protecting civilians, climate security and making the Council more efficient. Climate security means the effects of climate change on peace and security.
44828.m: Climate security was one of Switzerland's four priorities on the Security Council.

44829.q: For the seats of which regional group did Switzerland stand for the Security Council?
44829.e: The Western European and Other States Group also includes Canada, Australia and New Zealand, for example. In 2022 there were only two candidates for its two seats becoming free.
44829.m: Switzerland stood in the Western European and Other States Group.

44830.q: What conclusion did the Federal Council reach in 2015 in its report on neutrality and a Security Council seat?
a: A seat is compatible with neutrality
Only a popular vote can decide
Switzerland would have to leave the UN
44830.e: The report stated that the law of neutrality mainly concerns wars between states and that Security Council decisions do not fall under it. As a member, Switzerland could preserve its neutrality.
44830.m: According to the Federal Council, a Security Council seat is compatible with neutrality.

44831.q: What did Switzerland campaign for in particular on the Syria file in the Security Council in 2023?
44831.e: Together with Brazil, Switzerland drafted the texts on cross-border humanitarian aid. After the earthquake in February 2023 this was especially urgent.
44831.m: Switzerland campaigned in the Security Council for humanitarian aid in Syria.

44832.q: Which four countries form the G4, which jointly seek permanent seats on the Security Council?
44832.e: The G4 support each other's claims to permanent seats. They point to their population, economic strength or contributions to the UN.
44832.m: Germany, Japan, India and Brazil want permanent seats as the G4.

44833.q: What do countries such as Italy and Pakistan want instead of new permanent seats on the UN Security Council?
a: One joint seat just for the EU
44833.e: The group “Uniting for Consensus”, led by Italy, rejects new permanent seats, for example for Germany, India or Brazil. Instead it proposes more elected or longer-term non-permanent seats.
44833.m: Italy and Pakistan want more elected seats rather than new permanent ones.

44834.q: What does the African Union demand for the reform of the UN Security Council?
a: Permanent seats for Africa, including the veto
Moving the Security Council to Africa
One joint seat for Africa and Europe
44834.e: In the 2005 Ezulwini Consensus, the African Union demands at least two permanent seats with all rights, including the veto, plus more non-permanent seats. So far Africa has no permanent seat.
44834.m: Africa demands permanent seats on the Security Council.

44835.q: How many times has the UN Security Council been enlarged since 1945?
a: Never, it has always had 15 members
Twice, by five seats each time
44835.e: The only enlargement so far came into force in 1965: the non-permanent seats rose from six to ten. Since then all reform attempts have failed.
44835.m: The Security Council has been enlarged only once, in 1965.

44836.q: What is the main reason Security Council reform has failed so far?
a: Countries cannot agree on who gets new seats
The Secretary-General blocks it with his veto
The International Court of Justice has banned it
44836.e: Since 2009 countries have negotiated on it in the General Assembly, so far without result. Amending the Charter needs two thirds of UN members and the approval of all five permanent members.
44836.m: Security Council reform fails because countries cannot agree.

44837.q: According to most reform proposals, which right of today's five permanent members should new permanent members not receive?
44837.e: For example, a UN expert panel proposed six new permanent seats without a veto in 2004. A veto for more countries would make the Council even slower to act.
44837.m: New permanent seats would usually come without a veto.

44838.q: Which body was created in 2005 as part of UN reform to help countries rebuild after conflicts?
44838.e: The Peacebuilding Commission was founded jointly by the General Assembly and the Security Council. It aims to prevent countries from falling back into violence after a war.
44838.m: The Peacebuilding Commission helps countries make a fresh start after wars.

44839.q: Which new UN body emerged in 2006 from Kofi Annan's reform proposals and replaced the Commission on Human Rights?
44839.e: In 2005 Kofi Annan proposed a Human Rights Council in his report “In Larger Freedom”. It was created in 2006 and is based in Geneva.
44839.m: The Human Rights Council in Geneva grew out of Annan's reform plan.

44840.q: Near which city did Dag Hammarskjöld's plane crash in 1961?
44840.e: The plane crashed at night shortly before landing near Ndola in Northern Rhodesia, today's Zambia. The exact cause has still not been finally established.
44840.m: Dag Hammarskjöld died in 1961 in a crash near Ndola.

44841.q: In which conflict did Dag Hammarskjöld want to mediate on his last journey?
44841.e: Hammarskjöld wanted to negotiate a ceasefire between UN troops and the breakaway province of Katanga. The UN mission in the Congo was then its largest operation.
44841.m: Hammarskjöld died on a mediation journey during the Congo Crisis.

44842.q: Which office did Dag Hammarskjöld hold from 1953 to 1961?
44842.e: The Swede Dag Hammarskjöld was the second Secretary-General of the UN. He died in office in 1961 in a plane crash in Africa.
44842.m: Dag Hammarskjöld was UN Secretary-General from 1953 to 1961.

44843.q: Which Secretary-General said that the UN was not created to take mankind to heaven, but to save humanity from hell?
44843.e: The saying is attributed to Dag Hammarskjöld and often quoted to describe the UN's realistic aims. He said it in a speech in California in 1954.
44843.m: According to Hammarskjöld, the UN is above all meant to prevent the worst.

44844.q: Which award did Dag Hammarskjöld receive in 1961 after his death?
44844.e: Hammarskjöld was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1961 after his death. He is still one of the few people to have received it posthumously.
44844.m: Hammarskjöld received the Nobel Peace Prize after his death.

44845.q: Whose release from Chinese captivity did Dag Hammarskjöld achieve in 1955 after talks in Beijing?
44845.e: The airmen had been captured during the Korean War. Hammarskjöld travelled to Beijing in person in early 1955, even though the People's Republic of China was not represented at the UN at the time.
44845.m: Hammarskjöld used quiet diplomacy to get captured airmen released.

44846.q: In which subject did Dag Hammarskjöld earn his doctorate before becoming a top civil servant in Sweden?
44846.e: His doctoral thesis on the spread of business cycle fluctuations appeared in 1933. He then became, among other things, state secretary in the Swedish finance ministry.
44846.m: Dag Hammarskjöld was a trained economist.

44847.q: With whom did Kofi Annan share the Nobel Peace Prize in 2001?
44847.e: The Nobel Committee honoured Annan and the UN for their work for a better organised and more peaceful world. It was the hundredth year of the prize.
44847.m: Kofi Annan and the UN received the Nobel Peace Prize together.

44848.q: Which area of the UN Secretariat did Kofi Annan head before he became Secretary-General?
44848.e: As Under-Secretary-General he was responsible for peace operations, including during the crises in Rwanda and Bosnia. He later admitted the UN's mistakes in these crises.
44848.m: Before his election, Kofi Annan was responsible for UN peace operations.

44849.q: At which institution in Switzerland did Kofi Annan study for a year in the early 1960s?
44849.e: After his bachelor's degree in the USA, Annan spent a year at the Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva. He then began his career at the UN.
44849.m: Kofi Annan studied international relations in Geneva.

44850.q: Which country did Kofi Annan come from?
44850.e: Kofi Annan was born in Kumasi in Ghana in 1938. From 1997 to 2006 he was the first UN Secretary-General from sub-Saharan Africa.

44851.q: In which country did Kofi Annan mediate in 2008 after serious unrest following a presidential election?
44851.e: After the disputed election at the end of 2007, violence in Kenya left over a thousand people dead. Annan brokered a power-sharing deal between the Kibaki and Odinga camps.
44851.m: Kofi Annan brokered a power-sharing deal in Kenya in 2008.

44852.q: Which UN programme for Iraq led to a major corruption scandal during Annan's term of office?
44852.e: Under the programme, Iraq was allowed to sell oil despite sanctions in order to buy food and medicine. An inquiry under Paul Volcker uncovered bribery and failings in the UN administration.
44852.m: The Oil-for-Food scandal overshadowed Kofi Annan's term of office.

44853.q: Which group of former statesmen did Kofi Annan chair from 2013?
44853.e: The Elders were founded in 2007 at Nelson Mandela's suggestion and work for peace and human rights. Annan was a member from the start and chair until his death.
44853.m: Kofi Annan led the group The Elders.

44854.q: Which Portuguese party does António Guterres belong to?
44854.e: Guterres was secretary-general of the Partido Socialista and led it to election victory in 1995. This made him Portugal's head of government.
44854.m: António Guterres comes from Portugal's Socialist Party.

44855.q: In which year was António Guterres appointed for a second term as Secretary-General?
44855.e: The General Assembly confirmed him in June 2021 on the Security Council's recommendation, without a rival candidate. The second term began on 1 January 2022.
44855.m: António Guterres was confirmed for a second term in 2021.

44856.q: Because of which situation did António Guterres invoke Article 99 of the Charter in December 2023?
a: The war in the Gaza Strip
44856.e: With this rarely used article, the Secretary-General can draw the Security Council's attention to a danger on his own initiative. Guterres warned of a collapse of humanitarian supplies in Gaza.
44856.m: In 2023 Guterres used his rare right to call on the Security Council over Gaza.

44857.q: Which UN organisation did António Guterres head from 2005 to 2015, before he became Secretary-General?
44857.e: Guterres was UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), based in Geneva, for ten years. This period saw large movements of refugees, for example from Syria.
44857.m: Before his election as Secretary-General, Guterres headed UNHCR.

44858.q: Who was António Guterres's direct predecessor as UN Secretary-General?
44858.e: The South Korean Ban Ki-moon was Secretary-General from 2007 to 2016. Guterres took office on 1 January 2017.

44859.q: Which economic strategy did the EU adopt in 2000 under Portugal's Council presidency, when Guterres was head of government?
44859.e: The Lisbon Strategy aimed to make the EU the world's most competitive knowledge-based economy by 2010. As Prime Minister, Guterres was then chairing the European Council.
44859.m: The EU's Lisbon Strategy was adopted in 2000 with Guterres chairing the Council.

44860.q: What did António Guterres call for in March 2020 because of the Covid-19 pandemic?
a: A ban on all air travel
44860.e: Guterres urged all parties to conflicts to lay down their weapons so that the fight against the virus could go ahead. Many countries and groups supported the appeal, and the Security Council followed in July 2020.
44860.m: During the pandemic Guterres demanded a global ceasefire.

44861.q: Which report has UNDP published every year since 1990?
44861.e: The Human Development Report has been published on behalf of UNDP since 1990. The World Development Report, by contrast, comes from the World Bank.
44861.m: The Human Development Report is UNDP's most important report.

44862.q: Which three dimensions does the Human Development Index (HDI) combine?
a: Health, education and standard of living
44862.e: The HDI combines life expectancy, years of schooling and gross national income per person. It is meant to measure development more broadly than income alone.
44862.m: The HDI measures a long, healthy life, education and a decent standard of living.

44863.q: Which value does the Human Development Index (HDI) use to measure health?
44863.e: The HDI measures health through life expectancy, education through years of schooling and standard of living through income per person. It was developed in 1990 by the economist Mahbub ul Haq with Amartya Sen.
44863.m: In the HDI, life expectancy stands for health.

44864.q: Where does the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) have its headquarters?
44864.e: UNDP has its headquarters in New York, close to UN Headquarters. It has offices in around 170 countries.
44864.m: UNDP is based in New York.

44865.e: UNDP, founded in 1965, helps countries build institutions, fight poverty and develop sustainably. Refugees are looked after by UNHCR, and food aid is provided by WFP.
44865.m: UNDP is the UN's development network.

a: Through compulsory contributions based on the UN scale
Through customs duties on developing countries
44866.e: UNDP receives no compulsory contributions, only voluntary payments from countries and other donors. A large part of this is tied to specific projects.
44866.m: UNDP depends on voluntary contributions from donors.

44867.q: Which index did UNDP introduce in 2010 to measure disadvantages between women and men?
44867.e: The Gender Inequality Index takes into account reproductive health, empowerment through power and education, and the labour market. The Global Gender Gap Index, by contrast, comes from the WEF.
44867.m: UNDP's Gender Inequality Index measures inequality between the sexes.

44868.q: Which poverty index did UNDP develop in 2010 together with the University of Oxford?
44868.e: The Multidimensional Poverty Index measures shortfalls in health, education and standard of living within the same household. It was created with the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative.
44868.m: The Multidimensional Poverty Index shows poverty beyond income.

44869.q: Which global agenda has UNDP supported as the central guideline of its work since 2016?
44869.e: Since 2016 the 2030 Agenda with 17 Sustainable Development Goals has applied. The eight Millennium Goals ended in 2015.
44869.m: The 2030 Agenda contains 17 Sustainable Development Goals.

44870.q: In which city does the environment programme UNEP have its headquarters?
44870.e: UNEP is based in Nairobi, Kenya. It was the first UN organisation with its headquarters in a developing country.
44870.m: The environment programme UNEP is based in Nairobi.

44871.q: Which conference led to the founding of UNEP in 1972?
a: Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm
Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro
44871.e: The 1972 UN conference in Stockholm was the first big world conference on the environment. In the same year, the General Assembly decided to found UNEP.
44871.m: UNEP was created in 1972 after the Stockholm environment conference.

44872.q: What is the task of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)?
a: It coordinates the UN's environmental work worldwide
It runs its own power stations
44872.e: UNEP monitors the state of the environment, advises countries and looks after important environmental agreements. Its first head was the Canadian Maurice Strong.
44872.m: UNEP is the UN's voice for the environment.

44873.q: Which international day is marked every year on 5 June under UNEP's leadership?
44873.e: World Environment Day recalls the opening of the Stockholm conference on 5 June 1972. It has been marked since 1974.

44874.q: Which 1987 agreement to protect the ozone layer was negotiated under UNEP's umbrella?
44874.e: The Montreal Protocol bans CFCs and other ozone-depleting substances step by step. Its secretariat is based at UNEP in Nairobi.
44874.m: The Montreal Protocol protects the ozone layer.

44875.q: Which body did UNEP and the WMO found together in 1988?
44875.e: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change summarises the state of knowledge on climate change. It was set up in 1988 by UNEP and the WMO.
44875.m: The IPCC climate panel is a joint creation of UNEP and the WMO.

44876.q: Which annual report does UNEP publish on the gap between climate pledges and the emission cuts needed?
44876.e: The Emissions Gap Report compares expected emissions with the paths needed for 1.5 or 2 degrees. It appears every year before the climate conference.
44876.m: UNEP's Emissions Gap Report measures the gap in climate protection.

44877.q: Which chemicals conventions share a secretariat in Geneva, run by UNEP?
44877.e: The three conventions deal with hazardous waste, hazardous chemicals in trade and persistent organic pollutants. Their joint secretariat is mostly in Geneva; part of the Rotterdam secretariat works at the FAO in Rome.
44877.m: The Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions are looked after jointly in Geneva.

44878.q: Which environmental award has UNEP given to people and organisations since 2005?
44878.e: With the Champions of the Earth award, UNEP honours outstanding work for the environment. It is regarded as the UN's highest environmental award.
44878.m: Champions of the Earth is the UN's environmental award.

44879.q: Which UN organisation received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020 for fighting hunger?
44879.e: The World Food Programme (WFP) was honoured for its work against hunger and for peace in conflict areas. For this it also runs depots of relief supplies, for example in Brindisi.
44879.m: The World Food Programme received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020.

44880.q: What was the aim of the WFP programme “Purchase for Progress”, launched in 2008?
44880.e: With Purchase for Progress, the WFP bought food directly from smallholder farmers in developing countries. This was meant to increase their income and access to markets.
44880.m: The WFP also wants to strengthen smallholder farmers through its purchases.

44881.q: In which city does the World Food Programme (WFP) have its headquarters?
44881.e: The WFP is based in Rome, as is the Food and Agriculture Organization, FAO. Some units, such as the Innovation Accelerator, are in other cities, for example Munich.
44881.m: The World Food Programme is based in Rome.

44882.q: Which air transport service for humanitarian workers does the WFP run?
44882.e: The UN Humanitarian Air Service (UNHAS) flies aid workers and goods into crisis areas that are hard to reach. The WFP runs it on behalf of the humanitarian community.
44882.m: The WFP runs the UN's humanitarian air service.

44883.q: Which form of aid does the WFP increasingly use instead of food deliveries when local markets work?
44883.e: With cash or vouchers, people can buy at local markets. This strengthens the local economy and saves transport costs.
44883.m: Cash aid strengthens local markets and gives people choice.

44884.q: Which humanitarian cluster does the WFP lead within the UN coordination system?
44884.e: The WFP leads the Logistics Cluster and the Emergency Telecommunications Cluster. In this way it organises transport and storage for many aid agencies.
44884.m: The WFP coordinates the logistics of humanitarian aid.

44885.q: What does the WFP publish with its “Hunger Map”?
a: A world map of food insecurity
A list of the biggest grain exporters
A map of the most fertile soils
A ranking of food prices in cities
44885.e: The Hunger Map shows where people do not have enough to eat. It is constantly updated with data and estimates.
44885.m: The WFP's Hunger Map shows where hunger exists.

44886.q: Which WFP programme is meant to encourage children to go to school?
44886.e: The WFP supports school meals in many countries. A hot meal at school improves nutrition and attendance, especially among girls.
44886.m: School meals fight hunger and support education.

44887.q: Which early warning report on looming hunger crises do the WFP and FAO publish together?
44887.e: The Hunger Hotspots report names regions where the food situation is likely to get worse in the following months. The Global Hunger Index, by contrast, comes from aid agencies.
44887.m: The Hunger Hotspots report warns of coming hunger crises.

44888.q: In which city is the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) based?
44888.e: WIPO is based in Geneva, where its predecessor organisation BIRPI was already located. It is a UN specialised agency.

44889.q: What does the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) protect?
44889.e: WIPO has been a UN specialised agency since 1974. It administers agreements on patents, trademarks, designs and copyright.
44889.m: WIPO looks after the protection of intellectual property.

44890.q: Which 1886 copyright agreement is administered by WIPO today?
44890.e: The Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works was concluded in Bern in 1886. It is still the basis of international copyright today.
44890.m: The Berne Convention of 1886 governs copyright internationally.

44891.q: Which agreement concluded in 1883 is regarded as the basis of the international protection of patents and trademarks?
44891.e: The Paris Convention of 1883 concerns industrial property such as patents, trademarks and designs. Among other things, it introduced the right of priority.
44891.m: The Paris Convention has protected industrial property since 1883.

44892.q: Which WIPO system makes international patent applications easier with a single application?
44892.e: With the 1970 Patent Cooperation Treaty, a single application can seek patent protection in many countries at once. The patents themselves are still granted nationally or regionally.
44892.m: The PCT allows a single international patent application.

44893.q: What is WIPO's Madrid System responsible for?
44893.e: Through the Madrid System, a trademark can be protected in many member states with one application. For designs there is the Hague System.
44893.m: The Madrid System is used for international trademark protection.

44894.q: What position did Switzerland take in WIPO's Global Innovation Index 2025?
44894.e: Switzerland has topped the Global Innovation Index without a break since 2011, including in 2025. Its universities, patents and research spending, for example, are praised.
44894.m: According to WIPO, Switzerland is the most innovative country in the world.

44895.q: In which Swiss city were WIPO's predecessors first based, before they moved to Geneva?
44895.e: The United International Bureaux for the Protection of Intellectual Property (BIRPI) administered the Paris and Berne Conventions. They were first based in Bern, later in Geneva.
44895.m: WIPO's predecessors were first based in Bern.

44896.q: What is the WIPO Arbitration and Mediation Center particularly known for?
44896.e: The Center rules on abusively registered domain names using the UDRP procedure. It handles thousands of such cases every year.
44896.m: WIPO settles disputes over domain names.

44897.q: What is the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) responsible for?
a: Cooperation on weather, climate and water
44897.e: The WMO has been a UN specialised agency since 1951. It makes sure that weather services work together and share data worldwide.
44897.m: The WMO is the UN organisation for weather, climate and water.

44898.q: Which Swiss measuring station is one of the global stations of the WMO's Global Atmosphere Watch programme?
44898.e: On the Jungfraujoch, at around 3,580 metres, greenhouse gases and pollutants are measured in clean air. The station is one of the few global stations of the GAW programme.
44898.m: On the Jungfraujoch, Switzerland measures the atmosphere for the WMO.

44899.e: The WMO is based in Geneva. Reading is home to the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which is not a UN organisation.
44899.m: The World Meteorological Organization is based in Geneva.

44900.q: What has been new about the WMO's leadership since 2024?
a: For the first time a woman heads the organisation
It is led jointly by two people
Its headquarters have moved to New York
44900.e: The Argentinian Celeste Saulo succeeded Petteri Taalas on 1 January 2024. She is the WMO's first female Secretary-General.
44900.m: Since 2024 a woman has led the WMO for the first time.

44901.q: What does the WMO's annual “Greenhouse Gas Bulletin” report on?
a: The concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere
44901.e: The bulletin analyses worldwide measurements of CO2, methane and nitrous oxide in the air. So it shows what is building up in the atmosphere, not what individual countries emit.
44901.m: The WMO's Greenhouse Gas Bulletin shows the concentration of greenhouse gases in the air.

44902.q: According to the WMO, which year has been the warmest since records began (as of 2026)?
44902.e: According to the WMO, the global average temperature in 2024 was around 1.55 degrees above the pre-industrial level. This means 2024 beat the record year 2023, and 2025 also stayed slightly below it.
44902.m: According to the WMO, 2024 was the warmest year since records began.

44903.q: Which task do the WMO's regional committees take on for tropical cyclones?
a: They set the lists of names
They steer the storms away with aircraft
44903.e: The names of hurricanes and typhoons come from lists kept by WMO committees. The names of especially destructive storms are retired.
44903.m: The WMO manages the names of tropical cyclones.

44904.q: What is the name of the WMO's worldwide programme for sharing weather observations, which started in 1963?
44904.e: Through the World Weather Watch, the weather services of all member states share observations in real time. Without these data, global weather models would not be possible.
44904.m: Weather data are shared worldwide through the World Weather Watch.

44905.q: In which year did the first United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) take place?
44905.e: The first UNCTAD conference met in Geneva in 1964. It led to a permanent body of the UN General Assembly.

44906.q: What has UNCTAD mainly worked for since it was founded?
a: Better trade opportunities for developing countries
44906.e: UNCTAD wants to help developing countries benefit from world trade. Its first Secretary-General, the Argentinian Raúl Prebisch, called for fair trade rules for this.
44906.m: UNCTAD works for developing countries in world trade.

44907.q: Which group of countries was founded in 1964 at the first UNCTAD conference?
44907.e: 77 developing countries signed a joint declaration in 1964. The G77 now has over 130 states but has kept its name.
44907.m: The Group of 77 was formed at the first UNCTAD conference.

44908.q: Which thesis, held by Prebisch and Singer, shaped early UNCTAD?
a: The terms of trade for commodity exporters worsen in the long run
Free trade benefits all countries equally
Commodity prices rise faster than industrial prices in the long run
Developing countries should export only farm products
44908.e: According to the Prebisch-Singer thesis, the prices of raw materials fall relative to manufactured goods. That is why UNCTAD called for industrialisation and trade advantages for developing countries.
44908.m: The Prebisch-Singer thesis warns of falling commodity prices.

44909.q: Which system of preferences for developing countries was agreed at the 1968 UNCTAD conference in New Delhi?
44909.e: Under the Generalised System of Preferences, industrialised countries grant developing countries lower tariffs on a one-sided basis. Switzerland also applies such a system.
44909.m: The Generalised System of Preferences lowers tariffs for developing countries.

44910.q: Which annual report on foreign direct investment does UNCTAD publish?
44910.e: The World Investment Report analyses worldwide flows of direct investment. The World Trade Report, by contrast, comes from the WTO.
44910.m: UNCTAD's World Investment Report tracks direct investment.

44911.q: Which organisation in Geneva do UNCTAD and the WTO run together?
44911.e: The International Trade Centre (ITC) helps small and medium-sized businesses in developing countries to export. It is a joint agency of UNCTAD and the WTO.
44911.m: The International Trade Centre belongs jointly to UNCTAD and the WTO.

44912.q: Who has led UNCTAD since 2021 as the first woman in the post (as of 2025)?
44912.e: The Costa Rican Rebeca Grynspan became Secretary-General of UNCTAD in 2021. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, by contrast, heads the WTO.
44912.m: Rebeca Grynspan is the first woman at the head of UNCTAD.

44913.q: Which conference recommended creating a High Commissioner for Human Rights in 1993?
a: World Conference on Human Rights in Vienna
World Conference on Women in Beijing
44913.e: The 1993 Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action called for such an office. The General Assembly created it in the same year.
44913.m: The office of High Commissioner for Human Rights goes back to the 1993 Vienna conference.

44914.q: In which Swiss city is the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights based?
44914.e: The OHCHR is in the Palais Wilson in Geneva, the former seat of the League of Nations Secretariat. Geneva is an important centre of international human rights work.
44914.m: The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights is in Geneva.

44915.q: Which office did Mary Robinson hold before she became UN High Commissioner for Human Rights in 1997?
44915.e: Mary Robinson was Ireland's first female President from 1990 to 1997. As High Commissioner she made the young office known internationally.
44915.m: The former Irish President Mary Robinson was High Commissioner for Human Rights.

44916.q: Which High Commissioner for Human Rights was killed in the 2003 attack on the UN headquarters in Baghdad?
44916.e: The Brazilian Sérgio Vieira de Mello was special envoy in Iraq and died on 19 August 2003. This date is now World Humanitarian Day.
44916.m: Sérgio Vieira de Mello died in an attack in Baghdad in 2003.

44917.q: Which procedure has reviewed the human rights situation in all UN member states since 2008, supported by the OHCHR?
44917.e: In the Universal Periodic Review, every state is reviewed by the Human Rights Council roughly every four and a half to five years. Other states make recommendations.
44917.m: In the Universal Periodic Review all states are reviewed regularly.

44918.q: Who was Michelle Bachelet before she became UN High Commissioner for Human Rights in 2018?
44918.e: Michelle Bachelet was President of Chile twice. She was High Commissioner from 2018 to 2022, followed by Volker Türk.
44918.m: The former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet led the UN human rights office.

44919.q: Which Austrian has been High Commissioner for Human Rights since 2022 (as of 2025)?
44919.e: Volker Türk succeeded Michelle Bachelet in October 2022. Before that he worked for UNHCR for a long time.
44919.m: Volker Türk is High Commissioner for Human Rights.

44920.q: Since when has the office of UN High Commissioner for Human Rights existed?
a: Since the UN was founded in 1945
Since the end of the First World War
44920.e: The UN General Assembly created the office in 1993 after the Vienna World Conference. The Ecuadorian José Ayala-Lasso was the first to hold it, from 1994.
44920.m: The office of High Commissioner for Human Rights has existed since 1993.

44921.e: UNAIDS is in Geneva, close to the WHO. It coordinates the work of several UN organisations against HIV.

44922.q: Which disease is the UN programme UNAIDS fighting?
44922.e: UNAIDS was founded in 1996 and coordinates the work of several UN organisations against HIV. Its first head was the Belgian researcher Peter Piot.
44922.m: UNAIDS coordinates the worldwide fight against HIV.

44923.q: Why is UNAIDS structured differently from most UN organisations?
a: It coordinates several UN organisations together
It is a private drug company
It belongs to the WHO alone
It is funded only by Switzerland
44923.e: UNAIDS is a joint programme involving, for example, the WHO, UNICEF and the World Bank. Since 2019 it has been led by the Ugandan Winnie Byanyima.
44923.m: UNAIDS is a joint programme of several UN organisations.

44924.q: What do the UNAIDS “95-95-95” targets stand for?
a: Diagnosed, treated and with a suppressed viral load
44924.e: By 2025, 95 per cent of people with HIV should know their status, 95 per cent of them should be on treatment, and 95 per cent of those should have a suppressed viral load. There is still no vaccine against HIV.
44924.m: The 95-95-95 targets concern diagnosis, treatment and viral load.

44925.q: What does effective HIV treatment achieve in the people affected?
a: The virus can no longer be detected in the blood
The virus disappears from the body for ever
You are then protected against all viruses
You must stop the medicine after a week
44925.e: The medicines suppress the virus's reproduction so strongly that it can no longer be detected in the blood. But they cannot cure HIV, so they have to be taken for life.
44925.m: Effective HIV treatment pushes the viral load below the detection limit.

44926.q: Which goal for 2030 is UNAIDS pursuing as part of the 2030 Agenda?
a: Ending AIDS as a public health threat
Wiping out HIV worldwide like smallpox
44926.e: Target 3.3 of the 2030 Agenda names ending the AIDS epidemic as a health threat. This means a sharp fall in new infections and deaths.
44926.m: UNAIDS wants to end AIDS as a health threat by 2030.

44927.q: What is special about the UNAIDS Programme Coordinating Board?
a: Representatives of civil society also sit on it
Only drug companies have a vote
It meets only every ten years
44927.e: UNAIDS was the first UN programme to include civil society organisations, among them people living with HIV, in its governing body. However, they have no vote there.
44927.m: At UNAIDS, civil society has a say in the governing body.

44928.q: According to UNAIDS, how many people worldwide were living with HIV (as of 2024)?
44928.e: UNAIDS estimated around 40.8 million people living with HIV in 2024. Most of them live in eastern and southern Africa.
44928.m: About 40 million people worldwide live with HIV.

44929.q: In which year was the forerunner of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) founded?
44929.e: In 1951 a provisional committee was set up in Brussels to help resettle migrants from war-torn Europe. The IOM later grew out of it.
44929.m: The roots of the IOM go back to 1951.

44930.q: Since which year has the IOM been part of the UN system as a related organisation?
44930.e: At the 2016 UN summit for refugees and migrants, an agreement between the UN and the IOM was signed. Since then the IOM has been a related organisation of the UN.
44930.m: The IOM has been part of the UN system since 2016.

44931.e: The IOM has its headquarters in Geneva, more precisely in Grand-Saconnex. It is active in over 100 countries worldwide.
44931.m: The IOM's headquarters are in Geneva.

44932.q: Who has led the IOM since 2023 as the first woman in the post (as of 2025)?
44932.e: The American Amy Pope took office as Director General in October 2023. Filippo Grandi, by contrast, was High Commissioner for Refugees.
44932.m: Amy Pope is the first woman at the head of the IOM.

44933.q: What are people called who flee war or disasters but stay in their own country?
44933.e: Internally displaced people do not cross a national border and are therefore not refugees under the Geneva Convention. The IOM records their numbers with the Displacement Tracking Matrix.
44933.m: Internally displaced people are displaced within their own country.

44934.q: Which IOM project documents deaths and missing people on migration routes?
44934.e: Since 2014 the Missing Migrants Project has collected data on people who die or disappear while fleeing or migrating. The Mediterranean is one of the deadliest routes.
44934.m: The Missing Migrants Project counts the dead on migration routes.

44935.q: Which framework adopted in Marrakesh in 2018 does the IOM particularly support?
a: Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration
44935.e: The legally non-binding migration compact was adopted in Marrakesh in December 2018. Switzerland did not approve it at the time, because the Federal Council first wanted to involve parliament.
44935.m: The 2018 migration compact is not legally binding.

44936.q: Which report does the IOM publish every two years?
44936.e: The World Migration Report gives an overview of migration figures and trends. Global Trends, by contrast, is a UNHCR report.
44936.m: The IOM's World Migration Report appears every two years.

44937.q: Where was the vaccine alliance Gavi officially launched in January 2000?
a: At the G8 summit in Genoa
44937.e: Gavi was presented at the World Economic Forum in Davos. Its headquarters are now in Geneva.
44937.m: The vaccine alliance Gavi was launched in Davos in 2000.

44938.q: Which foundation gave Gavi start-up funding of 750 million US dollars when it was founded?
44938.e: The Gates Foundation pledged 750 million dollars at the founding. It is still one of the most important funders today.
44938.m: The Gates Foundation helped to found Gavi.

44939.q: What kind of organisation is the vaccine alliance Gavi?
44939.e: In Gavi, governments, the WHO, UNICEF, the World Bank, foundations and vaccine makers work together. Gavi is not a UN organisation but a foundation under Swiss law with special status.

44940.q: Which initiative did Gavi lead from 2020 together with CEPI and the WHO?
44940.e: COVAX was meant to give all countries fair access to Covid-19 vaccines. By 2023 COVAX had delivered almost 2 billion vaccine doses.
44940.m: COVAX distributed Covid vaccines to poorer countries.

44941.q: In which city is the vaccine alliance Gavi based?
44941.e: Like the WHO, Gavi is based in Geneva. The city is one of the most important centres for international health organisations.
44941.m: The vaccine alliance Gavi is based in Geneva.

44942.q: What does Gavi's co-financing principle mean for the countries it supports?
a: They pay a growing share of vaccine costs themselves
They must hand their profits to Gavi
They always get vaccines completely free
They must build their own vaccine factories
44942.e: Countries contribute to the costs, and their share rises as their income grows. In the end they take over the vaccination programmes completely.
44942.m: Through co-financing, countries gradually take over their vaccination programmes.

44943.q: Which UN organisation buys most of the vaccines for Gavi?
44943.e: UNICEF's Supply Division in Copenhagen buys vaccines in large quantities. This lets Gavi get lower prices.
44943.m: UNICEF buys the vaccines for Gavi.

44944.q: According to its own figures, how many children has Gavi helped to vaccinate since 2000 (as of 2024)?
44944.e: Gavi says it has helped vaccinate over a billion children in low-income countries since 2000. It says this has prevented millions of deaths.
44944.m: Gavi has helped vaccinate over a billion children.

44945.q: According to UNRWA's definition, who counts as a Palestine refugee?
a: Someone who lived in Palestine between June 1946 and May 1948 and lost home and livelihood in the 1948 war
Someone who emigrated from the Gaza Strip after 1967
44945.e: What counts is having lived in Palestine from 1 June 1946 to 15 May 1948 and having lost home and means of living. Descendants in the male line can also be registered.
44945.m: UNRWA defines Palestine refugees through the 1948 war.

a: Palestine refugees in the Middle East
44946.e: UNRWA helps registered Palestine refugees and their descendants. For most other refugees, UNHCR is responsible.

44947.q: In which five fields of operation is UNRWA active?
a: Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip
Egypt, Iraq, Iran, Turkey and Cyprus
Israel, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar and Oman
Jordan, Egypt, Iraq, Yemen and Libya
44947.e: UNRWA runs schools, health centres and social services in these five areas. Most registered Palestine refugees live there.
44947.m: UNRWA works in five areas in the Middle East.

44948.q: What did the Israeli parliament decide about UNRWA in October 2024?
a: A ban on UNRWA activities on Israeli sovereign territory
Integrating UNRWA into the Israeli army
44948.e: The Knesset passed two laws banning UNRWA from operating on Israeli sovereign territory and from contact with Israeli authorities. They came into force at the end of January 2025.
44948.m: In 2024 Israel banned UNRWA from operating on its sovereign territory.

44949.q: How is the duration of UNRWA's mandate regulated?
a: The General Assembly extends the mandate for a few years at a time
The mandate is unlimited under the UN Charter
The Security Council renews it every year
Israel and Jordan decide on it
44949.e: UNRWA is a subsidiary body of the General Assembly, and its mandate is time-limited. It has been extended again and again since 1950, usually by three years.
44949.m: UNRWA's mandate has to be extended by the General Assembly.

44950.q: Which area of work is UNRWA's largest in terms of budget and staff?
44950.e: UNRWA runs hundreds of schools for hundreds of thousands of children. Most of its staff are teachers.
44950.m: Education is UNRWA's largest area of work.

a: Through compulsory contributions from all UN members
44951.e: Only a small part of UNRWA's budget comes from the regular UN budget. The rest depends on voluntary donations, which makes the agency vulnerable to financial crises.

44952.q: Which conflict led to the flight that caused UNRWA to be founded?
44952.e: In the 1948 war around 700,000 Arab Palestinians fled or were driven out. UNRWA was created for them.
44952.m: UNRWA was created after the 1948 Palestine war.

44953.q: Which 1944 agreement is the basis of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO)?
44953.e: The Convention on International Civil Aviation was signed in Chicago on 7 December 1944. ICAO came into being in 1947, when it entered into force.
44953.m: The 1944 Chicago Convention is the basis of ICAO.

44954.q: In which city is ICAO based?
44954.e: ICAO is based in Montreal, Canada. The headquarters of the airline association IATA are also there.

44955.q: What is the task of the International Civil Aviation Organization, ICAO?
a: Setting worldwide standards for civil aviation safety
Selling plane tickets for all airlines
44955.e: ICAO is a UN specialised agency. Its Council of 36 states adopts standards on things such as licences, air traffic control and accident investigation.
44955.m: ICAO sets the worldwide rules for civil aviation.

44956.q: Which spelling alphabet did ICAO lay down for radio communication?
44956.e: The ICAO alphabet has been in international use since the 1950s. Alfa is deliberately spelt with an f so that it is pronounced correctly everywhere.
44956.m: The ICAO alphabet begins with Alfa and Bravo.

44957.q: What is the name of the system adopted by ICAO in 2016 to offset CO2 emissions from international aviation?
44957.e: CORSIA requires airlines to offset increases in emissions on international flights through climate projects. It is the first global climate instrument for a whole economic sector.
44957.m: CORSIA is meant to offset the growth in aviation emissions.

44958.q: What are the technical rulebooks attached to the Chicago Convention called?
44958.e: The 19 annexes today contain standards and recommendations, for example on licences, air traffic control or accident investigation. Countries put them into national law.
44958.m: The annexes to the Chicago Convention contain the technical standards of aviation.

44959.q: What is the purpose of air accident investigations under ICAO rules?
44959.e: Annex 13 to the Chicago Convention states that investigations serve prevention, not the allocation of blame. In Switzerland, the STSB (SUST) is responsible for this.
44959.m: Air accidents are investigated to prevent future accidents.

44960.q: Which language must pilots and air traffic controllers master for international radio communication under ICAO rules?
44960.e: English is the language of international aviation radio. Since 2008, pilots and controllers have had to prove at least level 4 on the ICAO scale.
44960.m: English is compulsory in international aviation radio.

44961.q: What happens to a treaty between states that breaks a peremptory norm of international law (ius cogens)?
a: It is valid for only ten years
It must be confirmed by the people
It stays valid, but without penalties
44961.e: A treaty that breaks ius cogens is invalid from the start. This is laid down in the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.
44961.m: A treaty that breaks ius cogens is void.

44962.q: May two states agree in a treaty not to respect the ban on torture?
a: No, peremptory international law cannot be set aside
Yes, but only during a war
Yes, if the UN Security Council agrees
44962.e: The ban on torture is part of ius cogens. Such norms apply to all states and cannot be overridden by any treaty.
44962.m: No treaty may depart from peremptory international law.

44963.q: Who must recognise a rule as a peremptory norm of international law (ius cogens) for it to count as one?
a: The international community of states as a whole
The International Court of Justice alone
44963.e: Under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, a norm is peremptory if the international community of states as a whole recognises it. No single body can decide this on its own.
44963.m: Ius cogens rests on recognition by the whole community of states.

44964.q: Which of these norms is generally regarded as ius cogens?
44964.e: Like the bans on torture, genocide and aggression, the ban on slavery belongs to the recognised core of peremptory international law. Customs tariffs or visa rules, by contrast, can be freely negotiated.
44964.m: The ban on slavery is a peremptory norm of international law.

44965.q: Which ban did the International Court of Justice explicitly call ius cogens for the first time in 2006?
a: The ban on the death penalty
The ban on nuclear weapons tests
44965.e: In the case Congo v. Rwanda, the Court called the ban on genocide a peremptory norm. The death penalty, by contrast, is not generally banned under international law.
44965.m: The ban on genocide is part of peremptory international law.

44966.q: What happens in Switzerland if a popular initiative violates peremptory rules of international law?
a: The Federal Assembly declares it invalid
It is voted on only in the cantons
The Federal Supreme Court changes its text
It automatically lapses after five years
44966.e: Under Article 139 paragraph 3 of the Federal Constitution, the Federal Assembly declares a popular initiative wholly or partly invalid if it violates peremptory international law. This happened in 1996 with an asylum initiative because of the principle of non-refoulement.
44966.m: In Switzerland, popular initiatives must not violate peremptory international law.

44967.q: What does the Latin expression “erga omnes”, often found together with ius cogens in international law, mean?
44967.e: A state owes obligations erga omnes to the whole community of states, for example the ban on genocide. That is why all states may insist that they are respected.
44967.m: Obligations erga omnes apply towards all states.

44968.q: In which city was the 1969 Convention on the Law of Treaties, which first defined ius cogens, concluded?
44968.e: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties sets out how treaties between states are made, apply and end. It also describes peremptory international law.
44968.m: Ius cogens is defined in the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties.

44969.q: Which two elements are needed for customary international law to arise?
a: General practice and a belief that it is law
44969.e: Article 38(1)(b) of the ICJ Statute describes custom as evidence of a general practice accepted as law. So it needs state practice (consuetudo) and a belief that it is legally required (opinio iuris).
44969.m: Customary law arises from state practice and a belief that it is law.

44970.q: How does customary international law differ from a treaty?
a: It is not signed but grows out of the practice of states
It is issued by the UN Security Council
44970.e: A treaty is negotiated and signed. Customary law, by contrast, arises when states behave in the same way over a long time and feel legally bound in doing so.
44970.m: Customary law arises from how states behave, not from a signature.

44971.q: Which court decides disputes between states and applies treaties and customary international law?
44971.e: The International Court of Justice in The Hague relies on treaties, customary law and general principles of law. Court decisions and legal writings serve as aids.
44971.m: The International Court of Justice also applies customary international law.

44972.q: When is a state not bound by a new rule of customary international law?
a: If it has consistently objected to it from the start
If it has ignored it once
If it is not in the UN
If its parliament has not agreed
44972.e: A state that clearly and constantly objects to an emerging customary rule is not bound by it. This exception does not apply to peremptory rules such as the ban on torture.
44972.m: A state that objects early and consistently can avoid being bound by a new customary rule.

44973.q: According to the International Court of Justice, what is needed for a rule to become customary international law?
a: A widespread and uniform practice of states
The approval of the UN Secretary-General
A majority decision of the General Assembly
The signature of every state in the world
44973.e: In the North Sea cases of 1969, the ICJ required a widespread and uniform practice, backed by the belief that it is legally binding.
44973.m: Customary law needs widespread, uniform state practice.

44974.q: What was the name of the court in The Hague that settled disputes between states in the days of the League of Nations?
44974.e: The Permanent Court of International Justice worked from 1922. After the Second World War, the UN's International Court of Justice took its place.
44974.m: The Permanent Court of International Justice was the forerunner of the ICJ.

44975.q: What is meant by diplomatic asylum?
a: Protection for persecuted people in an embassy
44975.e: With diplomatic asylum, an embassy takes in a persecuted person. There are regional rules on this in Latin America, but it is not generally recognised worldwide.
44975.m: Diplomatic asylum is protection in an embassy.

44976.q: What is the task of the UN International Law Commission?
a: It writes down international law and develops it further
44976.e: The International Law Commission drafts treaties and summarises customary law. In 2018, for example, it set out how customary law can be identified.
44976.m: The International Law Commission codifies and develops international law.

44977.q: What does the 1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties regulate?
a: How states conclude, interpret and end treaties
The protection of prisoners of war
44977.e: The Convention is often called the “treaty on treaties”. It came into force in 1980. The rights of diplomats are governed by another Vienna Convention of 1961.
44977.m: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties is the “treaty on treaties”.

44978.q: What does the principle “pacta sunt servanda” mean?
a: The stronger party decides the treaty
44978.e: The principle is in Article 26 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties: every valid treaty binds the parties and must be carried out in good faith.
44978.m: Treaties must be kept in good faith.

44979.q: May a state end a treaty because circumstances have changed fundamentally?
a: Only exceptionally and under strict conditions
Yes, at any time without giving reasons
44979.e: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties allows a fundamental change of circumstances to be invoked only exceptionally. For boundary treaties it is ruled out completely.
44979.m: A fundamental change of circumstances can end a treaty only exceptionally.

44980.q: What are international treaties interpreted by first and foremost?
a: By their wording in context and by their object and purpose
By the will of the stronger state
By the law of the state that keeps the treaty
44980.e: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties requires interpretation in good faith, according to the ordinary meaning of the terms in their context and in the light of object and purpose. The preparatory work is only a supplementary means.
44980.m: Treaties are interpreted by wording, context, and object and purpose.

44981.q: May a state justify breaking a treaty with its own national law?
a: No, national law does not excuse a breach of treaty
Yes, national law always comes first
44981.e: Under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, a state may not use its internal law as a reason for not carrying out a treaty. This also applies to constitutional law, with one narrow exception.
44981.m: National law does not excuse a breach of treaty.

44982.q: Which people may represent their state when concluding a treaty without full powers?
a: Head of state, head of government and foreign minister
44982.e: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties names heads of state, heads of government and foreign ministers, who by virtue of their office do not need to present full powers. Other people generally need them.
44982.m: Head of state, head of government and foreign minister need no full powers.

44983.q: What is a one-sided statement called with which a state wants to exclude the legal effect of certain treaty provisions for itself?
44983.e: Reservations are dealt with in Articles 19 to 23 of the Vienna Convention. They are not allowed, among other things, if they are incompatible with the treaty's object and purpose.
44983.m: With a reservation, a state limits how far it is bound by a treaty.

44984.q: What applies to a treaty that was forced on a state by the threat or use of force?
a: It is valid but can be terminated
It is valid for only five years
It must be confirmed by the Security Council
44984.e: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties declares void any treaty brought about by force in violation of the UN Charter. The rule is linked to the ban on the use of force.
44984.m: A treaty obtained by force is void.

44985.q: What duty does a state have that has signed a treaty but not yet ratified it?
a: It must not defeat the treaty's object and purpose
It must apply all provisions at once
It must ratify within a year
It has no duties at all
44985.e: A signatory state must not do things that would defeat the treaty's object and purpose. This applies until it makes clear that it does not intend to become a party.
44985.m: A state that signs must not undermine the treaty in advance.

44986.q: What does state immunity mean in international law?
a: A state cannot simply be sued in the courts of another state
A state may never be attacked
Heads of state may never be arrested
A state pays no customs duties
44986.e: States are equal in rank. So no state should sit in judgement over another sovereign state. Immunity from foreign courts follows from this.
44986.m: A state does not judge another state of equal rank.

44987.q: For which acts does a state usually enjoy immunity before foreign courts?
a: For sovereign acts such as legislation or military operations
For buying goods from private firms
For rental contracts with private individuals
For the business of its state railway
44987.e: Today most states distinguish between sovereign and commercial acts. Immunity applies only to sovereign acts.
44987.m: States enjoy immunity for sovereign acts.

44988.q: For which type of acts do most states no longer grant immunity today?
44988.e: If a state buys goods like a private person, for example, it acts iure gestionis. Under the restrictive theory that prevails today, it can be sued for this before foreign courts.
44988.m: A state that acts like a trader is treated like a trader.

44989.q: Which organisation in Strasbourg drew up the European Convention on State Immunity in 1972?
44989.e: The Convention was drawn up by the Council of Europe and signed in Basel in 1972. It follows the rule that states enjoy immunity only for sovereign acts.
44989.m: The European Convention on State Immunity comes from the Council of Europe.

44990.q: Which case on immunity in claims over Second World War crimes did the ICJ decide in 2012?
44990.e: Italian courts had ruled against Germany over war crimes committed by the Wehrmacht. The ICJ decided that Italy had violated Germany's state immunity, even in the case of serious violations of international law.
44990.m: According to the ICJ, state immunity applies even to claims over war crimes.

44991.q: A foreign state buys goods in Switzerland like a private company and does not pay. What applies according to today's view?
a: It can be sued in a Swiss court
Only the UN Security Council can decide
Only the International Court of Justice is competent
44991.e: If a state acts like a private party, it enjoys no immunity. Swiss courts also require the deal to have a sufficient link to Switzerland.
44991.m: A state that acts like a trader can be sued like a trader.

44992.q: What is the immunity called that prevents the seizure of state assets such as central bank reserves?
44992.e: Even if a state loses a case, its assets used for sovereign purposes usually may not be seized. This immunity from enforcement is broader than immunity from the court proceedings themselves.
44992.m: Immunity from enforcement protects state assets used for sovereign purposes from seizure.

44993.q: Why is the 2004 UN Convention on State Immunity not yet in force (as of 2025)?
a: Too few states have ratified it
The Security Council blocked it with a veto
The International Court of Justice declared it invalid
It only applies from the year 2050
44993.e: The UN General Assembly adopted the Convention in 2004. However, it needs 30 ratifications, and this number has not yet been reached.
44993.m: A convention only comes into force once enough states have ratified it.

44994.q: In which document was the right of peoples to self-determination named as an aim as early as 1945?
44994.e: Article 1 of the UN Charter names as an aim friendly relations based on equal rights and self-determination of peoples.
44994.m: The UN Charter already names the self-determination of peoples.

44995.q: How did the right of peoples to self-determination become binding treaty law in 1966?
