45214.m: In the ordinary legislative procedure the Council mostly votes by qualified majority.

45215.q: What happens if Parliament rejects the Council's position by an absolute majority at second reading?
45215.e: If Parliament rejects the Council's position at second reading by a majority of its members, the proposed act is deemed not to have been adopted.
45215.m: If Parliament rejects it at second reading, the law fails.

45216.q: Why is the EU's ordinary legislative procedure called “ordinary”?
a: It is the usual procedure for most EU laws
It is used only in emergencies
It applies only to laws on public order
It needs no approval from Parliament
45216.e: Since the Treaty of Lisbon, this procedure has been the normal case. It is set out in Article 294 TFEU.
45216.m: The ordinary procedure is the normal way EU laws are made.

45217.q: What distinguishes an EU regulation from an EU directive?
a: The regulation applies directly in all states
The regulation must first be transposed
The regulation applies only to some states
The regulation is not legally binding
45217.e: Under Article 288 TFEU, a regulation applies generally and directly in every member state. A directive must first be transposed into national law.
45217.m: An EU regulation applies directly; a directive must be transposed.

45218.q: What is binding on member states in an EU directive?
a: The exact wording of the law
45218.e: A directive is binding as to the result to be achieved but leaves the choice of form and methods to the states.
45218.m: With a directive, the goal is binding but the way to reach it is free.

45219.q: What legal form does the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) take?
45219.e: The GDPR (Regulation 2016/679) has applied directly in all member states since 25 May 2018. It replaced the 1995 Data Protection Directive.
45219.m: The GDPR is a regulation and applies directly throughout the EU.

45220.q: Which EU legal acts are NOT legally binding under Article 288 TFEU?
45220.e: Regulations, directives and decisions are binding; recommendations and opinions have no binding force.
45220.m: EU recommendations and opinions are not binding.

45221.q: What does a member state face if it does not transpose an EU directive on time?
45221.e: Infringement proceedings can end before the Court of Justice, which under Article 260 TFEU can impose lump sums or penalty payments.
45221.m: Late transposition can lead to infringement proceedings.

45222.q: Which court has the final say on interpreting EU law?
a: The Court of Justice of the EU in Luxembourg
The European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg
The International Court of Justice in The Hague
The Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe
45222.e: The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) makes sure that EU law is applied in the same way everywhere. The court in Strasbourg, by contrast, belongs to the Council of Europe.
45222.m: The Court of Justice in Luxembourg gives the binding interpretation of EU law.

45223.q: What is it called when a state adopts stricter rules than required when transposing a directive?
45223.e: Gold-plating means going beyond a directive when transposing it into national law, for example by adding extra obligations.
45223.m: Gold-plating means transposing a directive more strictly than necessary.

45224.q: What is a “decision” within the meaning of Article 288 TFEU?
a: A legal act binding in its entirety, often for specific addressees
A law only for non-EU states
A judgment of the Court of Justice
45224.e: A decision is binding in its entirety; if it is addressed to specific parties, such as a company, it applies only to them.
45224.m: An EU decision is binding and is often addressed to specific parties.

45225.q: Who takes part in a trilogue in the EU legislative procedure?
a: Parliament, the Council and the Commission
The Council, the Court of Justice and the ECB
Parliament, the Council of Europe and the Commission
The Commission, the Court of Auditors and the Council
45225.e: In a trilogue, representatives of Parliament and the Council negotiate, while the Commission mediates and advises.
45225.m: In a trilogue, Parliament, the Council and the Commission negotiate.

45226.q: Is the trilogue laid down in the EU treaties as a formal procedure?
a: Yes, as part of the preliminary ruling procedure
Yes, as a task of the Court of Auditors
45226.e: Trilogues are informal negotiations. How they work is described in a joint declaration and in the 2016 interinstitutional agreement, not in the treaties.
45226.m: The trilogue is an informal negotiating format.

45227.q: What is a frequent criticism of trilogues?
a: Election campaigns that are too long
Interest rates that are too high
45227.e: Critics complain that trilogues take place behind closed doors and that interim results are hard to follow. The European Ombudsman called for more transparency in 2016.
45227.m: Trilogues are often criticised for a lack of transparency.

45228.q: What happens after a successful agreement in a trilogue?
a: Parliament and the Council must formally approve it
The law applies at once without a vote
The Court of Justice confirms it
45228.e: The provisional agreement is then endorsed in Coreper and in the responsible parliamentary committee, and afterwards formally adopted by the plenary and the Council.
45228.m: A trilogue agreement must be formally confirmed by Parliament and the Council.

45229.q: Why are trilogues especially often held at the first reading?
a: To adopt laws faster, without a second reading
Because the first reading is secret
Because the Commission then has no say
Because the Council must then decide unanimously
45229.e: Thanks to trilogues, most laws are now adopted at the first reading, which shortens the procedure a lot.
45229.m: Trilogues allow quick agreements at the first reading.

45230.q: What is the working document in a trilogue called that shows the bodies' positions side by side in columns?
45230.e: The four-column document shows the Commission proposal, the positions of Parliament and the Council, and a column for the compromise text.
45230.m: In a trilogue people work with a four-column document.

45231.q: Which person in the European Parliament leads on a legislative file and helps negotiate it in the trilogue?
a: The rapporteur of the responsible committee
The President of the European Council
45231.e: The rapporteur drafts the committee's report and negotiates in the trilogue together with the committee chair and the shadow rapporteurs of the other political groups.
45231.m: In a trilogue, the main voice for Parliament is the responsible rapporteur.

45232.q: Who represents the Council of the EU in trilogues?
a: The President of the Court of Justice
45232.e: The Council is represented by the current presidency country, usually by its Permanent Representative or deputy, on the basis of a mandate from Coreper.
45232.m: In a trilogue the Council presidency represents the member states.

45233.q: How often do European elections take place?
45233.e: The European Parliament's term is five years; the last election took place in June 2024.
45233.m: European elections take place every five years.

45234.q: Which country has the most seats in the European Parliament?
45234.e: Seats are roughly based on population. As the EU country with the largest population, Germany has the maximum of 96 seats.
45234.m: As the largest EU country, Germany has the most seats in the European Parliament.

45235.q: What does the principle of “degressive proportionality” mean for the allocation of seats in the European Parliament?
a: Small states have more seats per inhabitant than large ones
All states have the same number of seats
Seats depend only on economic strength
Large states have more seats per inhabitant
45235.e: An MEP from Malta represents far fewer people than one from Germany, so that small countries are also properly represented.
45235.m: In European elections, small states have more seats per inhabitant.

45236.q: Which voting system must all member states use in European elections?
45236.e: Since 2002 the Electoral Act has required proportional representation in all states; details such as thresholds are set by the states themselves.
45236.m: European elections use proportional representation in all states.

45237.q: From what age could people in Germany vote in the 2024 European elections for the first time?
45237.e: Germany lowered the voting age for the 2024 European elections from 18 to 16. Each member state sets the minimum age for European elections itself.
45237.m: In Germany, people could vote from 16 in the 2024 European elections.

45238.q: Roughly what was the EU-wide turnout in the 2024 European elections?
45238.e: According to the results published by the European Parliament, EU-wide turnout in 2024 was about 51%, similar to 2019.
45238.m: Turnout in the 2024 European elections was about half.

45239.q: Which political group became the largest in the European Parliament in the 2024 elections?
45239.e: The Christian Democratic EPP won the most seats in 2024, ahead of the Social Democrats.
45239.m: The EPP became the largest group in the 2024 European elections.

45240.q: What does the lead candidate principle (Spitzenkandidat) in European elections say?
a: The lead candidate of the strongest party should become Commission President
The Council President is directly elected
The strongest party provides the ECB President
45240.e: The European parties nominate lead candidates before the election; under the principle, the candidate of the most successful party family should become President of the Commission.
45240.m: Under the lead candidate principle, the election winner should lead the Commission.

45241.q: Who in 2014 became the first President of the European Commission under the lead candidate principle?
45241.e: Jean-Claude Juncker from Luxembourg was lead candidate of the EPP, which became the largest force in 2014; he led the Commission from 2014 to 2019.
45241.m: In 2014 Jean-Claude Juncker became the first lead candidate to become Commission President.

45242.q: Who was the EPP's lead candidate in 2019 but did not become Commission President?
45242.e: Although the EPP became the largest force in 2019, Manfred Weber did not find a majority in the European Council. Instead, Ursula von der Leyen, who had not been a lead candidate, was proposed.
45242.m: Manfred Weber failed in 2019 despite the EPP's election win.

45243.q: According to the EU Treaty, what must the European Council take into account when proposing someone for Commission President?
a: The result of the European elections
The views of the national central banks
An opinion from the Court of Justice
45243.e: The EU Treaty requires the European Council to take the election result into account. But there is no automatic rule that the lead candidate of the strongest party is chosen.
45243.m: The treaties only require the election result to be taken into account.

45244.q: How is the Commission President elected after the European Council's proposal?
a: By the European Parliament, with a majority of its members
Unanimously by the Council of the EU
By the Court of Justice of the EU
45244.e: The European Council proposes a person by qualified majority; Parliament elects them with a majority of its members.
45244.m: The European Parliament elects the Commission President.

45245.q: Who was the EPP's lead candidate in the 2024 European elections?
45245.e: Ursula von der Leyen stood as the EPP's lead candidate in 2024 and was elected by Parliament for a second term in July 2024.
45245.m: Ursula von der Leyen was the EPP's lead candidate in 2024.

45246.q: Which body pushed the lead candidate principle especially hard in 2014?
a: The Court of Justice of the EU
45246.e: Parliament wanted to increase its influence on the choice of Commission President and make European elections more personal and exciting.
45246.m: The European Parliament campaigned for lead candidates.

45247.q: Which EU office did Martin Schulz hold when he was the Social Democrats' lead candidate in 2014?
45247.e: Martin Schulz was President of the European Parliament from 2012 to 2017 and stood in 2014 as lead candidate of the European Social Democrats.
45247.m: Martin Schulz stood in the 2014 European elections as President of Parliament.

45248.q: Which treaty created today's office of High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy?
45248.e: The Treaty of Lisbon (2009) combined the former office of High Representative for the CFSP with that of the Commissioner for External Relations.
45248.m: Today's office of High Representative comes from the Treaty of Lisbon.

45249.q: Who is the EU's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy (as of 2026)?
45249.e: The former Estonian Prime Minister Kaja Kallas took office on 1 December 2024, together with the second von der Leyen Commission.
45249.m: Kaja Kallas has been the EU's High Representative since December 2024.

45250.q: Which second role does the High Representative hold at the same time?
a: Judge at the Court of Justice
45250.e: The High Representative is also Vice-President of the Commission; this is why people speak of the “double hat”.
45250.m: The High Representative is also Vice-President of the Commission.

45251.q: Which diplomatic service reports to the High Representative?
a: The General Secretariat of the Council of Europe
45251.e: The EEAS began its work in 2011 and runs more than 140 EU delegations worldwide, including one in Bern.
45251.m: The European External Action Service is the EU's diplomatic service.

45252.q: Who was the first High Representative after the Treaty of Lisbon?
45252.e: The British politician Catherine Ashton held the office from 2009 to 2014. Before that she had been EU Trade Commissioner.
45252.m: Catherine Ashton was the first High Representative after Lisbon, in 2009.

45253.q: Who held the forerunner office of High Representative for the CFSP from 1999 to 2009?
45253.e: The Spaniard Javier Solana, previously NATO Secretary General, was High Representative for the Common Foreign and Security Policy for ten years.
45253.m: Javier Solana was the first High Representative for the CFSP.

45254.q: Who appoints the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy?
a: The European Council by qualified majority, with the Commission President's agreement
The people in a direct election
The Court of Justice of the EU
The Council of the EU unanimously, with no further approval
45254.e: Under Article 18 TEU the European Council appoints the High Representative; as a member of the Commission, the person must also be confirmed by Parliament together with the Commission.
45254.m: The European Council appoints the EU's High Representative.

45255.q: Who was the EU's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy from 2019 to 2024?
45255.e: The Spaniard Josep Borrell held the office from December 2019 to November 2024; before that he had been President of the European Parliament.
45255.m: Josep Borrell was the High Representative from 2019 to 2024.

45256.q: What are the reports called in which the European Court of Auditors examines particular policy areas or programmes in depth?
45256.e: Besides the annual report, the Court of Auditors publishes many special reports every year, for example on farm subsidies or coronavirus aid.
45256.m: The Court of Auditors publishes in-depth audits in special reports.

45257.q: What happens if Parliament and the Council already agree at the first reading?
a: The Court of Justice must approve it
There is a referendum in all states
45257.e: If the Council approves Parliament's first-reading position, the act is adopted. Many EU laws are passed this way today.
45257.m: If there is agreement at the first reading, an EU law is adopted.

45258.q: Which country is one of the states with the fewest seats in the European Parliament?
45258.e: Small states such as Malta, Luxembourg and Cyprus have six seats each, the guaranteed minimum. Per inhabitant, however, they are better represented than large states.
45258.m: The smallest EU states, such as Malta, have six seats each in the European Parliament.

45259.q: What did Robert Schuman propose on 9 May 1950?
a: Managing French and German coal and steel jointly
A joint army of all Western Europeans
45259.e: The declaration was read out in the Clock Room of the French Foreign Ministry in Paris. It led in 1951 to the European Coal and Steel Community.
45259.m: In 1950 Schuman proposed joint management of coal and steel.

45260.q: What was the ECSC's supranational executive body called?
45260.e: The High Authority could take decisions binding on the member states. This made it the first supranational body in Europe and a forerunner of the Commission.
45260.m: The High Authority was the first supranational body of European integration.

45261.q: Which present-day EU body goes back to the ECSC's Common Assembly?
45261.e: The Common Assembly was made up of members of the national parliaments. It developed into the European Parliament, which has been directly elected since 1979.
45261.m: The European Parliament has its roots in the Common Assembly of the Coal and Steel Community.

45262.q: Which ECSC court was the forerunner of today's Court of Justice of the EU?
a: ECSC Court of Justice in Luxembourg
International Court of Justice in The Hague
Permanent Court of Arbitration in Geneva
45262.e: The ECSC got its own Court of Justice in Luxembourg in 1952. In 1958 it became the joint Court of Justice of the three Communities.
45262.m: Even the Coal and Steel Community had its own court in Luxembourg.

45263.q: Which two Communities were founded in 1957 by the Treaties of Rome?
45263.e: On 25 March 1957 the six founding states signed the treaties on the European Economic Community and the European Atomic Energy Community on the Capitoline Hill in Rome. The ECSC had existed since 1952.
45263.m: The Treaties of Rome created the EEC and Euratom.

45264.q: What did the EEC complete in 1968 by abolishing customs duties between its members?
45264.e: From 1 July 1968, customs duties between the six states disappeared, and a common external tariff applied to other countries.
45264.m: The EEC customs union was completed in 1968.

45265.q: How many states founded the European Economic Community in 1957?
45265.e: Belgium, Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands had already formed the Coal and Steel Community. The 1955 Messina conference prepared the Treaties of Rome.

45266.q: In the Maastricht three-pillar model, what was the second pillar?
a: Cooperation in Justice and Home Affairs
45266.e: The first pillar was the European Communities, the second the CFSP, the third cooperation in justice and home affairs. The second and third pillars were organised between governments.
45266.m: Foreign and security policy was the EU's second pillar after Maastricht.

45267.q: What was the European Economic Community renamed by the Maastricht Treaty?
45267.e: Maastricht dropped the word “Economic” from the name, because the Community now covered other policy areas too. The EEC became the EC.
45267.m: Since Maastricht, the EEC has simply been called the European Community.

45268.q: In which country is the city that gave its name to the 1997 EU treaty which brought Schengen into EU law?
45268.e: The Treaty of Amsterdam was signed in 1997 and came into force in 1999. Among other things, it brought the Schengen agreements into the EU's legal framework.
45268.m: The Treaty of Amsterdam came into force in 1999.

45269.q: Which set of rules on open internal borders, previously agreed between governments, was brought into EU law by the Treaty of Amsterdam?
a: The Dublin agreement on double taxation
45269.e: The Schengen agreements had come about outside the treaties. Amsterdam brought them into the EU's legal framework.
45269.m: With Amsterdam, Schengen became part of EU law.

45270.q: Who was the first High Representative for the Common Foreign and Security Policy, an office created by the Amsterdam Treaty?
45270.e: The Spanish politician and former NATO Secretary General Javier Solana held the office from 1999 to 2009.
45270.m: Javier Solana was the EU's first High Representative for foreign policy.

45271.q: Which EU body gained particular influence from the extension of the co-decision procedure in the Treaty of Amsterdam?
45271.e: Amsterdam extended co-decision to many areas and simplified it. This put Parliament on an equal footing with the Council on many legislative questions.
45271.m: The Treaty of Amsterdam strengthened the European Parliament as co-legislator.

45272.q: Which new chapter was added to the EC Treaty by the Treaty of Amsterdam in view of high unemployment?
45272.e: The member states committed themselves to coordinating their employment policies. This gave rise to the European Employment Strategy.
45272.m: With Amsterdam, employment became a shared concern of the EU.

45273.q: Since the Treaty of Amsterdam, which tool has allowed a group of member states to move ahead in one area without the others?
45273.e: Enhanced cooperation allows a multi-speed Europe within the framework of the treaties. It was later used, for example, for the EU patent.
45273.m: Thanks to enhanced cooperation, some states can move ahead within the EU.

45274.q: Which option did the Treaty of Amsterdam introduce against member states that seriously and persistently breach basic values such as democracy?
a: Suspending certain rights, such as voting rights in the Council
Cutting the number of its MEPs
45274.e: The procedure under Article 7 of the EU Treaty allows a state to be stripped of rights for a serious breach of the basic values. Expulsion is not provided for.
45274.m: Article 7 can strip states that breach the basic values of their voting rights.

45275.q: What was the main aim of the Treaty of Nice?
a: To prepare the institutions for the big enlargement
To regulate a member state's withdrawal
To dissolve the Coal and Steel Community
45275.e: With many Central and Eastern European states joining, the way the institutions worked had to be adapted. Nice mainly reorganised the weighting of votes and the size of the Commission.
45275.m: The Treaty of Nice was meant to get the EU ready for enlargement.

45276.q: Which EU treaty followed the Treaty of Amsterdam and came into force in 2003?
45276.e: The Treaty of Nice was signed in 2001 and came into force on 1 February 2003. It was later replaced by the Treaty of Lisbon.
45276.m: The Treaty of Nice has applied since 2003.

45277.q: Under the Treaty of Nice, what mainly determined how many votes a state had in the Council of the EU?
45277.e: Large states such as Germany and France got 29 votes each, little Malta only 3. Smaller states were favoured relative to their population.
45277.m: Under Nice, states with larger populations had more votes in the Council.

45278.q: Which two states, with 27 votes each in the Council under Nice, got almost as much weight as the largest states?
45278.e: Spain and Poland got 27 votes each, although they had far fewer inhabitants than Germany. This arrangement later became a point of dispute.
45278.m: Spain and Poland were heavily weighted in the Nice system.

45279.q: Which country rejected the Treaty of Nice in a first referendum in 2001?
45279.e: Irish voters said no in June 2001. After assurances on neutrality, they approved it in October 2002.
45279.m: Ireland only accepted the Treaty of Nice at the second attempt.

45280.q: Which document was solemnly proclaimed at the Nice summit in December 2000 but not yet made legally binding?
a: The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union
The European Convention on Human Rights
45280.e: The Charter of Fundamental Rights was drawn up by a convention and proclaimed in Nice. It only became legally binding some years later.
45280.m: The EU Charter of Fundamental Rights was proclaimed in Nice in 2000.

45281.q: Under the Treaty of Nice, what did the largest member states have to give up from the 2004 Barroso Commission onwards?
a: Their language as an official language
45281.e: Before that, the five largest states each had two commissioners. Since the Barroso Commission, which took office in November 2004, each member state has had one commissioner.
45281.m: Since Nice, each member state has only one commissioner.

45282.q: Which body drew up the draft of the EU Constitutional Treaty?
a: The European Convention under Valéry Giscard d'Estaing
The Council of Europe in Strasbourg
45282.e: The Convention met from 2002 to 2003 and was made up of representatives of governments, parliaments and EU bodies. It was chaired by the former French President Giscard d'Estaing.
45282.m: The draft constitution came from the European Convention under Giscard d'Estaing.

45283.q: When and where was the Treaty establishing a Constitution for Europe signed?
45283.e: The heads of state and government signed the treaty in Rome, in the same place as the founding treaties of 1957.
45283.m: The Constitutional Treaty was signed in Rome in 2004.

45284.q: Which two founding states rejected the Constitutional Treaty in referendums in 2005?
45284.e: France voted no on 29 May 2005 with about 55 per cent, the Netherlands on 1 June 2005 with about 62 per cent. This meant the treaty had failed.
45284.m: The no votes in France and the Netherlands sank the EU constitution in 2005.

45285.q: Which country was the first to approve the Constitutional Treaty in a referendum, in February 2005?
45285.e: In Spain, about three quarters of voters said yes on 20 February 2005, though turnout was low at about 42 per cent.
45285.m: Spain was the first country to say yes to the EU constitution in a referendum.

45286.q: Which title was planned in the Constitutional Treaty for the EU's top foreign representative?
a: President of the Foreign Affairs Council
45286.e: The state-like title “Union Minister for Foreign Affairs” was later dropped. The tasks were largely kept in the successor treaty under a different title.
45286.m: The title “Union Minister for Foreign Affairs” failed along with the Constitutional Treaty.

45287.q: What did the EU call the period after the failed constitutional referendums of 2005?
45287.e: In June 2005 the European Council decided on a period of reflection. Only in 2007 was a new reform project agreed, without the word constitution.
45287.m: After the constitution failed, the EU took a period of reflection.

45288.q: Which state-like symbols were to be written into the Constitutional Treaty but were left out of the successor treaty?
a: Coat of arms, crown and seal
45288.e: The Constitutional Treaty named the flag, anthem, motto, currency and Europe Day. To avoid the impression of a superstate, the symbols were left out of the later treaty text, but they are still used in everyday life.
45288.m: The EU symbols disappeared from the treaty text after the Constitutional Treaty.

45289.q: Who was elected as the first permanent President of the European Council, an office created by the Treaty of Lisbon?
45289.e: The Belgian politician Herman Van Rompuy held the office from 2009 to 2014. Before that, the chair rotated every six months with the Council presidency.
45289.m: Herman Van Rompuy was the first permanent President of the European Council.

45290.q: Which double majority has applied to the qualified majority in the Council since the Treaty of Lisbon?
a: 55 per cent of states and 65 per cent of the population
50 per cent of states and 50 per cent of the population
66 per cent of states and 75 per cent of the population
60 per cent of states and 60 per cent of the population
45290.e: The double majority system replaced the weighting of votes from 2014. A decision needs at least 55 per cent of member states, together representing at least 65 per cent of the EU population.
45290.m: The double majority requires 55 per cent of states and 65 per cent of the population.

45291.q: What has the former EC Treaty been called since the Treaty of Lisbon?
a: Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union
Treaty on the European Single Market
45291.e: Lisbon amended the existing treaties instead of replacing them. The EC Treaty became the TFEU, which together with the EU Treaty forms the basis of the EU.
45291.m: The TFEU is the renamed former EC Treaty.

45292.q: Which diplomatic service was built up on the basis of the Treaty of Lisbon?
45292.e: The European External Action Service began its work in 2011. It supports the High Representative and runs the EU delegations around the world, including in Bern.
45292.m: The European External Action Service is the EU's diplomatic corps.

45293.q: Since when did the euro exist as book money before the cash followed?
45293.e: On 1 January 1999 the exchange rates were fixed irrevocably, and the euro was introduced for transfers and financial markets.
45293.m: The euro was book money from 1999 and cash from 2002.

45294.q: How many states introduced euro cash on 1 January 2002?
45294.e: Greece joined the eleven founding states of the monetary union in 2001. So twelve states issued the new cash.
45294.m: Twelve states started with euro cash in 2002.

45295.q: After the euro was introduced in Germany, how did people roughly convert Deutschmark prices into euros?
a: Not at all, 1 Deutschmark was 1 euro
45295.e: The fixed rate was 1.95583 Deutschmarks to one euro. In everyday life people therefore halved Deutschmark prices to estimate the euro price.
45295.m: One euro was worth just under 2 Deutschmarks.

45296.q: What do the euro banknotes show as their designs?
a: Imaginary windows, gateways and bridges in different architectural styles
Famous people from all member states
Real landmarks such as the Eiffel Tower
45296.e: The designs stand for openness and connection. Invented buildings were chosen on purpose so that no country would be favoured.
45296.m: The euro notes show invented buildings from different periods.

45297.q: Which euro banknote has not been newly issued since 2019?
45297.e: The ECB stopped issuing the 500-euro note, partly because of concerns about its misuse for illegal money. Notes already issued remain legal tender.
45297.m: The 500-euro note has not been issued since 2019.

45298.q: Which of these small European states uses the euro on the basis of an agreement with the EU?
45298.e: Monaco, San Marino, the Vatican and Andorra may use the euro on the basis of agreements. Liechtenstein, by contrast, uses the Swiss franc.
45298.m: Monaco pays in euros, Liechtenstein in Swiss francs.

45299.q: Roughly how much money did the first aid package for Greece in May 2010 involve?
45299.e: The euro states and the IMF promised Greece loans of around 110 billion euros. In return, the country had to carry out strict austerity measures.
45299.m: The first Greek package of 2010 was worth around 110 billion euros.

45300.q: Which three institutions formed the so-called troika that monitored the aid programmes?
a: European Parliament, Council and Court of Justice
Eurogroup, BIS and Council of Europe
45300.e: The troika checked whether Greece and other programme countries were carrying out the agreed reforms. Payment of further loans depended on this.
45300.m: The troika was made up of the European Commission, the ECB and the International Monetary Fund.

45301.q: Which permanent rescue fund of the euro states was set up in 2012?
45301.e: The ESM replaced the temporary European Financial Stability Facility. It is based in Luxembourg and can grant loans to euro states in difficulty.
45301.m: The ESM is the permanent rescue fund of the eurozone.

45302.q: Which ECB President calmed the markets in July 2012 with the promise to do whatever was needed to save the euro?
45302.e: Mario Draghi said “whatever it takes” in London. After that, interest rates for crisis countries fell sharply, although the ECB at first hardly had to buy any bonds.
45302.m: Mario Draghi's “whatever it takes” is seen as a turning point in the euro crisis.

45303.q: How did the Greek people decide on the creditors' austerity conditions in the 2015 referendum?
a: The referendum was called off at short notice
45303.e: About 61 per cent voted no. A few days later, the government nevertheless accepted a third aid programme with tough conditions.
45303.m: Greece voted a clear no in the 2015 referendum but then accepted a new programme.

45304.q: Which measure did the Swiss National Bank take in September 2011 because of the franc's sharp rise during the euro crisis?
a: A minimum exchange rate of 1.20 francs per euro
Introducing the euro as a second currency
A fixed rate of 1 franc per euro
A ban on buying foreign currency
45304.e: Many investors fled into the franc, which rose strongly in value. The SNB defended the minimum rate of 1.20 francs until January 2015.
45304.m: In 2011 the SNB introduced a minimum euro rate of 1.20 francs.

45305.q: What was the one-billion-franc contribution called with which Switzerland supported the states that joined in 2004?
45305.e: In 2006 voters approved the law on cooperation with Eastern Europe on which the contribution is based. With it, Switzerland funded projects in the new member states to reduce economic differences.
45305.m: With the enlargement contribution, Switzerland supported the new EU states.

45306.q: In which Swiss city is the foundation set up by Jean Monnet, which keeps his archive, based?
45306.e: Monnet founded the Fondation Jean Monnet pour l'Europe in 1978 and handed his archives over to it. It is located on the campus of the University of Lausanne.
45306.m: Jean Monnet's archive is in Lausanne.

45307.q: In which year did the European Council set out the Copenhagen criteria?
45307.e: In June 1993, in Copenhagen, the European Council laid down the conditions that Central and Eastern European states must meet to join.
45307.m: The Copenhagen criteria have applied since 1993.

45308.q: Which of these is one of the political Copenhagen criteria?
a: Stable institutions guaranteeing democracy, the rule of law, human rights and protection of minorities
A budget deficit of at most 3 per cent
A population of at least one million
45308.e: Candidate countries must have a stable democratic order based on the rule of law. The protection of minorities is also expressly mentioned.
45308.m: Anyone who wants to join the EU must guarantee democracy and human rights.

45309.q: What does the economic Copenhagen criterion require?
a: A functioning market economy that can cope with competitive pressure in the single market
Its own currency with a fixed rate to the euro
A trade surplus with the EU
An unemployment rate below 5 per cent
45309.e: A candidate country's economy must be strong enough to keep up with the competition in the single market.
45309.m: Candidate countries need a competitive market economy.

45310.q: What is the whole body of EU law that a candidate country must take over called?
45310.e: The acquis includes the EU's treaties, laws, court rulings and agreements. Taking it over is the subject of the accession negotiations, which are divided into chapters.
45310.m: The acquis communautaire is the EU's shared body of law.

45311.q: Besides the requirements for candidates, which condition on the EU's own side did the Copenhagen Council name?
a: The EU's capacity to take in new members
A joint army of the member states
45311.e: The EU must be able to take in new members without losing the momentum of integration. This absorption capacity is often called the fourth criterion.
45311.m: The EU itself must also be ready for enlargement.

45312.q: With which country did the EU start accession negotiations in 2005 that are now practically frozen because of shortcomings in democracy and the rule of law?
45312.e: Turkey has been a candidate since 1999, and negotiations began in 2005. Because of backsliding on the political Copenhagen criteria, they have made no progress for years.
45312.m: Accession talks with Turkey are frozen because of the Copenhagen criteria.

45313.q: Who must agree to the admission of a new member to the EU?
45313.e: The Council of the EU must decide unanimously, and the consent of the European Parliament is also needed. After that, all member states must ratify the accession treaty.
45313.m: Every EU state can block a new accession.

45314.q: How long is the negotiating period under Article 50 if it is not extended?
45314.e: The treaties cease to apply two years after notice of withdrawal is given, even without an agreement. The European Council can extend the period unanimously in agreement with the state.
45314.m: Under Article 50, there are in principle two years for withdrawal negotiations.

45315.q: When did the United Kingdom become the first state to trigger the Article 50 procedure?
45315.e: Prime Minister Theresa May handed over the notice of withdrawal on 29 March 2017. Because of extensions, the procedure finally took almost three years.
45315.m: The UK triggered its withdrawal on 29 March 2017.

45316.q: What share of the vote was for leaving in the Brexit referendum of 23 June 2016?
45316.e: Just under 51.9 per cent voted “Leave”. In Scotland and Northern Ireland, however, there were majorities for remaining.
45316.m: The Brexit referendum narrowly favoured leaving, with about 52 per cent.

45317.q: On which date did the United Kingdom leave the EU?
45317.e: After several extensions, the withdrawal took effect on 31 January 2020. A transition period applied until the end of 2020.
45317.m: The UK has not been an EU member since 31 January 2020.

45318.q: What does Article 50 of the EU Treaty regulate?
a: The election of the European Parliament
45318.e: Article 50 was introduced in 2009 by the Treaty of Lisbon. The United Kingdom was the first state to use it, for Brexit.
45318.m: Article 50 is the EU's exit clause.

45319.q: Which procedure must a state that has left under Article 50 go through if it wants to become a member again?
a: The normal accession procedure under Article 49
A simple notification to the Council
A vote in the European Parliament alone
A judgment of the European Court of Justice
45319.e: Article 50(5) states that rejoining is treated like any other accession. So the state must meet all the conditions again.
45319.m: A state that has left must apply to join again in order to return.

45320.q: Which territory left the European Communities as early as 1985, long before Article 50 existed?
45320.e: As part of Denmark, Greenland belonged to the EC and voted to leave in 1982, mainly because of fisheries policy. Since 1985 it has been an associated overseas territory.
45320.m: Greenland left the EC as early as 1985.

45321.q: How did the Schuman Declaration describe the planned Coal and Steel Community with regard to Europe's future?
a: As a first step towards the European federation
As a replacement for the United Nations
As a temporary emergency solution for five years
As a military alliance against the East
45321.e: The declaration did not see the Coal and Steel Community as the final goal but as a first concrete step towards a European federation.
45321.m: Schuman saw the Coal and Steel Community as a first step towards a federal Europe.

45322.q: Which political movement did Robert Schuman belong to?
45322.e: Schuman was a member of the Christian Democratic Mouvement républicain populaire (MRP). Many of Europe's founding fathers, such as Adenauer and De Gasperi, came from this movement.
45322.m: Robert Schuman was a Christian Democratic politician.

45323.q: Which office did Robert Schuman hold when he presented his declaration in 1950?
a: President of the Coal and Steel Community
45323.e: Schuman was Foreign Minister from 1948 to early 1953, and briefly Prime Minister before that. He developed his plan together with Jean Monnet.
45323.m: In 1950 Schuman was France's Foreign Minister.

45324.q: Which award of the city of Aachen did Robert Schuman receive in 1958?
45324.e: The International Charlemagne Prize of Aachen honours services to European unity. Schuman received it in 1958 for his 1950 plan.
45324.m: Robert Schuman received the Aachen Charlemagne Prize in 1958.

45325.q: Which day in the EU marks the Schuman Declaration every year?
45325.e: 9 May recalls Schuman's 1950 proposal, which is regarded as the birth of European unity.
45325.m: 9 May is the EU's Europe Day.

45326.q: Which states founded the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951?
a: France, Germany, Italy and the Benelux countries
France, Germany, the UK and Italy
45326.e: The six founding states were France, the Federal Republic of Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. The UK only joined the Communities in 1973.
45326.m: The ECSC was founded by six states, including France and Germany.

45327.q: Which French Foreign Minister proposed founding the Coal and Steel Community in 1950?
45327.e: With the Schuman Declaration of 9 May 1950, Robert Schuman proposed managing coal and steel jointly. Jean Monnet had drawn up the plan but was not Foreign Minister.
45327.m: The 1950 Schuman Declaration is seen as the starting point of European unity.

45328.q: Why did France and Germany want to manage coal and steel jointly from 1951?
a: So that a new war between them would be impossible
Because neither country had any coal left
So that the USA would stop supplying steel
45328.e: Coal and steel were important for making weapons. Whoever controls them jointly cannot secretly arm against the other. In this way the ECSC replaced mistrust with cooperation.
45328.m: The ECSC was meant to prevent a new war between France and Germany.

45329.q: What did the 1956 Spaak Report, which prepared the Treaties of Rome, recommend?
45329.e: The committee under the Belgian Foreign Minister Paul-Henri Spaak recommended a common market and an atomic energy community. These became the EEC and Euratom in 1957.
45329.m: The Spaak Report proposed a common market.

45330.q: Which EEC body was meant to represent the common interest independently of governments and propose laws?
45330.e: The first Commission President, Walter Hallstein, shaped the Commission from 1958 to 1967 as a strong, independent body. To this day it has the right to propose EU laws.
45330.m: In the EU, the Commission proposes the laws.

45331.q: Which aim does the preamble of the 1957 EEC Treaty name?
a: To lay the foundations of an ever closer union among the peoples of Europe
To found a European federal state within ten years
To manage the member states' colonies jointly
To build a military alliance against the Soviet Union
45331.e: The phrase “ever closer union” can still be found in the EU Treaty today. It expresses that integration is an open-ended process.
45331.m: The Treaties of Rome aimed at an ever closer union of the peoples of Europe.

45332.q: Which advisory body for municipalities and regions was created by the Maastricht Treaty?
a: Congress of Local and Regional Authorities
45332.e: The Committee of the Regions gives representatives of regional and local authorities a voice in lawmaking. It began its work in 1994.
45332.m: The Committee of the Regions was created by the Maastricht Treaty.

45333.q: Which principle, under which the Community acts only if aims cannot be adequately achieved at a lower level, was laid down in Maastricht?
45333.e: The subsidiarity principle protects the powers of the member states and regions. It is also laid down in the Swiss Federal Constitution for the relationship between the Confederation and the cantons.
45333.m: Under the subsidiarity principle, the lowest possible level should decide.

45334.q: Which legal status for all nationals of the member states was introduced by the Maastricht Treaty?
a: European nationality instead of national nationality
European right of residence for non-EU countries
45334.e: Since Maastricht, anyone who is a national of a member state is also a citizen of the Union. Union citizenship adds to national citizenship but does not replace it, and gives, for example, the right to vote in local elections in the state of residence.
45334.m: Since Maastricht, Union citizenship has added to national citizenship.

45335.q: In which area, besides monetary union, did the United Kingdom get an exemption at Maastricht?
45335.e: The other eleven states agreed on a social protocol in which the UK did not take part. Only in 1997 did the country join the social policy.
45335.m: After Maastricht, the UK at first stayed out of the common social policy.

45336.q: Which office, which citizens can turn to over maladministration in the EU, was created by the Maastricht Treaty?
a: Advocate General at the Court of Justice
45336.e: The European Ombudsman investigates complaints about maladministration in the EU institutions. The Ombudsman is elected by the European Parliament.
45336.m: For maladministration in the EU, the European Ombudsman can help.

45337.q: Which new aim for home affairs and justice policy was set out in the Treaty of Amsterdam?
a: An area of freedom, security and justice
An area without taxes or charges
A single criminal code for all states
45337.e: Amsterdam moved asylum, immigration and visas into the Community area. The overall aim was described as an area of freedom, security and justice.
45337.m: Since Amsterdam, the EU has aimed for an area of freedom, security and justice.

45338.q: Why did the Treaty of Nice raise the maximum number of seats in the European Parliament?
a: Because many new member states were about to join
45338.e: With the eastern enlargement of 2004, ten new states joined. Nice therefore raised the ceiling to 732 seats. Later the number was adjusted several times.
45338.m: The Treaty of Nice enlarged Parliament for the enlargement.

45339.q: Which country approved the Constitutional Treaty in a referendum in July 2005, despite the no votes in France and the Netherlands?
45339.e: The people of Luxembourg approved the treaty on 10 July 2005 with about 57 per cent. Other countries postponed their planned votes.
45339.m: Luxembourg said yes to the EU constitution in 2005 despite the crisis.

45340.q: Which tool did national parliaments get with the Treaty of Lisbon to monitor compliance with subsidiarity?
a: The reasoned opinion in the early warning mechanism
A veto on every EU law
The right to remove EU judges
45340.e: If a third of national parliaments object, the Commission must review its proposal. This is called the “yellow card”.
45340.m: With a reasoned opinion, national parliaments can show the Commission the yellow card.

45341.q: Since the Treaty of Lisbon, what must the European Council take into account in its proposal for Commission President?
a: The result of the European Parliament elections
The view of the UN General Assembly
The order of the Council presidencies
45341.e: The European Council proposes a person, taking the election result into account. Parliament then elects them with a majority of its members.
45341.m: Since Lisbon, the European election result counts in choosing the Commission President.

45342.q: According to the European Commission, which letter inspired the euro sign?
45342.e: The epsilon refers to the cradle of European civilisation and to the first letter of the word Europe. The two horizontal lines are meant to represent stability.
45342.m: The euro sign is derived from the Greek epsilon.

45343.q: Which euro country asked the EU and the IMF for help in November 2010, mainly because of problems with its banks?
45343.e: The Irish state had rescued its banks after a property bubble burst and got into trouble as a result. It received an aid programme of around 85 billion euros.
45343.m: In 2010 Ireland needed a rescue because of its banking crisis.

45344.q: Which euro country, when it was rescued in 2013, also made bank customers with deposits over 100,000 euros share the losses?
45344.e: In the rescue of Cyprus, large bank deposits had to contribute to the costs for the first time. Deposits up to 100,000 euros stayed protected.
45344.m: In Cyprus in 2013, wealthy bank customers also had to contribute to the rescue.

45345.q: What happened in 2012 to Greek government bonds held by private creditors?
a: The creditors gave up about half
Greece repaid them in full early
The euro states took them over at full value
The ECB cancelled them with no loss for the creditors
45345.e: In the debt cut, private creditors gave up about 53.5 per cent of the face value of their bonds. It was the largest restructuring of a state's debt up to that time.
45345.m: In 2012 private creditors gave up about half of their claims on Greece.

45346.q: In which city was the accession treaty for the ten new member states signed on 16 April 2003?
45346.e: Greece held the Council presidency at the time. The signing took place with the Acropolis as a backdrop.
45346.m: The accession treaty for the big enlargement was signed in Athens in 2003.

45347.q: Which three existing EU states opened their labour markets straight away in 2004 to workers from the new member states?
45347.e: Most of the old members used transitional periods. Only the UK, Ireland and Sweden immediately granted largely free access to their labour markets.
45347.m: The UK, Ireland and Sweden opened their labour markets immediately in 2004.

45348.q: Until when did Germany and Austria restrict the free movement of workers from most of the states that joined in 2004?
45348.e: The accession treaties allowed transitional periods of at most seven years. Germany and Austria used them in full, until 1 May 2011.
45348.m: Germany and Austria used the full seven-year transitional period.

45349.q: How did Swiss voters decide in 2005 on extending the free movement of persons to the new EU states?
a: Approved with about 56 per cent yes
Rejected with about 56 per cent no
Approved with about 75 per cent yes
Rejected with just under 50.3 per cent no
45349.e: On 25 September 2005 the people approved extending the free movement agreement. This meant the bilateral approach also applied to the new member states.
45349.m: In 2005 Switzerland extended the free movement of persons to the new EU states.

45350.q: When were passport checks at the land borders with most of the states that joined in 2004 dropped?
45350.e: Nine of the ten states joined the Schengen area in December 2007, and at airports this followed in March 2008. Cyprus is not yet fully part of it.
45350.m: Most of the new EU states of 2004 became part of the Schengen area at the end of 2007.

45351.q: What is the French modernisation programme led by Jean Monnet from 1946 called?
45351.e: As head of the planning commission, Monnet drew up a plan to rebuild the French economy. It focused on coal, steel, energy and transport.
45351.m: The Monnet Plan was meant to modernise France after the war.

45352.q: Which proposal did Jean Monnet make in June 1940 to keep France in the war?
a: A union between France and Britain
45352.e: With British partners, Monnet drafted a Franco-British union with joint citizenship. Churchill agreed, but the French government refused and signed the armistice.
45352.m: In 1940 Monnet proposed a union between France and Britain.

45353.q: Which office did Jean Monnet hold in Geneva from 1920 to 1923?
a: Deputy Secretary-General of the League of Nations
President of the International Committee of the Red Cross
Director of the International Labour Organization
League of Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
45353.e: After the First World War, the young Monnet became Deputy Secretary-General of the newly founded League of Nations, based in Geneva. There he learned the limits of purely intergovernmental cooperation.
45353.m: Jean Monnet worked for the League of Nations in Geneva in the 1920s.

45354.q: Which project, partly shaped by Monnet, failed in the French National Assembly in 1954?
45354.e: The Defence Community went back to the Pleven Plan, which Monnet had suggested. After it failed, integration concentrated on the economy.
45354.m: The European Defence Community failed in 1954 because of France.

45355.q: Which Community emerged in 1951 from the Schuman Plan drafted by Jean Monnet?
45355.e: Monnet drafted the plan that the French Foreign Minister Robert Schuman presented in 1950. The Coal and Steel Community placed coal and steel under a joint authority, whose first President was Monnet.
45355.m: The Coal and Steel Community grew out of the Schuman Plan in 1951.

45356.q: What can the EU do if a member state seriously violates its basic values such as democracy and the rule of law?
a: Strip it of voting rights in the Council
Expel it from the EU at once
45356.e: The procedure under Article 7 of the EU Treaty can go as far as removing voting rights. The treaties do not provide for expulsion from the EU. Procedures have been brought against Poland and Hungary, for example.
45356.m: A state that violates the EU's basic values can lose voting rights.

45357.q: Who led the Brexit negotiations on the EU side?
45357.e: The Frenchman Michel Barnier was the European Commission's chief negotiator for the withdrawal and then for the trade agreement.
45357.m: Michel Barnier negotiated Brexit for the EU.

45358.q: What was the fallback arrangement in the first withdrawal agreement called, which was meant to prevent a hard border on the island of Ireland?
45358.e: The backstop would, if necessary, have kept the United Kingdom in a customs union with the EU. It was controversial and was replaced in 2019 by the Northern Ireland Protocol.
45358.m: The backstop was meant to prevent a hard border in Ireland.

45359.q: How many sectoral agreements make up the Bilateral Agreements I package?
45359.e: The Bilateral Agreements I consist of seven agreements, including the one on the free movement of persons. They were signed on 21 June 1999 and came into force in 2002.
45359.m: The Bilateral Agreements I consist of seven linked agreements.

45360.q: What does the public procurement agreement of the Bilateral Agreements I regulate?
a: Tenders for public contracts, including those of municipalities
45360.e: The agreement extends the rules of the World Trade Organization, for example to municipalities and railways. Swiss and EU companies can thus bid for each other's public contracts.
45360.m: The procurement agreement opens public contracts to companies from Switzerland and the EU.

45361.q: For which product has there been complete free trade between Switzerland and the EU since 2007, thanks to the agricultural agreement?
45361.e: Tariffs and quotas for cheese were removed step by step. Since 1 June 2007 the cheese trade has been fully liberalised.
45361.m: Since 2007 cheese can be traded duty-free between Switzerland and the EU.

45362.q: Which agreement is NOT part of the Bilateral Agreements I package?
45362.e: The taxation of savings agreement was only concluded with the Bilateral Agreements II. Land transport, air transport and research are part of the Bilateral Agreements I.
45362.m: Tax matters were only added with the Bilateral Agreements II.

45363.q: Under the land transport agreement, to what weight limit for lorries did Switzerland have to raise its previous 28-tonne limit step by step?
45363.e: In the land transport agreement Switzerland accepted the EU's 40-tonne limit. In return it was allowed to levy the distance-related heavy vehicle charge (LSVA).
45363.m: The land transport agreement allowed 40-tonne lorries in Switzerland.

45364.q: Which charge was Switzerland allowed to levy on heavy goods traffic thanks to the land transport agreement?
45364.e: Since 2001 the LSVA has been calculated according to weight and kilometres driven. Its revenue helps finance railway expansion such as the NRLA.
45364.m: The LSVA charges lorries according to weight and distance driven.

45365.q: Which vote result of 6 December 1992 led Switzerland to take the bilateral path with the EU?
45365.e: The people and the cantons narrowly rejected joining the European Economic Area. Afterwards Switzerland sought market access through individual sectoral treaties.
45365.m: After the EEA ‘no’ of 1992, Switzerland chose the bilateral path.

45366.q: In which city were the Bilateral Agreements II signed?
45366.e: The Bilateral Agreements II were signed in Luxembourg on 26 October 2004. They extended cooperation beyond economic interests, for example to security and asylum.
45366.m: The Bilateral Agreements II were signed in Luxembourg.

45367.q: With roughly what percentage of yes votes was association with Schengen and Dublin approved on 5 June 2005?
45367.e: A referendum was called against the Schengen and Dublin agreements. The people voted yes with 54.6 percent.
45367.m: The Schengen and Dublin agreements were approved in 2005 with just under 55 percent.

45368.q: From 2017, what procedure replaced the taxation of savings agreement of the Bilateral Agreements II?
45368.e: The taxation of savings agreement provided for a tax retention on interest income of EU citizens. It was replaced by an agreement on the automatic exchange of information (AEOI) on financial accounts.
45368.m: Since 2017 Switzerland has automatically exchanged account information with the EU.

45369.q: In which city is the European Environment Agency, which Switzerland joined with the Bilateral Agreements II, based?
45369.e: With the environment agreement of the Bilateral Agreements II, Switzerland joined the European Environment Agency in Copenhagen. It collects and compares environmental data from all over Europe.
45369.m: Switzerland supplies its environmental data to the European Environment Agency in Copenhagen.

45370.q: What does the pensions agreement of the Bilateral Agreements II regulate?
a: Double taxation of retired EU officials
The export of pension fund money
The retirement age for cross-border commuters
45370.e: Former EU officials who live in Switzerland should not have to pay tax twice on their pension. The EU already taxes these pensions at source.
45370.m: The pensions agreement prevents double taxation of retired EU officials.

45371.q: What cooperation does the anti-fraud agreement of the Bilateral Agreements II mainly regulate?
a: Administrative assistance on smuggling and indirect taxes
45371.e: The agreement improves cooperation against smuggling and fraud involving customs duties, VAT and subsidies. It mainly concerns indirect taxes.
45371.m: The anti-fraud agreement targets smuggling and fraud involving indirect taxes.

45372.q: Which area was promoted by the MEDIA agreement of the Bilateral Agreements II?
45372.e: Through the MEDIA programme, Swiss filmmakers gained access to EU funding for development and distribution. From 2014 Switzerland was no longer involved.
45372.m: The MEDIA programme supports European films and audiovisual works.

45373.q: Which existing agreement would NOT have been covered by the Institutional Framework Agreement?
45373.e: The framework agreement was to apply to five market access agreements, including free movement of persons, land and air transport. Schengen and Dublin have their own rules on adopting law.
45373.m: The framework agreement only concerned the agreements on access to the EU single market.

45374.q: Which point of dispute in the framework agreement involved, among other things, state guarantees for cantonal banks?
45374.e: The EU wanted rules against state aid that distorts competition. In Switzerland people feared consequences for cantonal banks or cantonal energy companies.
45374.m: State aid was a particularly sensitive issue for the cantons in the framework agreement.

45375.q: Which EU directive was one of the three main points of dispute in the framework agreement?
45375.e: The Citizens' Rights Directive regulates, among other things, the residence of EU citizens and their access to social benefits. Switzerland feared higher social assistance costs.
45375.m: The Citizens' Rights Directive was one of the sticking points of the framework agreement.

45376.q: According to the framework agreement, which court was to give binding rulings in disputes over the interpretation of EU law?
45376.e: Disputes were to go before an arbitration tribunal. If the interpretation of EU law was at stake, it would have had to refer the matter to the European Court of Justice (ECJ).
45376.m: The role of the ECJ was a controversial part of the framework agreement.

45377.q: Which principle of adopting law did the framework agreement provide for the single market agreements?
a: Automatic adoption of law without a referendum
45377.e: Switzerland would have had to adopt developments in EU law in the areas concerned, but using its own democratic procedures such as the referendum.
45377.m: With dynamic adoption of law, Switzerland continuously adapts agreements to new EU law.

45378.q: Which industry felt a direct consequence right after the breakdown in 2021, because the EU no longer updated the Mutual Recognition Agreement (MRA)?
45378.e: From the end of May 2021, Swiss medical devices were treated as third-country products in the EU. Manufacturers needed additional authorised representatives in the EU.
45378.m: After the framework agreement collapsed, medical technology lost its easier market access.

45379.q: Which President of the Swiss Confederation met Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels in April 2021 for talks on the framework agreement?
45379.e: Guy Parmelin was President of the Confederation in 2021 and travelled to Brussels on 23 April 2021. The meeting brought no breakthrough.
45379.m: The summit in April 2021 could not save the framework agreement.

45380.q: In which city is the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), in which Switzerland is to take part under the Switzerland-EU package, based?
45380.e: The food safety agreement creates a common food safety area covering the whole food chain. This includes taking part in EFSA, which is based in Parma.
45380.m: The food safety agreement links Switzerland to EFSA in Parma.

45381.q: Which top EU politician announced the conclusion of negotiations together with Viola Amherd in Bern in December 2024?
45381.e: The President of the European Commission travelled to Bern for this. The Commission conducts negotiations with third countries on behalf of the EU.
45381.m: The European Commission negotiates with Switzerland on behalf of the EU.

45382.q: How are the institutional questions dealt with in the Switzerland-EU package, unlike in the failed framework agreement?
a: Separately in each single market agreement
In an additional declaration by the Federal Council
Not at all, they were dropped
45382.e: Adoption of law, dispute settlement and monitoring are built directly into the individual single market agreements. This is known as the vertical approach.
45382.m: In the Switzerland-EU package, the institutional rules are built into each single market agreement.

45383.q: Besides electricity and food safety, which new agreement is part of the Switzerland-EU package?
45383.e: The health agreement allows closer cooperation on cross-border health threats such as pandemics. It gives Switzerland access to the relevant EU bodies.
45383.m: The health agreement strengthens cooperation against cross-border health threats.

45384.q: Under the Switzerland-EU package, what may the EU do if Switzerland does not adopt a development in EU law?
a: Impose sanctions on the Swiss franc
45384.e: Switzerland keeps the right to reject adoption, for example by referendum. The EU can then take compensatory measures, whose proportionality can be reviewed by an arbitration tribunal.
45384.m: If Switzerland rejects new EU law, only proportionate compensatory measures are allowed.

45385.q: In the Switzerland-EU package, which body decides on disputes if the Joint Committee cannot agree?
45385.e: An arbitration tribunal with equal representation from both sides decides the dispute. If the interpretation of EU law is involved, it obtains an interpretation from the European Court of Justice.
45385.m: Disputes in the Switzerland-EU package are decided by a joint arbitration tribunal.

45386.q: Which EU education programme is Switzerland planned to take part in again from 2027?
45386.e: Since 2014 Switzerland had only been a partner country in Erasmus+ and financed its own replacement scheme. The package provides for association from 2027.
45386.m: From 2027 Swiss students should again be able to take full part in Erasmus+.

45387.q: In which year did the Federal Council open the consultation on the Switzerland-EU package?
45387.e: The Federal Council opened the consultation in June 2025 and it lasted until the end of October 2025. Parties, cantons and associations could give their views.
45387.m: The consultation on the Bilateral Agreements III took place in 2025.

45388.q: What was dropped at Switzerland's land borders in 2008 when it joined the Schengen area?
a: The obligation to carry an identity document
45388.e: Since 12 December 2008 Switzerland has applied Schengen at its land borders. People are now only checked at random, but goods are still checked by customs.
45388.m: Since 2008 there have been no systematic checks on persons at Switzerland's land borders.

45389.q: What did Swiss airports have to set up for Schengen in 2009?
a: Separate areas for Schengen and other flights
Their own runways for planes from the EU
A second security check for every flight
45389.e: On flights within the Schengen area there is no longer a systematic passport check, but on other flights there is. That is why airports separated the passenger flows; Schengen has applied there too since March 2009.
45389.m: At airports, Schengen and non-Schengen flights are kept separate.

45390.q: Which checks still take place at the Swiss border despite Schengen, because Switzerland is not part of the EU customs union?
45390.e: Schengen only concerns the movement of people. As Switzerland has its own customs duties, the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security continues to check goods.
45390.m: Schengen removes checks on persons, but not Swiss customs checks.

45391.q: What is the shared wanted-persons database of the Schengen states, to which the Swiss police are also connected, called?
45391.e: The Schengen Information System (SIS) lists wanted persons, missing people and stolen items. It makes up for the removal of systematic border checks.
45391.m: The SIS allows the police to search for people across Europe.

45392.q: What is the system called that, since October 2025, biometrically records entries and exits of third-country nationals at the Schengen external borders?
45392.e: The Entry/Exit System (EES) is gradually replacing the stamping of passports. It records facial images and fingerprints, also at Swiss airports.
45392.m: The EES digitally records travellers from third countries at the Schengen external borders.

45393.q: Which development of Schengen law did voters approve on 19 May 2019 with about 64 percent yes?
45393.e: Adopting the stricter EU Firearms Directive was approved with 63.7 percent yes. A ‘no’ could have put the Schengen association at risk.
45393.m: In 2019 Switzerland adopted the stricter EU Firearms Directive.

45394.q: Which EU agency was the subject of the proposal approved on 15 May 2022 with about 72 percent yes?
45394.e: As a Schengen state, Switzerland takes part in the European Border and Coast Guard Agency. The people approved the higher Swiss contribution with 71.5 percent.
45394.m: As a Schengen state, Switzerland takes part in Frontex.

45395.q: Which neighbouring country of Switzerland only joined the Schengen area in December 2011?
45395.e: Liechtenstein became an operational part of Schengen on 19 December 2011. Until then there were special arrangements at the border with Switzerland.
45395.m: Liechtenstein has been part of the Schengen area since 2011.

45396.q: What does the Dublin system mainly regulate?
a: Which state examines an asylum application
45396.e: The Dublin rules determine which state is responsible for examining an asylum application. This is meant to ensure each application is examined only once.
45396.m: Dublin determines which state must deal with an asylum application.

45397.q: What does the so-called sovereignty clause in the Dublin system allow?
a: To examine an application voluntarily itself
To reject asylum seekers without examination
To force another state to take over
45397.e: A state can examine an asylum application even though another state would actually be responsible under Dublin. This happens, for example, for humanitarian reasons.
45397.m: With the sovereignty clause, a state can voluntarily take on an asylum application.

45398.q: Which problem is the Dublin system meant to prevent?
a: Multiple asylum applications in several states
Customs fraud at the external borders
45398.e: Without Dublin, asylum seekers could submit applications in several countries one after another. The system sets a single responsibility.
45398.m: Dublin is meant to prevent asylum seekers from applying in several states.

a: Return to the responsible Dublin state
Deportation to the country of origin
Removal to a safe third country outside Europe
45399.e: If another Dublin state is responsible, Switzerland transfers the person there. The asylum application is then examined on its merits in that state.
45399.m: In a Dublin transfer, a person is handed over to the responsible European state.

45400.q: Which criterion takes priority over the place of first entry when determining Dublin responsibility?
a: Family members in a Dublin state
The language of the asylum seeker
The wish of the asylum seeker
The economic strength of the state
45400.e: The Dublin criteria have an order of priority. Family unity, especially for unaccompanied minors, comes before first entry.
45400.m: In Dublin, family unity takes priority over the place of first entry.

45401.q: Which regulation from 2013 long formed the basis of the Dublin system?
45401.e: The Dublin III Regulation of 2013 replaced the Dublin II Regulation of 2003. Switzerland adopted it as a development of the Dublin acquis.
45401.m: The Dublin III Regulation dates from 2013.

45402.q: Which group of states is associated with Dublin as non-EU states, alongside Switzerland?
a: Monaco, San Marino and the Vatican
45402.e: Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland are Dublin states without EU membership. They are also associated with Schengen.
45402.m: Four non-EU states apply the Dublin rules.

45403.q: How did voters decide in 2006 on the Eastern Europe Cooperation Act, the basis for the Swiss enlargement contribution?
45403.e: A referendum was called against the law. On 26 November 2006, 53.4 percent voted yes.
45403.m: In 2006 voters narrowly said yes to aid for Eastern Europe.

45404.q: How large was Switzerland's first enlargement contribution for new EU member states in total?
45404.e: At first 1 billion francs was planned for the ten states that joined in 2004. With contributions for Bulgaria, Romania and Croatia, the total came to about 1.3 billion francs.
45404.m: Switzerland's first enlargement contribution amounted to about 1.3 billion francs.

45405.q: Which country received the largest share of Switzerland's first enlargement contribution?
45405.e: As the most populous new member, Poland was the largest recipient. Projects in transport, the environment and research, for example, were supported.
45405.m: Poland was the largest recipient of the Swiss enlargement contribution.

45406.q: Which two federal agencies jointly implement the Swiss contribution to selected EU states?
45406.e: The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC) and the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) manage the projects. The State Secretariat for Migration is involved in the migration part.
45406.m: SDC and SECO implement the Swiss contribution in the partner countries.

45407.q: How has the money from the Swiss contribution reached the recipients so far?
a: Through projects in the partner countries
As a payment to the European Commission
45407.e: Switzerland funds specific projects that it agrees with the partner countries. It does not pay the contribution into the EU budget.
45407.m: The Swiss contribution funds specific projects rather than the EU budget.

45408.q: Under the Switzerland-EU package, for periods of how many years is the Swiss cohesion contribution set each time?
45408.e: The periods match the EU's multiannual financial framework, which lasts seven years each time. This makes the contribution legally binding and predictable for the first time.
45408.m: The cohesion contribution is set in step with the EU's seven-year financial framework.

45409.q: Under the Switzerland-EU package, how much is Switzerland to pay each year as a cohesion contribution in the period 2030 to 2036?
45409.e: The package regulates the contribution in a legally binding way for the first time. For the years 2030 to 2036, 350 million francs per year are planned.
45409.m: From 2030 a cohesion contribution of 350 million francs per year is planned.

45410.q: Who can trigger the guillotine clause of the Bilateral Agreements I by terminating an agreement?
a: Only the European Court of Justice
Only a single EU member state
45410.e: Each contracting party can terminate an agreement. So both Switzerland and the EU could trigger the clause.
45410.m: Both contracting parties can trigger the guillotine clause.

45411.q: Under the guillotine clause, how long after one agreement of the Bilateral Agreements I is terminated do the other agreements also cease to apply?
45411.e: The other agreements cease to apply six months after the notice of termination is received. This leaves little time for new negotiations.
45411.m: The guillotine clause takes effect six months after a termination.

45412.q: Which EU interest was the main reason for the guillotine clause?
a: Not letting free movement of persons be separated
Tying the Swiss franc to the euro
Bringing Switzerland into the customs union
45412.e: The EU wanted to prevent Switzerland from keeping only the agreements that benefited it. Above all, free movement of persons was to be inseparably linked to market access.
45412.m: The guillotine clause ties market access to free movement of persons.

45413.q: Where does the name ‘guillotine clause’ come from?
a: From the blade used for executions
45413.e: The guillotine was a falling blade often used during the French Revolution. The image stands for all agreements falling away at one stroke.
45413.m: The name of the clause recalls the blade that cuts everything off at once.

45414.q: Does the guillotine clause also apply to the 1972 free trade agreement between Switzerland and the EEC?
a: No, it is independent of it
Yes, it would also fall away
Yes, but only after five years
45414.e: The guillotine clause only links the agreements of the Bilateral Agreements I. The 1972 free trade agreement for industrial goods would remain in place after a termination.
45414.m: The 1972 free trade agreement is not linked to the Bilateral Agreements I.

45415.q: Which two agreements of the Bilateral Agreements II are also legally linked to each other?
45415.e: The association agreements on Schengen and Dublin depend on each other. If one ends, the other ends too.
45415.m: For Switzerland, Schengen and Dublin only come together.

45416.q: Which agreement of the Bilateral Agreements I would also have fallen away because of the guillotine clause if the Limitation Initiative had been implemented in 2020?
45416.e: The initiative demanded an end to free movement of persons. Through the guillotine clause, agreements such as the one on air transport would also have lapsed.
45416.m: If free movement had ended, the guillotine clause would also have affected air transport.

45417.q: Which group in Switzerland campaigned particularly strongly for the flanking measures?
45417.e: The trade unions made their support for free movement of persons depend on effective wage protection. The EU, on the other hand, criticised some measures as barriers to trade.
45417.m: The trade unions are seen as the main defenders of the flanking measures.

45418.q: What are the flanking measures mainly meant to protect against?
45418.e: They are meant to prevent the wages and working conditions usual in Switzerland from being undercut. To this end there are checks, and breaches are penalised.
45418.m: The flanking measures protect Swiss wages from being undercut.

45419.q: Which law obliges foreign companies that send workers to Switzerland to observe minimum pay and working conditions?
45419.e: The Posted Workers Act applies to companies from abroad that temporarily deploy staff in Switzerland. It is a core element of the flanking measures.
45419.m: The Posted Workers Act also applies to companies that send staff to Switzerland from abroad.

45420.q: Under the previous rule, how far in advance did foreign companies have to report an assignment in Switzerland?
45420.e: The so-called eight-day rule gives the authorities time for checks. The EU criticised it as an obstacle to the free movement of services.
45420.m: The eight-day rule was a point of dispute with the EU.

45421.q: Who is represented on the tripartite commissions of the flanking measures?
45421.e: Tripartite means in three parts: authorities, employer and employee representatives work together. They monitor the labour market in sectors without a generally binding collective labour agreement.
45421.m: The state, employers and employees sit together on the tripartite commissions.

45422.q: Who checks compliance with collective labour agreements that have been declared generally binding?
45422.e: Joint commissions consist of equal numbers of employer and employee representatives from a sector. They check businesses for breaches of the collective labour agreement.
45422.m: Joint commissions monitor the collective labour agreements in their sector.

45423.q: Which instrument can authorities issue in the case of repeated wage dumping in a sector without a collective labour agreement?
a: Standard employment contract with minimum wages
45423.e: If the tripartite commissions find repeated abuses, a standard employment contract with mandatory minimum wages can be issued. It then applies to the whole sector.
45423.m: A standard employment contract can set minimum wages in sectors without a collective labour agreement.

45424.q: Which period does the EU research framework programme Horizon Europe cover?
45424.e: Horizon Europe followed Horizon 2020 and runs for seven years. It funds research and innovation across Europe.

45425.q: Roughly how large is the budget of Horizon Europe?
45425.e: Horizon Europe has about 95.5 billion euros, considerably more than Horizon 2020 with about 77 billion euros. This makes it one of the largest research funding programmes in the world.
45425.m: With about 95 billion euros, Horizon Europe is one of the largest research programmes in the world.

45426.q: Which EU research programme was the direct predecessor of Horizon Europe?
45426.e: Horizon 2020 ran from 2014 to 2020. Horizon Europe, the EU's ninth research framework programme, is its successor.
45426.m: Horizon 2020 was followed by Horizon Europe.

45427.q: From which date does Switzerland's association with Horizon Europe apply retroactively?
45427.e: The agreement was signed on 10 November 2025 and applies retroactively from 1 January 2025. Swiss researchers could therefore already apply for calls in 2025.
45427.m: Switzerland is again associated with Horizon Europe retroactively from 2025.

45428.q: Which programme is part of the association agreement signed in 2025, together with Horizon Europe?
