45428.e: The agreement covers Horizon Europe, the Euratom programme for research and training, and Digital Europe. Euratom concerns nuclear and fusion research.
45428.m: Besides Horizon Europe, Switzerland is also associated with Euratom and Digital Europe.

45429.q: Which federal office financed transitional measures for Swiss researchers while Switzerland was not associated?
a: State Secretariat for Education, Research and Innovation
45429.e: SERI funded successful Swiss projects directly when no EU money was flowing. In some cases the Swiss National Science Foundation also stepped in with replacement programmes.
45429.m: SERI stepped in to replace missing EU research funding.

45430.q: From when was Switzerland fully associated again with the predecessor programme Horizon 2020?
45430.e: From 2014 Switzerland was only partly associated, because extending free movement of persons to Croatia was blocked. After ratifying the Croatia protocol on free movement, it was fully associated again from 2017.
45430.m: In Horizon 2020, Switzerland was fully involved again from 2017.

45431.q: What is meant by the ‘autonomous adoption’ of EU law?
a: Voluntary alignment with EU law without a treaty obligation
An obligation to adopt it through an international treaty
Review of EU law by the Federal Supreme Court
Adoption of EU law by the cantons alone
45431.e: Switzerland voluntarily adapts its own laws to EU law, even though no treaty obliges it to. This is meant to avoid barriers to trade.
45431.m: With autonomous adoption, Switzerland takes over EU law voluntarily.

45432.q: After which popular vote did Switzerland increasingly begin to adopt EU law voluntarily?
a: After the no to the EEA in 1992
After the yes to joining the UN in 2002
After the yes to Schengen in 2005
After the yes to women's suffrage in 1971
45432.e: After the no to the European Economic Area, Switzerland still adapted many laws to EU law. It wanted to avoid disadvantages for the economy.
45432.m: After the EEA ‘no’, Switzerland often adopted EU law voluntarily.

45433.q: Which principle did Switzerland introduce unilaterally on 1 July 2010 so that products approved in the EU can be sold more easily?
45433.e: Products that are lawfully sold in the EU or EEA may, in principle, also be sold in Switzerland. Switzerland introduced the principle unilaterally to lower prices.
45433.m: The Cassis de Dijon principle has applied in Switzerland since 2010.

45434.q: What is the main economic motive behind autonomous adoption?
45434.e: The EU is Switzerland's most important trading partner. Identical regulations make exports easier because products do not have to be tested twice.
45434.m: Identical product regulations make trade with the EU easier.

45435.q: With autonomous adoption, what does Switzerland lack compared with an EU member?
a: A say in drafting the rules
45435.e: Switzerland adopts rules it did not help decide in the EU institutions. However, Switzerland's democratic procedures remain in place.
45435.m: With autonomous adoption, Switzerland takes over rules it had no say in.

45436.q: How does dynamic adoption of law differ from autonomous adoption?
a: It only applies to the cantons
It does not need parliament's approval
45436.e: With autonomous adoption, Switzerland decides freely. With dynamic adoption of law, it commits in an agreement to adopt new EU law in certain areas.
45436.m: Dynamic adoption of law is based on a treaty; autonomous adoption is not.

45437.q: Where does the Cassis de Dijon principle get its name from?
a: From a court case about a French liqueur
From the city where the EU was founded
From a treaty between Switzerland and France
45437.e: In 1979 the European Court of Justice ruled that the blackcurrant liqueur Cassis de Dijon may be sold in Germany. This gave rise to the principle of mutual recognition of products.
45437.m: The Cassis de Dijon principle goes back to a ruling about a liqueur.

45438.q: Why did the electricity agreement between Switzerland and the EU fail to materialise for many years?
a: The EU tied it to a solution of the institutional questions
The EU has no common power grid
Switzerland is a member of the EU
45438.e: Negotiations began in 2007. The EU only wanted to conclude new market access agreements once questions such as adoption of law and dispute settlement were settled. Only in the Switzerland-EU package was the agreement fully negotiated.
45438.m: The electricity agreement was held up for a long time by the institutional questions.

45439.q: What is the place in Aargau where the power grids of Germany, France and Switzerland were first connected in 1958?
45439.e: The ‘Star of Laufenburg’ is seen as the birth of the European interconnected grid. Switzerland was thus part of the European electricity system from the very beginning.
45439.m: In 1958 the Star of Laufenburg connected the power grids of three countries.

45440.q: Without an electricity agreement, which procedure of the EU electricity market is Switzerland excluded from?
45440.e: In market coupling, quantities of electricity and cross-border capacities are allocated together. Without taking part, grid capacities at Swiss borders are used less efficiently.
45440.m: Without an electricity agreement, Switzerland remains excluded from European market coupling.

45441.q: Which company operates the Swiss electricity transmission grid?
45441.e: Swissgrid is the national grid company and operates the extra-high-voltage grid. It is a member of ENTSO-E, the association of European transmission system operators.

45442.q: Which authority supervises the electricity market in Switzerland?
a: The Swiss Federal Office of Energy alone
45442.e: ElCom is the independent regulatory authority for electricity. It monitors, for example, grid usage tariffs and security of supply.
45442.m: ElCom monitors the Swiss electricity market.

45443.q: In principle, what would change for Swiss households with the electricity agreement?
a: They could freely choose their electricity supplier
They would have to buy electricity from the EU
They would no longer pay grid fees
They could no longer feed in solar power
45443.e: The agreement provides for the complete opening of the electricity market. Small customers could, however, stay in the regulated basic supply.
45443.m: With the electricity agreement, households too would get a free choice of electricity supplier.

45444.q: What physical problem arises in the Swiss grid when electricity flows unplanned through Switzerland between EU countries?
a: Unplanned loop flows put strain on the grid
The electricity loses its frequency completely
45444.e: Physically, electricity follows the path of least resistance, including through neighbouring grids. Without coordination with the EU, this can endanger Switzerland's grid security.
45444.m: Unplanned electricity flows through Switzerland make grid control harder.

45445.q: What was the result of the vote on the Limitation Initiative in September 2020?
a: Clearly rejected, with about 62 percent no
Narrowly rejected, with about 51 percent no
45445.e: On 27 September 2020, 61.7 percent voted no. The large majority of cantons also rejected the initiative.
45445.m: The Limitation Initiative was clearly rejected in 2020.

45446.q: Which organisations launched the Limitation Initiative?
a: SP and the Trade Union Federation
45446.e: The Swiss People's Party and the Campaign for an Independent and Neutral Switzerland submitted the initiative in 2018. The Federal Council and parliament recommended rejecting it.
45446.m: The Limitation Initiative came from the SVP and the AUNS.

45447.q: Which canton was one of only four cantons to approve the Limitation Initiative?
45447.e: Schwyz, Glarus, Appenzell Innerrhoden and Ticino voted yes. In Ticino, competition from cross-border commuters is an important issue.
45447.m: Only four cantons said yes to the Limitation Initiative.

45448.q: What, at its core, did the Limitation Initiative demand?
a: An end to free movement of persons with the EU
A complete ban on cross-border commuters
The abolition of the right to asylum
45448.e: The initiative wanted to control immigration independently. For this, the free movement agreement with the EU would have had to be ended.
45448.m: The Limitation Initiative wanted to end free movement of persons.

45449.q: Why was the vote on the Limitation Initiative postponed from May to September 2020?
a: Because of a case at the Federal Supreme Court
Because of the National Council elections
45449.e: The Federal Council cancelled the voting date of 17 May 2020 because of the pandemic. The proposal then went to the polls on 27 September 2020.
45449.m: The pandemic postponed the vote on the Limitation Initiative.

45450.q: Which initiative on immigration had the people already narrowly approved on 9 February 2014?
45450.e: The Mass Immigration Initiative was approved with 50.3 percent yes. It demanded quotas without directly terminating free movement of persons.
45450.m: The Mass Immigration Initiative was narrowly approved in 2014.

45451.q: With which measure was the Mass Immigration Initiative implemented from July 2018, before the Limitation Initiative came to a vote?
45451.e: In occupations with high unemployment, vacancies must first be reported to the regional employment centres. This solution was often called ‘domestic priority light’.
45451.m: The job vacancy reporting obligation gives jobseekers in Switzerland an information advantage.

45452.q: Under an agreement from 2023, up to what share of their working time may cross-border commuters from France work from home without their taxation changing?
45452.e: Switzerland and France agreed that teleworking up to 40 percent of working time does not change which country taxes. This made a rule from the pandemic period permanent.
45452.m: Cross-border commuters from France may work up to 40 percent from home.

45453.q: From which country do more than half of the cross-border commuters in Switzerland come?
45453.e: Most cross-border commuters live in France and work mainly in the Lake Geneva region and north-western Switzerland. They are followed by Italy and Germany.
45453.m: Most cross-border commuters in Switzerland live in France.

45454.q: Which canton employs the most cross-border commuters?
45454.e: Geneva is almost completely surrounded by France and has a large labour market. More than a quarter of all cross-border commuters work there.
45454.m: Geneva is the canton with the most cross-border commuters.

45455.q: Which permit do cross-border commuters from the EU receive in Switzerland?
45455.e: Permit G is the cross-border commuter permit. Permit B is for residents, C for settled residents and L for short-term residents.

45456.q: What was abolished for cross-border commuters from the EU with full free movement of persons?
a: The obligation to have health insurance
The obligation to have a permit
45456.e: In the past, cross-border commuters had to live and work in a border zone. Today EU citizens can live anywhere in the EU and work as cross-border commuters anywhere in Switzerland.
45456.m: Cross-border commuters from the EU are no longer tied to border zones.

45457.q: In principle, which state pays unemployment benefit to a cross-border commuter who loses their job in Switzerland?
a: Switzerland as the state of employment
45457.e: Under the EU rules on coordinating social security, the state of residence is responsible for fully unemployed cross-border commuters. Switzerland adopts these rules through the free movement agreement.
45457.m: Unemployed cross-border commuters receive benefits in principle from their state of residence.

45458.q: With which neighbouring country has a new agreement on the taxation of cross-border commuters applied since July 2023?
45458.e: The new agreement with Italy came into force in July 2023. Since then, new cross-border commuters have also been taxed in Italy, with Switzerland collecting part of the tax.
45458.m: A new tax agreement has applied to cross-border commuters from Italy since 2023.

45459.q: To which area outside Switzerland was neutrality extended in 1815?
45459.e: Northern Savoy then belonged to the Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont. It was included in Swiss neutrality so that Geneva was better protected militarily.
45459.m: The neutrality of 1815 also included Northern Savoy.

45460.q: In 1815, what did the powers guarantee Switzerland in addition to recognising its neutrality?
a: A seat on the council of the great powers
45460.e: The powers guaranteed Switzerland's inviolability and independence within its 1815 borders. In return Switzerland committed to neutrality in future conflicts.
45460.m: In 1815 neutrality and the inviolability of the territory went together.

45461.q: For what strategic reason was a neutral Switzerland in the interest of the great powers in 1815?
a: It served as a buffer between France and Austria
It gave Russia access to the Mediterranean
It was to serve Prussia as a troop base
It alone controlled trade on the Rhine
45461.e: Austria, France and Prussia each wanted to draw Switzerland into their sphere of influence. A neutral Switzerland prevented any one power from controlling the important Alpine passes.
45461.m: In 1815 neutral Switzerland was a buffer between the great powers.

45462.q: Which document governed relations between the cantons from 1815 and replaced the Act of Mediation?
45462.e: The Federal Treaty of 1815 created a loose confederation of sovereign cantons. It applied until the Federal Constitution of 1848.
45462.m: From 1815 to 1848 the Federal Treaty formed the basis of the Confederation.

45463.q: Whose side did Switzerland take in 1815 after Napoleon's return from Elba?
a: The side of the Ottoman Empire
45463.e: During the Hundred Days, Switzerland sided with the Allies. Federal troops under General Bachmann briefly advanced into the Franche-Comté in July 1815.
45463.m: In 1815 Switzerland stood with the Allies against Napoleon's France.

45464.q: What was special about Neuchâtel after it joined the Confederation in 1815?
a: It was both a canton and a Prussian principality
It remained a subject territory of Bern
It had no government of its own
It also belonged to France at the same time
45464.e: The King of Prussia remained Prince of Neuchâtel. Only with the Neuchâtel affair of 1856 and 1857 did Prussia give up its rights.
45464.m: Until 1857 Neuchâtel was both a canton and a Prussian principality.

45465.q: Which Savoyard town became part of the canton of Geneva through the Treaty of Turin in 1816?
45465.e: So that Geneva would have a connected territory, Sardinia-Piedmont gave up several municipalities, including Carouge. The borders followed the decisions of Vienna and Paris.
45465.m: Carouge has belonged to the canton of Geneva since 1816.

45466.q: What is the period of Swiss history called that began in 1815 and lasted until about 1830?
45466.e: During the Restoration the old elites regained their power in many cantons. From about 1830 the liberal Regeneration followed.
45466.m: The Restoration began in Switzerland in 1815.

45467.q: At which conference were the rights and duties of neutral states in land warfare first comprehensively codified?
45467.e: In 1907 the Second Hague Peace Conference adopted Hague Convention V on neutrality in land warfare. It still forms the core of the law of neutrality today.
45467.m: The law of neutrality was set down in 1907 at the Second Hague Peace Conference.

45468.q: Under Hague Convention V, what are warring parties expressly forbidden to do?
45468.e: The territory of neutral powers is inviolable. Belligerents may not move troops or convoys of munitions or supplies across it.
45468.m: Warring parties may not cross neutral territory.

45469.q: In which city did the two great peace conferences of 1899 and 1907, which set rules for war and neutrality, take place?
45469.e: The Hague Peace Conferences created important conventions of the law of war. Hague Convention V of 1907 governs neutrality in land warfare.
45469.m: The Hague Conventions come from the conferences in The Hague.

45470.q: Under the law of neutrality, which supply is forbidden to a neutral state itself?
a: War material from state stocks to warring parties
Medicines for hospitals in the war zone
Goods from private companies to third countries
45470.e: The neutral state may not supply warring parties, directly or indirectly, with weapons or ammunition from its own stocks. Humanitarian aid, however, remains allowed.
45470.m: A neutral state does not supply its own weapons to warring parties.

45471.q: Under Hague Convention V, which installations may warring parties not set up on neutral territory?
a: Radio stations for communicating with their troops
45471.e: Article 3 forbids belligerents to set up radio or telegraph stations on neutral territory to communicate with their armed forces.
45471.m: Warring parties may not operate military radio stations on neutral territory.

45472.q: According to Hague Convention V, what may warring parties not do on the territory of a neutral state?
45472.e: No corps of combatants may be formed and no recruiting agencies opened on neutral territory to assist the belligerents.
45472.m: No one may recruit soldiers for a warring party on neutral soil.

45473.q: Under Hague Convention V, which people may a neutral state allow to be transported across its territory?
a: Prisoners of war near the front
45473.e: The neutral state may allow the passage of the wounded and sick, provided the trains carry neither combat personnel nor war material. It must ensure that safety and control are maintained.
45473.m: The wounded and sick may be transported across neutral territory.

45474.q: According to Hague Convention V, what applies to prisoners of war who escape to neutral territory?
a: They must serve in the neutral state's army
45474.e: Escaped prisoners of war who reach neutral territory are set free. The neutral state may, however, assign them a place of residence.
45474.m: A prisoner of war who flees to a neutral country is free.

45475.q: Is a neutral state liable if individuals cross the border to join a warring party?
a: No, it is not responsible for that
Yes, it then counts as a warring party
Only if there are more than a hundred
45475.e: Article 6 states that the responsibility of the neutral state is not engaged when individuals cross the border. Only the organised formation of troops and recruiting are forbidden.
45475.m: A neutral state is not liable for individual volunteers who go to war.

45476.q: Whose interests did Switzerland represent in Cuba from 1961 to 2015?
45476.e: After the break between Washington and Havana in 1961, Switzerland represented the USA in Cuba. The mandate ended in 2015 when the embassies reopened.
45476.m: For more than fifty years Switzerland was the protecting power of the USA in Cuba.

45477.q: After which conflict did Switzerland take on protecting power mandates between Russia and Georgia in 2009?
45477.e: After the war in August 2008, Georgia and Russia broke off relations. Since 2009 Switzerland has represented the interests of each state in the other country.
45477.m: Since the Caucasus war, Switzerland has been protecting power for Russia and Georgia.

45478.q: What led Switzerland to represent Mexico's interests in Ecuador in 2024?
a: Ecuador's police stormed the Mexican embassy
A border war between the two states
A dispute over oil in the Pacific
A Mexican trade boycott against Ecuador
45478.e: After the Ecuadorian police stormed the Mexican embassy in Quito in April 2024, Mexico broke off relations. Since then Switzerland has looked after Mexico's interests in Ecuador.
45478.m: Since 2024 Switzerland has been Mexico's protecting power in Ecuador.

45479.q: Why, for example, has Switzerland represented Iran's interests in Egypt since 1979?
a: Because the two states broke off relations
Because Switzerland is allied with both states
Because Iran no longer has diplomats
45479.e: After the Islamic Revolution, Iran and Egypt broke off relations in 1979. A neutral third state then keeps up contact and helps the citizens.
45479.m: A protecting power steps in when two states no longer have relations.

45480.q: Whose interests has Switzerland represented in Iran since 1980?
45480.e: After the hostage crisis at the US embassy in Tehran, the USA broke off relations in 1980. Since then the Swiss embassy in Tehran has looked after US interests; since 2019 Switzerland has also represented Iran in Canada.
45480.m: Switzerland has been the protecting power of the USA in Iran since 1980.

45481.q: Which 1961 agreement in diplomatic law provides that a third state may take over protecting a state's interests?
45481.e: The Vienna Convention allows the protection of interests and citizens to be entrusted to a third state when relations are broken off.
45481.m: The Vienna Convention of 1961 is the legal basis for protecting powers.

45482.q: Under the Geneva Conventions, what task does a protecting power have in a war?
a: Monitoring the treatment of prisoners of war
Supplying the warring parties with weapons
Ending the war on behalf of the UN
Setting the borders of the warring parties
45482.e: Protecting powers may visit prison camps and check whether the Geneva Conventions are being respected. Switzerland played this role especially in the Second World War.
45482.m: A protecting power checks how prisoners of war are treated.

45483.q: When did the Summit on Peace in Ukraine take place at the Bürgenstock?
45483.e: The high-level summit took place on 15 and 16 June 2024 at the Bürgenstock resort. It was preceded by several meetings of national security advisers.
45483.m: The Bürgenstock summit took place in June 2024.

45484.q: According to the Bürgenstock final communiqué, which nuclear power plant should return to full Ukrainian control?
45484.e: Europe's largest nuclear power plant has been occupied by Russia since 2022. The communiqué called for safe operation under full Ukrainian control.
45484.m: The occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant was a topic of the summit.

45485.q: Which of these participating states did not sign the Bürgenstock final communiqué?
45485.e: India, Saudi Arabia and South Africa took part but did not sign the declaration. Among other things, they demanded that Russia be included in future.
45485.m: India did not support the Bürgenstock final communiqué.

45486.q: In which Swiss town did national security advisers meet in January 2024 to prepare a Ukraine peace summit?
45486.e: The meeting on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum was the fourth after Copenhagen, Jeddah and Malta. Afterwards Switzerland announced it would organise a summit.
45486.m: The peace summit was prepared in Davos in January 2024.

45487.q: How many points did President Zelensky's peace formula, on which the Bürgenstock summit was based, have?
45487.e: The peace formula had ten points, including nuclear safety and the withdrawal of Russian troops. Only three of them were dealt with at the Bürgenstock.
45487.m: Zelensky's peace formula had ten points.

45488.q: How many states signed the final communiqué of the Bürgenstock summit immediately after it?
45488.e: At first 80 states and four European organisations signed. By autumn 2024 the number of states had risen to 89.
45488.m: About 80 states supported the Bürgenstock communiqué straight away.

45489.q: What did the final communiqué of the Bürgenstock summit demand regarding prisoners of war?
a: The release of all through a full exchange
Their naturalisation in the detaining state
45489.e: All prisoners of war were to be freed through a full exchange. In addition, deported Ukrainian children and unlawfully detained civilians were to return.
45489.m: The communiqué called for the exchange of all prisoners of war.

45490.q: Who represented the USA at the 2024 Bürgenstock summit?
45490.e: President Biden did not attend in person. Vice President Kamala Harris travelled to the Bürgenstock and announced aid for Ukraine.
45490.m: Kamala Harris represented the USA at the Bürgenstock in 2024.

45491.q: Which state was deliberately not invited to the 2024 Bürgenstock summit?
45491.e: Switzerland did not invite Russia to this first meeting. China was invited but declined, India took part and Brazil attended as an observer.
45491.m: Russia was not at the Bürgenstock summit.

45492.q: Who was President of the Confederation in 2022 when Switzerland adopted the sanctions against Russia?
45492.e: Ignazio Cassis was President of the Confederation and head of the FDFA in 2022. He said that playing into the hands of an aggressor is not neutral.
45492.m: Ignazio Cassis was President of the Confederation in 2022.

45493.q: Why, in the Federal Council's view, are economic sanctions compatible with the law of neutrality?
a: The law of neutrality only concerns military matters
The sanctions only apply to private individuals
Switzerland is a member of the EU
45493.e: The law of neutrality mainly governs military duties, such as not taking part in wars. Economic measures are not covered by it, but they do affect neutrality policy.
45493.m: The law of neutrality does not forbid economic sanctions.

45494.q: How did Switzerland respond to the Russian annexation of Crimea in 2014?
a: It prevented circumvention without fully adopting the sanctions
It adopted all EU sanctions immediately
It broke off relations with Russia
It imposed a complete trade embargo
45494.e: In 2014 Switzerland did not fully adopt the EU sanctions. But it took measures so that the sanctions could not be circumvented via Switzerland.
45494.m: After the annexation of Crimea, Switzerland mainly prevented the circumvention of sanctions.

45495.q: Which measure is typically part of the financial sanctions against Russia?
a: Freezing the assets of listed persons
Seizing Russian ships on the Rhine
45495.e: The assets of people and companies on the sanctions lists are frozen. In addition, import and export bans apply to certain goods.
45495.m: Financial sanctions freeze the assets of listed persons.

45496.q: Since December 2022, which measure also limits trade in Russian crude oil by sea for Switzerland?
45496.e: Switzerland adopted the G7 and EU price cap on Russian oil. Services such as transport or insurance are only allowed if the oil is sold below the price cap.
45496.m: A price cap applies to Russian crude oil.

45497.q: What is the aim of the REPO Task Force, founded by the G7 states in 2022?
a: Tracking down the assets of Russian oligarchs
45497.e: The task force is meant to find and freeze the money of sanctioned Russian elites. Switzerland works with it but is not a member.
45497.m: The REPO Task Force searches for the assets of Russian elites.

45498.q: Which precious metal from Russia has Switzerland no longer been allowed to import since August 2022?
45498.e: With the EU's seventh sanctions package, Switzerland adopted an import ban on Russian gold. This hit Switzerland particularly hard as an important location for gold refineries.
45498.m: Since 2022 Russian gold may no longer be imported into Switzerland.

45499.q: Which measure affected air traffic from 28 February 2022?
a: The airspace was closed to Russian flights
All flights to Ukraine were banned
Swiss airlines could no longer fly to Asia
Russian pilots had to stay in Switzerland
45499.e: Switzerland closed its airspace to aircraft from Russia, with exceptions for humanitarian and diplomatic flights. In doing so it followed its neighbouring states.
45499.m: Swiss airspace is closed to Russian flights.

45500.q: What does a foreign buyer promise with a non-re-export declaration?
a: Not to pass on the material without consent
To use the material only for training
To return the material after ten years
To store the material only at home
45500.e: With this declaration, the buyer state undertakes not to pass on Swiss war material to third parties without Switzerland's permission. It is meant to prevent weapons from reaching conflict zones.
45500.m: A non-re-export declaration forbids passing material on without Swiss consent.

45501.q: In 2022, which state wanted to pass on Swiss-made ammunition for the Gepard anti-aircraft tank to Ukraine?
45501.e: Germany had supplied Gepard tanks to Ukraine and wanted to pass on Swiss ammunition for them. Switzerland rejected the request.
45501.m: In 2022 Switzerland refused to let Germany pass on Gepard ammunition.

45502.q: Which principle did Switzerland cite when it refused in 2022 to allow Gepard ammunition to be passed on to Ukraine?
45502.e: Under the law of neutrality and the War Material Act, Switzerland may not supply weapons to one warring party only. This also applies to passing them on through third countries.
45502.m: Switzerland justified its no to passing on ammunition with its neutrality.

45503.q: Which Swiss-developed wheeled armoured vehicles did Denmark want to pass on to Ukraine?
45503.e: The Piranha is built by Mowag in Kreuzlingen. Switzerland refused to allow it to be passed on, for reasons of neutrality and war material law.
45503.m: Denmark was not allowed to pass on Swiss Piranha vehicles to Ukraine.

45504.q: Under the War Material Act, which criterion in principle rules out export permits?
a: The recipient country is involved in an armed conflict
The recipient country is not an EU member
The recipient country is outside Europe
The recipient country is a monarchy
45504.e: Exports are not permitted if the destination country is involved in an internal or international armed conflict. In addition, there is the equal treatment rule of the law of neutrality.
45504.m: Switzerland does not permit war material exports to countries at war.

45505.q: How did voters decide in 2009 on the popular initiative for a ban on war material exports?
a: A clear no, by about two thirds
45505.e: On 29 November 2009, 68.2 percent voted no, and all the cantons also rejected it. The Federal Council had argued mainly with jobs and supplies for the army.
45505.m: An export ban on war material clearly failed in 2009.

45506.q: What did the counter-proposal to the ‘Correction Initiative’, which came into force on 1 May 2022, change?
a: The approval criteria are now in the law instead of the ordinance
War material exports were banned completely
Exports to countries at war were allowed
The people now decide on every export
45506.e: The criteria were written into the law, so parliament rather than the Federal Council alone decides on changes. The initiators therefore withdrew their initiative conditionally.
45506.m: Since 2022 parliament has set the rules for war material exports in the law.

45507.q: Which argument did the Swiss arms industry put forward against the strict re-export ban?
a: Foreign customers would avoid Swiss suppliers
The army did not need its own industry
Exports had been completely banned since 2022
45507.e: Companies warned that states like Germany would no longer buy Swiss components if they could not pass them on in an emergency. This would endanger the country's own defence industry.
45507.m: The industry feared losing customers because of the re-export ban.

45508.q: Which federal agency issues permits for the export of war material in Switzerland?
45508.e: The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs examines the applications together with the FDFA. Sensitive cases are decided by the Federal Council.
45508.m: SECO approves the export of war material.

45509.q: In which city is the OSCE Secretariat based?
45509.e: The OSCE Secretariat is in Vienna. From 2017 to 2020 it was headed by the Swiss diplomat Thomas Greminger.
45509.m: The OSCE Secretariat is in Vienna.

45510.q: Who holds the chairmanship of the OSCE?
a: The foreign minister of the chairing country
The President of the European Parliament
The oldest head of state of the member states
45510.e: The chairmanship rotates annually among the participating states. Switzerland held it, for example, in 1996 with Flavio Cotti.
45510.m: The OSCE chairmanship is held by the foreign minister of the chairing country.

45511.q: In which country did the OSCE organise the first post-war elections in 1996 under Swiss chairmanship?
45511.e: After the Dayton Agreement of 1995, the OSCE was given the task of preparing elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They took place in September 1996.
45511.m: In 1996 the OSCE organised elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

45512.q: Which Federal Councillor is the OSCE Chairperson-in-Office in 2026?
45512.e: The chairmanship is held by the foreign minister of the chairing country. For Switzerland in 2026 this is the head of the FDFA.
45512.m: Ignazio Cassis chairs the OSCE in 2026.

45513.q: What is the body made up of the previous, current and next OSCE chairmanships called?
45513.e: The Troika ensures continuity between the annually changing chairmanships. It discusses current business together.
45513.m: The OSCE Troika links three successive chairmanships.

45514.q: In which conflict did a Swiss diplomat mediate for the OSCE in a contact group in 2014?
45514.e: Heidi Tagliavini represented the OSCE in the Trilateral Contact Group with Ukraine and Russia. The group negotiated the Minsk Protocol.
45514.m: In 2014 a Swiss diplomat mediated for the OSCE in Ukraine.

45515.q: Which agreement on eastern Ukraine was signed in the Trilateral Contact Group in September 2014?
45515.e: The Minsk Protocol provided for a ceasefire monitored by the OSCE. In 2015 it was supplemented by a further Minsk agreement.
45515.m: The Minsk Protocol of 2014 was meant to end the war in eastern Ukraine.

45516.q: What did the popular vote of 10 June 2001 on the Military Act make possible?
45516.e: Voters narrowly approved the change. Since then Swiss soldiers on peace support missions may be armed for self-defence.
45516.m: Since 2001 Swiss peacekeeping troops may be armed.

45518.q: Until when did parliament extend the Swisscoy mission in June 2023?
45518.e: The mandate is extended for three years at a time. In June 2023 parliament approved an extension until the end of 2026.
45518.m: Parliament extends the Swisscoy mission by three years at a time.

45519.q: What does the name ‘Swisscoy’ stand for?
45519.e: The name is short for ‘Swiss Company’, a Swiss military company. It dates from the early days, when the unit was about the size of a company.

45520.q: Under the leadership of which organisation is KFOR, in which Swisscoy takes part?
45520.e: KFOR is led by NATO and is based on a mandate from the UN Security Council. As a non-member, Switzerland takes part through the Partnership for Peace.
45520.m: KFOR in Kosovo is led by NATO.

45521.q: What is the task of Swisscoy's Liaison and Monitoring Teams (LMT)?
a: Keeping in contact with the population and observing the situation
Taking over police duties for municipalities
45521.e: The LMT live in houses in the middle of towns and villages and talk to the authorities and the population. This way KFOR spots tensions early.
45521.m: Swisscoy's LMT observe the situation in direct contact with the population.

45522.q: On what legal basis is the KFOR mission in Kosovo, in which Swisscoy takes part, founded?
a: A resolution of the UN Security Council
A decision of the Federal Council alone
A ruling of the International Court of Justice
A treaty between Switzerland and Serbia
45522.e: The basis is UN Security Council Resolution 1244 of 1999. For Switzerland, such a mandate is a condition for taking part in a peace mission.
45522.m: KFOR is based on a mandate from the UN Security Council.

45523.q: What is Swisscoy's EOD team responsible for?
a: Disposing of unexploded and other explosive ordnance
Providing medical care to the population
45523.e: EOD stands for Explosive Ordnance Disposal. The specialists defuse and destroy ammunition and explosives from earlier conflicts.
45523.m: Swisscoy's EOD team removes dangerous explosive ordnance.

45524.q: How is cooperation in the Partnership for Peace basically organised?
a: Each state chooses its own programmes
All states must complete the same exercises
The partners pay a fixed membership fee
45524.e: Each partner state sets out in an individual programme which areas it wants to take part in. Switzerland focuses, for example, on training, disarmament and disaster relief.
45524.m: In the Partnership for Peace each state decides its own cooperation.

45525.q: What does Switzerland contribute in particular to the Partnership for Peace?
a: The three Geneva centres for security issues
Its own combat units for NATO missions
45525.e: The Geneva Centre for Security Policy, the Geneva Centre for Security Sector Governance and the Geneva International Centre for Humanitarian Demining offer courses and expertise.
45525.m: Switzerland contributes to the partnership with its Geneva centres.

45526.q: What was NATO's main aim with the Partnership for Peace in 1994?
a: Building trust with states of the former Eastern Bloc
45526.e: After the end of the Cold War, NATO wanted to work with former opponents and neutral states. The programme also served as a first step towards later membership.
45526.m: The Partnership for Peace was meant to build trust after the Cold War.

45527.q: Which neutral neighbour of Switzerland takes part in the Partnership for Peace but is not a NATO member?
45527.e: Like Switzerland, Austria is neutral and has taken part in the Partnership for Peace since 1995. Germany, Italy and France are NATO members.
45527.m: Austria takes part in the Partnership for Peace without being a NATO member.

45528.q: Which militarily neutral state joined the Partnership for Peace in 1999?
45528.e: Ireland joined in 1999 after a long domestic debate about its neutrality. It is still not a NATO member today.
45528.m: Ireland has been part of the Partnership for Peace since 1999.

45529.q: What is Switzerland's aim in taking part in the Partnership's Planning and Review Process (PARP)?
a: Improving its army's ability to work with others
Providing troops for NATO combat missions
Buying weapons more cheaply from NATO
45529.e: PARP helps partner states shape their armed forces so that they can work with others. This is called interoperability, for example for peace missions.
45529.m: Through PARP, Switzerland improves its army's interoperability.

45530.q: Which two politicians met at the summit in Geneva in 1985?
a: John F. Kennedy and Nikita Khrushchev
45530.e: From 19 to 21 November 1985, US President Reagan and Soviet party leader Gorbachev met for the first time. Kennedy and Khrushchev had met in Vienna in 1961.
45530.m: Reagan and Gorbachev first met in Geneva in 1985.

45531.q: Which principle on nuclear war was set out in the joint statement of 1985?
a: It cannot be won and must never be fought
It is only allowed for defence
It may only be fought with UN approval
It is ruled out after ten years of disarmament
45531.e: Both sides declared that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. The sentence was often repeated later.
45531.m: In Geneva the superpowers declared that a nuclear war must never be fought.

45532.q: Where in Geneva did Reagan and Gorbachev hold their most famous one-to-one talk in 1985?
a: By the fireside in a pool house
On a boat on Lake Geneva
In the hall of the UN General Assembly
45532.e: On the first day the two withdrew to the villa's pool house and talked by the fireplace. The conversation became a symbol of the new trust.
45532.m: The fireside chat of 1985 became the symbol of the Geneva summit.

45533.q: Which US arms programme was the biggest point of dispute at the 1985 Geneva summit?
45533.e: Reagan wanted to keep the space-based missile defence, which Gorbachev firmly rejected. That is why no disarmament treaty was reached in Geneva.
45533.m: The SDI missile defence prevented a major agreement in 1985.

45534.q: What was the outcome of the 1985 Geneva summit?
a: No disarmament treaty, but new trust
The abolition of all nuclear weapons
The end of the Warsaw Pact
45534.e: No disarmament treaty was signed in Geneva, mainly because of the dispute over SDI. But the two leaders built trust and agreed on further meetings and exchange programmes.
45534.m: The Geneva summit brought no treaty, but the start of détente.

45535.q: Why was Geneva a suitable place for the meeting of the two superpowers in 1985?
a: Switzerland is neutral and experienced in diplomacy
Geneva lies exactly between Washington and Moscow
Switzerland was a NATO member at the time
Geneva is the Soviet Union's headquarters in the West
45535.e: As a neutral state with many international organisations, Switzerland offered a safe and impartial venue. A summit had already taken place in Geneva in 1955.
45535.m: Neutral Switzerland is a popular venue for summits.

45536.q: Which disarmament treaty followed the Geneva and Reykjavík summits in 1987?
a: The INF Treaty on intermediate-range missiles
45536.e: In the INF Treaty, the USA and the Soviet Union committed to scrapping all land-based intermediate-range missiles. The Geneva summit had created the trust needed for this.
45536.m: The INF Treaty of 1987 was a result of the summit diplomacy from 1985.

45537.q: Which states had already met for a summit in Geneva in 1955?
a: USA, Soviet Union, Great Britain and France
Soviet Union, Poland, East Germany and Hungary
45537.e: In 1955 the heads of government of the four victorious powers of the Second World War discussed Germany and disarmament in Geneva. Geneva was already a place of summit diplomacy then.
45537.m: The four victorious powers already met in Geneva in 1955.

45538.q: Which organisation launched the Neutrality Initiative?
a: Group for a Switzerland without an Army
45538.e: Pro Schweiz launched the initiative in November 2022. The committee was made up mainly of SVP politicians.
45538.m: The Neutrality Initiative comes from Pro Schweiz.

45539.q: Which decision by the Federal Council in 2022 prompted the Neutrality Initiative?
a: Adopting the EU sanctions against Russia
45539.e: After the Russian attack on Ukraine, Switzerland adopted the EU's sanctions. Critics saw this as a violation of neutrality and launched the initiative.
45539.m: Adopting the EU sanctions triggered the Neutrality Initiative.

45540.q: Roughly how many valid signatures did the Federal Chancellery count for the Neutrality Initiative?
45540.e: Just under 130,000 signatures were valid. A popular initiative needs 100,000 valid signatures.
45540.m: The Neutrality Initiative succeeded with about 130,000 signatures.

45541.q: Where did the Neutrality Initiative want to set out Switzerland's neutrality in detail?
a: In a treaty with the UN
45541.e: A popular initiative always changes the Federal Constitution. The initiative called for a new Article 54a for this.
45541.m: The Neutrality Initiative wanted to anchor neutrality in the constitution.

45542.q: How did the text of the Neutrality Initiative describe Switzerland's neutrality?
45542.e: The first paragraph said that Switzerland is neutral and that its neutrality is perpetual and armed. This formula matches existing practice.
45542.m: The initiative called neutrality perpetual and armed.

45543.q: According to the text of the Neutrality Initiative, which sanctions would still have been allowed?
45543.e: The initiative wanted to ban non-military coercive measures against warring states. Obligations towards the UN and measures against the circumvention of other countries' sanctions were exempted.
45543.m: Under the initiative, Switzerland could only have adopted UN sanctions.

45544.q: Under the Neutrality Initiative, when would cooperation with a military alliance have been permitted?
a: In the event of a direct military attack on Switzerland
After a decision by the Federal Council
45544.e: The initiative wanted to ban joining military or defence alliances. Cooperation would only have been allowed in the event of a direct attack or preparations for one.
45544.m: The initiative would only have allowed alliance cooperation in the event of an attack on Switzerland.

45545.q: What position did the Federal Council take in its dispatch on the Neutrality Initiative?
45545.e: In its dispatch of November 2024 the Federal Council recommended rejection. It feared that a rigid rule would take away the flexibility of neutrality policy.
45545.m: The Federal Council rejected the Neutrality Initiative without a counter-proposal.

45546.q: How did voters decide on the Neutrality Initiative on 27 September 2026?
45546.e: The initiative was clearly rejected with 70.15 percent no votes, and by the cantons too. A stricter definition of neutrality in the constitution thus found no majority.
45546.m: The Neutrality Initiative was clearly rejected in 2026.

45547.q: Which former Federal Councillor announced a popular initiative for comprehensive neutrality in March 2022?
45547.e: In March 2022 Christoph Blocher announced an initiative for ‘integral neutrality’. The reason was the adoption of the EU sanctions against Russia.
45547.m: Christoph Blocher was behind the start of the Neutrality Initiative.

45548.q: Which task did the fourth paragraph of the Neutrality Initiative give Switzerland?
a: It should be available as a mediator
It should build a professional army
45548.e: Switzerland was to use its neutrality to prevent and resolve conflicts and be available as a mediator. This matches today's policy of good offices.
45548.m: Under the initiative, Switzerland was to mediate in conflicts.

45549.q: For what period does the Federal Council set its Foreign Policy Strategy each time?
45549.e: The strategy applies for one legislative period, for example from 2024 to 2027. After that the Federal Council draws up a new one.
45549.m: The Foreign Policy Strategy applies for four years at a time.

45550.q: What are mediation between conflicting parties and protecting power mandates, with which Switzerland helps in foreign policy, called?
45550.e: With its good offices, Switzerland offers mediation, venues for negotiations and protecting power mandates. They are an important part of Swiss peace policy.
45550.m: Good offices are a hallmark of Swiss foreign policy.

45551.q: Which region has top geographical priority in the Foreign Policy Strategy 2024 to 2027?
45551.e: The strategy aims for a stable and prosperous Europe. This includes developing relations with the EU further.
45551.m: Europe is the top priority of Swiss foreign policy.

45552.q: Which department draws up the Foreign Policy Strategy for the Federal Council?
45552.e: The Federal Department of Foreign Affairs coordinates foreign policy and draws up the strategy. It is adopted by the Federal Council as a whole.
45552.m: The FDFA draws up the Foreign Policy Strategy.

45553.q: Which parliamentary bodies does the Federal Council consult on important foreign policy plans such as the strategy?
45553.e: Under the Parliament Act, the Federal Council consults the committees responsible for foreign policy on important plans and on guidelines. This lets parliament help shape foreign policy.
45553.m: The Federal Council consults the Foreign Affairs Committees on important plans.

45554.q: In which document does the Federal Council report each year on the implementation of the Foreign Policy Strategy?
45554.e: The Foreign Policy Report is published every year and shows the state of the goals. Parliament takes note of it.
45554.m: The Foreign Policy Report gives yearly information on the strategy's goals.

45555.q: Which aim does the Federal Constitution expressly name for Swiss foreign policy?
a: Alleviating need and poverty in the world
45555.e: The constitution names, among other things, the alleviation of need and poverty, respect for human rights and the peaceful coexistence of peoples. Foreign policy is a matter for the Confederation.
45555.m: The constitution also commits foreign policy to alleviating need and poverty.

45556.q: Who adopts Switzerland's Foreign Policy Strategy?
a: The Federal Council as a whole
The people at the ballot box
45556.e: The FDFA draws up the strategy, but it is adopted by the Federal Council as a body. Parliament is consulted on important plans.
45556.m: The Federal Council adopts the Foreign Policy Strategy.

45557.q: Which authorities does the Federal Constitution expressly task with taking measures to safeguard neutrality?
a: The Federal Assembly and the Federal Council
The Federal Supreme Court and the cantons
The army and the National Bank
45557.e: Articles 173 and 185 oblige the Federal Assembly and the Federal Council to take measures to safeguard external security, independence and neutrality. The constitution has no separate article on neutrality.
45557.m: According to the constitution, the Federal Assembly and the Federal Council must safeguard neutrality.

45558.q: Which strategy came directly before the Foreign Policy Strategy 2024 to 2027?
45558.e: The Federal Council sets its foreign policy for one legislative period at a time. The predecessor was the Foreign Policy Strategy 2020 to 2023.
45558.m: The Foreign Policy Strategy is renewed every four years.

45559.q: Under the North Atlantic Treaty, which states can be invited to join?
a: Only states with an Atlantic coast
45559.e: Under Article 10, the members can unanimously invite any European state that can contribute to the security of the North Atlantic area. All NATO enlargements are based on this.

45560.q: How many states signed the North Atlantic Treaty as founding members?
45560.e: The founding members were the USA, Canada, Great Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Norway, Denmark, Iceland, Italy and Portugal. That makes twelve states.

45561.q: On what occasion did NATO invoke the collective defence clause of Article 5 for the only time so far?
a: Terrorist attacks in the USA in 2001
45561.e: After the attacks on the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, the North Atlantic Council declared the case for collective defence on 12 September 2001. An attack on one member was thus treated as an attack on all.
45561.m: Article 5 was invoked for the first time after the attacks of 11 September 2001.

45562.q: What exactly does Article 5 oblige the allies to do when it is invoked?
a: Give assistance with measures of their own choosing
Formally declare war on the attacker
45562.e: Each member gives assistance with the measures it considers necessary, including armed force. The article contains no automatic duty to intervene militarily.
45562.m: Article 5 requires assistance, but leaves the type of help to each member.

45563.q: Which area does NATO's collective defence clause cover?
a: Europe, North America and the North Atlantic
45563.e: Article 6 covers the territory of the members in Europe and North America and the North Atlantic north of the Tropic of Cancer. Colonies further south were not included.
45563.m: NATO's collective defence clause applies to the North Atlantic area.

45564.q: Can a state leave NATO again?
a: Yes, after giving notice with a waiting period
Only with the consent of all members
45564.e: A member can give notice of withdrawal to the government of the USA. The withdrawal takes effect one year after notice is given.
45564.m: Leaving NATO is possible with one year's notice.

45565.q: Against what threat were NATO's measures directed after it first invoked collective defence in 2001?
45565.e: After the attacks of 11 September 2001, NATO monitored shipping in the Mediterranean, for example with Operation Active Endeavour, to ward off terrorism.
45565.m: NATO's first case of collective defence was directed against terrorism.

45566.q: Which three states joined NATO in 1999 in the first enlargement round after the Cold War?
a: Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary
The Czech Republic, Slovenia and Lithuania
45566.e: Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary were admitted on 12 March 1999. All three had previously been members of the Warsaw Pact.
45566.m: Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary joined NATO in 1999.

45567.q: How many states were admitted in 2004 in NATO's largest enlargement round so far?
45567.e: In March 2004 seven states from Central and Eastern Europe joined at the same time. No other round has been so large.
45567.m: The largest NATO enlargement brought seven new members in 2004.

45568.q: Which former Soviet republics have been NATO members since 2004?
45568.e: The three Baltic states were part of the Soviet Union until 1991. They are still the only former Soviet republics in the alliance.
45568.m: The Baltic states are the only former Soviet republics in NATO.

45569.q: Who has to agree for a new state to be admitted to NATO?
45569.e: New members are invited unanimously, and then all member states must ratify the accession. That is why individual countries such as Turkey or Hungary were able to delay accessions.
45569.m: Joining NATO needs the consent of all members.

45570.q: How did Russia view NATO's eastward enlargement?
a: As a threat to its security
As a step towards its own membership
As purely a matter for the EU
45570.e: Russia criticised the admission of former Eastern Bloc states from the start. It saw it as the Western alliance advancing to its borders.
45570.m: Russia sees NATO's eastward enlargement as a threat.

45571.q: Which state was only able to join NATO in 2020 after settling the name dispute with Greece?
45571.e: Greece blocked its accession for a long time because of the name ‘Macedonia’. After the Prespa Agreement of 2018 the state was renamed and was admitted in 2020 as the 30th member.
45571.m: North Macedonia became a NATO member after the Prespa Agreement.

45572.q: Which Balkan state was admitted to NATO in 2017 as its 29th member?
45572.e: Montenegro joined on 5 June 2017, although Russia sharply criticised its accession. The state had only separated from Serbia in 2006.
45572.m: Montenegro has been a member of NATO since 2017.

45574.q: As which member did Sweden join NATO in March 2024?
45574.e: Sweden was admitted on 7 March 2024. Since then the alliance has had 32 members.

45575.q: Which event led Finland and Sweden to give up their non-alignment in 2022?
45575.e: After Russia's attack on Ukraine in February 2022, support for joining NATO rose sharply in both countries. In May 2022 they submitted their applications together.
45575.m: The war against Ukraine brought Finland and Sweden into NATO.

45576.q: Which NATO country demanded concessions from Sweden, including on action against the PKK?
45576.e: Turkey accused Sweden of tolerating Kurdish groups that it classifies as terrorist. Only after commitments from Sweden did the Turkish parliament approve in January 2024.
45576.m: Turkey delayed Sweden's accession for a long time.

45577.q: Which member state was the last to ratify Sweden's accession in February 2024?
45577.e: The Hungarian parliament approved on 26 February 2024. After that Sweden was able to deposit its instrument of accession.
45577.m: Hungary was the last country to give the green light for Sweden's accession.

45578.q: Which term describes Finland's foreign policy in the Cold War, which paid great attention to Soviet interests?
45578.e: Finland remained formally neutral and democratic, but avoided anything that might annoy the Soviet Union. The term was often used critically in the West.
45578.m: Finlandisation describes a policy of deferring to a powerful neighbour.

45579.q: At which NATO summit did Turkey, Finland and Sweden sign a memorandum on the accession process in June 2022?
45579.e: On the sidelines of the Madrid summit, the three states agreed on a trilateral memorandum. After that, both countries were officially invited to join.
45579.m: Finland and Sweden were invited to join in Madrid in 2022.

45580.q: Under what name did NATO carry out its air strikes against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1999?
45580.e: Allied Force began on 24 March 1999 and targeted military and strategic sites in Serbia and Kosovo. Deliberate Force, by contrast, was a mission in Bosnia in 1995.
45580.m: NATO's air war in the Kosovo war was called Operation Allied Force.

45581.q: Roughly how long did the NATO air strikes in the Kosovo war last?
45581.e: The strikes began on 24 March and ended on 10 June 1999. That makes 78 days.
45581.m: The air war over Kosovo lasted 78 days.

45582.q: Why is the NATO mission in the Kosovo war still disputed under international law today?
a: There was no mandate from the UN Security Council
It was carried out without a decision of the North Atlantic Council
It violated the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty
45582.e: Russia and China would have blocked a mandate in the Security Council, so NATO acted without one. Supporters spoke of a humanitarian intervention, critics of a breach of the ban on the use of force.
45582.m: NATO's Kosovo mission took place without a UN mandate.

45583.q: Which negotiations failed in February and March 1999, shortly before the NATO air strikes began?
45583.e: At the Château de Rambouillet near Paris, an agreement on autonomy for Kosovo was to be reached. The Yugoslav side rejected the draft.
45583.m: The failure at Rambouillet preceded the Kosovo war.

45585.q: What is the contingent called with which the Swiss Armed Forces take part in KFOR in Kosovo?
45585.e: Swisscoy has been deployed in Kosovo since 1999 and is made up of volunteers. Swissint, on the other hand, is the army's competence centre for missions abroad.
45585.m: Switzerland takes part in KFOR with Swisscoy.

45586.q: What special significance did the Kosovo war have for the German Bundeswehr?
45586.e: With Tornado fighter jets, Germany took part in combat for the first time since the Second World War. There had already been missions abroad without a combat role, for example in Somalia.
45586.m: In the Kosovo war the Bundeswehr fought for the first time since 1945.

45587.q: What was ISAF's task at the start, after the UN created it in December 2001?
45587.e: With Resolution 1386 the UN Security Council authorised an international force for the capital. Later its mission was extended to the whole of Afghanistan.
45587.m: ISAF first secured Kabul and later the whole of Afghanistan.

45588.q: In which year did NATO take command of ISAF?
45588.e: In August 2003 the leadership passed from changing lead nations to NATO. This gave the mission a permanent command structure.

45589.q: Why was taking over ISAF a turning point for NATO?
a: First mission outside the Euro-Atlantic area
First mission with its own nuclear weapons
45589.e: Until then NATO had only operated in Europe. With Afghanistan it took on a major mission far outside its treaty area for the first time.
45589.m: With ISAF, NATO became active outside Europe for the first time.

45590.q: When did the ISAF mission in Afghanistan end?
45590.e: ISAF ended on 31 December 2014, and responsibility for security passed to the Afghan forces. A smaller training mission then remained in the country.
45590.m: ISAF was ended at the end of 2014.

45591.q: What was the NATO mission called that trained and advised Afghan security forces from 2015?
45591.e: Resolute Support ran from 2015 to 2021 and had no combat role. It ended with the withdrawal of international troops and the Taliban takeover.
45591.m: Resolute Support followed ISAF as a training mission.

45592.q: At which conference was an interim government for Afghanistan agreed at the end of 2001?
45592.e: At the Petersberg near Bonn, Afghan groups agreed in December 2001 on an interim administration under Hamid Karzai. The agreement also provided for an international security force.
45592.m: The Petersberg Conference set Afghanistan's political new start in 2001.

45593.q: What were the Provincial Reconstruction Teams within ISAF?
45593.e: The teams combined soldiers with civilian experts to promote security and reconstruction in the provinces. Germany led such teams, for example, in Kunduz and Faizabad.
45593.m: Provincial Reconstruction Teams combined the military and civilian reconstruction.

45594.q: What is NATO's aim with nuclear sharing?
a: Involving states without their own nuclear weapons in deterrence
Abolishing all nuclear weapons in Europe
Giving every member its own nuclear weapons
45594.e: The USA stores atomic bombs in some European states, whose aircraft would use them in an emergency. In this way non-nuclear states also share in deterrence.
45594.m: Nuclear sharing involves states without nuclear weapons in deterrence.

45595.q: What task would the German Air Force have in an emergency under nuclear sharing?
a: Delivering US atomic bombs to target with its own aircraft
Deciding alone on a nuclear strike
45595.e: The bombs are believed to be at Büchel air base and remain under American control. In an emergency, German pilots would use them after release.
45595.m: Under nuclear sharing, German aircraft would carry US atomic bombs.

45596.q: Which fighter jet is to replace the Tornado in Germany as the delivery system for nuclear sharing?
45596.e: In 2022 the German government decided to buy F-35As from the USA. The Tornado is outdated and must be replaced.
45596.m: Germany will use the F-35A for nuclear sharing in future.

45597.q: Which NATO member with its own nuclear weapons does not take part in the alliance's Nuclear Planning Group?
45597.e: France wants to decide alone about its nuclear weapons and therefore does not take part in the Nuclear Planning Group. The other members discuss nuclear policy there.
45597.m: France stays away from NATO's Nuclear Planning Group.

45598.q: In peacetime, who has control of the nuclear weapons stored under nuclear sharing?
45598.e: The weapons remain under the guard and codes of American soldiers. Only after release by the US President and NATO approval could pilots from the host countries use them.
45598.m: In peacetime, nuclear sharing weapons stay under American control.

45599.q: What is officially neither confirmed nor denied in nuclear sharing?
a: The exact storage sites of the nuclear weapons
That the USA has nuclear weapons
That Germany is a NATO member
45599.e: According to public estimates, US atomic bombs are stored in Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Italy and Turkey. The governments do not officially confirm this.
45599.m: The storage sites of the nuclear sharing weapons remain officially secret.

45600.q: What does NATO practise every year in the exercise ‘Steadfast Noon’?
a: Nuclear sharing procedures without real warheads
45600.e: In Steadfast Noon, the air forces of several states practise the procedures of nuclear sharing. No real nuclear weapons are used.
45600.m: Steadfast Noon is NATO's annual nuclear exercise.

45601.q: Which event of 2014 was the background to NATO's two percent target?
a: The fall of the Berlin Wall
45601.e: After the annexation of Crimea, the NATO states decided at the Wales summit in September 2014 to raise their defence spending to two percent of GDP.
45601.m: The two percent target was a response to the annexation of Crimea in 2014.

45602.q: Under the 2014 decision, by when were the NATO states to move towards the two percent target?
45602.e: The states committed to moving towards the guideline within a decade. Counting from 2014, that makes 2024.
45602.m: The two percent target was to be reached within ten years.

45603.q: To which figure does NATO's two percent target refer?
45603.e: Defence spending should be at least two percent of annual economic output, that is, gross domestic product. If the economy grows, the amount needed also rises.
45603.m: The two percent target measures defence spending against gross domestic product.

45604.q: According to NATO's 2014 guideline, what should a fixed share of defence spending be used for?
a: Major equipment and research and development
45604.e: Besides the two percent target there is a second guideline: at least 20 percent of spending should go on major weapons systems and research. This is meant to modernise equipment too.
45604.m: A fifth of defence spending should go on equipment and research.

45605.q: Which new spending target did NATO decide on at the summit in The Hague in 2025?
45605.e: The target is made up of 3.5 percent for core defence spending and 1.5 percent for related areas such as infrastructure and resilience. It replaces the previous guideline.
45605.m: Since 2025 NATO has aimed for spending of five percent of GDP by 2035.

45606.q: How large was the special fund that Germany created for the Bundeswehr in 2022?
45606.e: Shortly after the Russian attack on Ukraine, Chancellor Scholz announced the special fund. It was anchored in the Basic Law and is meant to help modernise equipment.
45606.m: In 2022 Germany created a special fund of 100 billion euros for the Bundeswehr.

45607.q: According to NATO estimates, which NATO member had the highest share of defence spending in GDP in 2024?
45607.e: According to NATO, Poland spent about 4.1 percent of its GDP on defence in 2024, putting it ahead of Estonia and the USA. The country is arming heavily because it is close to Russia and Belarus.
45607.m: In 2024 Poland had the highest defence share in NATO.

45608.q: Since when has the former CSCE been called the OSCE?
45608.e: The Budapest summit in December 1994 decided on the renaming, which took effect on 1 January 1995. The conference thus became an organisation with permanent structures.
45608.m: Since 1995 the CSCE has been called the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe.

45609.q: Which CSCE document of 1990 declared the era of confrontation and division in Europe to be over?
45609.e: The Charter of Paris for a New Europe was signed in November 1990. It committed to democracy, human rights and a market economy.
45609.m: In 1990 the Charter of Paris marked the end of the Cold War in Europe.

45610.q: How does the OSCE aim to strengthen trust between the armed forces of its participating states?
a: With information exchange and mutual inspections
With a ban on all military exercises
45610.e: In the Vienna Document, the states commit to exchanging data on their armed forces and allowing inspections. Transparency is meant to prevent misunderstandings.
45610.m: In the OSCE, military transparency is meant to build trust.

45611.q: By what procedure does the OSCE take its decisions?
a: By consensus of all participating states
With a veto only for great powers
45611.e: All decisions must be supported by all participating states. This strengthens legitimacy but can also paralyse the organisation.

45612.q: Which OSCE institution based in Warsaw is best known for election observation?
a: Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights
Representative on Freedom of the Media
45612.e: The office, known as ODIHR, observes elections in participating states and promotes human rights. The High Commissioner on National Minorities is based in The Hague.
45612.m: The OSCE office in Warsaw observes elections.

45613.q: In which country was the OSCE's largest civilian monitoring mission active from 2014 to 2022?
45613.e: The Special Monitoring Mission observed the situation in eastern Ukraine and the ceasefire. It was ended after the Russian attack in 2022.
45613.m: The OSCE monitored the situation in Ukraine from 2014 to 2022.

45614.q: In which phase of the Cold War does the Helsinki Final Act of 1975 fall?
a: The collapse of the Soviet Union
45614.e: The Final Act of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe was signed on 1 August 1975. It was a high point of détente between East and West.
45614.m: The Helsinki Final Act was a high point of détente.

45615.q: Which two non-European states signed the Helsinki Final Act in 1975?
45615.e: Besides 33 European states, the USA and Canada signed, making 35 states in total. In this way both blocs and the neutral states were involved.
45615.m: The USA and Canada also signed the Helsinki Final Act.

45616.q: What legal character does the Helsinki Final Act have?
a: A political declaration of intent without treaty obligation
A ruling of an international court
A resolution of the UN Security Council
45616.e: The Final Act is not an international treaty but a politically binding declaration. Its moral impact was nevertheless great.
45616.m: The Helsinki Final Act is politically but not legally binding.

45617.q: Which part of the Helsinki Final Act became particularly important for opposition figures in the Eastern Bloc?
a: The commitments on human rights and travel
45617.e: The so-called Basket III dealt with family reunification, travel and freedom of information. Civil rights movements later referred to it.
45617.m: Opposition figures in the Eastern Bloc referred to the human rights commitments of Helsinki.

45618.q: Which European state was the only one not to take part in the CSCE in 1975?
45618.e: Communist Albania under Enver Hoxha rejected the conference and isolated itself. It only joined the CSCE in 1991.
45618.m: Albania stayed away from the Helsinki conference in 1975.

45619.q: Which civil rights movement in Czechoslovakia referred to the Helsinki human rights provisions in 1977?
45619.e: Charter 77 called on the government to respect the rights promised in Helsinki. Its spokespeople included Václav Havel.
45619.m: Charter 77 referred to the Helsinki Final Act.

45620.q: In which group did Switzerland take part in the Helsinki conference?
a: Group of neutral and non-aligned states
45620.e: Switzerland, Austria, Sweden, Finland and other states mediated between East and West as a group of neutral and non-aligned countries. Federal President Pierre Graber signed for Switzerland.
45620.m: In Helsinki Switzerland mediated together with other neutral states.

45621.q: Which principle of the Final Act was particularly important for the Soviet Union because it consolidated the post-war order?
45621.e: The Soviet Union wanted the borders drawn in Europe after 1945 to be recognised. In return it accepted provisions on human rights, which opposition figures later used.
45621.m: With Helsinki, the Soviet Union wanted to secure the post-war borders.

45622.q: On which three pillars does the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty rest?
45622.e: Non-nuclear-weapon states renounce nuclear weapons, nuclear-weapon states are to disarm, and all may use nuclear energy peacefully. This bargain is seen as the core of the treaty.
45622.m: The Non-Proliferation Treaty combines non-proliferation, disarmament and peaceful use.

45623.q: Which five states are recognised as nuclear-weapon states in the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty?
a: USA, Russia, Great Britain, France, China
USA, Great Britain, France, Germany, Japan
45623.e: Only those states that had tested a nuclear weapon before 1967 count as nuclear-weapon states. They are also the five permanent members of the UN Security Council.
45623.m: The five recognised nuclear powers are the permanent members of the Security Council.

45624.q: How often are the review conferences of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty held?
45624.e: At the review conferences, the states parties assess how the treaty is being implemented. Several conferences ended without a joint final document.
45624.m: The Non-Proliferation Treaty is reviewed every five years.

45625.q: Which states have nuclear weapons but have never joined the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty?
45625.e: India and Pakistan have carried out nuclear tests, and Israel is regarded as a nuclear power without confirming it. All three have stayed out of the treaty.
45625.m: India, Pakistan and Israel are nuclear powers outside the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

45626.q: What did the states parties decide in 1995 about the duration of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty?
45626.e: The treaty was initially set for 25 years. The Review and Extension Conference of 1995 extended it without a time limit.
45626.m: Since 1995 the Non-Proliferation Treaty has applied indefinitely.

45627.q: Which organisation uses inspections to check that non-nuclear-weapon states use nuclear material only peacefully?
a: Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons
45627.e: The IAEA in Vienna concludes safeguards agreements with states and inspects facilities on site. This is meant to prevent material being diverted for weapons.
45627.m: The IAEA checks the peaceful use of nuclear material.

45628.q: What does Article VI of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty oblige the states parties to do?
45628.e: Article VI calls for negotiations in good faith on ending the arms race and on nuclear disarmament. Critics complain that the nuclear powers do too little to meet this obligation.
45628.m: Article VI obliges states to negotiate on disarmament.

45629.q: Where and when was the New START treaty signed?
45629.e: The treaty was signed in the Czech capital on 8 April 2010 and came into force in February 2011. It limits the strategic nuclear weapons of the USA and Russia.
45629.m: New START was signed in Prague in 2010.

45630.q: Which presidents signed the New START treaty?
a: George W. Bush and Vladimir Putin
45630.e: At the time, the two presidents wanted to revive relations between the USA and Russia. The treaty was seen as a success of this rapprochement.
45630.m: Obama and Medvedev concluded New START.

45631.q: What did the New START treaty limit?
a: The strategic nuclear weapons of the USA and Russia
The number of soldiers in Europe
The nuclear power plants of both countries
45631.e: New START set upper limits for deployed strategic warheads and delivery systems, about 1,550 warheads per side. It was the last major arms control treaty between the two powers.
45631.m: New START limited the strategic nuclear weapons of the USA and Russia.

45632.q: How was compliance with New START checked?
a: Through checks by the Swiss army
Only with statements by the presidents
45632.e: The two states were allowed to inspect the other side's bases and exchanged data. Since Russia suspended its participation in 2023, no more inspections have taken place.
45632.m: New START was checked with mutual inspections.

45633.q: In 2021, until when was New START extended?
45633.e: Shortly before it expired, the USA and Russia agreed in 2021 on the one-time possible extension of five years. On 5 February 2026 the treaty finally expired.
45633.m: New START was extended by five years in 2021.

45634.q: What did Russia announce in February 2023 in connection with New START?
45634.e: President Putin declared that Russia was suspending its participation but not formally withdrawing. Inspections and data exchange no longer took place after that.
45634.m: In 2023 Russia suspended its participation in New START.

45635.q: Why is the expiry of New START in February 2026 seen as a turning point?
a: No treaty limits the nuclear weapons of the USA and Russia any more
Russia had to give up all its nuclear weapons
45635.e: New START was the last treaty limiting the strategic nuclear arsenals of both countries. With its end, binding limits are missing for the first time in decades.
45635.m: With New START, the last nuclear weapons treaty between the USA and Russia expired.

45636.q: In which year was the INF Treaty signed?
45636.e: The treaty was signed in Washington on 8 December 1987. It came into force in 1988.

45637.q: Which two states concluded the INF Treaty on intermediate-range weapons in 1987?
45637.e: Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev signed the treaty in Washington. Land-based missiles with a range of 500 to 5,500 kilometres were banned.
45637.m: The INF Treaty was an agreement between the USA and the Soviet Union.

45638.q: Which intermediate-range weapons systems were covered by the INF Treaty?
a: Systems on land, at sea and in the air
45638.e: The treaty only applied to missiles and cruise missiles launched from the ground. Weapons on ships, submarines and aircraft remained allowed.
45638.m: The INF Treaty only concerned land-based weapons.

45639.q: What was new about the INF Treaty compared with earlier arms control treaties?
a: It abolished an entire category of weapons
It limited nuclear tests for the first time
It banned chemical weapons for the first time
It applied to space weapons for the first time
45639.e: Earlier agreements such as SALT only set upper limits. The INF Treaty required the complete destruction of all systems in one category, with on-site checks.
45639.m: The INF Treaty was the first to eliminate a whole class of nuclear weapons.

45640.q: Which accusation did the USA give as the reason for leaving the INF Treaty in 2019?
a: Russia had developed banned cruise missiles
Russia had carried out nuclear tests
45640.e: The USA accused Russia of breaching the treaty with the 9M729 cruise missile. Russia denied this, and the treaty ended on 2 August 2019.
45640.m: The INF Treaty ended in 2019 after accusations against Russia.

45641.q: The deployment of which Soviet intermediate-range missiles led to the debate over NATO's response in the 1970s?
45641.e: The SS-20 could reach targets all over Western Europe. In 1979 NATO responded with the Double-Track Decision, which provided for negotiations and its own missiles.
45641.m: The Soviet SS-20 triggered NATO's Double-Track Decision.

45642.q: Which American missiles were deployed in West Germany from 1983?
45642.e: After the negotiations failed, Pershing II missiles and cruise missiles were deployed, accompanied by large peace demonstrations. They were removed again because of the INF Treaty.
45642.m: The Pershing II was stationed in West Germany from 1983.

45643.q: Roughly how many missiles were destroyed under the INF Treaty by 1991?
45643.e: By the deadline of 1 June 1991, a total of 2,692 missiles had been destroyed, most of them Soviet. Inspectors monitored the destruction on site.
45643.m: The INF Treaty led to the destruction of about 2,700 missiles.

45644.q: What does the abbreviation MAD stand for in deterrence theory?
45644.e: MAD means mutually assured destruction. Because an attacker would itself be destroyed, no one should start a nuclear war.
45644.m: MAD describes deterrence through mutually assured destruction.

45645.q: What is meant by second-strike capability?
a: The ability to strike back devastatingly after an attack
The ability to intercept missiles in flight
The ability to hit two targets at once
45645.e: Anyone who can still strike back after an enemy first strike makes an attack pointless. Second-strike capability is therefore seen as the core of stable deterrence.
45645.m: Second-strike capability makes a nuclear first strike pointless.

45646.q: Which three components make up the so-called nuclear triad?
45646.e: The triad spreads nuclear weapons across land-based intercontinental missiles, submarine-launched missiles and strategic bombers. This means an enemy cannot knock out all systems at once.
45646.m: The nuclear triad consists of land-based missiles, submarines and bombers.

45647.q: Which US strategy of the 1950s threatened to answer any Soviet attack with an all-out nuclear strike?
45647.e: Secretary of State John Foster Dulles presented the strategy in 1954. It was considered not very credible once the Soviet Union could itself threaten the USA with nuclear weapons.
45647.m: Massive retaliation relied on the threat of a total nuclear strike.

45648.q: Which strategy did NATO adopt in 1967 so that it could respond to attacks in stages?
45648.e: Flexible response provided for answering conventionally, with tactical or with strategic nuclear weapons, depending on the type of attack. This was meant to make the threat more credible.
45648.m: From 1967 NATO relied on flexible response.

45649.q: Why did the USA and the Soviet Union limit their missile defences in the ABM Treaty in 1972?
a: So that mutual deterrence remained stable
Because missile defence was technically impossible
