To save money for space travel
Because the UN had demanded it
45649.e: An effective defence could have allowed one side to risk a first strike. By limiting it, both remained vulnerable and therefore deterred.
45649.m: The ABM Treaty ensured mutual vulnerability.

45650.q: Which Soviet officer correctly judged a missile alert to be a false alarm in 1983?
45650.e: In September 1983 the early warning system reported supposed US missiles. Petrov did not pass the alert on as an attack and so may have prevented a counter-strike.
45650.m: In 1983 Stanislav Petrov may have prevented a nuclear war.

a: A combination of military and non-military means
The use of nuclear weapons only
45651.e: Hybrid warfare combines, for example, disinformation, cyber attacks, economic pressure and covert troops. It often stays below the threshold of open war.
45651.m: Hybrid warfare mixes military and non-military means.

45652.q: What were the soldiers without insignia who appeared in Crimea in 2014 called?
45652.e: The soldiers wore uniforms without markings, and Russia at first denied its involvement. Later President Putin admitted that Russian troops had been deployed.
45652.m: The little green men in Crimea are seen as an example of hybrid warfare.

45653.q: In which city is the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats, founded in 2017, located?
45653.e: The Hybrid CoE was jointly supported by EU and NATO states and set up in the Finnish capital. It researches hybrid threats and advises its members.
45653.m: The Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats is in Helsinki.

45654.q: Which country became the target of massive cyber attacks in 2007 after a dispute over a Soviet war memorial?
45654.e: After the Bronze Soldier was moved, attacks paralysed the websites of the government, banks and media. The case is considered one of the first major cyber attacks on a state.
45654.m: Estonia suffered large-scale cyber attacks in 2007.

45655.q: After which Russian Chief of the General Staff is an often-quoted 2013 article on modern warfare named?
45655.e: Gerasimov described the growing importance of non-military means in conflicts. In the West this gave rise to the controversial term ‘Gerasimov doctrine’.
45655.m: Gerasimov's 2013 article shaped the debate on hybrid wars.

45656.q: In security policy, what is the area between peace and open war, where hybrid actors often operate, called?
45656.e: In the grey zone, actions deliberately stay below the threshold of an armed attack. This makes a clear military response more difficult.
45656.m: Hybrid actors use the grey zone between peace and war.

45657.q: At which border was migration deliberately used as a means of political pressure against the EU in 2021?
a: The border between Belarus and Poland
The border between Serbia and Hungary
The border between Ukraine and Romania
The border between Norway and Russia
45657.e: The Belarusian regime let migrants enter the country and brought them to the borders with Poland and Lithuania. The EU regarded this as a hybrid attack.
45657.m: In 2021 Belarus used migration as a hybrid means of pressure.

45658.q: What did the US Air Force shoot down off the east coast of the USA in February 2023, straining relations with China?
45658.e: The balloon had crossed the American continent for several days, and the USA classified it as a spy balloon. China spoke of a weather balloon blown off course, and the US Secretary of State postponed a trip to China because of it.
45658.m: The balloon incident of 2023 strained relations between the USA and China.

45659.q: Which term coined by political scientist Graham Allison describes the danger of war when a rising power challenges an established power?
45659.e: Allison refers to the ancient historian Thucydides, who explained the Peloponnesian War by the rise of Athens and the fear of Sparta. He applies the image to the relationship between China and the USA.
45659.m: The Thucydides Trap describes the danger of war between a rising and an established power.

45660.q: Which goods were at the centre of the sweeping US export controls on China in October 2022?
45660.e: In October 2022 the USA restricted the export of advanced computer chips and the machines to make them to China. The aim was to slow China's progress in artificial intelligence and military technology.
45660.m: In the technology race with China, the USA relies on export controls for semiconductors.

45661.q: What is the rapprochement between the USA and the People's Republic of China called, which began in 1971 with the visit of an American sports team?
45661.e: In 1971 the US table tennis team travelled to China at its invitation. The visit is seen as having opened the door to the later normalisation of relations.
45661.m: The ping-pong diplomacy of 1971 started the rapprochement between the USA and China.

45662.q: Since when has the USA had official diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China?
45662.e: On 1 January 1979 the USA established diplomatic relations with Beijing. At the same time it broke off official relations with the government in Taipei.
45662.m: The USA has recognised the People's Republic of China diplomatically since 1979.

45663.q: In which year did the People's Republic of China join the World Trade Organization (WTO)?
45663.e: China became a member of the WTO in December 2001. Joining sped up China's rise to become the world's largest exporting nation.
45663.m: China has been a member of the World Trade Organization since 2001.

45664.q: What was the strategic reorientation of US foreign policy towards the Asia-Pacific region under President Barack Obama called?
45664.e: From 2011 the Obama administration shifted its foreign policy and military focus more strongly to Asia. The main background was China's growing power.
45664.m: With the ‘Pivot to Asia’, Obama focused US policy more strongly on Asia.

45665.q: What is the 2022 US law called that supports semiconductor production in the USA with billions in subsidies to reduce dependence on Asia?
45665.e: The law provides about 52 billion US dollars for chip factories and research. It is part of the technology race with China.
45665.m: With the CHIPS and Science Act, the USA supports domestic chip production.

45666.q: Which party withdrew to Taiwan in 1949 after its defeat in the Chinese Civil War?
45666.e: After the victory of the Communists under Mao Zedong, the Kuomintang under Chiang Kai-shek fled to Taiwan. There the Republic of China continued to exist.
45666.m: After 1949 the Kuomintang governed the Republic of China on Taiwan.

45667.q: What happened to China's seat at the UN in 1971?
a: It passed from the Republic of China on Taiwan to the People's Republic of China
It was shared between Taiwan and Beijing
45667.e: With General Assembly Resolution 2758, the People's Republic was recognised as the only lawful representative of China. Taiwan thus lost its seat, including on the Security Council.
45667.m: Since 1971 the People's Republic of China has represented the country at the UN.

45668.q: What does the US Taiwan Relations Act regulate?
a: Unofficial relations and arms supplies for Taiwan's self-defence
A formal defence pact with a duty of assistance
Diplomatic recognition of Taiwan as a state
A free trade agreement between the USA and Taiwan
45668.e: The US law governs relations with Taiwan without official recognition and allows arms supplies for its defence. It contains no explicit duty of military assistance.
45668.m: The Taiwan Relations Act allows the USA to supply arms to Taiwan without a formal alliance.

45669.q: What is the position called that there is only one China, which the People's Republic demands of its diplomatic partners?
45669.e: States that establish diplomatic relations with Beijing must recognise the One-China policy. That is why most countries, including Switzerland, have no official relations with Taiwan.
45669.m: Anyone wanting diplomatic relations with Beijing must accept the One-China policy.

45670.q: Which Taiwanese company is the world's largest contract manufacturer of semiconductors, making Taiwan particularly important economically?
45670.e: TSMC makes a large share of the world's most advanced computer chips. This key role is often called Taiwan's ‘silicon shield’.
45670.m: Taiwan's semiconductor industry makes the island important in world politics.

45671.q: Roughly how wide is the Taiwan Strait at its narrowest point?
45671.e: The strait between mainland China and Taiwan is about 126 kilometres wide at its narrowest point. A military crossing would still be very demanding logistically.
45671.m: The Taiwan Strait is about 130 kilometres wide at its narrowest point.

45672.q: What triggered the so-called Third Taiwan Strait Crisis in 1995/96?
a: Chinese missile tests off Taiwan around the first direct presidential election
A naval battle between Taiwan and Japan
45672.e: China fired missiles into the waters around Taiwan to intimidate the island before the 1996 election. The USA then sent two aircraft carrier groups into the region.
45672.m: The Taiwan crisis of 1995/96 showed how quickly the conflict can escalate militarily.

45673.q: Who has been President of Taiwan since May 2024 (as of 2025)?
45673.e: Lai Ching-te of the Democratic Progressive Party won the election in January 2024. He succeeded Tsai Ing-wen, who had served two terms.
45673.m: Lai Ching-te has been President of Taiwan since 2024.

45674.q: What is the line called with which China claims a large part of the South China Sea?
45674.e: The nine-dash line covers about 90 percent of the South China Sea. It overlaps with the claims of several neighbouring states.
45674.m: China bases its claims in the South China Sea on the nine-dash line.

45675.q: Which country took China to an arbitration tribunal in The Hague, which rejected China's historical claims in 2016?
45675.e: The tribunal under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea sat at the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague and ruled in 2016 that the nine-dash line has no basis in the law of the sea. China does not recognise the ruling.
45675.m: The 2016 arbitration ruling found for the Philippines against China.

45676.q: Which group of islands in the South China Sea is claimed in whole or in part by China, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and Taiwan?
45676.e: No other island group in the region has as many claims as the Spratly Islands. The waters are rich in fish and probably in raw materials.
45676.m: The Spratly Islands are the most disputed island group in the South China Sea.

45677.q: Which shoal has China effectively controlled since a stand-off with the Philippines in 2012?
45677.e: After a weeks-long stand-off between ships of both countries in 2012, Chinese ships stayed at Scarborough Shoal. Filipino fishermen have only had limited access since then.
45677.m: Since 2012 China has controlled Scarborough Shoal.

45678.q: From which state did China capture the Paracel Islands in a short naval battle in 1974?
45678.e: In a battle in January 1974, China drove South Vietnamese troops off the islands. Vietnam still claims the Paracel Islands today.
45678.m: China has controlled the Paracel Islands since 1974.

45679.q: What does the ‘Malacca dilemma’, a term coined by Chinese leader Hu Jintao in 2003, refer to?
a: China's dependence on a narrow strait for oil transport
The dispute over fishing rights off Malaysia
A border conflict between Malaysia and Thailand
The ageing of the Chinese merchant fleet
45679.e: A large part of China's oil imports passes through the Strait of Malacca, which could be blocked in a conflict. This explains China's interest in controlling sea routes and in land routes.
45679.m: The Malacca dilemma describes China's vulnerable energy supply by sea.

45680.q: What did the Philippines deliberately run aground on Second Thomas Shoal in 1999 to secure its claim?
45680.e: The decommissioned landing ship BRP Sierra Madre has since served as an outpost with a small crew. Chinese ships repeatedly obstruct its resupply.
45680.m: On Second Thomas Shoal the Philippines maintains its claim with a stranded ship.

45681.q: With what measure has China greatly expanded its presence in the South China Sea since about 2013?
a: Building artificial islands with military facilities
Laying an undersea cable to Australia
45681.e: China has built up reefs into artificial islands and built harbours, radar facilities and runways on them. Neighbouring states and the USA criticise this militarisation.
45681.m: China is turning artificial islands in the South China Sea into bases.

45682.q: In which year did Xi Jinping announce the New Silk Road initiative?
45682.e: In 2013 Xi Jinping first presented a land corridor and then a maritime route. This grew into China's largest infrastructure programme.
45682.m: The New Silk Road was announced in 2013.

45683.q: Which region of the world serves as the New Silk Road's land bridge between China and Europe?
45683.e: The land routes lead from China through states such as Kazakhstan to Russia, Iran and Europe. It was also there that Xi Jinping first presented the land route in 2013.
45683.m: Central Asia is the land bridge of the New Silk Road.

45684.q: What is the English name of the New Silk Road?
45684.e: In English the initiative is called the Belt and Road Initiative, abbreviated BRI. ‘Belt’ stands for the land routes, ‘Road’ for the sea routes.
45684.m: The New Silk Road is called the Belt and Road Initiative in English.

45685.q: Which G7 country was the only one to join the New Silk Road in 2019 and then withdrew at the end of 2023?
45685.e: In 2019 Italy signed a memorandum of understanding with China, which was criticised by its Western partners. At the end of 2023 Rome did not renew the agreement.
45685.m: From 2019 to 2023 Italy was the only G7 country in the New Silk Road.

45686.q: Which accusation is often made against China in connection with the New Silk Road?
a: It drives poorer countries into a debt trap
It only builds roads in Europe
It gives all buildings away to the UN
It bans the trade in silk
45686.e: Critics say China grants large loans that countries can hardly repay, and so gains influence. A well-known example is the port of Hambantota in Sri Lanka. Experts disagree about this claim.
45686.m: The New Silk Road is criticised because of possible debt traps.

45687.q: Through which country does the New Silk Road economic corridor run that gives China access to the Arabian Sea?
45687.e: The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor connects Xinjiang province with the port of Gwadar. In this way China bypasses the Strait of Malacca.
45687.m: The economic corridor through Pakistan takes China to the Arabian Sea.

45688.q: Which multilateral bank, whose founding members include Switzerland, was set up on China's initiative in 2015?
45688.e: The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, based in Beijing, finances infrastructure in Asia. Switzerland joined it as a founding member, even though the USA was sceptical.
45688.m: Switzerland is a founding member of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.

45689.q: Which German geographer coined the term ‘Silk Road’ in 1877 for the historical trade routes between China and the West?
45689.e: Ferdinand von Richthofen used the term in his work on China. The Chinese initiative deliberately draws on this image.
45689.m: The term Silk Road comes from Ferdinand von Richthofen.

45690.q: Who coined the abbreviation ‘BRIC’ for emerging economies in 2001?
a: The economist Jim O'Neill of Goldman Sachs
The World Bank in an annual report
45690.e: In a study, Jim O'Neill grouped Brazil, Russia, India and China together under the abbreviation BRIC. Only later did the countries form a political group from it.
45690.m: The abbreviation BRIC originally came from a bank economist.

45691.q: In which Russian city did the first summit of the enlarged BRICS group take place in 2024?
45691.e: Russia held the chair in 2024 and invited the members to Kazan. President Putin wanted to show that Russia was not isolated despite sanctions.
45691.m: The 2024 BRICS summit took place in Kazan.

45692.q: Which country joined in 2010/2011 as the fifth member, turning BRIC into BRICS?
45692.e: South Africa was invited at the end of 2010 and took part in a summit for the first time in 2011. This meant Africa was also represented in the group.
45692.m: With South Africa, BRIC became the BRICS group.

45693.q: Where is the New Development Bank of the BRICS states based?
45693.e: The New Development Bank was agreed in 2014 and is based in Shanghai. It is meant to offer an alternative to the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund.
45693.m: The BRICS New Development Bank is based in Shanghai.

45694.q: Which country turned down the 2023 invitation to join BRICS after a change of government?
45694.e: Argentina had been invited in 2023, but the new government under Javier Milei decided not to join. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates joined in 2024.
45694.m: Argentina decided not to join BRICS.

45695.q: In which city did the 2023 BRICS summit decide on the group's first major enlargement?
45695.e: At the summit in Johannesburg, six countries were invited to join. The enlargement took effect on 1 January 2024.
45695.m: The BRICS enlargement was decided in Johannesburg in 2023.

45696.q: Which populous Southeast Asian country became a full member of BRICS in January 2025?
45696.e: In January 2025 Indonesia became the first Southeast Asian country to join BRICS. It is the fourth most populous country in the world.
45696.m: Indonesia has been a member of BRICS since 2025.

45697.q: In which city did the 2025 BRICS summit take place?
45697.e: Brazil held the chair in 2025 and invited the members to Rio de Janeiro in July. The chair rotates annually among the members.
45697.m: The 2025 BRICS summit took place in Brazil.

45698.q: Which NATO member has been an SCO dialogue partner since 2012?
45698.e: Turkey is linked to the SCO as a dialogue partner, even though it belongs to NATO. President Erdoğan has even raised the idea of full membership.
45698.m: Turkey is a NATO state and at the same time an SCO dialogue partner.

45699.q: What was the predecessor group of the SCO called, founded in 1996 to build trust at the borders?
45699.e: The Shanghai Five consisted of China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan. They agreed on disarmament and confidence-building measures along the former Sino-Soviet border.
45699.m: The SCO grew out of the Shanghai Five group.

45700.q: Which two states became full members of the SCO at the same time in 2017?
45700.e: In 2017 the two rivals India and Pakistan joined the SCO. As a result, the organisation represents a large part of the world's population.
45700.m: India and Pakistan have been members of the SCO since 2017.

45701.q: Which two great powers dominate the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation?
45701.e: The SCO was founded in Shanghai in 2001 by China, Russia and four Central Asian states. Later India, Pakistan, Iran and Belarus, among others, joined.
45701.m: China and Russia are the leading powers of the SCO.

45702.q: Which European state became a full member of the SCO in 2024?
45702.e: Belarus was admitted at the 2024 summit in Astana. It is closely allied with Russia.
45702.m: Belarus has been a member of the SCO since 2024.

45703.q: According to its charter, which ‘three evils’ does the SCO want to fight together?
45703.e: Fighting these three evils is a core aim of its security cooperation. Critics complain that the terms can also be used against opposition figures and minorities.
45703.m: The SCO is directed against terrorism, separatism and extremism.

45704.q: Apart from China and Russia, from which region of the world do the founding members of the SCO come?
45704.e: Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan were co-founders of the SCO in 2001. The SCO's anti-terrorism structure is based in Tashkent, the capital of Uzbekistan.
45704.m: The SCO was founded by China, Russia and Central Asian states.

45705.q: When did Ukraine officially receive the status of candidate for membership of the European Union?
45705.e: The European Council granted candidate status to Ukraine and Moldova in June 2022. At the end of 2023 the EU decided to open accession negotiations.
45705.m: Ukraine has been an EU candidate country since June 2022.

45706.q: Which flagship of the Russian Black Sea Fleet sank in April 2022 after Ukrainian fire?
45706.e: According to Ukraine, the missile cruiser Moskva was hit by anti-ship missiles and sank. It was one of the largest losses of a warship since the Second World War.
45706.m: With the Moskva, Russia lost the flagship of its Black Sea Fleet in 2022.

45707.q: Which nuclear power plant, the largest in Europe, did Russian troops occupy in March 2022?
45707.e: The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant has been under Russian control since March 2022. The International Atomic Energy Agency has observers on site.
45707.m: The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant has been occupied by Russia since 2022.

45708.q: In which Swiss city did the Ukraine Recovery Conference on rebuilding Ukraine take place in July 2022?
45708.e: The conference was jointly hosted by Switzerland and Ukraine and was the first to carry the name Ukraine Recovery Conference. Participants adopted principles for transparent reconstruction.
45708.m: The 2022 Ukraine Recovery Conference took place in Lugano.

45709.q: Which four Ukrainian regions did Russia declare annexed in September 2022, in breach of international law?
45709.e: After sham referendums, Russia declared at the end of September 2022 that these four regions had joined it. The UN General Assembly condemned the step by a large majority.
45709.m: Since 2022 Russia has claimed four Ukrainian regions in breach of international law.

45710.q: Which regional capital did Ukraine recapture in November 2022?
45710.e: After a Ukrainian counter-offensive, Russian troops withdrew across the Dnipro. Kherson was the only regional capital Russia had taken in 2022.
45710.m: Kherson was liberated by Ukraine in November 2022.

45711.q: When did the Swiss Federal Council decide to adopt the EU sanctions against Russia?
45711.e: Four days after the war began, the Federal Council adopted the EU sanctions. It considers this compatible with neutrality, as Switzerland does not support any warring party.
45711.m: Since February 2022 Switzerland has adopted the EU's sanctions against Russia.

45712.q: Who brokered the grain deal in July 2022 that allowed exports across the Black Sea?
45712.e: The agreement was signed in Istanbul and allowed grain exports from Ukrainian ports. Russia pulled out again in July 2023.
45712.m: The 2022 grain deal was brokered by the UN and Turkey.

45713.q: On which date did the referendum in Crimea, organised by Russia and not recognised internationally, take place?
45713.e: The referendum was held with Russian soldiers present and without monitoring by independent organisations. A few days later Russia declared that Crimea had joined it.
45713.m: The disputed Crimean referendum took place in March 2014.

45714.q: Which protest movement in Kyiv came directly before the annexation of Crimea?
45714.e: The protests began in November 2013 after the government had put an agreement with the EU on ice. In February 2014 President Yanukovych fled to Russia.
45714.m: In 2014 the Euromaidan led to the fall of President Yanukovych.

45715.q: Which Russian fleet has its main base in Sevastopol in Crimea?
45715.e: Russia had already leased the port of Sevastopol from Ukraine before 2014. The strategic importance of the base is seen as an important motive for the annexation.
45715.m: Sevastopol is the home port of the Russian Black Sea Fleet.

45716.q: Which body adopted Resolution 68/262 on the territorial integrity of Ukraine in March 2014?
45716.e: The General Assembly declared the referendum in Crimea invalid. In the Security Council, a resolution had previously failed because of Russia's veto.
45716.m: In 2014 the UN General Assembly reaffirmed Ukraine's territorial integrity.

45717.q: What consequence did the annexation of Crimea have for Russia's role in the group of leading industrial nations?
a: The G8 became the G7 again without Russia
Russia took over the G20 presidency
Russia became a member of the OECD
The G8 was expanded to include China
45717.e: The other states suspended cooperation with Russia in 2014 and met again as the G7. Russia has not returned since.
45717.m: Because of the annexation of Crimea, Russia was excluded from the G8.

45718.q: Across which strait does the bridge between Russia and Crimea, opened in 2018, run?
45718.e: The Crimean Bridge connects the Taman Peninsula with Crimea and is about 19 kilometres long. It has been the target of Ukrainian attacks several times during the war.
45718.m: The Crimean Bridge spans the Kerch Strait.

45719.q: Under which Soviet leader was Crimea transferred from the Russian to the Ukrainian Soviet Republic in 1954?
45719.e: Within the Soviet Union the transfer was considered an administrative act. When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Crimea became part of independent Ukraine.
45719.m: Crimea became part of Ukraine in 1954 under Khrushchev.

45720.q: In the Budapest Memorandum of 1994, what did Ukraine receive in return for giving up its nuclear weapons?
a: Assurances that its borders would be respected
A permanent seat on the Security Council
45720.e: Russia, the USA and Great Britain gave assurances that they would respect Ukraine's sovereignty and borders. With the annexation of Crimea, Russia broke this assurance.
45720.m: In the Budapest Memorandum, Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons in exchange for security assurances.

45721.q: According to UN estimates, in which year did India overtake China as the most populous country in the world?
45721.e: According to the UN, in spring 2023 India had more inhabitants than China, about 1.43 billion. China's population has been shrinking since 2022.
45721.m: India has been the most populous country in the world since 2023.

45722.q: Which space probe was the first to land near the Moon's south pole in August 2023?
45722.e: With Chandrayaan-3, India became the fourth country to achieve a soft landing on the Moon. Landing near the south pole was a first.
45722.m: In 2023 India, with Chandrayaan-3, was the first country to land near the Moon's south pole.

45723.q: Which organisation was admitted as a permanent member at the 2023 G20 summit in New Delhi?
45723.e: During its presidency, India campaigned for the African Union to be admitted. It likes to present itself as the voice of the Global South.
45723.m: Since 2023 the African Union has been a permanent member of the G20.

45724.q: In which year did India introduce sweeping economic liberalisation because of a balance of payments crisis?
45724.e: Under Finance Minister Manmohan Singh, India opened up its economy in 1991, cut tariffs and reduced licensing rules. This is seen as the start of its strong growth.
45724.m: The economic reforms of 1991 laid the foundation for India's rise.

45725.q: Which country did India overtake in nominal gross domestic product in 2022, becoming the world's fifth largest economy?
45725.e: Measured in US dollars, India's economic output in 2022 exceeded that of its former colonial power. Per head, however, India is still much poorer.
45725.m: In 2022 India overtook Great Britain in gross domestic product.

45726.q: Which Indian prime minister was one of the founders of the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961?
45726.e: Nehru did not want India to be subordinate to either bloc in the Cold War. Today's policy of ‘strategic autonomy’ builds on this tradition.
45726.m: Nehru shaped India's policy of non-alignment.

45727.q: In which border valley did deadly clashes between Indian and Chinese soldiers take place in June 2020?
45727.e: In the Galwan Valley in Ladakh, soldiers on both sides died in fighting without firearms. They were the first deaths on this border in decades.
45727.m: The clash in the Galwan Valley in 2020 sharpened the rivalry between India and China.

45728.q: What did the EFTA states, including Switzerland, sign with India in March 2024?
a: A trade and economic partnership agreement
An agreement on free movement of persons
45728.e: The agreement lowers tariffs and includes the aim that EFTA companies invest 100 billion US dollars in India. It came into force in October 2025.
45728.m: Through EFTA, Switzerland has concluded a free trade agreement with India.

45729.q: Which four states form the Quad security dialogue?
a: USA, Great Britain, Canada and Australia
Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and USA
India, Indonesia, Australia and New Zealand
45729.e: The Quad brings together four democracies in the Indo-Pacific region. It is not a formal military alliance.
45729.m: The Quad is made up of the USA, Japan, India and Australia.

45730.q: Which Japanese prime minister proposed the Quad dialogue in 2007?
45730.e: Shinzō Abe promoted cooperation between the democracies in the Indo-Pacific. He also shaped the idea of a free and open Indo-Pacific.
45730.m: Shinzō Abe is regarded as the intellectual father of the Quad.

45731.q: From which cooperation did the Quad originally emerge?
a: Disaster relief after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami
An alliance against pirates off Somalia
A trade agreement on rare earths
45731.e: After the devastating tsunami, the four states coordinated their navies for the relief effort. This gave rise to the idea of a regular dialogue.
45731.m: The Quad has its roots in the tsunami relief of 2004.

45732.q: Which country temporarily withdrew from the Quad in 2008?
45732.e: The Australian government under Kevin Rudd did not want to strain relations with China. The dialogue then lay dormant for about ten years.
45732.m: Australia temporarily left the Quad in 2008.

45733.q: In which year was the Quad dialogue revived at official level?
45733.e: On the sidelines of an ASEAN summit in Manila in 2017, representatives of the four states met again. The main reason was China's growing assertiveness in the Indo-Pacific.

45734.q: In which year did the first summit of the Quad heads of state and government take place?
45734.e: In March 2021 the four leaders met for the first time by video, and in September 2021 in person in Washington. This gave the Quad much more weight.
45734.m: The first Quad summit took place in 2021.

45735.q: How do the Quad states cooperate militarily, even though the Quad is not an alliance?
a: With a duty of assistance as in NATO
45735.e: Since 2020 all four states have taken part in the Malabar naval exercise. There is no duty of mutual defence.
45735.m: The Quad states train together at sea but are not an alliance.

45736.q: Which three states form the AUKUS pact?
45736.e: The name is made up of the abbreviations AU, UK and US. The pact focuses on security in the Indo-Pacific.
45736.m: AUKUS is a security pact between Australia, Great Britain and the USA.

45737.q: In which year was AUKUS announced?
45737.e: The three leaders announced the pact in September 2021. It came as a surprise to many allies.

45738.q: Which type of weapons system is Australia to receive under AUKUS?
45738.e: Australia is to get submarines with nuclear propulsion but conventional weapons. They can stay under water for a long time and operate far away.
45738.m: Through AUKUS, Australia is getting nuclear-powered submarines.

45739.q: Which country lost a multi-billion submarine contract from Australia because of AUKUS and temporarily withdrew its ambassadors?
45739.e: Australia cancelled a contract for conventional submarines with a French shipyard. France spoke of a breach of trust and recalled its ambassadors from Washington and Canberra.
45739.m: AUKUS caused a diplomatic crisis with France.

45740.q: Why are nuclear-powered submarines militarily particularly attractive for Australia?
a: They can stay submerged for very long and operate far away
They are cheaper than diesel submarines
45740.e: A nuclear power plant hardly ever needs refuelling and needs no air. The boats can therefore stay under water for months, which is important for the huge distances in the Pacific.
45740.m: Nuclear-powered submarines have an almost unlimited range under water.

45741.q: What is the second pillar (‘Pillar II’) of AUKUS about?
a: Jointly developing advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence and quantum technology
A free trade agreement between the three states
Training police forces in the Pacific
45741.e: The first pillar concerns the submarines, the second modern military technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum technology and hypersonic weapons. Other partners such as Japan can take part.
45741.m: The second pillar of AUKUS is for cooperation on future technologies.

45742.q: With which country had the USA already shared its submarine nuclear propulsion technology from 1958?
45742.e: A defence agreement of 1958 gave Great Britain access to this technology. Australia is only the second state with which the USA shares it.
45742.m: Before Australia, the USA had only helped Great Britain with submarine nuclear propulsion.

45743.q: What is meant by a multipolar world order?
a: A system with several roughly equally strong great powers
A system with exactly two superpowers
A system with a single superpower
45743.e: In political science, polarity refers to the distribution of power in the international system. In multipolarity, several centres of power share influence.
45743.m: In a multipolar world there are several great powers.

45744.q: Which commentator coined the term ‘unipolar moment’ in 1990 for the dominance of the USA after the Cold War?
45744.e: Krauthammer wrote that after the collapse of the Eastern Bloc, the USA was left as the only superpower. He expected that this situation would not last for ever.
45744.m: The term unipolar moment comes from Charles Krauthammer.

45745.q: How is the distribution of power between the USA and the Soviet Union in the Cold War described?
45745.e: In the Cold War, two superpowers and their alliance systems faced each other. Most other states aligned themselves with one of the two blocs.
45745.m: The Cold War was a bipolar world order.

45747.q: Which order emerged after the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and is seen as a historical example of a multipolar balance?
45747.e: Great Britain, Russia, Austria, Prussia and later France consulted one another in crises. The system contributed to a relatively long period of peace in Europe.
45747.m: The Concert of Europe was a multipolar balance in the 19th century.

45748.q: In which year did the first summit of the G20 heads of state and government take place?
45748.e: The G20 had existed since 1999 as a meeting of finance ministers. During the financial crisis of 2008, the heads of state and government met for the first time in Washington.
45748.m: Since the financial crisis of 2008, the leaders of the G20 states have met.

45749.q: Which political scientist published a book in 1996 about a ‘clash of civilisations’ after the end of the Cold War?
45749.e: Huntington expected that future conflicts would mainly run along cultural lines. His thesis was widely discussed and criticised.
45749.m: Samuel P. Huntington coined the thesis of the clash of civilisations.

45750.q: How many member states does the Arctic Council, founded in 1996, have?
45750.e: The members are Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Canada, Norway, Russia, Sweden and the USA. In addition, organisations of indigenous peoples are represented as permanent participants.
45750.m: The Arctic Council has eight member states.

45751.q: What role does Switzerland have in the Arctic Council?
45751.e: Only the eight Arctic states are full members. Switzerland has been an observer since 2017 and bases its interest on its polar and glacier research.
45751.m: Switzerland is an observer in the Arctic Council.

45752.q: Why are several states quarrelling over the Arctic seabed?
a: Because of suspected raw materials such as oil and gas
Because of the large freshwater lakes
45752.e: Large deposits of raw materials are thought to lie beneath the Arctic Ocean. That is why states such as Russia, Denmark and Canada claim parts of the seabed as an extension of their continental shelf.
45752.m: Raw materials make the Arctic seabed politically sought after.

45753.q: What did a Russian diving expedition do on the seabed beneath the North Pole in 2007?
a: It placed a Russian flag made of titanium
45753.e: The symbolic act led by Artur Chilingarov caused a stir internationally. It has no legal effect.
45753.m: In 2007 Russia symbolically placed a flag on the seabed at the North Pole.

45754.q: How did China describe itself in its 2018 Arctic white paper?
a: As the protecting power of the Arctic
45754.e: China does not border the Arctic Ocean but claims a say. In the white paper it also speaks of a ‘Polar Silk Road’.
45754.m: China calls itself a near-Arctic state.

45755.q: According to a 2022 study, how much faster than the global average has the Arctic warmed since 1979?
45755.e: The warming is shrinking the sea ice and making shipping routes and raw materials more accessible. This increases geopolitical competition.
45755.m: The Arctic is warming almost four times as fast as the Earth on average.

45756.q: Which state does Greenland belong to?
45756.e: Greenland is an autonomous part of the Kingdom of Denmark. The USA operates an important military base there, Pituffik Space Base.
45756.m: Greenland belongs to the Kingdom of Denmark.

45757.q: What are Canada and the USA arguing about regarding the Northwest Passage?
a: Whether it is Canadian internal waters or an international strait
The position of the land border in Alaska
45757.e: Canada regards the passage as its own waters, while the USA sees it as a strait with free passage. As the ice melts, the question is becoming more important.
45757.m: Canada and the USA disagree about the status of the Northwest Passage.

45758.q: In which city was the first Oslo Accord ceremonially signed on 13 September 1993?
45758.e: The negotiations took place in secret in Norway, but the Declaration of Principles was signed in front of the White House in Washington. There Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat shook hands in the presence of US President Bill Clinton.
45758.m: The Oslo Accord is named after Oslo but was signed in Washington.

45759.q: What is the official name of the first Oslo Accord of 1993?
a: Declaration of Principles on Interim Self-Government
Treaty on the Founding of a State of Palestine
Agreement on the Division of Jerusalem
Peace Treaty between Israel and Jordan
45759.e: Oslo I was a ‘Declaration of Principles’, a framework for an interim Palestinian self-government. It was not a final peace treaty and did not found a state.
45759.m: Oslo I only set out principles for an interim period, not a finished peace.

45760.q: What did the PLO recognise in the letters of mutual recognition of September 1993?
a: Israeli sovereignty over all of Jerusalem
The settlements in the West Bank
The borders of the 1947 UN Partition Plan as final
45760.e: Shortly before the signing, Arafat and Rabin exchanged letters. The PLO recognised Israel's right to exist and renounced violence, and Israel recognised the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people.
45760.m: With Oslo, Israel and the PLO recognised each other for the first time.

45761.q: Which institution was created as a result of the Oslo Accords?
45761.e: The Oslo Accords created a Palestinian self-government, the Palestinian Authority, headed by Yasser Arafat. UNRWA and the Arab League are older, and Hamas was founded independently in 1987.
45761.m: The Palestinian Authority is a result of the Oslo Accords.

45762.q: Into which areas did the Oslo II Accord of 1995 divide the West Bank?
45762.e: In Area A the Palestinian Authority handles civil and security matters, in Area B only civil matters. Area C, the largest part, remained under full Israeli control.
45762.m: Oslo II divided the West Bank into Areas A, B and C.

45763.q: Which three politicians received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1994 for the Oslo peace process?
45763.e: Yasser Arafat, Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres were honoured together in 1994. Begin and Sadat had already received the prize in 1978 for the Egyptian-Israeli peace.
45763.m: The 1994 Nobel Peace Prize went to Arafat, Rabin and Peres.

45764.q: Which event of November 1995 is seen as a severe setback for the Oslo peace process?
a: The outbreak of the Second Intifada
45764.e: On 4 November 1995 an Israeli right-wing extremist shot Prime Minister Rabin after a peace rally in Tel Aviv. Arafat only died in 2004, and the Second Intifada began in 2000.
45764.m: In 1995 Rabin was assassinated by an Israeli opponent of the peace process.

45765.q: Which questions did the Oslo Accords expressly leave for later final status negotiations?
a: Schools, hospitals and police in the Gaza Strip
Customs, currency and trade with Egypt
45765.e: The most difficult points of dispute were to be negotiated within an interim period of five years. These final status negotiations, for example at Camp David in 2000, failed.
45765.m: The big disputed questions such as Jerusalem and refugees remained unresolved at Oslo.

45766.q: Which UN body decided on the partition plan for the British Mandate of Palestine in 1947?
45766.e: On 29 November 1947, with Resolution 181, the General Assembly decided on partition into a Jewish and an Arab state. Jerusalem was to come under international administration.
45766.m: In 1947 the UN General Assembly adopted the partition plan for Palestine.

45767.q: Which line do proposals for a two-state solution usually refer to as the basis for the border?
a: The border of the Ottoman Empire in 1914
The course of the Jordan to the Mediterranean
45767.e: The Green Line arose from the armistice agreements of 1949 and applied until the Six-Day War of 1967. That is why people often speak of the ‘1967 borders’, with possible land swaps.
45767.m: The ‘1967 borders’ correspond to the Green Line of 1949.

45768.q: Which principle is associated with UN Security Council Resolution 242 of 1967?
45768.e: Resolution 242, after the Six-Day War, called for Israel's withdrawal from occupied territories and at the same time recognition of all states in the region. This gave rise to the formula ‘land for peace’.
45768.m: Resolution 242 stands for the principle of ‘land for peace’.

45769.q: Which four actors formed the Middle East Quartet, founded in 2002, which presented the ‘Roadmap’ for a two-state solution?
a: EU, Arab League, Turkey and Iran
UN, NATO, OSCE and World Bank
45769.e: In 2003 the Middle East Quartet presented the ‘Roadmap’, a step-by-step plan towards a Palestinian state alongside Israel. The plan was never implemented.
45769.m: The Middle East Quartet consists of the USA, the EU, Russia and the UN.

45770.q: Which three European states jointly recognised the State of Palestine in May 2024?
45770.e: Spain, Ireland and Norway recognised Palestine on 28 May 2024, citing the goal of a two-state solution. Sweden had already taken this step in 2014.
45770.m: Spain, Ireland and Norway recognised Palestine in May 2024.

45771.q: What status did Palestine receive at the UN in 2012?
a: Permanent member of the Security Council
45771.e: On 29 November 2012 the UN General Assembly upgraded Palestine to an observer state. Full membership would need a recommendation from the Security Council, where the USA has a veto.
45771.m: Palestine has been an observer state at the UN since 2012.

45772.q: Which Arab peace initiative of 2002 offered Israel normal relations if it withdrew to the 1967 lines?
a: The Arab Peace Initiative from Saudi Arabia
45772.e: The initiative proposed by Saudi Arabia was adopted at the Arab League summit in Beirut in 2002. It linked a Palestinian state with all Arab states normalising relations with Israel.
45772.m: The Arab Peace Initiative of 2002 originally came from Saudi Arabia.

45773.q: Which event on 7 October 2023 triggered the Gaza war?
a: A large-scale Hamas attack on Israel
An Israeli air strike on Lebanon
An Iranian missile attack on Tel Aviv
The killing of a Hamas leader in Qatar
45773.e: Armed fighters from Hamas and other groups broke into Israel from the Gaza Strip. It was the day on which the most Jewish people were killed since the Holocaust.
45773.m: The Gaza war began with the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

45774.q: Roughly how many people were killed in Israel in the attack of 7 October 2023?
45774.e: About 1,200 people were killed in the attack, most of them civilians, including many visitors to a music festival. About 250 people were taken to Gaza as hostages.
45774.m: About 1,200 people were killed in Israel on 7 October 2023.

45775.q: Since which year has Hamas controlled the Gaza Strip on its own?
45775.e: Hamas won the Palestinian parliamentary elections in 2006 and drove Fatah out of the Gaza Strip by force in 2007. Since then the Palestinian Authority has governed in the West Bank and Hamas in Gaza.
45775.m: Hamas has ruled the Gaza Strip alone since 2007.

45776.q: Which state filed a genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice in December 2023?
45776.e: South Africa based its case on the Genocide Convention of 1948. The International Court of Justice in The Hague ordered provisional measures in 2024; a ruling on the merits was still pending (as of 2025).
45776.m: In 2023 South Africa took Israel to the International Court of Justice.

45777.q: Against which Israeli politicians did the International Criminal Court issue arrest warrants in November 2024?
45777.e: The court accuses Prime Minister Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Gallant of war crimes, such as using starvation as a method of war. An arrest warrant was also issued against the Hamas military chief Mohammed Deif.
45777.m: The International Criminal Court prosecutes individuals, whereas the International Court of Justice deals with states.

45778.q: Which border crossing connects the Gaza Strip with Egypt?
45778.e: Rafah is the only crossing from Gaza that does not lead to Israel. Erez and Kerem Shalom are on the border with Israel, and the Allenby Bridge connects the West Bank with Jordan.
45778.m: The Rafah crossing leads from Gaza to Egypt.

45779.q: Which three states were the main mediators between Israel and Hamas in the Gaza war?
45779.e: As Israel and Hamas do not negotiate directly, Qatar, Egypt and the USA brokered the ceasefires and the exchange of hostages for Palestinian prisoners.
45779.m: Qatar, Egypt and the USA were the most important mediators in the Gaza war.

45780.q: Roughly how many people lived in the Gaza Strip before the war?
45780.e: About 2 million people lived on only about 360 square kilometres. This made the Gaza Strip one of the most densely populated areas in the world.
45780.m: Before the war about two million people lived in the small Gaza Strip.

45781.q: Which two Arab states were the first to sign the Abraham Accords with Israel on 15 September 2020?
45781.e: The signing took place at the White House, brokered by Donald Trump's administration. Egypt and Jordan had already made peace with Israel in 1979 and 1994.
45781.m: The Emirates and Bahrain were the first to sign the Abraham Accords in 2020.

45782.q: Why are the 2020 accords named after ‘Abraham’?
a: Abraham is seen as the forefather of Jews, Christians and Muslims
They were signed in the town of Abraham in Texas
A US diplomat called Abraham negotiated them
They go back to a plan by Abraham Lincoln
45782.e: The name is meant to emphasise the shared roots of the three Abrahamic religions. Abraham (Ibrahim in Arabic) is revered in Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
45782.m: As their forefather, Abraham links Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

45783.q: Which country joined the Abraham Accords in December 2020 after the USA recognised its claims to Western Sahara?
45783.e: In return for normalising relations with Israel, the USA recognised Morocco's sovereignty over the disputed Western Sahara. Western Sahara is also claimed by the Polisario independence movement.
45783.m: Morocco joined the Abraham Accords, and in return the USA recognised its claims to Western Sahara.

45784.q: Which plan did Israel set aside for the time being in connection with the agreement with the United Arab Emirates?
a: Annexing parts of the West Bank
45784.e: The Emirates justified normalisation by saying that Israel had suspended planned annexations in the West Bank. Israel spoke of a postponement, not a final renunciation.
45784.m: For the deal with the Emirates, Israel suspended annexation plans in the West Bank.

45785.q: Which African country also declared itself ready to join the Abraham Accords in January 2021?
45785.e: Sudan signed a declaration on the Abraham Accords in January 2021, partly because the USA removed it from its list of state sponsors of terrorism. Because of the later war in Sudan, implementation remained open.
45785.m: Sudan also declared in 2021 that it would join the Abraham Accords.

45786.q: Which normalisation, intensively negotiated before October 2023, stalled because of the Gaza war?
45786.e: Before the attack of 7 October 2023, a rapprochement between Israel and Saudi Arabia was considered possible. Since then Saudi Arabia has demanded a credible path to a Palestinian state in return.
45786.m: The Gaza war halted the rapprochement between Israel and Saudi Arabia.

45787.q: Why did many Palestinians criticise the Abraham Accords?
a: Arab states normalised relations without the conflict being resolved
The accords banned Palestinians from travelling
The accords dissolved the refugee agency UNRWA
45787.e: For a long time the Arab League's principle was to recognise Israel only after a Palestinian state existed. The Abraham Accords broke with this order.
45787.m: The Abraham Accords separated normalisation with Israel from the Palestinian question.

45788.q: In which city was the nuclear agreement with Iran (JCPOA) concluded in July 2015?
45788.e: On 14 July 2015 Iran and the group of the five permanent Security Council members plus Germany reached agreement in Vienna. Vienna is also the seat of the International Atomic Energy Agency.
45788.m: The nuclear agreement with Iran was concluded in Vienna in 2015.

45789.q: What was the aim of the 2015 nuclear agreement with Iran?
a: Iran should be unable to build an atomic bomb, and in return sanctions were lifted
Iran had to demolish all its nuclear power plants
Iran was given the right to its own nuclear weapons
45789.e: Iran limited its nuclear programme and allowed inspections. In return, economic sanctions were lifted.
45789.m: The Iran agreement traded nuclear inspections for sanctions relief.

45790.q: What is the group of states called that negotiated the nuclear agreement with Iran?
45790.e: P5+1 stands for the five permanent members of the UN Security Council (USA, Russia, China, Great Britain, France) plus Germany. The EU coordinated the negotiations.
45790.m: P5+1 means the five veto powers plus Germany.

45791.q: What is highly enriched uranium with about 90 percent uranium-235 needed for?
45791.e: Nuclear power plants manage with a few percent of uranium-235. The agreement therefore only allowed Iran low-enriched uranium, far below weapons level.
45791.m: Only very highly enriched uranium is suitable for nuclear weapons.

45792.q: Which organisation monitored compliance with the agreement in Iran?
a: The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW)
45792.e: IAEA inspectors regularly checked Iran's nuclear facilities on site. The OPCW is responsible for chemical weapons, not nuclear programmes.
45792.m: The IAEA in Vienna inspects nuclear facilities around the world.

45793.q: Which US President announced the USA's withdrawal from the nuclear agreement in May 2018?
45793.e: Trump called the agreement inadequate and relied on a policy of ‘maximum pressure’ with new sanctions. The agreement had been negotiated under Obama.
45793.m: Donald Trump took the USA out of the Iran nuclear agreement in 2018.

45794.q: What is the mechanism in the agreement called that allows earlier UN sanctions against Iran to come back into force automatically?
45794.e: Great Britain, France and Germany triggered the snapback in August 2025. At the end of September 2025 the earlier UN sanctions came back into force.
45794.m: The snapback automatically reinstates old UN sanctions.

45795.q: Which Iranian enrichment facility lies deep inside a mountain near Qom and was bombed by the USA in June 2025?
45795.e: Fordow was built so deep under rock that it was meant to be protected against ordinary air strikes. In June 2025 the USA used bunker-busting bombs against it. Bushehr is a nuclear power plant, Arak a heavy water reactor.
45795.m: The Fordow facility lies protected deep inside a mountain near Qom.

45796.q: In which town in southern Syria did the protests begin from which the civil war arose?
45796.e: In Daraa, young people were arrested and tortured for writing anti-government slogans on walls. The protests against this spread across the whole country.
45796.m: The Syrian revolution began in the town of Daraa.

45797.q: Who ruled Syria before Bashar al-Assad?
45797.e: Hafez al-Assad came to power in a coup in 1970 and ruled until his death in 2000. After that his son Bashar took over the presidency.
45797.m: The Assad family ruled Syria for more than fifty years.

45798.q: Who took over the leadership of Syria as interim president after the fall of Assad?
45798.e: Under the nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, Ahmed al-Sharaa was the leader of HTS. In January 2025 he was appointed interim president.
45798.m: Ahmed al-Sharaa has led Syria as interim president since 2025.

45799.q: Which state intervened militarily in the war on Assad's side from September 2015?
45799.e: Russia supported Assad mainly with air strikes and helped him recapture cities such as Aleppo. Iran and the Lebanese Hezbollah also fought on the regime's side.
45799.m: For years Russia, Iran and Hezbollah propped up the Assad regime.

45800.q: Which city did the terrorist militia ‘Islamic State’ declare its capital in Syria?
45800.e: In 2014 IS proclaimed a ‘caliphate’ and made Raqqa its centre. In 2017 the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces captured the city with US support.
45800.m: Raqqa was the Syrian capital of the so-called Islamic State.

45801.q: Which party was Syria's state party during the rule of the Assad family?
45801.e: The Arab nationalist Ba'ath Party had ruled Syria since 1963 and was the Assads' power base. The Muslim Brotherhood, on the other hand, was persecuted.
45801.m: Syria was ruled for decades by the Ba'ath Party.

45802.q: Which contested large city in the north did the Assad regime fully recapture with Russian help in December 2016?
45802.e: Eastern Aleppo had been in rebel hands since 2012 and was besieged and bombed for years. The recapture in 2016 was seen as a turning point in Assad's favour.
45802.m: The battle for Aleppo ended in 2016 with a victory for the regime.

45803.q: What are the volunteers of the Syrian civil defence called, who rescued people buried after bombings?
45803.e: The White Helmets pulled tens of thousands of people out of rubble in rebel areas. Blue Helmets, by contrast, are UN peacekeepers.
45803.m: In the Syrian war the White Helmets rescued people from the rubble.

45804.q: Which rebel group captured the Yemeni capital Sanaa in September 2014?
45804.e: The Houthis, officially Ansar Allah, come from northern Yemen and belong to the Shiite Zaydis. They drove the internationally recognised government out of Sanaa.
45804.m: The Houthis have controlled the capital Sanaa since 2014.

45805.q: Which country led a military coalition against the Houthis in Yemen from March 2015?
45805.e: Saudi Arabia intervened with a coalition of Arab states to support President Hadi's government. The most important partners included the United Arab Emirates.
45805.m: From 2015 Saudi Arabia led a coalition against the Houthis.

45806.q: Which state supports the Houthis politically and militarily?
45806.e: Iran supplies the Houthis with weapons and know-how and counts them as part of its ‘Axis of Resistance’. That is why the Yemen war is also seen as a proxy war between Saudi Arabia and Iran.
45806.m: The Yemen war is also seen as a proxy war between Saudi Arabia and Iran.

45807.q: Which strait did the Houthis make unsafe from the end of 2023 with attacks on merchant ships?
45807.e: Bab al-Mandab connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden. After the Gaza war began, the Houthis attacked ships there, and many shipping companies chose the detour around Africa.
45807.m: From 2023 the Houthis threatened shipping in the Bab al-Mandab.

45808.q: Which city in the south served as the substitute capital of Yemen's internationally recognised government?
45808.e: After losing Sanaa, the government moved its seat to Aden. The separatist Southern Transitional Council, which is supported by the Emirates, is also strong there.
45808.m: Aden is the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government.

45809.q: In which year were North and South Yemen united into one state?
45809.e: The Yemen Arab Republic in the north and the socialist People's Republic in the south united on 22 May 1990. The old divisions between north and south still shape the conflict today.
45809.m: Yemen has been united since 1990, but north and south remain divided.

45810.q: Which port city on the Red Sea was at the centre of the Stockholm Agreement of 2018?
45810.e: A large share of food and aid supplies entered the country through Hodeidah. In the Stockholm Agreement of December 2018, the warring parties agreed a ceasefire for the city under UN mediation.
45810.m: The Stockholm Agreement of 2018 was meant to protect the port of Hodeidah.

45811.q: Which disease spread in war-torn Yemen from 2016 in one of the largest epidemics of recent times?
45811.e: Destroyed water and sewage systems encouraged cholera, and over a million suspected cases were counted. The UN repeatedly called the situation in Yemen one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world.
45811.m: The war in Yemen caused a huge cholera epidemic.

45812.q: Which four states share most of the area where Kurds live?
45812.e: The Kurdish settlement area of Kurdistan stretches across these four states, with most Kurds living in Turkey. The Kurds are often regarded as the largest people without a state of their own.
45812.m: Kurdistan is spread across Turkey, Iraq, Iran and Syria.

45813.q: Which treaty of 1923, signed in a Swiss city, set Turkey's borders without providing for a Kurdish state?
45813.e: The Treaty of Sèvres of 1920 had still held out the prospect of autonomy for the Kurds. The Treaty of Lausanne replaced it in 1923 and no longer mentioned a Kurdish state.
45813.m: With the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923, hopes for a Kurdish state were dashed.

45814.q: Who founded the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) in 1978?
45814.e: From 1984 the PKK waged an armed struggle against the Turkish state. Öcalan was captured in Kenya in 1999 and has since been imprisoned on the prison island of İmralı.
45814.m: Abdullah Öcalan founded the PKK in 1978.

45815.q: Which city is the capital of the Kurdistan Region in Iraq?
45815.e: The Kurdistan Region in northern Iraq has its own government and parliament in Erbil. Its autonomy is anchored in the Iraqi constitution of 2005.
45815.m: Erbil is the capital of the Kurdish region in Iraq.

45816.q: What happened in the Kurdish town of Halabja in Iraq in 1988?
a: A poison gas attack by Saddam Hussein's regime
The proclamation of an independent Kurdistan
45816.e: In the poison gas attack on Halabja in March 1988, several thousand civilians died, according to frequent estimates 3,200 to 5,000. It was linked to the Anfal campaign against the Kurds in Iraq.
45816.m: Halabja stands for the poison gas attack on Kurds in 1988.

45817.q: What was the result of the independence referendum in Iraq's Kurdish region in September 2017?
a: Over 90 percent voted for independence, but it was not implemented
The region was recognised as a new UN state
The referendum was cancelled because of war
45817.e: About 93 percent voted yes, but the Iraqi government, the neighbouring states and most other states rejected the result. Baghdad then recaptured the disputed city of Kirkuk.
45817.m: The 2017 Kurdish referendum produced a clear yes with no consequences for independence.

45818.q: Which step did the PKK announce in May 2025?
a: Its dissolution and the end of the armed struggle
The founding of its own state
45818.e: Following a call from its imprisoned founder Öcalan, the PKK decided to dissolve itself and lay down its weapons. This was meant to end a conflict with Turkey that had lasted over 40 years.
45818.m: In 2025 the PKK decided to dissolve itself.

45819.q: To which state did Nagorno-Karabakh belong under international law, even though most of its inhabitants were Armenian?
45819.e: In the Soviet Union, Nagorno-Karabakh was an autonomous region within Azerbaijan. From 1988 the Armenian majority wanted to join Armenia, which led to the conflict.
45819.m: Under international law, Nagorno-Karabakh belonged to Azerbaijan.

45820.q: In which year did the first Nagorno-Karabakh war end with a ceasefire?
45820.e: In the ceasefire of May 1994, Armenian forces controlled Nagorno-Karabakh and surrounding Azerbaijani areas. Hundreds of thousands of people had been driven out on both sides.
45820.m: The first war over Nagorno-Karabakh ended with a ceasefire in 1994.

45821.q: What did the self-proclaimed Armenian republic in Nagorno-Karabakh call itself from 2017?
45821.e: Artsakh is an old Armenian name for the region. The republic was not recognised by any UN member, not even by Armenia.
45821.m: The Armenians of Nagorno-Karabakh called their republic Artsakh.

45822.q: Which OSCE group was meant to mediate in the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict from 1992?
45822.e: The Minsk Group was jointly led by the USA, Russia and France. In about 30 years it achieved no lasting solution.
45822.m: The OSCE Minsk Group mediated in Nagorno-Karabakh without success.

45823.q: Roughly how long did the second Nagorno-Karabakh war in autumn 2020 last?
45823.e: The war lasted from 27 September to 10 November 2020, when Russia brokered a ceasefire. Azerbaijan recaptured large areas, also with the help of Turkish drones.
45823.m: The second Karabakh war in 2020 lasted only 44 days.

45824.q: What was the only road link between Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh called, which Azerbaijan blocked from December 2022?
45824.e: Because of the blockade of the Lachin corridor, Nagorno-Karabakh lacked food, medicines and fuel for months. It prepared the way for the 2023 offensive.
45824.m: The Lachin corridor was Nagorno-Karabakh's lifeline to Armenia.

45825.q: What followed the Azerbaijani military offensive in Nagorno-Karabakh in September 2023?
a: Almost the entire Armenian population fled to Armenia
A UN peacekeeping force took over the administration
45825.e: After a one-day offensive, the authorities of Artsakh capitulated. Over 100,000 Armenians fled, and the Republic of Artsakh dissolved itself as of 1 January 2024.
45825.m: After the 2023 offensive, almost all Armenians left Nagorno-Karabakh.

45826.q: Where did the leaders of Armenia and Azerbaijan sign a joint peace declaration in August 2025?
a: At the White House in Washington
At the Palais des Nations in Geneva
45826.e: With Donald Trump as mediator, Ilham Aliyev and Nikol Pashinyan agreed on the key points of a peace. These include a transport route through the Armenian province of Syunik.
45826.m: In 2025 Armenia and Azerbaijan agreed key points for peace in Washington.

45827.q: What is meant by the Sahel?
a: A dry transition belt south of the Sahara
The coastal area on the Mediterranean
The tropical rainforest of the Congo
45827.e: The Sahel stretches from the Atlantic to the Red Sea between desert and savannah. States such as Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger suffer there from poverty, droughts and violence.
45827.m: The Sahel is the dry zone on the southern edge of the Sahara.

45828.q: In which country did the crisis begin in 2012 that later spread across the whole Sahel?
45828.e: In 2012 Tuareg rebelled in northern Mali, then jihadist groups took over large areas. From there the violence spread to Burkina Faso and Niger.
45828.m: The Sahel crisis began in Mali in 2012.

45829.q: Which country carried out a major counter-terrorism mission in the Sahel from 2014 with Operation Barkhane?
45829.e: France intervened in Mali in 2013 with Operation Serval and extended it in 2014 into Barkhane, covering the whole Sahel. After tensions with the new military governments, Barkhane ended in 2022.
45829.m: France fought jihadists in the Sahel with Operation Barkhane.

45830.q: Which UN peacekeeping mission ended its deployment in Mali at the end of 2023 at the request of the military government?
45830.e: MINUSMA had been in Mali since 2013 and was considered one of the most dangerous UN missions. MONUSCO is in the Congo, UNIFIL in Lebanon and UNMIK in Kosovo.
45830.m: The UN mission MINUSMA left Mali at the end of 2023.

45831.q: Which three military governments founded the ‘Alliance of Sahel States’ (AES) in 2023?
45831.e: After coups in all three countries, they formed an alliance. At the beginning of 2025 they left the West African economic community ECOWAS.
45831.m: Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger form the Alliance of Sahel States.

45832.q: After France's withdrawal, which state became Mali's most important security partner with the Wagner Group and later the ‘Africa Corps’?
45832.e: From the end of 2021, Mali's military government brought Russian mercenaries of the Wagner Group into the country. In 2025 the Africa Corps, controlled by the Russian Ministry of Defence, took over this role.
45832.m: Russia replaced France as the security partner of Mali's military government.

45833.q: With which terrorist network is the group JNIM, active in the Sahel, linked?
45833.e: JNIM was formed in 2017 as an alliance of several jihadist groups under the umbrella of al-Qaeda. In the Sahel it competes with offshoots of the ‘Islamic State’.

45834.q: Which terrorist group kidnapped about 276 schoolgirls in Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria in 2014?
45834.e: The kidnapping triggered the worldwide campaign ‘Bring Back Our Girls’. Boko Haram is active around Lake Chad in Nigeria, Niger, Chad and Cameroon.
45834.m: In 2014 Boko Haram abducted the schoolgirls of Chibok.

45835.q: Which two groups have been fighting each other in Sudan since April 2023?
a: The army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
45835.e: The Sudanese army under Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the RSF militia under Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, are fighting for power. In 2021 the two had still carried out a coup together.
45835.m: Since 2023 the army has been fighting the RSF militia in Sudan.

45836.q: From which militias did the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) emerge?
a: From the Janjaweed militias in the Darfur conflict
From the bodyguard of the King of Egypt
From the liberation movement of South Sudan
45836.e: From 2003 the Janjaweed were involved in serious crimes in Darfur. Under President Omar al-Bashir they were reorganised into the RSF in 2013.
45836.m: The RSF descend from the Janjaweed of Darfur.

45837.q: Which long-time ruler was overthrown in Sudan in 2019 after mass protests?
45837.e: Omar al-Bashir had ruled Sudan since 1989 and was wanted by the International Criminal Court for crimes in Darfur. After protests, the military removed him in April 2019.
45837.m: Omar al-Bashir was overthrown in 2019 after thirty years in power.

45838.q: Which statement about displacement in the Sudan war is correct (as of 2025)?
a: Sudan has the largest displacement crisis in the world
The displacement only affects the capital
45838.e: According to the UN, over 12 million people have been displaced inside and outside the country. Many fled to neighbouring countries such as Chad, Egypt and South Sudan.
45838.m: The war in Sudan has caused the largest displacement crisis in the world.

45839.q: Which western Sudanese region is particularly badly affected by violence against civilians by the RSF?
45839.e: In Darfur there were massacres of population groups such as the Masalit. In October 2025 the RSF captured the city of El Fasher, the army's last major stronghold in Darfur.
45839.m: Darfur is once again the scene of serious violence against civilians.

45840.q: Where did the Sudanese army government move its seat because of the fighting in Khartoum?
45840.e: Port Sudan lies on the Red Sea, far from the main combat areas. Juba is the capital of South Sudan, which has been independent since 2011.
45840.m: Sudan's army government is based in Port Sudan on the Red Sea.

45841.q: What did a famine review committee find for the Zamzam camp in Darfur in August 2024?
45841.e: The committee of the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) confirmed famine in the Zamzam refugee camp near El Fasher. Siege and blocked aid deliveries are seen as the main causes.
45841.m: In the Sudan war, a famine was officially declared in 2024.

45842.q: Which state is often accused by experts and the UN of supporting the RSF with weapons?
45842.e: UN expert reports and investigations point to arms deliveries to the RSF via neighbouring countries. The United Arab Emirates denies the accusations.
45842.m: Outside powers are prolonging the war in Sudan through arms supplies.

45843.q: Which rebel group captured the city of Goma in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo in January 2025?
45843.e: M23 took Goma, the capital of North Kivu province, in January 2025 and in February also Bukavu in South Kivu. The FDLR is an opposing Hutu militia.
45843.m: In 2025 M23 captured the cities of Goma and Bukavu.

45844.q: Which neighbouring country is accused by the UN of supporting M23?
45844.e: UN experts reported Rwandan troops and weapons with M23. Rwanda justifies its actions with the threat from the Hutu militia FDLR in the Congo.
45844.m: Rwanda is accused of supporting the M23 rebels.

45845.q: Where does the rebel group M23 get its name from?
a: From a peace agreement of 23 March 2009
From the 23rd province of the Congo
45845.e: M23 stands for ‘Mouvement du 23 mars’. The rebels accused the government of not keeping to the agreement of 23 March 2009.
45845.m: M23 is named after the agreement of 23 March 2009.

45846.q: Which event in a neighbouring country in 1994 triggered a refugee movement that still destabilises the eastern Congo today?
a: The fall of Gaddafi in Libya
45846.e: After the genocide against the Tutsi, over a million Hutu, including many perpetrators, fled into the eastern Congo. This gave rise to armed groups such as the FDLR and to the Congo wars.
45846.m: The 1994 genocide in Rwanda is one root of the conflict in the eastern Congo.

45847.q: Which raw materials play a major role in the conflict in the east of the DR Congo?
45847.e: Armed groups finance themselves through mining and smuggling minerals. Coltan provides tantalum, which is used in capacitors in mobile phones and computers.
45847.m: Coltan from the eastern Congo is found in many mobile phones.

45848.q: What is the UN peacekeeping mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo called?
45848.e: MONUSCO has been deployed since 2010 and grew out of the older mission MONUC. It is one of the UN's largest peacekeeping missions.
45848.m: MONUSCO is the UN peacekeeping mission in the Congo.

45849.q: Which Congolese doctor from Bukavu received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2018 for his help for women who became victims of violence in war?
45849.e: At Panzi Hospital in Bukavu, Denis Mukwege treats thousands of women who were seriously injured in the war. He shared the prize with the Yazidi Nadia Murad.
45849.m: Denis Mukwege received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2018.

45850.q: Which term is used for the Second Congo War of 1998 to 2003 because many states were involved in it?
45850.e: The states involved in the Second Congo War included Rwanda, Uganda, Angola, Zimbabwe and Namibia. Millions of people died through violence, hunger and disease.
45850.m: The Second Congo War is also called Africa's World War.

45851.q: What did UN Security Council Resolution 47 of 1948 call for in Kashmir?
a: A plebiscite on which country it should belong to
45851.e: The resolution provided for the people of Kashmir to decide in a plebiscite whether to join India or Pakistan. This vote never took place.
45851.m: The promised plebiscite on Kashmir was never held.

45852.q: Since which event have India and Pakistan been quarrelling over Kashmir?
a: Since the partition of British India in 1947
Since the end of the First World War
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union
Since the founding of Bangladesh in 1971
45852.e: India and Pakistan came into being at independence in 1947. The ruler of Kashmir joined India, after which the first war over the area broke out. Since 1949 a UN mission has monitored the ceasefire line.
45852.m: The Kashmir conflict began with the partition of British India in 1947.

45853.q: What step did the Indian government take in Kashmir on 5 August 2019?
a: It revoked the special status under Article 370
It handed Kashmir over to Pakistan
45853.e: Article 370 of the Indian constitution had granted Jammu and Kashmir far-reaching autonomy. After it was revoked, the state was divided into two union territories governed directly from Delhi.
45853.m: In 2019 India revoked Kashmir's autonomy under Article 370.

45854.q: Besides Gilgit-Baltistan, what does Pakistan call the part of Kashmir it administers?
45854.e: ‘Azad’ means ‘free’. India, on the other hand, calls the area Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. Ladakh and Jammu belong to the Indian part.
45854.m: Azad Kashmir is the part of Kashmir administered by Pakistan.

45855.q: What was India's military operation of May 2025 after the terrorist attack in Pahalgam called?
45855.e: In the attack in April 2025, gunmen killed 26 people in Pahalgam, most of them tourists. India then attacked targets in Pakistan, and after a few days of mutual attacks a ceasefire followed.
45855.m: After the Pahalgam attack, India attacked Pakistan in 2025 with Operation Sindoor.

45856.q: Which agreement of 1960 governs the use of the water of the Indus and its tributaries between India and Pakistan?
45856.e: The Indus Waters Treaty was concluded with World Bank mediation and survived several wars. After a terrorist attack in Kashmir in April 2025, India suspended it.
45856.m: The Indus Waters Treaty of 1960 divides the rivers between India and Pakistan.

45857.q: With which declaration did the second war over Kashmir end in 1966, with the Soviet Union as mediator?
45857.e: After the war of 1965, Indian Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri and Pakistani President Ayub Khan met in Tashkent. Both sides withdrew their troops to the pre-war lines.
45857.m: The Kashmir war of 1965 ended with the Tashkent Declaration.

45858.q: Which organisation was replaced by the African Union in 2002?
45858.e: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) had been founded in Addis Ababa in 1963. In 2002 in Durban it was replaced by the African Union, which focuses more on integration and conflict resolution.
45858.m: The African Union is the successor to the Organisation of African Unity.

45859.q: What is the task of the African Union's Peace and Security Council?
a: To prevent and resolve conflicts in Africa
To set tariffs in the African single market
To elect the judges of the International Criminal Court
To manage a common African currency
45859.e: The council was set up in 2004. It can decide on peace missions and suspend states after a coup.
45859.m: The AU Peace and Security Council deals with conflicts in Africa.

45860.q: Which country left the AU's predecessor organisation in 1984 and only returned in 2017?
45860.e: Morocco left the OAU in 1984 because the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (Western Sahara) had been admitted. In January 2017 Morocco became a member of the African Union again.
45860.m: Morocco returned to the African Union in 2017 after more than thirty years away.

45861.q: What step did the African Union achieve on the international stage in September 2023?
a: A permanent seat on the UN Security Council
45861.e: At the summit in New Delhi, the AU was admitted as a permanent member of the Group of Twenty. Before that, only one African state, South Africa, had been represented.
45861.m: Since 2023 the African Union has had a permanent seat at the G20 table.

45862.q: What does the African Union usually do when the military stages a coup in a member state?
a: It expels the country for ever
It takes over the country's government itself
It moves its headquarters to the country
45862.e: The AU rejects unconstitutional changes of government. In recent years, for example, Mali, Guinea, Burkina Faso and Niger were suspended after coups.
45862.m: After a coup, the AU suspends the country concerned.

45863.q: What is the idea of unity and solidarity among all Africans, to which the African Union refers, called?
45863.e: Pan-Africanism arose in the 19th and 20th centuries as a response to slavery and colonial rule. It shaped the founding of the OAU and later the AU.
45863.m: The African Union stands in the tradition of Pan-Africanism.

45864.q: What is the aim of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA)?
a: A common market with fewer tariffs in Africa
A common army for the whole of Africa
A single official language for Africa
45864.e: The free trade area is meant to reduce tariffs between African states and strengthen trade within the continent. Trading under the agreement began in 2021.
45864.m: The AfCFTA is meant to make trade between African states easier.

45866.q: With which treaty was the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) founded in 1975?
45866.e: On 28 May 1975, 15 West African states signed the founding treaty in Lagos. The aim was the economic integration of the region.
45866.m: ECOWAS was founded in 1975 with the Treaty of Lagos.

45867.q: In which city is the ECOWAS Commission based?
45867.e: The ECOWAS Commission is in Abuja, the capital of Nigeria. The Community Court of Justice is also based there.
45867.m: ECOWAS is run from Abuja in Nigeria.

45868.q: Which three states left ECOWAS in January 2025?
45868.e: The three Sahel states led by military governments had announced their withdrawal in January 2024. It took effect a year later, in January 2025.
45868.m: Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger left ECOWAS in 2025.

45869.q: What is the confederation called that three Sahel states led by military governments founded in Niamey in July 2024?
45869.e: The Alliance of Sahel States (AES) was formed in 2023 as a defence alliance and was developed into a confederation in Niamey in July 2024. It is seen as a rival model to ECOWAS.
45869.m: Three Sahel states under military rule form the Alliance of Sahel States.

45870.q: In which country did the ECOWAS force ECOMOG first intervene militarily in 1990?
45870.e: The ECOWAS Monitoring Group was sent into the Liberian civil war in 1990. It was one of the first peacekeeping missions in Africa by a regional economic organisation.
45870.m: The ECOMOG force was first deployed in Liberia in 1990.

45871.q: What was the aim of the ECOWAS intervention in the Gambia in January 2017?
