a: To enforce the handover of power to the election winner
To end a border conflict with Senegal
To fight pirates on the coast
45871.e: President Yahya Jammeh refused to step down after losing the election. Under pressure from ECOWAS troops he left the country, and Adama Barrow took office.
45871.m: In 2017 ECOWAS enforced a peaceful change of power in the Gambia after an election.

45872.q: What is the long-planned common currency of ECOWAS to be called?
45872.e: For decades ECOWAS has pursued the project of a single currency called the Eco. Its introduction has been postponed several times.
45872.m: West Africa's planned common currency is called the Eco.

45873.q: Which country left ECOWAS in 2000 and has not been a member since?
45873.e: Mauritania left in 2000 and turned more towards the Arab Maghreb Union. Later it concluded an association agreement with ECOWAS.
45873.m: Mauritania has not belonged to ECOWAS since 2000.

45874.q: What was the main aim of the SADC's predecessor organisation, founded in 1980?
a: Less dependence on apartheid South Africa
Defence against the colonial power Portugal
45874.e: SADCC was founded in Lusaka in 1980 to reduce economic dependence on apartheid South Africa. In 1992 it was turned into SADC.
45874.m: SADC's predecessor wanted to reduce dependence on the apartheid state.

45875.q: In which city was the treaty founding SADC signed in 1992?
45875.e: The SADC Treaty was signed in the Namibian capital Windhoek on 17 August 1992. Since then 17 August has been SADC Day.
45875.m: SADC was founded in Windhoek in 1992.

45876.q: Where is the SADC Secretariat located?
45876.e: The SADC Secretariat is based in Gaborone, the capital of Botswana. The community's programmes are coordinated from there.
45876.m: The SADC Secretariat is in Gaborone in Botswana.

45877.q: When did South Africa join SADC?
a: In 1994, after the end of apartheid
In 1992, at the signing in Windhoek
45877.e: The apartheid regime was the very reason the predecessor organisation was founded. Only after the first free elections in 1994 did South Africa become a member.
45877.m: South Africa only became a member of SADC after the end of apartheid in 1994.

45878.q: Which island state was admitted to SADC in 2017 as its 16th member?
45878.e: The Comoros became a full member of SADC in 2017. Madagascar, Mauritius and the Seychelles had already joined earlier.
45878.m: The Comoros have been a member of SADC since 2017.

45879.q: Why was the SADC Tribunal suspended in 2010?
a: After rulings against Zimbabwe's land reform
Because of a dispute over its seat in Gaborone
Because there were not enough judges
After a corruption scandal in the secretariat
45879.e: The tribunal had ruled in favour of white farmers against expropriations in Zimbabwe. Zimbabwe refused to implement the rulings, and the heads of state then shut the court down.
45879.m: The SADC Tribunal was shut down after rulings against Zimbabwe.

45880.q: In which province of Mozambique did SADC deploy a military mission against insurgents from 2021?
45880.e: From 2021 the SADC Mission in Mozambique (SAMIM) supported the government against Islamist insurgents in the north. It ended in 2024.
45880.m: From 2021 SADC fought insurgents in Cabo Delgado.

45881.q: Which group of states formed the political core when SADC's predecessor organisation was founded?
a: The members of the Southern African Customs Union
45881.e: The Frontline States, such as Tanzania, Zambia, Botswana, Mozambique and Angola, supported liberation movements in southern Africa. Their cooperation gave rise to SADCC in 1980.
45881.m: The Frontline States against apartheid laid the foundation for SADC.

45882.q: With which document was the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) founded in 1967?
45882.e: On 8 August 1967 the foreign ministers of five states signed the Bangkok Declaration. A legally binding founding treaty only followed with the Charter of 2008.
45882.m: ASEAN was founded in 1967 with the Bangkok Declaration.

45883.q: Which state was NOT one of the five founding members of ASEAN?
45883.e: The founding members were Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. Vietnam only joined in 1995.
45883.m: Vietnam has only been a member of ASEAN since 1995.

45884.q: In which city is the ASEAN Secretariat located?
45884.e: The ASEAN Secretariat was set up in 1976 and is based in the Indonesian capital Jakarta.
45884.m: The ASEAN Secretariat is in Jakarta.

45885.q: Which state was admitted to ASEAN in October 2025 as its eleventh member?
45885.e: East Timor (Timor-Leste) became a full member at the summit in Kuala Lumpur in October 2025. It was the first enlargement since Cambodia was admitted in 1999.
45885.m: Since 2025 East Timor has been the eleventh member of ASEAN.

45886.q: Which principles characterise the so-called ‘ASEAN Way’?
45886.e: The ASEAN states traditionally decide unanimously and do not interfere in each other's internal affairs. Critics see this as a weakness, for example in dealing with Myanmar.
45886.m: The ASEAN Way is based on consensus and non-interference.

45887.q: Which free trade agreement, in force since 2022, links ASEAN with China, Japan and Australia, among others?
a: Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific
45887.e: RCEP was signed by 15 states in 2020 and came into force on 1 January 2022. It is considered the largest free trade area in the world by population and economic output.
45887.m: RCEP links ASEAN with China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand.

45888.q: Since when has ASEAN had its own legal personality thanks to its charter?
45888.e: The ASEAN Charter came into force in December 2008. It made the association an intergovernmental organisation with legal personality.
45888.m: Since its Charter of 2008, ASEAN has been a legal person in its own right.

45889.q: What is the plan called that ASEAN adopted in April 2021 after the military coup in Myanmar?
45889.e: The Five-Point Consensus called, among other things, for an end to violence, dialogue among all parties and humanitarian aid. The military government hardly implemented it.
45889.m: After the coup in Myanmar, ASEAN adopted a Five-Point Consensus in 2021.

45890.q: Which treaty established the Southern Common Market (Mercosur) in 1991?
45890.e: Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay signed the Treaty of Asunción on 26 March 1991. It provided for a common market.
45890.m: Mercosur was founded in 1991 with the Treaty of Asunción.

45891.q: Which four states founded Mercosur in 1991?
45891.e: The four states signed the Treaty of Asunción in 1991. Later Venezuela (now suspended) and Bolivia joined.
45891.m: Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay founded Mercosur.

45892.q: In which city is the Mercosur Secretariat based?
45892.e: The secretariat and the Mercosur Parliament (Parlasur) are in the Uruguayan capital Montevideo.
45892.m: The Mercosur Secretariat is in Montevideo.

45893.q: Which country became a full member of Mercosur in July 2024?
45893.e: Bolivia had begun the accession process in 2015. At the summit in Asunción in July 2024 it was formally admitted as the fifth active full member.
45893.m: Bolivia has been a full member of Mercosur since 2024.

45894.q: What status do Chile, Colombia and Peru have in relation to Mercosur?
45894.e: Associated states take part in meetings and have trade agreements with Mercosur but do not belong to the customs union. They include several South American states.
45894.m: Chile, Colombia and Peru are associated with Mercosur but are not full members.

45895.q: Why was Paraguay temporarily suspended from Mercosur in 2012?
a: Because of the impeachment of President Lugo
Because of a border war with Bolivia
Because of a trade dispute with Brazil
45895.e: The other members considered the swift removal of Fernando Lugo a breach of the democratic order. After the 2013 elections Paraguay took full part again.
45895.m: Paraguay was suspended in 2012 after President Lugo was removed.

45896.q: When and where did the EFTA states, including Switzerland, sign their free trade agreement with Mercosur?
45896.e: Negotiations were concluded in July 2025, and the signing followed on 16 September 2025 in Rio de Janeiro. For Switzerland the agreement still needs approval by parliament.
45896.m: Switzerland signed the free trade agreement with Mercosur in 2025 as part of EFTA.

45897.q: Where were the negotiations on the partnership agreement between the EU and Mercosur concluded in December 2024?
45897.e: After about 25 years of negotiations, the European Commission and the Mercosur states announced the conclusion at the summit in Montevideo. Farmers in Europe in particular criticised the agreement.
45897.m: The agreement between the EU and Mercosur was negotiated in Montevideo in 2024.

45898.q: What is the main aim of the Andean Community?
a: Economic integration and free trade among its members
A common army of the Andean states
Protecting the glaciers in the Andes
A common currency like the euro
45898.e: The Andean Community began in 1969 as the Andean Pact. It has created a free trade area and wants to link its members' economies more closely.
45898.m: The Andean Community promotes trade between the Andean states.

45899.q: Which four states are full members of the Andean Community (as of 2025)?
45899.e: Several former members have left over the decades. Today four states form the community, and further states are associated.
45899.m: Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia and Peru form the Andean Community.

45900.q: Which South American economic bloc, which includes Brazil and Argentina, is often compared with the Andean Community?
45900.e: Mercosur was founded in 1991 and is the largest economic bloc in South America. The Andean Community and Mercosur work together in some areas.
45900.m: Besides the Andean Community, Mercosur is South America's most important economic bloc.

45901.q: Which country announced its withdrawal from the Andean Community in 2006?
45901.e: President Hugo Chávez justified the withdrawal with the free trade agreements that Colombia and Peru had made with the USA.
45901.m: Venezuela turned its back on the Andean Community in 2006.

45902.q: In which city is the General Secretariat of the Andean Community based?
45902.e: The General Secretariat, the executive body, is in the Peruvian capital Lima.
45902.m: The General Secretariat of the Andean Community is in Lima.

45903.q: What is the task of the Court of Justice of the Andean Community?
a: It gives binding interpretations of community law
It replaces the national constitutional courts
It elects the presidents of the member states
45903.e: The Andean Court ensures that the common rules are applied in the same way in all member states. Its rulings are binding, but the national courts continue to exist.
45903.m: The Andean Court interprets the law of the Andean Community.

45904.q: With what can citizens of the Andean Community travel between the member states?
a: With their identity card, without a passport
With a common Andean passport as the only document
45904.e: Within the Andean Community, a national identity card is enough for travel. This is meant to make exchange between the countries easier.
45904.m: In the Andean Community you travel with your identity card.

45905.q: Which states belong to the Organization of American States?
a: States of North, Central and South America and the Caribbean
Only the states of South America
The USA and its allies in Europe
45905.e: The OAS was founded in 1948 and brings together states from the whole American continent, including the USA, Canada and Brazil. Its forerunner was the Pan-American Union.
45905.m: The OAS unites states from all over the Americas.

45906.e: The OAS General Secretariat is based in Washington, D.C. The Permanent Council also meets there.
45906.m: The OAS headquarters is in Washington, D.C.

45907.q: Which country was excluded from taking part in the OAS in 1962?
45907.e: After the revolution and its rapprochement with the Soviet Union, Cuba's government was excluded at Punta del Este in 1962. The decision was lifted in 2009, but Cuba did not return.
45907.m: Cuba was excluded from taking part in the OAS in 1962.

45908.q: What can the OAS do if democracy is abolished by force in a member state?
a: Exclude the state from taking part
Remove the head of state itself
45908.e: The Inter-American Democratic Charter of 2001 allows a state to be suspended after a breach of the democratic order. This needs a two-thirds majority.
45908.m: The OAS can exclude states after a breach of democracy.

45909.q: Where is the Inter-American Court of Human Rights based?
45909.e: The court was set up in San José in 1979. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, on the other hand, works in Washington.
45909.m: The Inter-American Court of Human Rights sits in San José.

45910.q: Which country completed its withdrawal from the OAS in November 2023?
45910.e: Nicaragua had announced its withdrawal in 2021 after the OAS criticised its elections. After the two-year notice period, it took effect in November 2023.

45911.q: Which member state pays the largest share of the OAS budget?
45911.e: The USA pays about half of the OAS's regular contributions. The headquarters is also in Washington.
45911.m: The USA is the largest funder of the OAS.

45912.q: What status does Switzerland have in the Organization of American States?
45912.e: Switzerland is one of about 70 states with permanent observer status. It can take part in meetings but cannot vote.
45912.m: Switzerland is a permanent observer at the OAS.

45913.q: Unlike CELAC, which organisation also includes the USA and Canada?
a: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)
45913.e: Almost all states of the Americas are represented in the OAS, including the USA and Canada. CELAC, founded in 2011, was deliberately created without these two countries.
45913.m: Unlike the OAS, CELAC includes neither the USA nor Canada.

45914.q: Which two states of the Americas do not belong to CELAC?
45914.e: CELAC includes all 33 states of Latin America and the Caribbean. The USA and Canada are deliberately not part of it, unlike in the OAS.
45914.m: Only the USA and Canada are missing from CELAC.

45915.q: How many member states does CELAC have?
45915.e: All independent states of Latin America and the Caribbean are members, 33 countries in total.

45916.q: What is an important aim of CELAC?
a: To strengthen cooperation in Latin America and the Caribbean
To form a military alliance against Europe
To prepare for joining the EU
45916.e: CELAC is a forum for political coordination. It wants the region to act together more strongly, without the USA and Canada.
45916.m: CELAC is meant to strengthen cooperation in Latin America and the Caribbean.

a: By a presidency that changes every year
By a permanent secretariat in Panama
By a council of the five largest states
45917.e: CELAC has no permanent secretariat. One member state takes over the pro tempore presidency each time, for example Colombia in 2025.
45917.m: CELAC is led by a rotating pro tempore presidency.

45918.q: Which country suspended its participation in CELAC from 2020 to 2023?
45918.e: Under President Jair Bolsonaro, Brazil withdrew in 2020. After Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva took office, it returned in 2023.
45918.m: Brazil paused its participation in CELAC under President Bolsonaro.

45919.q: With which partner did CELAC hold a summit in Brussels in July 2023 for the first time in eight years?
45919.e: The EU-CELAC summit in Brussels was the first meeting of its kind since 2015. It was meant to revive relations between Europe and Latin America.
45919.m: In 2023 CELAC met the EU for a summit in Brussels.

45920.q: In which city is the Arab League based?
45920.e: The General Secretariat is in the Egyptian capital Cairo. Only from 1979 to 1990 was it temporarily in Tunis.
45920.m: The Arab League is based in Cairo.

45921.q: Which state was suspended from the Arab League in 1979 because of its peace treaty with Israel?
45921.e: In 1979, after the Camp David Accords, Egypt made peace with Israel. The other members then suspended it until 1989.
45921.m: Egypt was temporarily excluded from the Arab League because of its peace with Israel.

45922.q: How many members does the Arab League have (as of 2025)?
45922.e: The Arab League has 22 members, from Morocco to Oman, including Palestine.

45923.q: When was Syria readmitted to the Arab League after its suspension?
45923.e: Syria had been suspended in November 2011 because of the violent crackdown on protests. It returned in May 2023, and Bashar al-Assad attended the summit in Jeddah.
45923.m: Syria was readmitted to the Arab League in 2023.

45924.q: What did the Arab Peace Initiative of 2002 offer Israel?
a: Normal relations in return for withdrawal to the 1967 borders
A trade treaty in return for oil supplies
A seat in the Arab League
45924.e: The initiative, adopted at the summit in Beirut, held out the prospect of normal relations with Israel. In return Israel was to withdraw to the 1967 borders and a Palestinian state was to be created.
45924.m: The Arab Peace Initiative of 2002 linked recognition with a withdrawal to the 1967 borders.

45925.q: Unlike the Arab League, which organisation also includes non-Arab Muslim states such as Turkey, Iran and Indonesia?
45925.e: The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) has 57 member states on several continents. The Arab League, by contrast, includes only Arab states.
45925.m: Non-Arab Muslim states are also represented in the OIC.

45926.q: What decision did the Arab League take on Libya in March 2011?
a: It called for a no-fly zone
It moved its headquarters to Tripoli
45926.e: The League had already suspended Libya and asked the UN Security Council for a no-fly zone. This contributed to Resolution 1973.
45926.m: In 2011 the Arab League supported a no-fly zone over Libya.

45927.q: Which of these countries is a member of the Gulf Cooperation Council, which links six Arab states on the Persian Gulf?
45927.e: The Gulf Cooperation Council consists of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman. It was founded in 1981, and all its members are also in the Arab League.
45927.m: Qatar is one of the six states of the Gulf Cooperation Council.

45928.q: Which event of 1979 gave an important push to the founding of the Gulf Cooperation Council?
45928.e: After the revolution in Iran, the Gulf monarchies feared it might spread to their countries. Together with the war between Iran and Iraq, this led to the founding of the council in 1981.
45928.m: The Iranian Revolution pushed the Gulf monarchies into cooperation.

45929.q: Which joint project of the Gulf Cooperation Council has still not been realised?
45929.e: A Gulf currency was planned for a long time, but Oman and the United Arab Emirates pulled out. A customs union (2003), a common market (2008) and the General Secretariat in Riyadh, on the other hand, do exist.
45929.m: There is still no common Gulf currency today.

45930.q: In which city is the General Secretariat of the Gulf Cooperation Council located?
45930.e: The council's General Secretariat is based in the Saudi capital Riyadh.
45930.m: The General Secretariat of the Gulf Cooperation Council is in Riyadh.

45931.q: What did the Gulf Cooperation Council introduce in January 2008?
45931.e: The Gulf Common Market was meant to give citizens of the member states equal rights to work, live and invest in all six countries.
45931.m: Since 2008 the Gulf Cooperation Council has had a common market.

45932.q: In which member state did the Gulf Cooperation Council deploy its ‘Peninsula Shield’ force in 2011?
45932.e: During the protests of the Arab Spring, mainly Saudi Arabia and the Emirates sent troops to Bahrain to support the government.
45932.m: The Peninsula Shield force was deployed in Bahrain in 2011.

45933.q: Through which organisation does Switzerland have a free trade agreement with the states of the Gulf Cooperation Council?
45933.e: Switzerland concludes many free trade agreements together with the other EFTA states. The agreement with the six Gulf states has applied since 2014.
45933.m: Through EFTA, Switzerland has a free trade agreement with the Gulf states.

45934.q: What step towards economic integration did the Gulf Cooperation Council take in 2003?
45934.e: From 2003 a common external tariff applied. A common currency was planned but has not yet been introduced.
45934.m: The Gulf Cooperation Council has been a customs union since 2003.

45935.q: How many member states does the Commonwealth of Nations have (as of 2025)?
45935.e: After Gabon and Togo joined in 2022, the Commonwealth has 56 members. They are on every inhabited continent.

45936.q: What did the London Declaration of 1949 make possible in the Commonwealth?
45936.e: India wanted to become a republic and still stay in the Commonwealth. The London Declaration made this possible, and since then the monarch has been the symbolic head.
45936.m: Since 1949 republics can also be members of the Commonwealth.

45937.q: Which country joined the Commonwealth in 1995 as the first member with no historical link to the British Empire?
45937.e: Mozambique was a Portuguese colony but was admitted in 1995. Later Rwanda followed in 2009, and Gabon and Togo in 2022.
45937.m: In 1995 Mozambique was the first Commonwealth member without a British colonial past.

45938.q: Which declaration of 1991 committed the Commonwealth states to democracy, human rights and the rule of law?
45938.e: The Harare Declaration set out shared political values. Since then a member can be suspended for serious breaches.
45938.m: The Harare Declaration of 1991 made democracy a core value of the Commonwealth.

45939.q: In which city did the first British Empire Games, today's Commonwealth Games, take place in 1930?
45939.e: The first Games were held in 1930 in Hamilton in Ontario, Canada. Since 1978 they have been called the Commonwealth Games.
45939.m: The Commonwealth Games began in 1930 in Hamilton in Canada.

45940.q: Which law of 1931 gave dominions such as Canada and Australia full legislative independence?
45940.e: The Statute of Westminster turned the Balfour Declaration of 1926 into law. It is regarded as the legal basis of the modern Commonwealth.
45940.m: The Statute of Westminster of 1931 made the dominions legally independent.

45941.q: Where did the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) take place in 2024?
45941.e: The meeting in Samoa was the first held in a Pacific island state. A new secretary-general was also elected there.
45941.m: In 2024 the Commonwealth summit took place in a Pacific island state for the first time.

45942.q: Who has been Secretary-General of the Commonwealth since April 2025?
45942.e: Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey, Ghana's former foreign minister, was elected in 2024 and succeeded Patricia Scotland (as of 2025).
45942.m: Since 2025 Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey from Ghana has led the Commonwealth Secretariat.

45943.q: Under what name was the Pacific Islands Forum founded in 1971?
45943.e: The organisation was set up in Wellington in 1971 as the South Pacific Forum. In 2000 it got its present name.
45943.m: Until 2000 the Pacific Islands Forum was called the South Pacific Forum.

45944.q: In which city is the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat based?
45944.e: The secretariat is in Suva, the capital of Fiji.
45944.m: The Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat is in Suva in Fiji.

45945.q: Besides the island states, which two large states are members of the Pacific Islands Forum?
45945.e: Australia and New Zealand have been members since it was founded. They pay a large share of the budget.
45945.m: Australia and New Zealand belong to the Pacific Islands Forum.

45946.q: Which issue did the Boe Declaration of 2018 call the greatest threat to the Pacific region?
45946.e: The declaration, adopted in Nauru, declared climate change the single greatest threat to the security and livelihoods of the region.
45946.m: For the Pacific Islands Forum, climate change is the greatest threat.

45947.q: What does the Treaty of Rarotonga, signed in 1985, establish?
a: A nuclear-weapon-free zone in the South Pacific
A customs union of the island states
45947.e: The treaty bans the possession, stationing and testing of nuclear weapons in the region. One background was the French nuclear tests in Polynesia.
45947.m: The Treaty of Rarotonga makes the South Pacific a nuclear-weapon-free zone.

45948.q: Which danger particularly threatens low-lying member states of the Pacific Islands Forum such as Kiribati or Tuvalu?
45948.e: Many atolls are only a few metres above the sea. If the sea level rises, they face flooding and salty drinking water.
45948.m: Rising sea levels threaten low-lying island states in the Pacific.

45949.q: Which member of the Pacific Islands Forum led a stabilisation mission in the Solomon Islands from 2003?
45949.e: After serious unrest, the RAMSI mission was meant to restore law and order. Australia provided most of the personnel, and the mission lasted until 2017.
45949.m: Australia led the stabilisation mission in the Solomon Islands.

45950.q: Which of these countries is a member of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC)?
45950.e: APEC brings together economies around the Pacific. Chile lies on the Pacific and is a member; Brazil, Argentina and India do not belong.
45950.m: APEC members lie on the Pacific, for example Chile.

45951.q: Why does APEC speak of ‘member economies’ rather than member states?
a: So that Taiwan and Hong Kong can also take part
Because it is a sub-organisation of the WTO
45951.e: Taiwan takes part as ‘Chinese Taipei’ and Hong Kong as ‘Hong Kong, China’. The term economy avoids the question of recognition as a state.
45951.m: APEC speaks of economies so that Taiwan and Hong Kong can take part too.

45952.q: How many member economies does APEC have?
45952.e: APEC includes 21 member economies around the Pacific. Since 1998 there has been a freeze on new members.

45953.q: What does APEC mainly work for?
a: Open trade and investment in the Asia-Pacific region
45953.e: APEC wants to lower tariffs and make investment easier. It is a forum for economic cooperation, not a military alliance.
45953.m: APEC promotes free trade around the Pacific.

45954.q: What is special about APEC decisions?
a: They are voluntary and not legally binding
They must be confirmed by the UN Security Council
They immediately become law in all members
They need a referendum in each member
45954.e: APEC decides by consensus, and the members implement the goals voluntarily. Unlike the WTO, it cannot enforce rules.

45955.q: Where is the APEC Secretariat located?
45955.e: The APEC Secretariat was set up in Singapore in 1993. It supports the host country, which changes each year.
45955.m: The APEC Secretariat works in Singapore.

45956.q: How often do the APEC heads of state and government meet for a summit?
45956.e: A summit has been held every year since 1993. The host changes with the annual chair.
45956.m: The APEC summit takes place every year.

45957.e: China took over the chair in 2026 after South Korea. The leaders' summit takes place in Shenzhen.

45958.q: What is the WTO body called that decides on trade disputes between member states by adopting panel reports?
45958.e: The Dispute Settlement Body is made up of all WTO members and adopts the reports of the panels and the Appellate Body. It can also authorise countermeasures.
45958.m: Trade disputes in the WTO are decided by the Dispute Settlement Body.

45959.q: What does the ‘negative consensus’ rule mean when panel reports are adopted in the WTO?
a: A report is adopted unless all members reject it.
A report needs the approval of all members.
A report needs a two-thirds majority.
Only the parties to the dispute vote on the report.
45959.e: Since 1995 reports have been adopted automatically unless all members unanimously oppose them. This means the losing party can no longer block the decision, as was possible under the old GATT.
45959.m: A WTO panel report can only be stopped by unanimous rejection.

45960.q: Which first step is required in the WTO dispute settlement procedure before a panel can be set up?
a: Consultations between the parties to the dispute
A referendum in the complaining country
A ruling of the International Court of Justice
A vote in the UN Security Council
45960.e: First the parties must seek agreement in consultations. Only if these fail within 60 days can the complaining party request a panel.
45960.m: Every WTO dispute begins with consultations between the parties.

45961.q: Since when has the WTO's Appellate Body no longer been able to function?
45961.e: In December 2019 the terms of further members expired, and the USA blocked new appointments. Since then the three members needed to hear appeals have been missing.
45961.m: Since the end of 2019 the WTO Appellate Body has been blocked.

45962.q: Which country has been blocking the appointment of new members to the WTO Appellate Body for years?
45962.e: The USA argues that the Appellate Body oversteps its powers. New members can only be chosen by consensus, so a single veto is enough.
45962.m: The USA is preventing the appointment of new judges to the WTO Appellate Body.

45963.q: What is meant by an “appeal into the void” in WTO dispute settlement?
a: An appeal against a panel report that is never dealt with because there is no appeal body
A complaint against a country that is not a WTO member
An appeal against a decision of the Ministerial Conference
A complaint submitted after the deadline has passed
45963.e: A losing country can lodge an appeal even though the Appellate Body is not working. The panel report therefore never becomes legally binding and has no effect.
45963.m: Anyone who appeals “into the void” today prevents a WTO ruling from becoming binding.

45964.q: How have some WTO members such as Switzerland and the EU handled appeals since 2020, even though the Appellate Body is blocked?
a: With an arbitration procedure as an interim solution
With rulings of the International Court of Justice
With votes in the UN General Assembly
45964.e: The Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement (MPIA) replaces the Appellate Body with arbitration panels between the participating states. The USA does not take part.
45964.m: Some WTO states use an arbitration procedure to get around the blocked Appellate Body.

45965.q: What may a country do if it has won a WTO dispute and the loser still does not follow the rules?
a: Take countermeasures such as punitive tariffs with WTO approval
Expel the loser from the WTO
Close the border with the losing country
Have a fine paid to the UN
45965.e: If the loser does not implement the decision, the WTO can allow the winner to suspend concessions, for example through higher tariffs. This retaliation must match the damage suffered.
45965.m: If a ruling is not followed, the WTO can allow retaliatory tariffs.

45966.q: What does the WTO's most-favoured-nation principle state?
a: Trade advantages for one member apply immediately to all members.
Domestic and foreign goods must be treated equally within the country.
Every country may favour one preferred partner.
45966.e: If a WTO member lowers the tariff for one country, it must grant this advantage immediately and unconditionally to all other members. This prevents discrimination between trading partners.
45966.m: Under the most-favoured-nation principle, a tariff advantage for one WTO partner applies to all.

45967.q: In which agreement of 1947 was most-favoured-nation treatment for trade in goods laid down?
a: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)
45967.e: Most-favoured-nation treatment is right in the first article of the GATT. Since 1995 the GATT has been part of the World Trade Organization (WTO).
45967.m: Most-favoured-nation treatment is anchored in the GATT of 1947.

45968.q: Which principle complements most-favoured-nation treatment and forbids treating imported goods worse than domestic ones once they have crossed the border?
45968.e: National treatment (Article III GATT) requires imports to be treated the same as domestic products in terms of taxes and regulations. Together with most-favoured-nation treatment, it forms the principle of non-discrimination.
45968.m: National treatment protects imports from being disadvantaged compared with domestic goods.

45969.q: Which exception to most-favoured-nation treatment does Article XXIV of the GATT allow?
a: Free trade areas and customs unions
45969.e: Countries may grant each other advantages in free trade areas or customs unions without giving them to all WTO members. The condition is that substantially all trade is liberalised.
45969.m: Free trade agreements are a permitted exception to most-favoured-nation treatment.

45970.q: Which rule allows industrialised countries to grant developing countries lower tariffs one-sidedly without breaching most-favoured-nation treatment?
45970.e: The Enabling Clause of 1979 allows preference systems for developing countries. Switzerland also grants such countries lower tariffs through its preference system.
45970.m: Thanks to the Enabling Clause, developing countries may be given preference.

45971.q: What has most-favoured-nation treatment usually been called in US legal language since 1998?
45971.e: The US Congress replaced the term with “Normal Trade Relations” because most-favoured-nation wrongly sounded like a special privilege. In substance it is the normal treatment of all partners.
45971.m: Instead of most-favoured-nation, the USA speaks of “Normal Trade Relations”.

45972.q: Which condition characterises most-favoured-nation treatment in the GATT?
a: It applies unconditionally, so without anything in return.
It applies only if counter-tariffs are equally high.
It applies only to neighbouring states.
It applies only to industrial goods from Europe.
45972.e: GATT most-favoured-nation treatment is “unconditional”: an advantage must be granted to all members, even if they make no corresponding concessions themselves.
45972.m: In the GATT, most-favoured-nation treatment applies without requiring anything in return.

45973.q: What can a WTO member do if another member charges it higher tariffs than it charges everyone else?
a: Start a dispute settlement procedure at the WTO
Take the case to the International Criminal Court
Ask the UN Security Council for sanctions
Nothing, it has to accept the tariffs
45973.e: Such unequal treatment violates most-favoured-nation treatment. Disputes between members are decided by the WTO dispute settlement procedure in Geneva.
45973.m: Anyone who violates most-favoured-nation treatment can be taken to the WTO.

45974.q: The export of which two metals, important for semiconductors, did China restrict in August 2023 in response to Western chip controls?
45974.e: China is by far the largest producer of gallium and germanium. With export licences, Beijing showed that it too can put pressure on important supply chains.
45974.m: China uses its power over rare metals as leverage in the technology dispute.

45975.q: What did the USA accuse China of in 2018 to justify its punitive tariffs?
a: Forced technology transfer and theft of intellectual property
Wages that were too high in Chinese factories
45975.e: The USA relied on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. It accused China of forcing foreign firms to hand over technology and of violating patents.
45975.m: The US tariffs of 2018 were aimed at China's unfair technology practices.

45976.q: What did the USA and China agree after their talks in Geneva in May 2025?
a: To cut their additional tariffs on each other sharply for a limited time
To abolish all tariffs for ever
45976.e: For 90 days the USA lowered its additional tariffs from 145 to 30 per cent, and China its counter-tariffs from 125 to 10 per cent. The reduction was later extended several times.
45976.m: In May 2025 the USA and China temporarily eased their tariff dispute.

45977.q: Which Chinese technology company did the USA put on the so-called Entity List in 2019, severely restricting deliveries of US technology?
45977.e: The USA justified the step with security concerns. Since then, firms have needed a licence to supply Huawei with US technology.
45977.m: In 2019 Huawei became the symbol of the technology dispute between the USA and China.

45978.q: In which Swiss city did the USA and China hold talks in May 2025, after which they temporarily cut their tariffs on each other sharply?
45978.e: In Geneva the two countries agreed to reduce tariffs of over 100 per cent considerably for 90 days. Switzerland acted as host.
45978.m: The talks to ease the tariff dispute took place in Geneva in May 2025.

45979.q: What is the strategy of deliberately reducing economic dependence on China without breaking off relations completely called?
45979.e: De-risking means reducing risk, for example through new suppliers in other countries. Decoupling, on the other hand, means largely separating the economies.
45979.m: De-risking aims to reduce dependence on China without stopping trade.

45980.q: Which goods have been especially at the centre of US export controls towards China since 2022?
45980.e: From October 2022 the USA restricted the export to China of modern computer chips and the machines used to make them. The aim is to slow China's progress in artificial intelligence and military technology.
45980.m: Modern computer chips are at the centre of the technology dispute with China.

45981.q: Which US farm product did China hit particularly hard with counter-tariffs in the 2018 tariff round?
45981.e: China was the biggest buyer of American soya beans. With counter-tariffs China deliberately hit agriculture in the USA, after which the US government made aid payments to farmers.
45981.m: With tariffs on soya beans, China hit US agriculture.

45982.q: In which year did the Bretton Woods Conference take place, at which the post-war monetary order was laid down?
45982.e: In July 1944 representatives of 44 states met in Bretton Woods in the US state of New Hampshire. They decided on fixed exchange rates and new international institutions.
45982.m: The Bretton Woods Conference took place in 1944.

45983.q: At what price was the US dollar tied to gold in the Bretton Woods system?
45983.e: The USA undertook to exchange dollars held by central banks for gold at 35 dollars per fine ounce. The other currencies had fixed rates against the dollar.
45983.m: In the Bretton Woods system an ounce of gold cost 35 dollars.

45984.q: Which two institutions were founded at the Bretton Woods Conference?
45984.e: The International Monetary Fund was to secure the monetary order, and the World Bank (IBRD) was to finance reconstruction. Both have their headquarters in Washington.
45984.m: Bretton Woods produced the IMF and the World Bank.

45985.q: Which British economist represented Britain at Bretton Woods and proposed an international clearing currency called the “bancor”?
45985.e: Keynes wanted a neutral world currency but did not prevail against the American Harry Dexter White. So the dollar became the leading currency.
45985.m: At Bretton Woods, Keynes proposed the artificial currency bancor.

45986.q: Which US president ended the dollar's convertibility into gold in August 1971?
45986.e: With the “Nixon shock” of 15 August 1971, the USA suspended the exchange of dollars for gold. This removed the foundation of the system.
45986.m: The Nixon shock of 1971 ended the dollar's link to gold.

45987.q: What does the Triffin dilemma describe in the Bretton Woods system?
a: The leading currency must flow plentifully, but this undermines confidence in its convertibility into gold.
Fixed exchange rates always lead to deflation.
Gold is too heavy for international transport.
Central banks cannot set interest rates.
45987.e: In 1960 the economist Robert Triffin realised that the world needs more and more dollars for growing trade, but the more dollars are held abroad, the less credible the USA's gold promise becomes.
45987.m: The Triffin dilemma shows the inner contradiction of a national leading currency.

45988.q: Since which year have the exchange rates of the major currencies floated, after the Smithsonian Agreement also failed?
45988.e: After the short-lived Smithsonian Agreement of 1971, the major countries gave up fixed rates in 1973. The Swiss franc was also floated in January 1973.
45988.m: Since 1973 the exchange rates of major currencies have been set by the market.

45989.q: In which year did Switzerland join the IMF and the World Bank after a popular vote?
45989.e: On 17 May 1992 the people approved joining the Bretton Woods institutions. Since then Switzerland has led its own voting group in the IMF.
45989.m: Switzerland has been a member of the IMF and the World Bank since 1992.

45990.q: What is a Special Drawing Right (SDR) of the IMF?
a: An international reserve asset that can be exchanged for currencies
A coin that the IMF gives to tourists
A World Bank loan for building projects
A right to deliveries of gold from Fort Knox
45990.e: The SDR is not a currency but a claim on freely usable currencies of IMF members. It supplements countries' currency reserves.
45990.m: A Special Drawing Right is a reserve asset at the IMF.

45991.q: Why did the International Monetary Fund create Special Drawing Rights in 1969?
a: Because gold and dollars were not enough as reserves
To cancel all the debts of poor countries
45991.e: In the system of fixed exchange rates there was a worldwide shortage of currency reserves. The IMF therefore created the SDR in 1969 as an additional reserve asset; the first allocation took place in 1970.
45991.m: Since 1969 Special Drawing Rights have supplemented gold and dollars as reserves.

45992.q: How many currencies make up the basket of the Special Drawing Right (as of 2025)?
45992.e: The basket contains the US dollar, the euro, the Chinese renminbi, the Japanese yen and the British pound. The Swiss franc is not part of it.
45992.m: The SDR basket is made up of five currencies.

45993.q: Which currency was newly added to the basket of the Special Drawing Right in 2016?
45993.e: The renminbi has been part of the basket since 1 October 2016. This was seen as recognition of China's growing importance in world trade.
45993.m: The renminbi has been part of the SDR basket since 2016.

45994.q: Which currency has the greatest weight in the basket of the Special Drawing Right (2022 review)?
45994.e: In the 2022 review the dollar was given a weight of about 43 per cent and the euro about 29 per cent. The weights are reset roughly every five years.
45994.m: The US dollar has the greatest weight in the SDR basket.

45995.q: Apart from being a currency reserve, what else is the Special Drawing Right used for?
a: As a unit of account for international organisations
As a cryptocurrency on the internet
As the national currency of small states
45995.e: The IMF and other organisations keep their accounts in SDRs, and international agreements also use it, for example for compensation for lost luggage on flights. Its currency code is XDR.
45995.m: The Special Drawing Right also serves as an international unit of account.

45996.q: Why did the IMF hand out more Special Drawing Rights than ever before in August 2021?
a: To help countries in the Covid crisis
To end the financial crisis of 2008
To finance the war in Ukraine
To add the renminbi to the basket
45996.e: The allocation of about 456 billion SDRs, roughly 650 billion dollars, strengthened the reserves of all members in proportion to their quotas.
45996.m: In 2021 the IMF strengthened reserves during the pandemic with a record allocation.

45997.q: What determines how many Special Drawing Rights a country receives in a general allocation?
45997.e: SDRs are distributed in proportion to quotas, which depend mainly on economic strength. That is why rich countries receive the most, which is often criticised.
45997.m: A country's SDR allocation depends on its IMF quota.

45998.q: Which country was at the centre of the euro crisis from 2010 after it had to revise its budget deficit sharply upwards?
45998.e: At the end of 2009 the new Greek government admitted that the deficit was much higher than reported. In 2010 Greece received the first rescue package from the EU and the IMF.
45998.m: The euro crisis began with Greece's debt problems.

45999.q: What was the group made up of the European Commission, the European Central Bank and the IMF, which monitored reforms in the crisis countries, called?
45999.e: The troika negotiated the conditions of the aid loans and checked austerity measures. It was highly controversial in the countries affected.
45999.m: The troika monitored the conditions for the crisis countries in the euro area.

46000.q: With which famous phrase did ECB President Mario Draghi calm the financial markets in July 2012?
46000.e: Draghi promised to do whatever was necessary to preserve the euro. The announcement alone clearly lowered the interest rates of the crisis states.
46000.m: Draghi's “Whatever it takes” became the turning point of the euro crisis.

46001.q: Which Latin American country stopped paying its government debts in December 2001, at the time the largest sovereign default in history?
46001.e: Argentina could no longer service debts of around 100 billion dollars. The fixed link of the peso to the dollar collapsed, and a severe economic crisis followed.
46001.m: Argentina suffered a huge sovereign default in 2001.

46002.q: Which country triggered the Latin American debt crisis with a halt to payments in August 1982?
46002.e: Rising US interest rates and falling oil prices made Mexico's dollar debts unbearable. Soon many other Latin American countries ran into payment difficulties; people speak of the “lost decade”.
46002.m: Mexico's halt to payments in 1982 triggered the Latin American debt crisis.

46003.q: What is the name of the permanent rescue fund of the euro countries founded in 2012 and based in Luxembourg?
46003.e: The ESM grants loans to euro countries in difficulty, linked to reform conditions. It replaced the temporary European Financial Stability Facility.
46003.m: The ESM is the permanent rescue fund of the eurozone.

46004.q: What upper limit for government debt in relation to GDP do the Maastricht criteria set?
46004.e: Government debt should be at most 60 per cent of GDP, and the annual deficit at most 3 per cent. Many euro countries clearly exceed the debt limit.
46004.m: Under Maastricht, government debt should not exceed 60 per cent of GDP.

46005.q: With which instrument has the Swiss Confederation protected itself against excessive debt since 2003?
46005.e: The people approved the debt brake in 2001 with about 85 per cent voting yes. It requires that spending does not exceed revenue over an economic cycle.
46005.m: Since 2003 the debt brake has limited the debt of the Confederation.

46006.q: In which year was the free trade agreement between Switzerland and China signed?
46006.e: The signing took place on 6 July 2013 in Beijing. Afterwards both countries still had to ratify the agreement.
46006.m: The agreement with China was signed in 2013.

46007.q: What was special about Switzerland's agreement with China within Europe?
a: Switzerland was the first country in continental Europe with a free trade agreement with China.
Switzerland was the only EFTA country without an agreement with China.
It was China's first agreement ever.
It was concluded together with the EU.
46007.e: Switzerland concluded the agreement bilaterally and not through EFTA. The EU still has no free trade agreement with China today.
46007.m: Switzerland was the first country in continental Europe to have a free trade agreement with China.

46008.q: How is the removal of tariffs divided in the agreement between Switzerland and China?
a: Switzerland mostly removed industrial tariffs at once, China step by step over years.
China removed all tariffs at once, Switzerland over 20 years.
Both countries kept all industrial tariffs.
46008.e: The agreement is asymmetrical: Switzerland quickly granted duty-free access, while China lowered many tariffs over transition periods of up to 15 years. Watches and machines, for example, benefited gradually.
46008.m: In the agreement with Switzerland, China removes its tariffs step by step.

46009.q: How were labour and employment issues dealt with in the free trade agreement between Switzerland and China?
a: In a separate agreement on cooperation in labour matters
In a binding human rights chapter with sanctions
Not at all, the subject was expressly excluded
Through an arbitration court of the International Labour Organization
46009.e: Labour issues were dealt with in a parallel agreement that provides for dialogue and cooperation, but no sanctions. Critics complain that human rights are not anchored firmly enough.
46009.m: In the agreement with China, labour issues are dealt with in a parallel agreement.

46010.q: What position does China hold in Switzerland's foreign trade after the EU and the USA?
46010.e: After the EU and the USA, China is Switzerland's third largest trading partner. The free trade agreement was meant to strengthen these relations further.
46010.m: China is Switzerland's third largest trading partner.

46011.q: Which Federal Councillor signed the free trade agreement with China for Switzerland?
46011.e: Johann Schneider-Ammann was head of the economics department at the time. He signed the agreement together with the Chinese trade minister Gao Hucheng.
46011.m: Johann Schneider-Ammann signed the agreement with China.

46012.q: When was the Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA) between EFTA and India signed?
46012.e: The agreement was signed on 10 March 2024 in New Delhi. Federal Councillor Guy Parmelin signed for Switzerland.
46012.m: The EFTA agreement with India was signed in March 2024.

46013.q: Since when has the agreement between EFTA and India been in force?
46013.e: After no referendum was called in Switzerland, the agreement came into force on 1 October 2025. As a result, tariffs on many Swiss exports to India are falling.
46013.m: The agreement with India has applied since October 2025.

46014.q: Which investment target does the agreement between EFTA and India contain?
46014.e: The EFTA states want to increase direct investment in India by 100 billion dollars within 15 years. It is the first free trade agreement with such an investment target.
46014.m: EFTA is aiming for 100 billion dollars of investment in India.

46015.q: Which Swiss export products benefit especially from the agreement between EFTA and India?
46015.e: With the agreement India lowers tariffs on many industrial goods. Typical Swiss exports such as machines, watches, pharmaceutical and chemical products benefit.
46015.m: Thanks to the agreement, Swiss industrial products become cheaper in India.

46016.q: What may India do if the EFTA states miss their investment target?
a: Temporarily withdraw tariff concessions after consultations
Sue the EFTA states at the International Court of Justice
Seize all Swiss firms in India
Demand a penalty payment from Switzerland
46016.e: The agreement provides a mechanism: if the target is not reached, India can rebalance concessions after talks. The states can only encourage investment by private firms, not order it.
46016.m: If EFTA misses the investment target, India can adjust tariff advantages.

46017.q: Which countries make up EFTA, which concluded the agreement with India?
46017.e: The European Free Trade Association was founded in 1960 and now has four members. It concludes free trade agreements with third countries jointly.
46017.m: EFTA consists of Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Iceland.

46018.q: Why is the free trade agreement with India considered particularly important for Switzerland?
a: India is the most populous country in the world
India is a member of EFTA
India is Switzerland's most important trading partner
India pays for its imports in francs
46018.e: With over 1.4 billion people, India is a huge, growing market. After about 16 years of negotiations, Swiss firms gained better access there.
46018.m: As the largest country in the world by population, India is an important future market for Switzerland.

46019.q: What is meant by protectionism in trade policy?
a: Protecting the domestic economy from foreign competition
Promoting world trade that is as free as possible
46019.e: Protectionist states make imports more expensive or restrict them, for example with tariffs, quotas or subsidies. This is meant to protect domestic firms and jobs.
46019.m: Protectionism protects a country's own economy from foreign competition.

46020.q: Which US tariff law of 1930 is seen as an example of how protectionism made the Great Depression worse?
46020.e: The law raised tariffs on thousands of imported goods. Other countries responded with counter-tariffs, and world trade collapsed sharply.
46020.m: The Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930 made the Great Depression worse.

46021.q: What is a non-tariff barrier to trade?
a: An import restriction that is not a tariff, such as a quota or strict standards
A particularly low tariff on raw materials
A tariff charged only on exports
46021.e: Non-tariff barriers work without tariffs, for example through quotas, technical regulations or complicated approval procedures. Switzerland partly removes them with the “Cassis de Dijon principle”.
46021.m: Quotas and regulations can hinder trade even without tariffs.

46022.q: What did the economist Friedrich List argue with the “infant industry tariff”?
a: Young industries need protection for a while
Tariffs should stay high for ever
Free trade benefits all countries equally
Only raw materials may be taxed at the border
46022.e: In the 19th century List argued that emerging countries should protect new industries for a limited time. Once the industry is strong enough, the protection should be removed again.
46022.m: The infant industry tariff is meant to protect young industries temporarily.

46023.q: What does “dumping” mean in foreign trade?
a: Selling goods abroad below the price in the home market
Throwing surplus goods into the sea
Banning exports in times of crisis
Buying foreign firms at top prices
46023.e: In dumping, exports are sold below their normal value to push out competitors. The WTO allows anti-dumping duties against this if damage is proven.
46023.m: Dumping means selling more cheaply abroad than at home.

46024.q: What does a safeguard clause allow under WTO law?
a: Temporary import restrictions after a sudden sharp rise in imports
Permanent tariffs against a single unpopular country
Leaving the WTO without a notice period
Export subsidies for all industrial goods
46024.e: If a domestic industry is threatened with serious harm because of sharply rising imports, a country may take temporary protective measures. Unlike anti-dumping duties, they do not require unfair behaviour by the exporter.
46024.m: A safeguard clause allows temporary protection against a sudden flood of imports.

46025.q: How does a tariff quota work, as Switzerland uses for many agricultural products?
a: Up to a fixed quantity a low tariff applies, above it a very high one.
Each importing firm may bring in only one product.
The tariff falls the more is imported.
Imports are only allowed on certain days of the week.
46025.e: Within the quota the low in-quota tariff rate is charged, outside it a prohibitively high out-of-quota rate. In this way Switzerland protects meat, vegetables and dairy products, for example.
46025.m: Tariff quotas let a certain quantity into the country cheaply and make the rest much more expensive.

46026.q: Who usually bears a large part of the cost of an import tariff?
a: Consumers and firms in the importing country
Only the government of the exporting country
The central bank of the exporting country
46026.e: A tariff is due on import and makes the goods more expensive at home. Depending on the market, the costs are borne mainly by domestic buyers and partly by the foreign producers.
46026.m: Tariffs make imports more expensive mainly for buyers in the country itself.

46027.q: What is the minimum rate of the global minimum tax of the OECD and G20?
46027.e: Large international corporations are to pay an effective profit tax of at least 15 per cent in every country. If the tax is lower, a top-up tax can be charged.
46027.m: The global minimum tax is 15 per cent.

46028.q: From what annual turnover does the global minimum tax apply to groups of companies?
46028.e: Only large corporations with a turnover of at least 750 million euros are affected. The vast majority of small and medium-sized companies in Switzerland are not affected.
46028.m: The minimum tax only applies to corporations with a turnover of over 750 million euros.

46029.q: When did the Swiss people approve the implementation of the OECD minimum tax?
46029.e: On 18 June 2023 about 79 per cent approved the constitutional amendment. The top-up tax has applied since 1 January 2024.
46029.m: Switzerland approved the minimum tax at the ballot box in 2023.

46030.q: How is the revenue from the Swiss top-up tax for the OECD minimum tax divided?
a: 75 per cent to the cantons, 25 per cent to the Confederation
50 per cent to the AHV, 50 per cent to the cantons
46030.e: The cantons receive three quarters because they are responsible for company taxes and are in tax competition. The Confederation receives one quarter.
46030.m: The cantons receive most of the minimum tax revenue.

46031.q: Under which name does the global minimum tax run in the OECD reform project?
46031.e: The OECD/G20 project consists of two pillars. Pillar One redistributes taxing rights to market countries, Pillar Two regulates the minimum tax.
46031.m: The minimum tax is the second pillar of the OECD tax reform.

46032.q: Which practice of corporations is the OECD project that led to the global minimum tax aimed at?
a: Trading shares on several stock exchanges
46032.e: The OECD/G20 project BEPS (“Base Erosion and Profit Shifting”) is aimed at tax tricks with which corporations shift profits to countries with low taxes. The minimum tax is one result of it.
46032.m: The minimum tax is meant to stop corporations shifting profits to tax havens.

46033.q: What is the aim of the global minimum tax?
a: To set a lower limit on tax competition for corporate profits
To lower income tax for private individuals
46033.e: States should no longer undercut each other with ever lower profit taxes. Corporations should bear a minimum tax burden everywhere, no matter where they declare their profits.
46033.m: The minimum tax puts a lower limit on tax competition.

46034.q: Which group agreed in June 2025 to exempt US corporations from parts of the global minimum tax?
46034.e: The G7 agreed on a “side-by-side” approach because the USA has its own minimum tax rules. In return the USA dropped planned retaliatory taxes.
46034.m: In 2025 the G7 agreed a special rule for US corporations on the minimum tax.

46035.q: Which canton is considered the most important location for Swiss commodity trading?
46035.e: Geneva is home to a particularly large number of big trading firms, as well as specialised banks, shipping companies and inspection companies. The sector is very important for Geneva's economy.
46035.m: Geneva is the most important centre of Swiss commodity trading.

46036.q: Which canton is the second most important location for commodity trading after Geneva and home to Glencore?
46036.e: With low taxes, Zug attracted trading firms as early as the 1950s. Today the corporation Glencore, among others, has its headquarters there.
46036.m: After Geneva, Zug is Switzerland's second largest commodity trading centre.

46037.q: What is meant by merchanting in commodity trading?
a: A Swiss firm buys goods abroad and sells them on abroad without the goods ever coming to Switzerland.
Goods are imported into Switzerland, processed and exported again.
Goods are only transported through the country on Swiss roads and railways.
Goods are stored permanently in Swiss free ports.
46037.e: In merchanting the goods never touch Switzerland, for example when oil is shipped directly from a producing country to a refinery in Asia. But they are bought, financed and sold by a firm in Switzerland.
46037.m: In merchanting, goods are traded from Switzerland without entering the country.

46038.q: Since taking over Xstrata in 2013, what has made Glencore different from a pure commodity trader?
a: It also extracts raw materials in its own mines
It now sells only to Swiss customers
It now trades only in food
It has become a state-owned company
46038.e: With the mining group Xstrata, Glencore took over many mines, for example for copper, coal and zinc. Since then the corporation from the canton of Zug has been both trader and producer.
46038.m: Glencore trades in raw materials and also extracts them itself.

46039.q: For which group of commodities is the trading centre of Geneva especially well known?
46039.e: Several of the world's largest oil traders are based in Geneva. Grain, sugar and other agricultural goods are also traded there.
46039.m: Geneva is a globally important centre for oil trading.

46040.q: Which popular initiative on commodity firms and other corporations won a majority of the people in 2020 but failed to win a majority of the cantons?
46040.e: On 29 November 2020 about 50.7 per cent voted yes, but most cantons rejected it. The initiative wanted to make corporations liable for human rights and environmental damage abroad.
46040.m: In 2020 the Responsible Business Initiative failed to win a majority of the cantons.

46041.q: Which commodity trader founded a trading company in Zug in 1974 from which Glencore later emerged?
46041.e: Marc Rich made Zug a commodity centre. In the 1990s his firm was taken over by its management and renamed Glencore.
46041.m: Marc Rich laid the foundation for Glencore in Zug.

46042.q: What does the automatic exchange of information (AEOI) on financial accounts regulate?
a: Banks report account data of foreign customers to their country of residence.
Banks publish all account balances on the internet.
Cantons exchange tax returns with each other.
Central banks report exchange rates to the IMF.
46042.e: Financial institutions record accounts of people who are tax resident abroad and report them to the Federal Tax Administration. It passes the data on to the partner states every year.
46042.m: With AEOI, tax authorities automatically receive account data from abroad.

46043.q: Since when has Switzerland applied the automatic exchange of information?
46043.e: Switzerland collected data from 1 January 2017 and exchanged it for the first time in autumn 2018. This ended banking secrecy towards foreign tax authorities.
46043.m: Switzerland has automatically exchanged account data since 2018.

46044.q: Which international organisation developed the standard for the automatic exchange of information?
46044.e: In 2014 the OECD adopted the Common Reporting Standard. Over 100 states, including Switzerland, apply it.
46044.m: AEOI is based on an OECD standard.

46045.q: In which law of 1934 is Swiss banking secrecy anchored in criminal law?
46045.e: Article 47 of the Banking Act makes breaching professional secrecy a criminal offence. It still applies to residents with respect to the Swiss tax authorities.
46045.m: Banking secrecy has been in the Banking Act since 1934.

46046.q: With which partner did Switzerland sign an agreement on the automatic exchange of information in 2015, replacing the earlier savings tax agreement?
46046.e: The agreement with the EU was signed in May 2015. It replaced the savings tax agreement of 2004, under which Switzerland had charged an anonymous withholding tax.
46046.m: Since the agreement with the EU, Switzerland exchanges account data instead of making anonymous tax deductions.

46047.q: Which US law of 2010 obliges foreign banks to report accounts of US taxpayers?
46047.e: The Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act forces banks worldwide to report to the US tax authority. Switzerland concluded an agreement on this with the USA in 2013.
46047.m: FATCA requires reports on accounts of US taxpayers.

46048.q: For whom does banking secrecy towards the tax authorities still apply in Switzerland despite AEOI?
a: For customers who are tax resident in Switzerland
For all customers from EU states
For all customers from the USA
46048.e: AEOI only covers accounts of people who are tax resident abroad. For residents there is no automatic exchange with the Swiss tax authorities.
46048.m: For residents, banking secrecy towards the tax authorities still applies.

46049.q: Which countries belong to the G7?
a: USA, Japan, Germany, France, United Kingdom, Italy, Canada
USA, China, Russia, India, Japan, Brazil, Germany
USA, Canada, Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru
Germany, France, Switzerland, Austria, Italy, Spain, Belgium
46049.e: The G7 brings together seven large industrialised countries with democratic governments. The European Union also takes part in the meetings.
46049.m: The G7 are seven large democratic industrialised states.

46050.q: Against what background did the heads of government of the later G7 meet for the first time in 1975?
a: The oil crisis and the end of the system of fixed exchange rates
The end of the Second World War
The fall of the Berlin Wall
The founding of the European Union
46050.e: The first world economic summit took place in 1975 at the Château de Rambouillet near Paris. The oil crisis and the end of the Bretton Woods system had shaken the world economy.
46050.m: The G7 was formed in 1975 in response to the economic crises of the 1970s.

46051.q: Which forum was founded in 1999 to include large emerging economies such as China, India and Brazil alongside the G7?
46051.e: After the Asian crisis of 1997 it became clear that world economic issues could not be solved without emerging economies. At first the finance ministers met, and since 2008 the heads of state and government have too.
46051.m: Since 1999 the G20 has added important emerging economies to the G7.

46052.q: Why was Russia excluded from taking part in what was then the G8 in 2014?
a: Because of the annexation of Crimea
Because of election fraud in Moscow
46052.e: After the annexation of the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, the other members suspended Russia's participation. Since then the group has met again as the G7.
46052.m: Since the annexation of Crimea in 2014, Russia has no longer been part of the group.

46053.q: What makes the G7 different from an international organisation such as the WTO?
a: It has no founding treaty and no permanent secretariat.
It has its own court with binding rulings.
It can make laws for all UN states.
46053.e: The G7 is an informal forum. The presidency changes every year, and the presiding country organises the summit.
46053.m: The G7 is an informal forum without a founding treaty.

46054.q: In which French town on Lake Geneva did the G7 summit take place in June 2026?
46054.e: France invited the leaders to Évian from 15 to 17 June 2026, where a G8 summit had already been held in 2003. The Swiss Army was allowed to deploy up to 5,000 soldiers to help with security.
46054.m: The 2026 G7 summit took place in Évian on Lake Geneva.

46055.q: What role did Swiss President Guy Parmelin take on at the 2026 G7 summit?
a: He welcomed the heads of state and government at Geneva Airport.
He signed the final declaration as a member.
He gave the opening speech at the UN.
46055.e: Many delegations arrived via Geneva Airport, where Parmelin greeted them. However, Switzerland is not a member of the G7 and was not officially invited to the summit.
46055.m: In 2026 President Parmelin welcomed the summit guests at Geneva Airport.

46056.q: Where did the 2025 G7 summit take place?
46056.e: Canada held the presidency in 2025 and invited the leaders to Kananaskis in the Rocky Mountains. A G8 summit had already taken place there in 2002.
46056.m: The 2025 G7 summit took place in Kananaskis.

46057.q: In which year did the IPCC publish its first assessment report?
46057.e: The first assessment report appeared in 1990 and provided an important basis for the Framework Convention on Climate Change of 1992. Since then reports have followed at intervals of five to nine years.
46057.m: The first IPCC assessment report appeared in 1990.

46058.q: What is the main task of the IPCC, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change?
a: It assesses the state of climate research.
It runs its own climate measuring stations.
It decides on binding climate targets.
It hands out money to climate projects.
46058.e: The IPCC does not do its own research but reviews and assesses the published scientific literature and summarises it in assessment reports. Binding decisions are made by states in their own negotiations.
46058.m: The IPCC summarises existing knowledge instead of doing research itself.

46059.q: Which topics do the three working groups of the IPCC deal with?
46059.e: Working Group I deals with the physical science basis, Working Group II with impacts, adaptation and vulnerability, and Working Group III with mitigation of climate change.
46059.m: The three IPCC working groups deal with basics, impacts and mitigation.

46060.q: Which award did the IPCC receive in 2007 together with Al Gore?
46060.e: In 2007 the Nobel Committee honoured the IPCC and former US Vice President Al Gore for their work spreading knowledge about human-made climate change.
46060.m: In 2007 the IPCC received the Nobel Peace Prize together with Al Gore.

46061.q: How is the “Summary for Policymakers” of an IPCC report approved?
a: Line by line by the governments
By the lead author teams alone
By a majority decision of the WMO
By a decision of the UN Security Council
46061.e: Government representatives approve the summary sentence by sentence in the plenary, and it must agree with the main scientific report. This way all member states support the key statements.
46061.m: Governments approve the IPCC summaries line by line.

46062.q: How does the Sixth Assessment Report of the IPCC (Working Group I, 2021) describe human influence on warming?
46062.e: The report states that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land. Earlier reports had still expressed the link with probability statements.
46062.m: According to the IPCC, human influence on warming has been unequivocally proven since 2021.

46063.q: Why does the IPCC use fixed expressions such as “likely” or “very likely”?
a: Each expression stands for a particular range of probability
So that the reports sound more exciting
So that each country can interpret the words differently
46063.e: The IPCC uses calibrated language: “likely” stands for 66 to 100 per cent, “very likely” for 90 to 100 per cent. This makes the statements comparable.
46063.m: In the IPCC report, each expression stands for a particular probability.

46064.q: Which climate researcher from Bern was co-chair of IPCC Working Group I for the Fifth Assessment Report (2013)?
46064.e: Thomas Stocker of the University of Bern led Working Group I from 2008 to 2015 together with Qin Dahe. The report on the physical science basis appeared in 2013.
46064.m: Thomas Stocker from Bern led an IPCC working group for the Fifth Assessment Report.

46065.q: On which treaty are the annual UN climate conferences (COP) based?
a: UN Framework Convention on Climate Change
46065.e: The Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was adopted at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 and came into force in 1994. The Conference of the Parties (COP) is its highest body.
46065.m: The climate conferences are the meetings of the parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.

46066.q: In which city did the first UN climate conference (COP1) take place in 1995?
46066.e: COP1 met in Berlin in 1995, chaired by the then German environment minister Angela Merkel. It adopted the “Berlin Mandate” for negotiations on binding reduction targets.
46066.m: The first UN climate conference took place in Berlin in 1995.

46067.q: How are decisions made at the UN climate conferences in practice?
46067.e: The parties have never agreed on a voting rule in the rules of procedure, so the consensus principle applies. This often makes agreements slow.
46067.m: Decisions at the climate conferences are made by consensus.

46068.q: In which city is the secretariat of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change based?
46068.e: The climate secretariat (UNFCCC Secretariat) moved to Bonn in 1996. It organises the negotiations and evaluates the reports of the states.
46068.m: The secretariat of the Framework Convention on Climate Change is based in Bonn.

46069.q: What did the final text of COP28 in Dubai (2023) contain for the first time?
a: A ban on new coal power stations
46069.e: The “UAE Consensus” calls for “transitioning away” from fossil fuels in energy systems. This was the first time fossil energy as a whole was named in a COP decision.
46069.m: At COP28, moving away from fossil fuels was agreed for the first time.

46070.q: Which new climate finance target did COP29 in Baku (2024) adopt?
46070.e: The New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) says industrialised countries should take the lead in mobilising at least 300 billion US dollars a year for developing countries by 2035. It replaces the previous 100 billion target.
46070.m: At COP29 a finance target of 300 billion dollars a year by 2035 was adopted.

46071.q: In which negotiating group does Switzerland take part at the UN climate conferences?
46071.e: Since 2000 Switzerland has formed the Environmental Integrity Group (EIG) with Mexico, South Korea, Liechtenstein, Monaco and Georgia. The group brings together states from different regions of the world.
46071.m: Switzerland negotiates in the Environmental Integrity Group.

46072.q: How often does the Global Stocktake under the Paris Agreement take place?
46072.e: Under Article 14 of the Paris Agreement, states review their joint progress every five years; the first stocktake was completed in 2023. Its results are to feed into the next national climate targets.
46072.m: The Global Stocktake checks progress on climate protection every five years.

46073.q: In which agreement did states commit to pursuing efforts to limit warming to 1.5 °C?
46073.e: Article 2 of the Paris Agreement of 2015 requires keeping warming well below 2 °C and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C.
46073.m: The 1.5 degree target is anchored in the Paris Agreement.

46074.q: With the 1.5 degree target, what is today's global average temperature compared with?
a: With the value of the year 2000
With the temperature of the last ice age
46074.e: Warming is measured against the time before industrialisation. The IPCC uses the average of the years 1850 to 1900 for this.
46074.m: The 1.5 degree target measures warming compared with pre-industrial times.

46075.q: Which group of states fought especially hard for the 1.5 degree target with the slogan “1.5 to stay alive”?
a: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
46075.e: For low-lying island states, even warming of 2 °C threatens their existence because of rising sea levels. The Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS) therefore pushed through the mention of 1.5 °C in Paris.
46075.m: The small island states campaigned especially hard for the 1.5 degree target.

46076.q: According to the IPCC special report of 2018, roughly when would global net CO2 emissions have to reach zero to stay within 1.5 °C?
46076.e: In pathways with no or limited overshoot, CO2 emissions fall by about 45 per cent from 2010 levels by 2030 and reach net zero around 2050.
46076.m: For 1.5 degrees, CO2 emissions must reach net zero around 2050.

46077.q: Which body regularly summarises the state of climate research for governments?
46077.e: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) evaluates research and publishes assessment reports. They form the basis for climate negotiations such as those in Paris.
46077.m: The IPCC summarises knowledge about climate change for politics.

46078.q: Why is the 1.5 degree target not automatically considered missed, even though in 2024 a calendar year was above 1.5 °C for the first time?
a: It refers to a long-term average.
It only applies from the year 2050.
46078.e: The target refers to warming averaged over about 20 years, while individual years vary, for example because of El Niño. According to the WMO, 2024 was about 1.55 °C above the pre-industrial level.
46078.m: The 1.5 degree target refers to a long-term average.

46079.q: What does “overshoot” mean in connection with the 1.5 degree target?
a: Temporarily exceeding it and then coming back down
Warming of more than three degrees
46079.e: In an overshoot, warming rises temporarily above 1.5 °C and is later brought down again by net negative emissions. Some damage may still remain.
46079.m: An overshoot is a temporary exceeding of the temperature limit.

46080.q: Which law, approved by Swiss voters in 2023, sets the goal of net zero by 2050 for Switzerland?
46080.e: On 18 June 2023 voters approved the federal act on climate protection targets, innovation and strengthening energy security with about 59 per cent yes. It anchors net zero by 2050.
46080.m: The Climate and Innovation Act requires Switzerland to reach net zero by 2050.

46081.q: Which states demanded a fund for loss and damage most strongly?
a: Poor countries that are badly affected by climate change
46081.e: Island states and developing countries in particular demanded help with climate damage for years. The fund was agreed at COP27 in Egypt in 2022.
46081.m: The fund for loss and damage goes back to demands by poor, badly affected countries.

46082.q: What is meant by “loss and damage” in climate policy?
a: Costs of expanding solar power systems
46082.e: It means climate impacts that can no longer be prevented by adaptation, for example from storms, droughts or rising sea levels. It therefore goes beyond mitigation and adaptation.
46082.m: Loss and damage are climate impacts that happen despite adaptation.

46083.q: Which institution manages the fund for loss and damage as trustee during a transition phase?
46083.e: For an initial four years the fund is hosted at the World Bank as a financial intermediary fund. Developing countries had criticised this solution at first.
46083.m: The World Bank is managing the fund for loss and damage for the time being.

46084.q: Which event would be a typical case for the fund for loss and damage?
a: An island state loses land because of rising sea levels
A country builds a new coal power station
A firm loses money on the stock exchange
46084.e: The fund is meant to support countries that suffer climate damage, for example from storms, droughts or rising sea levels. Small island states are especially affected.
46084.m: The fund helps countries that suffer damage from climate change.

46085.q: In the view of many developing countries, who should mainly pay into the fund for loss and damage?
a: Industrialised countries with high historical emissions
The poorest countries in the world
The island states affected by climate change
46085.e: Industrialised countries have emitted the most greenhouse gases since industrialisation. That is why many developing countries consider them responsible for paying for climate damage.
46085.m: Many developing countries believe the main causes of climate change should pay.
