46086.q: In which climate agreement of 2015 is loss and damage recognised as a separate topic?
46086.e: Article 8 of the Paris Agreement recognises that loss and damage must be averted, minimised and addressed. No duty to pay compensation follows from it.
46086.m: The Paris Agreement recognises loss and damage as a separate topic.

46087.q: Which example counts as non-economic loss and damage?
46087.e: Non-economic losses can hardly be measured in money, for example the loss of cultural heritage, homeland, identity or biodiversity. Destroyed infrastructure and failed harvests count as economic damage.
46087.m: The loss of cultural heritage is non-economic climate damage.

46088.q: Why are people who leave their country because of climate impacts usually not considered refugees under international law?
a: Climate impacts are not a ground for persecution.
They never cross a national border.
The UN banned the term in 2015.
46088.e: The Geneva Refugee Convention only protects people who are persecuted for certain reasons. Environmental changes such as droughts or rising sea levels are not among them.
46088.m: Climate migrants usually do not fall under the refugee definition of the Geneva Convention.

46089.q: Where do most people who are displaced by weather extremes and climate impacts go?
46089.e: The vast majority of displaced people stay in their own country or region, often only temporarily. They are then considered internally displaced persons.
46089.m: Most people displaced by climate stay in their own country.

46090.q: Which two states launched the Nansen Initiative in 2012 to protect people displaced across borders by disasters?
46090.e: The Nansen Initiative was a state-led consultation process that adopted a protection agenda in 2015, supported by over 100 states. It is named after the Norwegian polar explorer and refugee helper Fridtjof Nansen.
46090.m: Switzerland and Norway launched the Nansen Initiative for people displaced by disasters.

46091.q: Which agreement of 2015 is meant to limit global warming and so also reduce displacement caused by climate impacts?
46091.e: In the Paris Agreement almost all states committed to keeping warming well below 2 degrees. It also mentions loss and damage, for example through displacement.
46091.m: The Paris Climate Agreement of 2015 is meant to limit global warming.

46092.q: Why could many people from Kiribati in the Pacific lose their homeland?
a: Rising sea levels threaten the flat atolls
Volcanic eruptions are destroying the islands
The desert is spreading across the islands
Melting glaciers are flooding the rivers
46092.e: Most of Kiribati's atolls lie only a few metres above the sea. A man from Kiribati, Ioane Teitiota, therefore sought protection in New Zealand, and his case went before a UN committee in 2020.
46092.m: Rising sea levels threaten flat island states such as Kiribati.

46093.q: Which country allows up to 280 people from Tuvalu to immigrate each year under the Falepili agreement?
46093.e: Australia and Tuvalu signed the agreement in 2023. Because of rising sea levels, it offers Tuvaluans a special migration route.
46093.m: The Falepili agreement opens a route to Australia for people from Tuvalu.

46094.q: How many climate migrants within their own countries does the World Bank's Groundswell report (2021) consider possible by 2050 in the worst-case scenario?
46094.e: The report examines six world regions and expects up to 216 million internal migrants by 2050. Rapid emission cuts could reduce this number considerably.
46094.m: The World Bank expects up to 216 million internal climate migrants by 2050.

46095.q: In which year was the Geneva Refugee Convention adopted?
46095.e: The Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees was adopted in Geneva on 28 July 1951 and came into force in 1954. It was created under the impression of the refugee movements of the Second World War.
46095.m: The Geneva Refugee Convention dates from 1951.

46096.q: What did the 1967 Protocol to the Geneva Refugee Convention change?
a: It removed the time and geographical limits.
It created a category for climate refugees.
It founded the UN refugee agency.
It abolished the duty to hold asylum procedures.
46096.e: Originally the convention only applied to events before 1 January 1951 and could be limited to Europe. The New York Protocol made it applicable worldwide and without a time limit.
46096.m: The 1967 Protocol made the Refugee Convention applicable worldwide.

46097.q: Which reason is NOT one of the grounds for persecution in the Geneva Refugee Convention?
46097.e: The convention names five grounds: race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group and political opinion. Poverty alone does not justify refugee status.
46097.m: Economic hardship alone is not a ground for persecution under the Refugee Convention.

46098.q: Which UN organisation watches over the application of the Geneva Refugee Convention?
46098.e: The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) was founded in 1950 and is based in Geneva. States undertake to cooperate with it.
46098.m: UNHCR monitors compliance with the Refugee Convention.

46099.q: Under Article 28 of the Geneva Refugee Convention, which document do the contracting states issue to recognised refugees for travel abroad?
46099.e: Because refugees usually cannot use the passport of their home country, they receive a special travel document. It does not allow travel to the state that persecuted them.
46099.m: Recognised refugees travel with a refugee travel document.

46100.q: What does Article 31 of the Geneva Refugee Convention say about refugees who enter a country illegally?
a: No penalty if they report without delay
Detention until the application is decided
A fine equal to the travel costs
46100.e: Refugees who come directly from a persecuting state and report to the authorities without delay may not be punished for entering illegally. Fleeing is often only possible without valid papers.
46100.m: Refugees may not be punished for illegal entry if they report immediately.

46101.q: Which permit is usually issued in Switzerland to recognised refugees who have been granted asylum?
46101.e: Asylum seekers receive permit N during the procedure, provisionally admitted persons permit F and people in need of protection permit S. Anyone granted asylum gets a residence permit B.
46101.m: Recognised refugees with asylum receive permit B in Switzerland.

46102.q: Which Swiss law largely adopts the refugee definition of the Geneva Convention?
46102.e: Article 3 of the Asylum Act defines refugees in a similar way to the convention and also states that reasons for flight specific to women must be taken into account.
46102.m: The Asylum Act adopts the refugee definition of the Geneva Convention.

46103.q: What does the principle of non-refoulement forbid?
a: Sending someone back to a persecuting state
46103.e: Under Article 33 of the Geneva Refugee Convention, no state may expel or return a refugee to a territory where their life or freedom is threatened. The French word “refouler” means to push back.
46103.m: No one may be sent back to a country where they face persecution.

46104.q: What is the consequence in Switzerland of the ban on refoulement being counted as peremptory international law?
a: Only the Federal Supreme Court may apply it.
It only applies in border cantons.
It can be overturned by referendum.
46104.e: Under Article 139 paragraph 3 of the Federal Constitution, the Federal Assembly declares popular initiatives invalid if they violate peremptory norms of international law. The Federal Council and legal scholars count the principle of non-refoulement among them.
46104.m: In Switzerland, popular initiatives that violate peremptory international law are invalid.

46105.q: Under Article 33 paragraph 2 of the Refugee Convention, in which case may a refugee not rely on the ban on refoulement?
a: If they are a danger to the security of the country
If they do not know the national language
If they turned down a job
46105.e: The exception applies if there are serious reasons to regard a refugee as a danger to the security of the host state, or if they have been finally convicted of a particularly serious crime.
46105.m: The Refugee Convention allows exceptions to the ban on refoulement if state security is at risk.

46106.q: In what way does protection against being sent back to face torture under Article 3 ECHR go further than that of the Refugee Convention?
a: It applies without exception, even to offenders.
It only applies to recognised refugees.
It only applies within EU states.
46106.e: The ban on torture in the European Convention on Human Rights has no exceptions, not even for dangerous people. Article 3 of the UN Convention against Torture is just as absolute.
46106.m: No one may be deported to a state where they face torture.

46107.q: Whom does the Federal Constitution protect from deportation to a state where they face torture?
46107.e: Article 25 of the Federal Constitution protects refugees from deportation to a persecuting state. It protects all people without exception from deportation to a state where they face torture.
46107.m: No one may be deported to a state where they face torture.

46108.q: Does the ban on refoulement also apply when a state intercepts boat refugees on the high seas?
a: Yes, on the high seas too
Only with permission from the UN
46108.e: In 2012, in the case of Hirsi Jamaa v. Italy, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that pushbacks to Libya on the high seas violate the ECHR.
46108.m: The ban on refoulement also applies on the high seas.

a: Passing someone on via a third country
46109.e: A state also violates the principle if it takes a person to a third country, which then passes them on to the persecuting state. This is also called chain deportation.
46109.m: Chain deportation via third countries also violates the ban on refoulement.

46110.q: What is the EU agency Frontex responsible for?
a: Helping to protect the Schengen external borders
46110.e: Frontex helps the Schengen states monitor the common external borders, for example with staff, aircraft and situation reports. Border control, however, remains the task of the states.
46110.m: Frontex supports the Schengen states in protecting the external borders.

46111.q: Why was Frontex greatly expanded after 2015?
a: Because of the many refugees who came to Europe
46111.e: In 2015 more than a million people came to Europe. After that, Frontex received more money, more staff and a wider mandate.
46111.m: After 2015 Frontex was greatly expanded because of the refugee movements.

46112.q: What was the result of the Swiss popular vote of 15 May 2022 on expanding Frontex?
a: Approved with about 72 per cent yes
Rejected with about 55 per cent no
Approved with about 51 per cent yes
Rejected with about 62 per cent no
46112.e: A referendum had been called against adopting the new EU regulation. Voters clearly approved the proposal with about 71.5 per cent yes.
46112.m: In 2022 Switzerland clearly voted for a bigger contribution to Frontex.

46113.q: Why does Switzerland take part in Frontex even though it is not an EU member?
46113.e: As a Schengen-associated state, Switzerland adopts developments of Schengen law, which include Frontex. It provides staff and money and has limited voting rights on the management board.
46113.m: Switzerland takes part in Frontex because it belongs to the Schengen area.

46114.q: To what size is the Frontex standing corps meant to grow by 2027?
46114.e: The 2019 regulation provides for a standing corps that is to grow to about 10,000 officers by 2027. It is made up of Frontex staff and staff from the member states.
46114.m: The Frontex standing corps is to include about 10,000 people by 2027.

46115.q: Why did Frontex director Fabrice Leggeri resign in 2022?
a: After a dispute about the budget
Because his term of office ended
46115.e: The European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) had investigated, among other things, whether Frontex had covered up illegal pushbacks in the Aegean. Leggeri resigned in April 2022.
46115.m: Fabrice Leggeri resigned in 2022 after investigations into pushbacks.

46116.q: Which post within Frontex monitors respect for fundamental rights?
46116.e: The Fundamental Rights Officer checks operations, deals with complaints and is supported by fundamental rights monitors. This post was strengthened after criticism of human rights violations.
46116.m: At Frontex, a Fundamental Rights Officer monitors respect for human rights.

46117.q: Across which sea do particularly many refugees try to reach Italy?
46117.e: Many boats set off from Libya or Tunisia towards Italy. Frontex supports Italy there with Operation Themis.
46117.m: The central Mediterranean route leads to Italy.

46118.q: In which year did the revised International Health Regulations (IHR 2005) come into force?
46118.e: The World Health Assembly adopted the revision in 2005; the regulations came into force on 15 June 2007. They are legally binding for the states parties.
46118.m: The International Health Regulations of 2005 have applied since 2007.

46119.q: Under the International Health Regulations, who declares a “public health emergency of international concern”?
46119.e: The Director-General decides after consulting an emergency committee of experts. The declaration (PHEIC) comes with recommendations to the states.
46119.m: The WHO Director-General declares an international health emergency.

46120.q: For which event was a “public health emergency of international concern” declared for the first time in 2009?
46120.e: The new influenza A/H1N1 in 2009 was the first case in which the revised regulations were applied. SARS in 2003 came before they came into force.
46120.m: The first international health emergency in 2009 was for swine flu.

46121.q: On which date did the WHO declare COVID-19 a public health emergency of international concern?
46121.e: The emergency was declared on 30 January 2020. On 11 March 2020 the Director-General also described the situation as a pandemic.
46121.m: COVID-19 was declared an international health emergency on 30 January 2020.

46122.q: Which federal office is Switzerland's national focal point for the International Health Regulations?
46122.e: Every state party must name a national IHR focal point that can be reached around the clock. In Switzerland the FOPH takes on this task and exchanges reports with the WHO.
46122.m: In Switzerland the FOPH is the focal point for the International Health Regulations.

46123.q: Within what time must a state notify the WHO of an event that could be an international emergency?
46123.e: Article 6 of the regulations requires notification within 24 hours after the state has assessed the event using the decision instrument in the annex.
46123.m: Possible international health emergencies must be reported within 24 hours.

46124.q: Which new alert level did the amendments to the International Health Regulations adopted in 2024 introduce?
46124.e: In 2024 the World Health Assembly adopted the category of pandemic emergency as the highest level. The amendments came into force for most states parties in September 2025.
46124.m: Since the 2024 revision, the Health Regulations include a pandemic emergency.

46125.q: Which three diseases were covered by the International Health Regulations of 1969 in the end?
46125.e: In the end the old regulations were limited to three notifiable diseases. The 2005 revision, by contrast, covers all events that can endanger public health internationally.
46125.m: The old Health Regulations only covered cholera, plague and yellow fever.

46126.q: When did the World Health Assembly adopt the WHO Pandemic Agreement?
46126.e: The 78th World Health Assembly in Geneva adopted the agreement on 20 May 2025, with no votes against and some abstentions. It is meant to prepare the world better for future pandemics.
46126.m: The WHO Pandemic Agreement was adopted in May 2025.

46127.q: Which event prompted the WHO Pandemic Agreement?
46127.e: The experience of Covid-19 showed how badly prepared the world was. Negotiations therefore began at the end of 2021 and led to the agreement in 2025.
46127.m: The WHO Pandemic Agreement is a lesson from the Covid-19 pandemic.

46128.q: From when is the WHO Pandemic Agreement binding for an individual state?
a: When the state has ratified it
As soon as the WHO has adopted it
When the WHO director orders it
46128.e: The World Health Assembly can adopt agreements with a two-thirds majority. But they only become binding for individual states once they ratify them.
46128.m: A WHO agreement only binds a state after ratification.

46129.q: Before the Pandemic Agreement, which agreement was the only one created under Article 19 of the WHO Constitution?
46129.e: The Framework Convention on Tobacco Control was adopted in 2003. The Pandemic Agreement is therefore only the second treaty of this kind.
46129.m: Before the Pandemic Agreement, the only WHO treaty was the tobacco convention.

46130.q: Which part of the Pandemic Agreement was still open when it was adopted and is to be dealt with in an annex?
a: The seat of a new pandemic fund
The election of a pandemic commissioner
46130.e: The Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing system (PABS) is meant to regulate how samples and gene sequences are shared and what the countries of origin receive in return. Only after it is adopted can the agreement be signed.
46130.m: Pathogen access and benefit sharing are dealt with in an annex to the Pandemic Agreement.

46131.q: Under the WHO Pandemic Agreement, what are participating manufacturers meant to do in a pandemic?
a: Make part of their production available to the WHO
46131.e: The plan is for manufacturers to make 20 per cent of their current production of vaccines, treatments and diagnostics available to the WHO, partly as a donation and partly at affordable prices.
46131.m: In a pandemic, manufacturers are to make part of their production available to the WHO.

46132.q: What does the WHO Pandemic Agreement expressly state about the sovereignty of states?
a: The WHO may close national borders.
The WHO imposes binding travel bans.
46132.e: The agreement makes clear that it gives the WHO no power to dictate national laws, such as lockdowns, vaccine mandates or entry bans. States decide for themselves.
46132.m: The Pandemic Agreement gives the WHO no power to order lockdowns or vaccine mandates.

46133.q: What must happen for the WHO Pandemic Agreement to come into force?
a: The UN Security Council must approve it
Every state in the world must sign it
A new pandemic must break out
46133.e: The agreement comes into force 30 days after the 60th ratification. In addition, the annex on pathogen access must first be adopted.
46133.m: The Pandemic Agreement needs enough ratifications to come into force.

46134.q: What was the aim of the COVAX initiative?
46134.e: COVAX was meant to give all countries, including poorer ones, equal access to vaccines against COVID-19. Rich countries also bought in and paid for doses for poorer countries.
46134.m: COVAX was meant to share Covid vaccines fairly among all countries.

46135.q: Which vaccine alliance led COVAX together with the WHO and the research initiative CEPI?
46135.e: Gavi, the vaccine alliance based in Geneva, organised the purchase and distribution of the doses. In this way donor countries paid for vaccines for 92 poorer countries.
46135.m: Gavi, the WHO and CEPI jointly led COVAX.

46136.q: Which country was the first to receive Covid vaccine doses through COVAX in February 2021?
46136.e: On 24 February 2021 about 600,000 doses of the AstraZeneca vaccine, made by the Serum Institute of India, arrived in Accra. Ivory Coast followed shortly afterwards.
46136.m: Ghana was the first country to receive vaccines through COVAX.

46137.q: Which international initiative was COVAX the vaccine pillar of?
46137.e: The Access to COVID-19 Tools Accelerator (ACT-A) was launched in April 2020 and had pillars for diagnostics, treatments, vaccines and health systems.
46137.m: COVAX was the vaccine pillar of the ACT Accelerator.

46138.q: Why did COVAX run into major supply shortages in spring 2021?
46138.e: COVAX depended heavily on the Serum Institute of India. Because of a severe wave of infections in its own country, India stopped exports, so millions of doses were missing.
46138.m: An Indian export stop caused shortages at COVAX in 2021.

46139.q: How many vaccine doses did COVAX originally want to provide by the end of 2021?
46139.e: The target of 2 billion doses by the end of 2021 was missed, partly because rich countries secured many doses directly. The first billion doses delivered was only reached in January 2022.
46139.m: COVAX missed its target of 2 billion doses by the end of 2021.

46140.q: When did the COVAX initiative end?
46140.e: COVAX was wound up on 31 December 2023, after almost 2 billion doses had been delivered to 146 countries and territories. Since then Covid vaccinations have run through regular Gavi programmes.
46140.m: COVAX ended at the end of 2023.

46141.q: In which year was the Montreal Protocol to protect the ozone layer signed?
46141.e: The protocol was signed on 16 September 1987 and came into force in 1989. That is why 16 September is the International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer.
46141.m: The Montreal Protocol was signed in 1987.

46142.q: Which groups of substances does the Montreal Protocol mainly regulate?
46142.e: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and halons release chlorine and bromine in the stratosphere, which destroy ozone catalytically. Their production was phased out step by step.
46142.m: The Montreal Protocol bans ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs and halons.

46143.q: Which substances did the Kigali Amendment of 2016 add to the Montreal Protocol?
46143.e: Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) often replaced CFCs and hardly harm the ozone layer, but they are powerful greenhouse gases. The Kigali Amendment came into force in 2019 and requires them to be reduced step by step.
46143.m: Since the Kigali Amendment, the Montreal Protocol also limits climate-damaging HFCs.

46144.q: Which milestone did the Montreal Protocol reach in 2009 as the first UN treaty to do so?
a: Nobel Peace Prize for the secretariat
46144.e: In 2009 the Montreal Protocol and the Vienna Convention were the first UN treaties that every state had joined. The treaty is therefore considered a particularly successful environmental agreement.
46144.m: The Montreal Protocol was the first UN treaty to be ratified by every state.

46145.q: Which researchers received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1995 for their work on ozone depletion?
46145.e: Paul Crutzen, Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland researched how nitrogen oxides and CFCs destroy ozone. Their warnings contributed greatly to the Montreal Protocol.
46145.m: Crutzen, Molina and Rowland received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for research on ozone depletion.

46146.q: In which place in the Grisons did the world's longest series of total ozone measurements begin in 1926?
46146.e: Total ozone has been measured at the Light Climatic Observatory in Arosa since 1926. The series is now continued by MeteoSwiss and helps to prove the effect of the Montreal Protocol.
46146.m: The world's longest ozone measurement series began in Arosa in 1926.

46147.q: According to the 2023 scientific assessment, when is the ozone layer over Antarctica expected to recover to its 1980 level?
46147.e: The 2023 UN assessment expects recovery over Antarctica around 2066, over the Arctic around 2045 and over the rest of the world around 2040. This assumes the rules continue to be followed.
46147.m: The ozone hole over Antarctica is likely to close by about 2066.

46148.q: Where and when was the Convention on Biological Diversity opened for signature?
a: In 1992 at the Earth Summit in Rio
46148.e: The Biodiversity Convention was signed in 1992 at the UN Conference on Environment and Development in Rio de Janeiro and came into force at the end of 1993.
46148.m: The Biodiversity Convention dates from the Earth Summit in Rio in 1992.

46149.q: Which of these is NOT a goal of the Biodiversity Convention?
a: A ban on all genetic engineering
46149.e: The convention's three goals are conservation of diversity, sustainable use of its components and fair sharing of the benefits from genetic resources. It does not contain a general ban on genetic engineering.
46149.m: The Biodiversity Convention aims at protection, sustainable use and fair sharing of benefits.

46150.q: According to the Kunming-Montreal framework, by how much a year should environmentally harmful subsidies fall by 2030?
46150.e: Target 18 requires incentives and subsidies harmful to biodiversity to be reduced or reformed by at least 500 billion US dollars a year by 2030.
46150.m: Harmful subsidies are to fall by at least 500 billion dollars a year by 2030.

46151.q: Which body, founded in 2012, provides scientific assessments of biodiversity, similar to the IPCC for the climate?
46151.e: IPBES is an intergovernmental platform with its secretariat in Bonn. Its global report of 2019 estimated that about one million species are threatened with extinction.
46151.m: IPBES assesses the state of biodiversity worldwide.

46152.q: What does the Nagoya Protocol of 2010 regulate?
46152.e: The Nagoya Protocol states that users of genetic resources need the consent of the country of origin and must share the benefits fairly. It came into force in 2014.
46152.m: The Nagoya Protocol regulates access to genetic resources and benefit sharing.

46153.q: What does the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) require by 2030?
46153.e: The “30 by 30” target aims to protect at least 30 per cent of land, inland water, coastal and marine areas effectively. The framework contains 23 targets for 2030 in total.
46153.m: By 2030, 30 per cent of land and sea areas are to be protected.

46154.q: According to the UN, how many of the 20 Aichi Biodiversity Targets for 2020 were fully achieved?
46154.e: The fifth Global Biodiversity Outlook (2020) found that none of the targets had been fully met and only some partly. The successor framework was adopted in 2022.
46154.m: None of the Aichi targets was fully achieved by 2020.

46155.q: What was a new fund created for at the COP16 biodiversity conference in Cali (2024)?
a: The use of digital sequence information
46155.e: Companies that profit from digitally stored gene sequences are to pay into the Cali Fund. The money is to benefit mainly the countries and indigenous communities the resources come from.
46155.m: The Cali Fund is meant to share profits from digital gene sequences more fairly.

46156.q: Which federal office takes the lead in implementing the Biodiversity Convention in Switzerland?
46156.e: The Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) coordinates the Swiss Biodiversity Strategy of 2012 and the action plan of 2017. This is how Switzerland meets its international commitments.
46156.m: The FOEN implements the Biodiversity Convention in Switzerland.

46157.q: At which event was the Millennium Declaration adopted in 2000?
a: At the UN Millennium Summit in New York
At the World Economic Forum in Davos
At the G8 summit in Genoa
At the World Bank meeting in Washington
46157.e: In September 2000 the heads of state and government met at the United Nations headquarters in New York. The declaration adopted there formed the basis of the development goals.
46157.m: The Millennium Declaration was made at the UN summit in New York.

46158.q: Which diseases did the sixth Millennium Development Goal expressly target?
46158.e: Goal 6 aimed to stop the spread of HIV/Aids and fight malaria and other serious diseases. Tuberculosis was also an important topic.
46158.m: The sixth Millennium Goal fought HIV/Aids and malaria.

46159.q: Which set of goals replaced the Millennium Development Goals in 2015?
a: The 2030 Agenda with 17 Sustainable Development Goals
The Kyoto Protocol with its climate targets
The Marshall Plan of the United Nations
46159.e: In September 2015 the UN General Assembly adopted the 2030 Agenda with the Sustainable Development Goals. Unlike the MDGs, they expressly apply to all countries, including Switzerland.
46159.m: The Millennium Goals were followed by the 17 goals of the 2030 Agenda.

46160.q: What was the topic of the third Millennium Development Goal?
46160.e: Goal 3 mainly required girls and boys to be treated equally in school education. The position of women in the economy and politics was also to be strengthened.
46160.m: The third Millennium Goal was about equality between women and men.

46161.q: According to the fifth Millennium Development Goal, by how much was maternal mortality supposed to fall?
46161.e: Goal 5 was about the health of mothers during pregnancy and birth. Maternal mortality did fall considerably, but the target was clearly missed.
46161.m: Maternal mortality was supposed to fall by three quarters.

46162.q: Which Millennium Development Goal included access to clean drinking water?
46162.e: The environmental goal included the target of halving the proportion of people without safe drinking water. According to the UN, this target was reached before 2015.
46162.m: Drinking water was part of the environmental goal of the Millennium Goals.

46163.q: Which year served as the starting year for measurement for most of the Millennium Development Goals?
46163.e: Progress was compared with the situation in 1990, even though the goals were only adopted in 2000. So successes from the 1990s also counted.
46163.m: The Millennium Goals measured progress from the year 1990.

46164.q: Which American economist led the UN Millennium Project, which worked out ways to reach the goals?
46164.e: Jeffrey Sachs was special adviser to the UN Secretary-General on the Millennium Goals. In 2005 his project presented a plan to halve poverty.
46164.m: Jeffrey Sachs led the UN Millennium Project.

46166.q: Which UN organisation publishes the Human Development Index (HDI) every year?
46166.e: The HDI appears in the UNDP's Human Development Report. It was first published in 1990.
46166.m: The HDI is calculated by the United Nations Development Programme.

46167.q: In which year did the first Human Development Report with the HDI appear?
46167.e: The first Human Development Report appeared in 1990. It was meant to show that development is more than economic growth.
46167.m: The HDI has been published since 1990.

46168.q: What is the version of the HDI that takes inequality within a country into account called?
46168.e: The IHDI lowers a country's value more, the more unequally health, education and income are distributed. It has been calculated since 2010.
46168.m: The IHDI shows how much development is lost through inequality.

46169.q: Since the 2010 report, how have the three sub-indices been combined into the HDI?
a: With the sum of all values
46169.e: The geometric mean is the cube root of the product of the three sub-indices. This way a poor value in one area can be offset less by good values elsewhere.
46169.m: Today the HDI uses the geometric mean.

46170.q: A country has the sub-indices 0.64 (health), 1.0 (education) and 0.8 (income). What is its HDI using the geometric mean?
46170.e: The product is 0.64 × 1.0 × 0.8 = 0.512. The cube root of 0.512 is 0.8, because 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.512.
46170.m: For the HDI you take the cube root of the product of the sub-indices.

46171.q: Which country tops the ranking in the Human Development Report 2025 (2023 data)?
46171.e: Iceland reached an HDI of 0.972, just ahead of the next countries. The Nordic countries traditionally do very well on the HDI.
46171.m: Iceland is at the top of the HDI in 2025.

46172.q: Into how many development groups does the UNDP divide countries according to their HDI?
46172.e: It distinguishes very high, high, medium and low human development. The groups make it easier to compare countries at a similar level.
46172.m: The HDI puts countries into four development groups.

46173.q: Which additional index did the UNDP introduce in 2020 to take environmental pressures such as CO2 emissions into account?
46173.e: The PHDI lowers a country's HDI more, the higher its CO2 emissions and raw material use per person. Rich countries often lose several places as a result.
46173.m: The PHDI links human development with pressure on the planet.

46174.q: What does the UNDP's Gender Development Index (GDI) compare?
a: The HDI of women with that of men
The proportion of women in parliament
46174.e: The GDI is the ratio between the HDI of women and the HDI of men. A value of 1 means they are equal.
46174.m: The GDI shows differences in the development of women and men.

46175.q: What does the Gini coefficient measure?
46175.e: The Gini coefficient is a statistical measure of unequal distribution. It is often applied to income or wealth.
46175.m: The Gini coefficient describes how unequally something is distributed.

46176.q: Which statistician is the Gini coefficient named after?
46176.e: Corrado Gini presented the measure in 1912. The Italian statistician studied population and distribution.
46176.m: Corrado Gini gave his name to the measure of inequality.

46177.q: Which Gini coefficient stands for perfectly equal distribution?
46177.e: At 0, everyone has exactly the same amount. The higher the value, the more unequal the distribution.
46177.m: A Gini coefficient of zero means complete equality.

46178.q: What does a Gini coefficient of 1 mean?
46178.e: The value 1 describes maximum inequality. All the income or wealth is then held by one single unit.
46178.m: At a value of one, inequality is at its maximum.

46179.q: From which graph is the Gini coefficient derived?
46179.e: The Lorenz curve shows which share of the population has which share of income. The Gini coefficient is the ratio of the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve to the whole area under the line.
46179.m: The Gini coefficient is worked out with the Lorenz curve.

46180.q: The area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve is 0.15, and the area under the Lorenz curve is 0.35. What is the Gini coefficient?
46180.e: The Gini coefficient is area A divided by A plus B. So 0.15 / (0.15 + 0.35) = 0.15 / 0.5 = 0.3.
46180.m: You divide the area above the Lorenz curve by the whole triangle area.

46181.q: How does the Gini coefficient of incomes typically change because of taxes and social transfers?
46181.e: Progressive taxes and transfers such as pensions or social assistance redistribute income. That is why the Gini of disposable incomes is lower than that of market incomes.
46181.m: Redistribution by the state lowers the Gini coefficient.

46182.q: What is true for Switzerland when comparing income and wealth?
a: Wealth is distributed much more unequally than income
Income is distributed more unequally than wealth
Both are distributed exactly the same
46182.e: The Gini of disposable incomes in Switzerland is about 0.3, while that of wealth is much higher. Wealth is inherited over generations and grows through investment income.
46182.m: In Switzerland wealth is distributed much more unequally than income.

46183.q: According to the World Bank, which country is among those with the highest Gini coefficient for incomes?
46183.e: With values above 0.6, South Africa has one of the most unequal income distributions in the world. The effects of apartheid are still felt there today.
46183.m: South Africa has one of the most unequal income distributions in the world.

46184.q: Why do poor people often not get a loan from ordinary banks?
a: They are not allowed to open an account
Loans are banned there by law
46184.e: Banks usually require collateral such as land or a house. In addition, the administrative costs are high in relation to very small amounts.
46184.m: Anyone without collateral rarely gets a loan from a normal bank.

46185.q: Apart from microloans, what else does the term microfinance include?
a: Savings accounts and insurance for poor people
46185.e: Microfinance means all financial services for people on low incomes. Besides loans, these include saving, insurance and money transfers.
46185.m: Microfinance also offers poor people savings and insurance.

46186.q: Which danger of microloans became apparent in some countries?
a: Borrowers getting into too much debt through high interest and too many loans
Interest rates so low that they ruined the banks
A ban on all loans by the UN
46186.e: Around 2010, for example in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, many people took out several loans at the same time and could not repay them. The government then severely restricted the lenders.

46187.q: In which Swiss city was BlueOrchard, one of the first commercial investment funds for microfinance, set up in 2001?
46187.e: BlueOrchard was founded in Geneva and invests investors' money in microfinance institutions. Switzerland is considered an important location for microfinance investment.
46187.m: Geneva is a centre for investment in microfinance.

46188.q: In which country was the Grameen Bank founded?
46188.e: Muhammad Yunus founded the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh. Since 1983 it has been an independent bank by law.
46188.m: The Grameen Bank comes from Bangladesh.

46189.q: What did Muhammad Yunus give poor women in Bangladesh from 1976 onwards to free them from moneylenders?
46189.e: Yunus first lent 42 women from the village of Jobra about 27 US dollars out of his own pocket. This gave rise to the idea of microloans and later the Grameen Bank.
46189.m: The Grameen Bank began with small loans to poor women.

46190.q: Who owns most of the Grameen Bank?
46190.e: The borrowers, most of them poor women, are also shareholders of the bank. Most recently the state of Bangladesh held about a quarter of the shares.
46190.m: The Grameen Bank is mostly owned by its customers.

46191.q: With which French food company did Grameen set up a social business in 2006 for cheap, nutritious yoghurt?
46191.e: Grameen Danone Foods makes an enriched yoghurt for children in Bangladesh. Profits are to stay in the company and not be paid out.
46191.m: Grameen and Danone produce yoghurt together to fight malnutrition.

46192.q: What happened between Muhammad Yunus and the Grameen Bank in 2011?
a: He sold the bank to investors
He moved the bank to India
He became an honorary citizen of Switzerland
46192.e: The central bank of Bangladesh dismissed Yunus, citing the age limit. Many saw this as a political conflict with the government of the time.
46192.m: In 2011 Yunus had to give up the leadership of the Grameen Bank.

46193.q: What does the abbreviation HIPC stand for?
46193.e: The initiative is aimed at heavily indebted poor countries. It is meant to reduce their debt burden to a bearable level.
46193.m: HIPC refers to the heavily indebted poor countries.

46194.q: Which two institutions run the HIPC initiative for heavily indebted poor countries?
46194.e: The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank started the initiative in 1996. A total of 39 countries are considered eligible or potentially eligible.
46194.m: The IMF and the World Bank run the HIPC initiative.

46195.q: What does a country receive if it successfully completes the HIPC initiative?
a: A large part of its foreign debt is cancelled
A permanent seat on the Security Council
46195.e: After several steps, from the decision point to the completion point, the debts are reduced to a bearable level. The money saved is to be used to fight poverty.
46195.m: The HIPC initiative reduces the debts of poor countries.

46196.q: Among other things, what must an HIPC country present and implement to receive full debt relief?
a: An application to join the EU
46196.e: A Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper is required, which must have been implemented for at least one year. This is so that the money saved benefits the poor.
46196.m: Debt relief is only given in return for an effective poverty strategy.

46197.q: Which initiative added full cancellation of certain multilateral debts to HIPC from 2005?
46197.e: Countries that have completed the HIPC process receive 100 per cent relief on certain debts to the IMF, the World Bank and the African Development Fund through the MDRI. It was prepared at the G8 summit in 2005.
46197.m: The MDRI cancelled HIPC countries' multilateral debts completely.

46198.q: What must HIPC countries do with the money they save thanks to debt relief?
a: Use it mainly to fight poverty
Pay it back to the World Bank
Keep it as a reserve in gold
46198.e: Debt relief is only given with a strategy to fight poverty. The money freed up is meant to go into schools and health, for example.
46198.m: Cancelled debts are meant to benefit the poor.

46199.q: In which region of the world are the great majority of HIPC countries?
46199.e: Of the 39 countries, 33 are in sub-Saharan Africa. In addition there are Afghanistan and some countries in Latin America and the Caribbean.
46199.m: Most HIPC countries are in sub-Saharan Africa.

46200.q: Which South American Andean country is one of the HIPC countries that received debt relief?
46200.e: Bolivia was one of the first countries to complete the HIPC process. In Latin America, Honduras, Nicaragua, Guyana and Haiti also benefited.
46200.m: Bolivia is one of the HIPC countries in South America.

46201.q: Which North African country reached the decision point of the HIPC initiative in 2021?
46201.e: After the fall of the long-time ruler Omar al-Bashir, the way to debt relief opened up. The war from 2023 slowed down the further process.
46201.m: Sudan was admitted to the HIPC initiative in 2021.

46202.q: Which body adopted the 0.7 per cent target in 1970?
46202.e: The General Assembly anchored the target in 1970 in a resolution on the Development Decade. It has often been confirmed since then.
46202.m: The UN General Assembly set the 0.7 per cent target in 1970.

46203.q: What does the 0.7 per cent target for development aid refer to?
a: The gross national income of the donor country
The state budget of the donor country
The exports of the donor country
The income of the receiving countries
46203.e: Rich countries are to spend 0.7 per cent of their gross national income (GNI) on official development aid every year. The target was set by the UN in 1970.
46203.m: The 0.7 per cent target measures development aid against gross national income.

46204.q: What are the international abbreviations for official development aid (in English and French)?
46204.e: In English it is called Official Development Assistance, in French Aide publique au développement. In Switzerland the abbreviation APD is common.
46204.m: Official development aid is called ODA or APD.

46205.q: Besides SECO, which federal agency is mainly responsible for Swiss development cooperation?
46205.e: The Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC) is part of the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs. It runs programmes in poor countries and provides humanitarian aid.
46205.m: The SDC is Switzerland's development agency.

46206.q: Roughly what was Switzerland's ODA rate in 2024?
46206.e: In 2024 Switzerland spent just under 0.5 per cent of its gross national income. Parliament had set a target of 0.5 per cent in 2011.
46206.m: At about 0.5 per cent, Switzerland is below the UN target.

46207.q: Which of these countries clearly exceeded the 0.7 per cent target in 2024?
46207.e: In 2024 Norway and Luxembourg reached about one per cent of their GNI. Only a few donor countries meet the target at all.
46207.m: Norway is one of the few countries above the 0.7 per cent target.

46208.q: Which controversial spending may a donor country partly count as development aid under the DAC rules?
a: Costs for asylum seekers in its own country in the first year
Interest on its own national debt
46208.e: Looking after asylum seekers at home may be counted during the first twelve months. Critics complain that this money does not go to poor countries.
46208.m: Asylum costs at home raise the official development aid rate.

46209.q: Which large donor country reached the 0.7 per cent target for the first time in 2016, partly because of high asylum costs at home?
46209.e: In 2016 Germany reached 0.70 per cent of its gross national income. A large part of this was spending on refugees in its own country.
46209.m: Germany met the UN target for the first time in 2016.

46210.q: How many of the 32 donor countries of the OECD Development Assistance Committee reached the 0.7 per cent target in 2024?
46210.e: Only Norway, Luxembourg, Sweden and Denmark were at 0.7 per cent or above in 2024. Most donor countries, including Switzerland, remain well below.
46210.m: Only very few countries meet the 0.7 per cent target.

46211.q: Which department is the Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit part of?
46211.e: The SHA belongs to the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs. It carries out projects of the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC).
46211.m: The SHA works on behalf of the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs.

46212.q: Who carries out the missions of the Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit?
a: Only professional soldiers of the army
Only employees of the Red Cross
46212.e: Several hundred experts are on standby, for example from medicine, construction, logistics or water supply. They are organised in expert groups.
46212.m: The SHA is made up of volunteer experts.

46213.q: What do the experts of the SHA expert group “Cash” do in a crisis?
a: They organise cash assistance for those affected
They guard banks in the crisis area
46213.e: Instead of handing out goods, those affected receive money and buy what they need most themselves. This also strengthens local markets.
46213.m: Cash assistance lets people in need decide for themselves what to buy.

46214.q: Which German federal agency has a range of worldwide missions comparable to that of the SHA?
a: The Federal Agency for Technical Relief (THW)
46214.e: Like Switzerland, the THW sends rescue and aid teams to disasters abroad, for example with its rapid deployment unit for rescue abroad. The Austrian Forces Disaster Relief Unit has a similar profile.
46214.m: The German THW carries out similar tasks to the SHA.

46215.q: Under whose leadership is the Swiss Rescue chain?
a: Under the leadership of the SHA
Under the leadership of the Red Cross
Under the leadership of the army
46215.e: The Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit secures the funding and decides on missions. The other partners contribute specialist knowledge and equipment.

46216.q: What is Swiss Rescue mainly used for?
a: Rescuing people buried after earthquakes abroad
Recovering avalanche victims in the Swiss Alps
Putting out forest fires in southern Europe
Looking after refugees at the borders
46216.e: Swiss Rescue has existed since 1981. It flies abroad with specialists, search dogs and equipment to search for people buried in collapsed buildings.
46216.m: Swiss Rescue searches for buried people after earthquakes abroad.

46217.q: Besides the SHA and REDOG, which organisation is a partner of Swiss Rescue?
46217.e: Swiss Air-Rescue is one link in the rescue chain. The partners contribute different skills.
46217.m: Rega is also a link in Swiss Rescue.

46218.q: According to the standards of which organisation is Swiss Rescue certified?
46218.e: The UN group INSARAG sets worldwide standards for rescue teams and checks them regularly. In an emergency, certified teams work according to common rules.

46219.q: To which country was Swiss Rescue sent after the severe earthquake in February 2023?
46219.e: After the earthquakes in the border area of Turkey and Syria, Swiss Rescue searched for buried people in Hatay. Turkey had already been a mission country several times.
46219.m: In 2023 Swiss Rescue helped after the earthquake in Turkey.

46220.q: How quickly should Swiss Rescue be ready to take off after an earthquake?
46220.e: Buried people usually only survive a few days. That is why Swiss Rescue must be able to take off within a few hours with staff, dogs and equipment.
46220.m: When searching for buried people, every hour counts.

46221.q: Which troops of the Swiss Army are part of Swiss Rescue?
a: The air force with fighter jets
46221.e: The rescue troops specialise in recovering people from collapsed buildings. They contribute heavy equipment and know-how.
46221.m: The army's rescue troops are also part of Swiss Rescue.

46222.q: To which country did Swiss Rescue travel after the severe Spitak earthquake in December 1988?
46222.e: Tens of thousands of people died in the earthquake in what was then a Soviet republic. Switzerland was among the foreign helpers.
46222.m: In 1988 Swiss Rescue helped after the earthquake in Armenia.

46223.q: To which country was Swiss Rescue sent after the earthquake of November 2019?
46223.e: An earthquake near the coastal city of Durrës caused many buildings to collapse. Swiss Rescue searched for buried people there.
46223.m: In 2019 Swiss Rescue was deployed in Albania.

46224.q: After which earthquake in an American city of millions did Swiss Rescue help in 1985?
46224.e: The earthquake of September 1985 destroyed large parts of Mexico City. In the same year Swiss Rescue was also deployed in Italy.
46224.m: In 1985 Swiss Rescue searched for buried people in Mexico.

46225.q: What legal form does Helvetas have?
46225.e: Helvetas is a politically and religiously independent association. It is supported by members, donors and volunteer regional groups.
46225.m: Helvetas is organised as an association.

46226.q: In which field has Helvetas become particularly well known, for example by building pipes and wells?
46226.e: Clean drinking water is one of its central areas of work. Helvetas also works for food security, education and income.
46226.m: Drinking water is a core topic of Helvetas.

46227.q: In which city was Helvetas founded?
46227.e: The founding meeting took place in Zurich on 18 June 1955. Its head office is still there today.

46228.q: What does the name of the aid organisation Helvetas recall?
46228.e: Helvetia is the Latin name of Switzerland. The aid organisation founded in 1955 has been called Helvetas since 1965.
46228.m: Helvetas recalls Helvetia, the Latin name of Switzerland.

46229.q: Roughly how many members and donors does Helvetas have?
46229.e: Helvetas is supported by a broad base among the population. In addition there are volunteer regional groups all over Switzerland.
46229.m: About 100,000 people support Helvetas as members or donors.

46230.q: What is Helvetas's position towards political parties and churches?
a: It is politically and religiously independent
It belongs to the Reformed Church
It is part of a party in the Federal Council
It is run by the Federal Council
46230.e: Helvetas is an independent association. It has offices in all the large language regions of Switzerland, for example in Zurich, Bern, Lausanne and Balerna.
46230.m: Helvetas is politically and religiously independent.

46231.q: Who makes up most of Helvetas's staff?
a: Local employees in the project countries
Employees at the Swiss head office
46231.e: Over 1,400 people work in the project countries, compared with about 130 in Switzerland. Local experts know the language and culture best.
46231.m: Helvetas works mainly with local experts.

46232.q: What importance does Helvetas have in the history of Swiss development cooperation?
a: It is one of the first private development organisations in Switzerland
It was the first federal office for development
It was the first Swiss bank for developing countries
It was the first army unit for disasters
46232.e: Helvetas was founded in 1955 as a private association, before the Confederation set up its own development aid. State development cooperation only followed in 1961.
46232.m: Helvetas is one of the first private development organisations in Switzerland.

46233.q: Which church is Caritas closely connected with?
46233.e: Caritas is the aid organisation of the Catholic Church; its name means love of one's neighbour in Latin. Its Reformed counterpart in Switzerland is HEKS.
46233.m: Caritas is the aid organisation of the Catholic Church.

46234.q: Which task does Caritas often take on in Switzerland on behalf of the public authorities?
a: Looking after asylum seekers and refugees
46234.e: Cantons commission Caritas to look after asylum seekers and recognised refugees. This includes accommodation and integration.
46234.m: In Switzerland Caritas looks after many asylum seekers and refugees.

46235.q: Which European network does Caritas Switzerland belong to?
46235.e: Caritas Europa brings together the national Caritas organisations of the continent. It represents their concerns to the European institutions.
46235.m: Caritas Switzerland is a member of Caritas Europa.

46236.q: Where is the worldwide umbrella organisation Caritas Internationalis based?
46236.e: The umbrella organisation is based in the Vatican, in the Palazzo San Calisto in Rome. This shows its link with the Catholic Church.
46236.m: Caritas Internationalis is based in Rome, in the Vatican.

46237.q: In how many countries is the Caritas network represented by member organisations?
46237.e: Caritas Internationalis includes organisations in 162 countries. This makes it one of the largest aid networks in the world.
46237.m: The Caritas network is active in over 160 countries.

46238.q: For which quality label was Caritas Switzerland one of the founding organisations in 1992?
46238.e: Together with other aid organisations, Caritas founded the foundation for fairly traded products. The label can now be found in almost every supermarket.
46238.m: Caritas helped bring the Max Havelaar label to Switzerland.

46239.q: Which award did Doctors Without Borders receive in 1999?
46239.e: The Nobel Committee honoured the organisation's pioneering humanitarian work on several continents. At the time it was already active in over 80 countries.
46239.m: Doctors Without Borders received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1999.

46240.q: Which later French foreign minister was one of the founders of Doctors Without Borders?
46240.e: Bernard Kouchner was a doctor in Biafra and a co-founder of the organisation. Later, from 2007 to 2010, he was France's foreign minister.
46240.m: Bernard Kouchner is one of the founders of Doctors Without Borders.

46241.q: What does Doctors Without Borders mean by the principle of “témoignage”?
46241.e: Unlike some aid organisations, MSF does not stay silent when it sees serious crimes. The organisation deliberately makes abuses public.
46241.m: Doctors Without Borders speaks publicly about what it sees on the ground.

46242.q: Where does by far the largest part of Doctors Without Borders' income come from?
46242.e: Well over 90 per cent of the organisation's funding comes from private donations. This secures its independence from governments.
46242.m: Private donations make Doctors Without Borders independent.

46243.q: In which city is the Swiss section of Doctors Without Borders based?
46243.e: The Swiss section was founded in Geneva in 1981. Geneva is also an important operational centre of the organisation.
46243.m: Doctors Without Borders Switzerland is based in Geneva.

46244.q: Which principles does Doctors Without Borders stress in its aid?
46244.e: Aid is given only according to need, regardless of origin, religion or politics. This also applies in war zones.
46244.m: Doctors Without Borders helps independently, neutrally and impartially.

46245.q: Out of experiences in which war did Doctors Without Borders arise?
46245.e: From 1968 to 1970 French doctors experienced a famine in the breakaway province of Biafra. They were unhappy at having to keep silent about what they had seen.
46245.m: Doctors Without Borders has its roots in the Biafran War.

46246.q: Which campaign did Doctors Without Borders start in 1999?
a: For a ban on nuclear power stations
For more female doctors in Europe
46246.e: The Access Campaign works for affordable medicines and vaccines in poor countries. It criticises, for example, high prices caused by patents.
46246.m: Doctors Without Borders fights for affordable medicines.

46247.q: Which umbrella organisation sets the international Fairtrade standards?
46247.e: Fairtrade International is an alliance of national Fairtrade organisations and producer networks. An independent certification body checks the standards.
46247.m: The Fairtrade standards come from Fairtrade International.

46248.q: What is the difference between fair trade and pure free trade?
a: Fair trade sets minimum social standards
Free trade is only allowed between poor countries
46248.e: In free trade the market mainly sets the price. Fair trade adds rules to it, such as minimum prices, workers' rights and a ban on exploitative child labour.
46248.m: Fair trade combines trade with minimum social standards.

46249.q: Why does an independent body check whether producers meet the Fairtrade standards?
a: So that the label stays credible
So that the products become cheaper
So that the producers pay no taxes
46249.e: Fairtrade separates setting the rules from checking them. The independent body FLOCERT inspects cooperatives and traders on site so that customers can trust the label.
46249.m: Independent checks make the Fairtrade label credible.

46250.q: What do cooperatives receive in Fairtrade trading in addition to the minimum price?
a: A permanent work contract in Europe
46250.e: With the Fairtrade premium, cooperatives fund schools, wells or better farming methods, for example. They decide together how it is used.
46250.m: The Fairtrade premium goes into the producers' community projects.

46251.q: What were the women called who drew attention to the situation of banana workers with a campaign in Frauenfeld in 1973?
46251.e: Led by Ursula Brunner, they demanded a fair price for bananas. The campaign is seen as pioneering work for fair trade in Switzerland.
46251.m: The banana women of Frauenfeld were pioneers of fair trade.

46252.q: Under which pen name did Eduard Douwes Dekker publish the novel “Max Havelaar”?
46252.e: Multatuli means “I have suffered much” in Latin. The novel appeared in 1860 and became a classic of Dutch literature.
46252.m: The author of “Max Havelaar” called himself Multatuli.

46253.q: On which island is the novel “Max Havelaar”, which denounces the exploitation of coffee farmers, set?
46253.e: The novel describes the oppression of the local population in the Dutch East Indies, today's Indonesia. The farmers had to grow coffee for export.
46253.m: “Max Havelaar” is set on the island of Java.

46254.q: In which country was the first Fairtrade label launched in 1988 under the name Max Havelaar?
46254.e: The church organisation Solidaridad and the priest Frans van der Hoff were behind the label. Other countries took up the idea in the following years.
46254.m: The Max Havelaar label was created in the Netherlands in 1988.

46255.q: What does the Max Havelaar Fairtrade label usually guarantee producers?
a: A minimum price and a premium for community projects
A fixed wage from the Swiss state
The sale of their whole harvest
46255.e: The minimum price protects against low world market prices. With the Fairtrade premium, cooperatives fund schools or wells, for example.
46255.m: Fairtrade secures minimum prices and a premium for community projects.

46256.q: Which two retailers had to launch fair products for the Confederation to pay the Max Havelaar Foundation a start-up contribution in 1992?
46256.e: The Federal Office for Foreign Economic Affairs made its start-up contribution conditional on the two largest retailers taking part. This brought the label quickly to the mass market.
46256.m: Migros and Coop made Max Havelaar well known in Switzerland.

46257.q: Under the Vienna Convention, what may the police of the receiving state not do to a diplomat?
a: Stop them at a traffic check
Point out an offence to them
46257.e: The person of a diplomat is inviolable; they may be neither arrested nor detained. The receiving state must even protect them from attacks.
46257.m: A diplomat may not be arrested in the host country.

46258.q: Under the Vienna Convention, what applies to the premises of an embassy?
a: They belong to the sending state
46258.e: The premises of the mission are inviolable; authorities of the receiving state may only enter with the consent of the head of mission. Contrary to a common mistake, however, this does not make the embassy territory of the sending state.
46258.m: An embassy is inviolable but remains territory of the receiving state.

46259.q: Under the Vienna Convention, what may the receiving state not do with the diplomatic bag?
46259.e: The diplomatic bag may be neither opened nor detained. This keeps confidential communication between the mission and its government protected.
46259.m: The diplomatic bag may not be opened.

46260.q: Under the Vienna Convention, who can waive a diplomat's immunity?
a: The court of the receiving state
46260.e: Immunity serves the state and not the person, so only the sending state can waive it. The waiver must be expressly stated.
46260.m: Only the sending state can lift its diplomat's immunity.

46261.q: Which duty do diplomats have towards the receiving state despite their immunity?
a: To pay tax there on everything
To give evidence in its courts
46261.e: The convention obliges diplomats to respect the laws of the receiving state and not to interfere in its internal affairs. Immunity means protection from prosecution, not freedom from rules.
46261.m: Even diplomats with immunity must respect the laws of the host country.

46262.q: Which treaty governs the work of consulates, as opposed to embassies?
a: The Charter of the United Nations
46262.e: Consular relations are governed by the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations of 1963. Consuls enjoy narrower protection there than diplomats.
46262.m: A separate Vienna Convention of 1963 applies to consulates.

46263.q: Under the Vienna Convention, which is the lowest of the three classes of heads of mission?
46263.e: The convention recognises ambassadors and nuncios, then envoys and internuncios, and finally chargés d'affaires. Chargés d'affaires are accredited to the foreign minister and not to the head of state.
46263.m: The chargé d'affaires is the lowest class of head of mission.

46264.q: Under the Vienna Convention, what must the receiving state do with a mission's buildings if diplomatic relations are broken off?
a: Continue to respect and protect them
Hand them over to the UN
46264.e: Even if relations are broken off or there is an armed conflict, the receiving state must respect and protect the mission's premises, property and archives. The sending state can entrust them to the care of a third state.
46264.m: Embassy buildings remain protected even after relations are broken off.

46265.q: What does the Latin expression “persona non grata” literally mean?
46265.e: “Persona non grata” literally means “person not welcome”. In diplomacy the expression refers to a diplomat whom the receiving state no longer accepts.
46265.m: A persona non grata is a person unwelcome in the host country.

46266.q: Does a state have to give reasons for declaring a diplomat persona non grata?
a: No, it does not have to give any reasons
Yes, in writing to the UN
46266.e: The Vienna Convention allows the declaration at any time and without explanation. In practice, though, reasons are often hinted at in public.
46266.m: A declaration of persona non grata needs no explanation.

46267.q: What must the sending state do if one of its diplomats has been declared persona non grata?
a: Recall them or end their work
Put them before its own court
Issue them with a new passport
46267.e: The sending state must recall the person or end their work at the mission. If it does not do so within a reasonable time, the receiving state can stop recognising them as a member of the mission.
46267.m: A diplomat declared persona non grata must be recalled.

46268.q: Under the Vienna Convention, from when can a person be declared persona non grata?
a: Even before they arrive in the country
Only after a year in office
46268.e: The convention states that a person can be declared not acceptable even before arriving in the territory. This way a state can prevent an entry from the start.
46268.m: A person can be declared persona non grata even before arriving.

46269.q: Under international law, may a state expel foreign diplomats?
a: Yes, it is unfriendly but allowed
46269.e: Expelling diplomats is a lawful but unfriendly measure. In international law such a step is called retorsion.
46269.m: Expelling diplomats is allowed but unfriendly.

46270.q: How do affected states often react when their diplomats are expelled?
a: By expelling the same number of diplomats
By complaining to the UN Security Council
46270.e: The usual answer follows the principle of reciprocity: the affected state in turn expels a similar number of diplomats. There have been such waves, for example, between Russia and Western states.
46270.m: Expulsions of diplomats are often answered with counter-expulsions.

46271.q: Can a state also force embassy employees without diplomatic status to leave?
a: Yes, it can declare them “not acceptable”
46271.e: For other staff, such as administrative employees, the Vienna Convention speaks of “not acceptable” instead of “persona non grata”. The result is the same.
46271.m: An embassy's administrative staff can also be declared not acceptable.

46272.q: Who issues an ambassador's letter of credence?
a: The head of state of the sending state
The parliament of the receiving state
The embassy of the receiving state
46272.e: The letter of credence is a letter from the head of state of the sending state to the head of state of the receiving state. It confirms that the person officially represents the state.
46272.m: The letter of credence comes from the head of state of the sending state.

46273.q: What is the letter called with which an ambassador is officially taken leave of at the end of their mission?
46273.e: The letter of recall, in French “lettre de rappel”, informs the receiving state that the mission has ended. Often the successor hands it over together with their own letter.
46273.m: A mission ends with the letter of recall.

46274.q: What is the letter of credence called in French, the traditional language of diplomacy?
46274.e: French was long the language of diplomacy, which is why many technical terms are French. The letter of credence is called “lettre de créance”.
46274.m: In French the letter of credence is called “lettre de créance”.

46275.q: What is the main difference between an embassy and a consulate?
a: The embassy represents the state politically, the consulate mainly looks after citizens
The consulate is always in the capital
Only the consulate may negotiate with the government
The embassy is only responsible for tourists
46275.e: The embassy in the capital maintains political relations with the government. Consulates deal mainly with passports, visas and help for their own nationals.
46275.m: Embassies are responsible for politics, consulates mainly for services to citizens.

46276.q: To whom does a new ambassador usually hand a copy of their letter of credence even before the formal presentation?
46276.e: After arriving, the ambassador gives the foreign ministry a copy of the letter of credence. Depending on the country's practice, they may then already take on certain tasks.
46276.m: A copy of the letter of credence goes first to the foreign ministry.

46277.q: Under the Vienna Convention, what does a state need in order to make a national of the receiving state one of its diplomats?
a: The consent of the receiving state
46277.e: In principle, diplomats should have the nationality of the sending state. People with the nationality of the receiving state may only be appointed with its consent.
46277.m: Citizens of the host country only become diplomats with its consent.

46278.q: In many states, who is the doyen of the diplomatic corps?
a: The ambassador who has been accredited the longest
The ambassador of the largest country
The ambassador of the neighbouring country
46278.e: Precedence within a class depends on the date of taking up office. In many countries with a Catholic tradition, however, the papal nuncio is traditionally the doyen.
46278.m: The doyen is usually the longest-serving ambassador in the country.

46279.q: Under the Vienna Convention, what determines the rank of ambassadors of the same class among themselves?
a: The date they took up office
The alphabetical order of the country names
46279.e: Within a class, the time when they took up their duties counts. This defused the old dispute about the precedence of powerful states.
46279.m: Among ambassadors, the order of taking up office applies.

46280.q: What did France receive in the Peace of Westphalia?
46280.e: France received the Habsburg rights and possessions in Alsace. Its possession of the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun was also confirmed.
46280.m: In 1648 France gained rights in Alsace.

46281.q: In which two cities was the Peace of Westphalia negotiated?
46281.e: The Catholic powers negotiated in Münster, the Protestant ones in Osnabrück. Both cities are in Westphalia, hence the name.
46281.m: The Peace of Westphalia was negotiated in Münster and Osnabrück.

46282.q: Which mayor of Basel achieved the separation of the Swiss Confederation from the Holy Roman Empire in 1648?
46282.e: Johann Rudolf Wettstein travelled to Westphalia as an envoy. He achieved the Confederation's release from the jurisdiction of the Empire, which is regarded as independence under international law.
46282.m: Johann Rudolf Wettstein secured the independence of the Swiss Confederation in 1648.

46283.q: Which country was recognised as independent by Spain as part of the Peace of Westphalia?
46283.e: In the Peace of Münster of January 1648, Spain recognised the Republic of the United Netherlands. This ended the Eighty Years' War.
46283.m: In 1648 Spain recognised the independence of the Netherlands.

46284.q: Which denomination was newly recognised in imperial law by the Peace of Westphalia?
46284.e: The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 had only recognised Catholics and Lutherans. In 1648 the Reformed, that is the Calvinists, were included too.
46284.m: From 1648 the Reformed were also recognised in the Empire.

46285.q: Which principle of the international order is often linked with the Peace of Westphalia?
a: The right of peoples to self-determination
The ban on wars of aggression
46285.e: The so-called Westphalian system stands for equal, sovereign states that do not interfere in each other's internal affairs. Historians stress, however, that this picture partly only developed later.
46285.m: The Peace of Westphalia is a symbol of the sovereignty of states.

46286.q: Which war did the Peace of Westphalia end in 1648?
46286.e: The Thirty Years' War lasted from 1618 to 1648 and devastated large parts of central Europe. The peace also settled the ownership of church property according to the situation in 1624.
46286.m: The Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648.

46287.q: Which area on the Baltic Sea did Sweden receive in the Peace of Westphalia?
46287.e: Among other things, Sweden received Western Pomerania and the bishoprics of Bremen and Verden. This made it an Imperial Estate and gave it control of important river mouths.
46287.m: In 1648 Sweden gained Western Pomerania on the Baltic Sea.

46288.q: Which four heads of government shaped the Paris Peace Conference of 1919 as the “Big Four”?
46288.e: Woodrow Wilson (USA), David Lloyd George (Britain), Georges Clemenceau (France) and Vittorio Emanuele Orlando (Italy) made the most important decisions. Clemenceau chaired the conference.
46288.m: Wilson, Lloyd George, Clemenceau and Orlando formed the “Big Four”.

46289.q: In which room was the Treaty of Versailles signed on 28 June 1919?
46289.e: The signing deliberately took place in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. The German Empire had been proclaimed there in 1871.
46289.m: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in the Hall of Mirrors.

46290.q: What role did the defeated Central Powers play in the negotiations at the Paris Peace Conference?
a: They were excluded from the negotiations
46290.e: Germany and its allies were not allowed to take part in the negotiations but were given the finished treaties to accept. In Germany people therefore spoke of a “dictated peace”.
46290.m: The losers of the First World War were excluded from the negotiations.

46291.q: Which Paris suburb treaty settled the peace with Austria in 1919?
46291.e: The Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye was signed in September 1919. Among other things, it banned the union of Austria with Germany.
46291.m: The peace treaty with Austria is called the Treaty of Saint-Germain.

46292.q: With which country was the Treaty of Trianon concluded in 1920?
46292.e: With the Treaty of Trianon of 4 June 1920, Hungary lost more than two thirds of its previous territory. The treaty still shapes Hungarian memory today.
46292.m: The Treaty of Trianon concerned Hungary.

46293.q: In which Swiss city did the League of Nations, founded at the Paris Peace Conference, have its seat?
46293.e: The Covenant of the League of Nations was part of the Paris peace treaties. Geneva was chosen as its seat; Switzerland joined in 1920 after a popular vote.
46293.m: The League of Nations had its seat in Geneva.

46294.q: Why did the USA never join the League of Nations, even though President Wilson had proposed it?
a: The Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles
The League refused to admit it
46294.e: Ratification needed a two-thirds majority in the US Senate, which was not reached. The USA later made a separate peace with Germany.
46294.m: The US Senate prevented the USA from joining the League of Nations.

46295.q: What is Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles usually called?
46295.e: Article 231 declared Germany and its allies responsible for the losses of the war. It served as the basis for the reparation demands and was fiercely opposed in Germany.
46295.m: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles is known as the war guilt clause.

46296.q: How long did the negotiations at Camp David last in September 1978?
46296.e: The talks began on 5 September and ended on 17 September 1978 with the signing at the White House. Several times they threatened to fail.
46296.m: The Camp David negotiations lasted 13 days.

46297.q: Which sensational step by Anwar Sadat in November 1977 paved the way for the Camp David talks?
a: His speech to the Knesset in Jerusalem
His withdrawal from the Arab League
His declaration of war on Syria
His visit to the Pope in Rome
46297.e: In November 1977 Sadat travelled to Israel as the first Arab head of state to do so and spoke to the Israeli parliament. He broke a taboo and opened the way to direct negotiations.
46297.m: Sadat's speech to the Knesset in 1977 prepared the way for Camp David.

46298.q: What did the Camp David Accords provide for the West Bank and the Gaza Strip?
a: Autonomy for a transition period of five years
The immediate founding of a Palestinian state
46298.e: A five-year autonomy status was planned for both areas, after which a final settlement was to follow. However, this part of the accords was never implemented.
46298.m: For the West Bank and Gaza, Camp David provided five years of autonomy.

46299.q: Which territory did Egypt get back from Israel as a result of the Camp David Accords?
46299.e: Israel had occupied Sinai in the Six-Day War of 1967. It withdrew completely by 1982.
46299.m: After Camp David, Egypt got the Sinai Peninsula back.

46300.q: Which award did Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin receive in the same year as the Camp David talks?
46300.e: Sadat and Begin jointly received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1978. Jimmy Carter, the mediator at Camp David, was only honoured with the prize in 2002.
46300.m: Sadat and Begin received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1978.

46301.q: How did the Arab League react in 1979 to Egypt's peace with Israel?
a: It moved its seat to Cairo
46301.e: The Arab League suspended Egypt's membership and moved its seat from Cairo to Tunis. Egypt was only readmitted in 1989.
46301.m: After making peace with Israel, Egypt was expelled from the Arab League.

46302.q: What fate befell Anwar Sadat in 1981?
a: He was assassinated at a military parade
46302.e: Islamist officers shot Sadat in October 1981 during a military parade in Cairo. Among other things, they rejected his peace with Israel.
46302.m: Anwar Sadat was assassinated at a parade in 1981.

46303.q: Which NATO force monitored the military implementation of the Dayton Agreement from December 1995?
46303.e: The Implementation Force (IFOR) replaced the UN protection force and secured the ceasefire. It numbered about 60,000 soldiers.
46303.m: From 1995 the NATO force IFOR secured the Dayton Agreement.

46304.q: Where exactly was the Dayton Agreement negotiated in November 1995?
a: At an air force base in Ohio
At the White House in Washington
At UN headquarters in New York
46304.e: The negotiations took place at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base near Dayton in the US state of Ohio. The sealed-off military base allowed negotiations away from the public eye.
46304.m: The Dayton Agreement was made at a military base in Ohio.

46305.q: Which US diplomat led the Dayton negotiations?
46305.e: Richard Holbrooke was the chief US negotiator. He had already spent months mediating between the parties to the conflict.
46305.m: Richard Holbrooke was the architect of the Dayton Agreement.

46306.q: Which three presidents signed the Dayton Agreement?
46306.e: Alija Izetbegović represented Bosnia and Herzegovina, Franjo Tuđman Croatia and the Serbian president Slobodan Milošević the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The Bosnian Serbs were involved through Milošević.
46306.m: Izetbegović, Tuđman and Milošević signed at Dayton.

46307.q: In which city was the Dayton Agreement officially signed on 14 December 1995?
46307.e: The treaty was initialled in Dayton on 21 November 1995. The formal signing followed in December at the Élysée Palace in Paris.
46307.m: The Dayton Agreement was formally signed in Paris.

46308.q: Which town could not be agreed on at Dayton, so that an arbitration ruling later made it a separate district?
46308.e: The status of Brčko remained open at Dayton because the town was strategically important. In 1999 an international arbitration tribunal decided to make it a neutral special district.
46308.m: After Dayton, Brčko became a separate district.

46309.q: Which office did the Dayton Agreement create to monitor the implementation of its civilian part?
46309.e: The High Representative monitors the implementation of the agreement. Since 1997 the holder can even pass laws and remove officials.
46309.m: The High Representative monitors the implementation of the Dayton Agreement.

46310.q: Under the Dayton Agreement, how is the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina made up?
a: One Bosniak, one Croat and one Serb
One president elected by the people
A Bosniak and a Serb taking turns
46310.e: The constitution in Annex 4 of the agreement provides for a three-member presidency. The chair rotates among the three members.
46310.m: Bosnia and Herzegovina has a three-member presidency.

46311.q: Which conflict was the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 meant to end?
